The Invisible World

Chemistry from the atom up. Twelve chapters on what everything is made of, how it changes, and how we know.

Written for Kym

Start reading

A letter to Kym

Dear Kym,

I should tell you something first: I am not a chemist. I don’t know much chemistry at all. What I have tried to do is make the book I would have loved to read when I was your age: one that tells you who found each idea and how, that lets you try things in the kitchen, and that never just hands you a fact to learn by heart. Much of what is in here was new to me too. I also had help: I made this book with the help of AI, which searched out the research, wrote the chapters to my design, and then checked them. The explanations draw on the free courses and books that MIT and OpenStax share with the world, and on what researchers have learned about the ideas students most often get wrong. Every fact, date and number was checked against reliable sources, more than once, by checkers whose only job was to find mistakes, and every number was worked out again from scratch. Even so, a few mistakes may have slipped through. If something here doesn’t match what you find somewhere else, don’t simply trust the book: tell me, and we will find out together which is right. And where the people who really know chemistry still argue about something, the book says so.

Pick up a pencil and look at the grey tip. Now think of a diamond on a ring, flashing in the light. The pencil tip is so soft that it rubs off onto paper every time you draw. The diamond is hard enough to scratch glass. Yet they are made of the same stuff. The grey part of a pencil is mostly graphite, with a little clay mixed in to make it firmer, and graphite and diamond are both made of carbon atoms and nothing else. What makes them different is not what the atoms are but how they are joined. In graphite the atoms sit in flat sheets that slide over each other, so layers flake off onto the page as you draw. In diamond every atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid three-dimensional frame, with no layers to slide.

That is the kind of surprise this book is full of. Chemistry is the study of what things are made of and how they change into other things. It explains why salt disappears in water and comes back as tiny cubes when the water dries up, why a cut apple goes brown, why a kettle of water can boil away without turning into anything new, why nimbu pani tastes sour, and how a battery pushes electricity through a wire. It explains you, too. The hydrogen in the water you drink was made in the first few minutes after the universe began. Most of the carbon, oxygen and iron in your body was made inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born.

The things that do all this are far too small to see. If you could shrink yourself ten billion times, you would be about the size of a single atom. No microscope that uses light will ever show you one clearly, because atoms are thousands of times smaller than the waves of light themselves. So how do we know anything about them? That question, how do we know?, is the most important one in this book, and you will see it again and again. Every chapter tells you about real experiments: a beam of particles fired at gold foil, X-rays bounced off a salt crystal, gases weighed before and after they react. Each one taught people something about a world they could not see.

Because we cannot see atoms, every picture of them is a model: a careful drawing that shows some things truthfully and leaves other things out on purpose. A map of Mumbai is useful precisely because it is not as big as Mumbai. The diagrams in this book are maps like that. They are good for counting particles and thinking about what pushes and pulls on them. They are wrong about sizes, colours and distances, and I will tell you where each one stops being trustworthy. When a better experiment shows that a model is too simple, we do not throw it away in embarrassment. We improve it. That is how science works.

You will sometimes hear people say things like “sodium wants to lose an electron so it can have a full shell.” Be suspicious of sentences like that. Atoms do not want anything. They have no wishes and no plans. Particles move the way they do because of forces (mostly electric attraction and repulsion), because they are always jiggling with heat, and because, in any ordinary chemical change, every atom is kept. This book tries to explain everything in those terms, and I think you will find the real explanations are more interesting than the made-up ones.

This is not a book of facts to memorise. It is an adventure story, and the heroes are real people: a French tax collector who weighed everything and lost his head in the Revolution, a Russian professor who left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found, a young man from a New Zealand farm who fired particles at gold and was astonished when some bounced back. Every idea in chemistry was found by someone who was puzzled, tried things, got them wrong, and tried again. When you see a word with a little book beside it, tap it, and you will get the whole story.

One more thing. Many sections ask you to make a prediction before you find out the answer. Please actually do it, in your head or on paper. A prediction that turns out wrong is not a failure. It is the most useful moment in learning, because it shows you exactly where your picture of the world needs to change. Nobody is grading you here. Take your time, go back whenever you like, and keep asking how we know.

With love,

Amar

P.S. The book goes with the chemistry lab app. Whenever you see a dashed box marked Try it, the matching investigation in the app has the same number, so you can build, change and test the thing you have just read about.

How this book works

This book is one long adventure. It follows people across two and a half thousand years, from Greek thinkers arguing about whether you can cut a pebble forever, to a schoolteacher in Manchester weighing the invisible, to a young scientist firing particles at gold in a darkened room, to the people who built the battery in your pocket. Each of them was trying to answer the same question you are about to ask: what is everything made of, and how do we know?

There are three volumes and twelve chapters, numbered from 0 because Chapter 0 is the warm-up. Each chapter is an episode: it opens with a puzzle, follows the people who cracked it, and then explains the idea plainly, one numbered section at a time. You can read straight through, or jump to anything that makes you curious. The numbers of the sections match the investigations in the lab app.

As you read, you will meet a few kinds of boxes. Each one has one job.

Story links
Some words in the text are marked like this. Each one opens a longer story beside the page: the full adventure of how that idea was found, with the idea explained slowly, step by step. They are all collected in Stories behind the ideas, and The adventure in time puts them in the order they happened.
The cast
Chemistry was made by people: shy schoolteachers, a bookbinder, a tax collector, alchemists, a girl who studied in a secret university. Their names are story links too, and tapping one opens their life story. The cast, near the front, introduces them all.
Scenes
A small pin and a place and date, like Manchester, 1909, means the story is taking you somewhere real.
Margin notes
When a new word matters, it is marked like this in the text and explained in the margin beside it (or just below, on a narrow screen). All of them are collected in Words worth knowing at the back.
How do we know?
The experiment or measurement behind an idea. Science is not a list of facts; it is a list of facts together with the reasons we believe them.
Careful
A tempting idea that is wrong, and why it is wrong. Most of these are ideas that lots of clever people have had, so if you have had them too, you are in good company.
Try it
Something to predict, sketch or do, usually with the matching investigation in the lab app.
Try it at home
A real experiment with things from the kitchen. Everything in these boxes is safe to do, but ask an adult first, and never taste anything unless the box says it is ordinary food.
Watch and turn
Many pictures come alive: a button under them starts an animation or a 3D model you can turn with your finger. They only move when you ask.
Check yourself
One question at the end of a section. The answers, with the reasoning, are at the back of the book.
Case file
A mystery at the end of each chapter. You get the clues; you work out what is going on. The solution is hidden until you ask for it.

Numbers in this book are real measured values unless the text says they are made up for a model. A few useful habits for reading them: 10⁶ means a million (a 1 followed by six zeros), and 10⁻⁶ means one millionth. The small number written low in H₂O counts atoms: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in each molecule. A small sign written high, as in Na⁺, shows an electric charge.

Four ideas that run through everything

Chemistry can look like an enormous pile of separate facts. It is not. Almost every explanation in this book is built from four ideas, used again and again in different combinations. When something puzzles you, it is worth asking which of the four is at work.

  1. Count everything.An atom’s number of protons decides which element it is. In ordinary chemical changes, atoms are never created or destroyed, and electric charge is never created or destroyed either. So you can always keep an account, like a shopkeeper’s ledger, of where every atom and every charge went.
  2. Opposite charges attract.Positive and negative charges pull on each other; like charges push apart; both effects get weaker with distance. This electric attraction is what holds atoms together, holds atoms to each other, and holds molecules near their neighbours.
  3. Jiggling against sticking.Every particle is always moving, and the hotter something is, the harder its particles jiggle. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas, and whether a reaction gets going, depends on a contest between that jiggling and the attractions or barriers holding things back.
  4. Huge numbers make steady averages.Even a drop of water holds more molecules than there are grains of sand on all of Earth’s beaches. With numbers that big, the random behaviour of single particles averages out into the steady, measurable things we see: a mass on a balance, the strength of a solution, a reaction that seems to have stopped but is secretly still going both ways.

And underneath all four is a fifth habit: keep what you observe separate from the model you use to explain it. The observation is what any careful person would measure. The model is our best explanation so far, and it can always be improved by a better experiment.

Chapter 0

The chemist’s way of seeing

The big questionA drop of water looks perfectly smooth. Chemists say it is made of about 1.7 × 10²¹ separate, jostling molecules. How can anyone know that about something nobody can see?

  1. 0.1What we see and what we think
  2. 0.2Powers of ten: from a flask to an atom

Abdera, a port town in northern Greece, about 420 BCE

Our adventure begins nearly two and a half thousand years ago, with a man and a question. The man was Democritus, and he is said to have laughed so much at the foolishness of the world that people called him the laughing philosopher. The question was one you can ask about anything around you: what happens if you keep cutting it?

Take a raindrop. Cut it in half (in your imagination) and you have two smaller drops. Cut those, and again, and again. Is there an end to the cutting? Democritus, and his teacher Leucippus before him, thought there must be. Somewhere, they said, you reach pieces so small they cannot be cut any further. They called them atomos, Greek for “uncuttable”. Nobody could see these pieces, and nobody could test the idea. Aristotle, the most admired thinker of the ancient world, rejected it, and for nearly two thousand years most people agreed with him.

The story behind this

Can you cut forever? The long argument about atomsFor more than two thousand years people argued about whether matter is made of tiny uncuttable pieces. A Manchester schoolteacher turned the argument into science.

Trinity College, Cambridge, the 1690s

Instead, for most of those two thousand years, the people who worked hardest on what things are made of were the alchemists. In workshops from Cairo to Prague they heated, dissolved, distilled and mixed, chasing one great dream: to turn “base” metals such as lead or mercury into gold. They never managed it, but they invented much of the equipment chemists still use, and they kept careful notes on how substances behave.

One of the most devoted alchemists of all is a surprise. Isaac Newton, the Cambridge professor who worked out the laws of motion and gravity, spent years at the furnace of a small laboratory in the garden beside his rooms at Trinity College, and secretly wrote about a million words about alchemy. He published almost none of it. In 1936 a large collection of his private papers was sold at auction at Sotheby’s in London, and the economist John Maynard Keynes bought many of them. After reading them, Keynes wrote that Newton was not the first of the age of reason but “the last of the magicians”.

The story behind this

Two thousand years of trying to make goldThe alchemists never made gold, but they invented the laboratory, and one of them found a glowing element while boiling down buckets of urine.

The alchemists’ dream will come back, with a twist, in Chapter 1. It took until the twentieth century to settle the argument beyond doubt, and the people who settled it had to learn two habits first. The first habit is keeping what you see separate from what you think is going on underneath. The second is learning to think with numbers far bigger and far smaller than anything in daily life. This short chapter is about those two habits. You will use them on every page that follows.

0.1What we see and what we think

Observation

Something you can see or measure directly, such as a colour, a mass, a temperature, or a change of state.

Fill a glass with water and be a scientist for a minute. What can you find out just by looking and measuring? It is clear and colourless. It takes the shape of the glass. A 100-millilitre glassful has a mass of about 100 grams. Put it in the freezer and it turns solid at 0 °C; heat it in a pan near sea level and it boils at 100 °C. These are observations: anyone with the right equipment can check them, anywhere in the world, and they will get the same results.

Inference

A conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence. In chemistry, our ideas about particles we cannot see are inferences, built into models.

Now here is a very different kind of sentence: water is made of tiny molecules, each one an oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms, H₂O. Democritus would have loved it. But notice: nobody has ever looked into a glass of water and seen that. It is an inference: an explanation worked out from many observations and tested against many more. It is an extremely good inference, supported by dozens of completely different kinds of experiment, which you will meet in this book. But it belongs in a different column from “boils at 100 °C”.

This is what makes chemistry such a detective game. A detective sees footprints, a broken window and an empty jewellery box: those are observations. “The thief came in through the window” is an inference. A good detective, like a good chemist, keeps the two apart and is always ready to change the inference when a new clue turns up.

Chemists move back and forth between three ways of describing the same thing, all the time. There is the bench view: what you see and measure in the lab or the kitchen. There is the particle view: the atoms and molecules that we think are doing the work. And there is the symbol view: the shorthand we write down, such as H₂O. A big part of learning chemistry is learning to move smoothly between the three, and to remember which one you are in.

Careful

“If you looked at water through a powerful enough magnifying glass, you would see the bent shape of the H₂O molecules, like in the diagrams.”

You would not, and not only because magnifying glasses are not strong enough. Light itself is the problem. Visible light is a wave, and its waves are between about 400 and 700 nanometres long. A water molecule is about 0.3 nanometres across: more than a thousand times smaller than the shortest wave of visible light. Light simply cannot pick out details that small. We know the shape of a water molecule from other kinds of evidence, which you will meet later. The diagrams are models drawn from that evidence, not photographs.

Understand itObservation and inference

What is it?

An observation is something anyone can see or measure for themselves, such as “water boils at 100 °C”. An inference is an explanation reasoned out from observations, such as “water is made of H₂O molecules”.

Why is it called this?

“Observe” comes from Latin observare, to watch over. “Infer” comes from Latin inferre, to carry in: you carry a conclusion in from the evidence.

What problem did it solve?

For centuries people argued about things nobody could see, with no way to settle the argument. Keeping the two columns apart shows which claims anyone can check and which still need more evidence.

Why does it work?

Anyone, anywhere, can repeat an observation, so it is hard to fool yourself about. An inference is kept only while it explains every observation and survives new tests; one stubborn new fact can overturn it.

How does it help?

It lets you build confident knowledge about things far too small to see, such as atoms, and it tells you what to test next when a clue does not fit.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

We trust the H₂O inference because many completely different kinds of experiment, from splitting water with electricity to watching specks jiggle under a microscope, all point the same way.

What it isn’t

An inference is not a wild guess or “just an opinion”. The best inferences, like atoms, rest on so much evidence that scientists rely on them every day.

Where does it stop working?

The line can blur: even reading a thermometer relies on ideas about how thermometers work. Scientists still keep the two as separate as they can.

Your turn

Explain Observation and inference to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

One drop, two glasses

You need two clear glasses of still water, one warm (from a hot tap, or mixed by an adult with a little water from the kettle: warm, not scalding) and one with ice water, and food colouring. Predict first: if you let one drop fall gently into each glass and do not stir, which will spread faster, or will they be the same? Write your prediction down. Then drop them in together and watch for ten minutes. Write down what you observe (colours, shapes, how long it took in each glass). Then write one inference about what might be happening, too small to see, that lets the colour spread out without anyone stirring it, and faster in one glass than the other. Keep the two lists separate: that is exactly what scientists do. (You will find out whether your inference was right in Chapter 3.)

The mystery box

Scientists spend their lives working out what is inside things they cannot open. Practise on a box. Ask someone to tape one or two objects to the inside of a shoebox (a cork, a small cup, a ruler laid across: anything, without telling you), drop in a marble, and tape the lid shut. Now tilt the box, roll the marble, listen to it and feel it stop. Draw your best map of what is inside, and write down which observation told you each thing. Only when you have made your best inference may you open the box. You have just done, with a marble, what the scientists in this book did with atoms. One of them, in Chapter 1, will do it by firing tiny particles at a sheet of gold.

Investigation 0.1

In the app, switch between the four samples: hydrogen gas, oxygen gas, a mixture of the two, and water. For each one, write down one thing you could observe about a real sample and one thing the particle picture claims. Which of your sentences could someone check with a thermometer or a balance?

Check yourself

Which of these is an observation and which is an inference? (a) “This liquid boils at 100 °C.” (b) “This liquid is made of H₂O molecules.”

Answer at the back of the book

0.2Powers of ten: from a flask to an atom

Powers of ten

A short way of writing big and small numbers. 10⁶ is a million; 10⁻⁶ is a millionth. Each step of 1 in the little number is a factor of ten.

If atoms exist, they must be unimaginably small, and there must be unimaginably many of them. To talk about numbers like that without filling the page with zeros, scientists use powers of ten. 10³ means 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. 10⁻³ means one thousandth, 0.001. A millimetre is 10⁻³ metres; a nanometre is 10⁻⁹ metres, a billionth of a metre.

Take a journey down Figure 0.2. Each step is ten times smaller than the one before. Ten steps take you from something you can hold, past a grain of salt, a red blood cell and a virus, all the way to a single molecule.

Mole

A counting unit, like a dozen, but much bigger: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ things (atoms, molecules, or whatever you say you are counting).

Avogadro’s constant

The number of things in one mole, 6.022 140 76 × 10²³. Since 2019 this is an exact number, fixed by definition.

Masses are just as extreme. One water molecule has a mass of about 3 × 10⁻²³ grams. Even an extremely sensitive laboratory balance can only detect about a ten-millionth of a gram, 10⁻⁷ g, which is still more than a thousand million million times the mass of one molecule. So you could never weigh molecules one at a time. Chemists solved that problem the way a rice seller does: they count by weighing, using a counting unit made for the job, called the mole. A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ things, a number called Avogadro’s constant. It was chosen so that a mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to the relative mass of its particles: 12 g for carbon-12 atoms, about 18 g for water molecules, roughly one big gulp.

The story behind this

The mole, step by stepHow chemists learned to count atoms by weighing them, and why the counting unit they invented is so enormous.

A drop of water. A typical raindrop-sized drop has a mass of about 0.05 g.

Number of moles = 0.05 g ÷ 18 g per mole ≈ 0.0028 moles.

Number of molecules ≈ 0.0028 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.7 × 10²¹.

That is 1,700,000,000,000,000,000,000 molecules in one drop.

When you have twice as many moles, you have twice the mass and twice the number of molecules. What you do not get is bigger molecules. A spoonful and a bucketful of water are made of exactly the same molecules; the bucket simply has more of them.

How many molecules in one drop?

You need a medicine dropper (or a straw you can pinch at the top), a 5 mL measuring spoon and a little water. Count how many drops it takes to fill the spoon. A spoonful of 5 mL of water has a mass of about 5 g, so divide 5 g by your number of drops to get the mass of one drop. Then follow the steps in the box above to work out how many molecules are in one of your drops. (With a typical dropper it takes about 100 drops, which gives about 0.05 g a drop.)

Paris, 1908

Back to Democritus. By 1900 most chemists used atoms every day, but some famous scientists in Europe, such as the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, still argued that atoms were only a handy way of talking, not real things. The person who changed their minds was Jean Perrin, a French physicist at the Sorbonne in Paris, patient and stubborn in equal measure. He looked through a microscope at tiny grains of resin, each about a thousandth of a millimetre across, floating in water. The grains never kept still. They jiggled and wandered, this way and that, for as long as he watched. The Scottish botanist Robert Brown, peering through his microscope at tiny specks released from pollen grains in water, had noticed this restless motion in 1827, and it is called Brownian motion after him.

In 1905 a young Albert Einstein, then working as a clerk in the patent office in Bern, Switzerland, had explained the jiggling: each grain is being battered by invisible water molecules from every side, and at each instant a few more hit one side than the other. He even worked out how far a grain should wander, depending on how many molecules there are. Perrin measured the wandering with enormous patience, marking each grain’s position again and again, and from it worked out the number of molecules in a mole. Then he measured that number in several other, completely different ways, and the answers agreed. Ostwald and most of the other doubters gave in. Perrin won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926.

A century later, scientists measured the number again, far more precisely, by counting the atoms in an almost perfect sphere of pure silicon, using X-rays to measure the spacing between them. The results were so good that in 2019 the number was fixed exactly: 6.022 140 76 × 10²³. Democritus’s uncuttable pieces had been counted.

Understand itAtom

What is it?

The smallest piece of an element that is still that element. Everything you can touch is built from atoms, joined together in different ways.

Why is it called this?

From the Greek atomos, “uncuttable”, the name Leucippus and Democritus gave their imagined smallest pieces. The name turned out to be wrong: in Chapter 1 you will see atoms opened up.

What problem did it solve?

It explained why substances combine in fixed amounts, and why melting, boiling and dissolving never make matter vanish: the same pieces are only being rearranged.

Why does it work?

Matter really is made of separate particles, far too small to see, and chemical changes rearrange them instead of creating or destroying them.

How does it help?

It lets chemists count by weighing, using the mole, and predict how much of each substance a change will need and make.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Perrin’s measurements of Brownian motion, and several other completely different methods, all gave the same number of molecules in a mole. That agreement convinced even the doubters.

What it isn’t

Not a tiny coloured ball like the drawings. Atoms have no colour, and as Chapter 1 shows, an atom is mostly empty space.

Where does it stop working?

“Uncuttable” fails: atoms have a nucleus and electrons inside, and nuclear processes can even turn one element into another.

Your turn

Explain Atom to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Keep the molar mass at 18 g per mole and change the amount from 0.25 mol to 2 mol. Before you look, predict what happens to the mass and to the number of molecules when you double the amount. Then predict what happens to the size of each molecule.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 0

The case of the vanishing water

A student puts 0.90 g of water into a strong, empty 2-litre glass flask, seals it, and weighs it: 250.90 g. She heats the flask to 120 °C until every drop has disappeared. Her friend says: “The water has broken up into hydrogen and oxygen gas, and the flask must be lighter now that the liquid has gone.”

  1. Weighed while still hot and sealed, the flask is 250.90 g.
  2. As the flask cools, droplets of colourless liquid form on the inside of the glass. The liquid boils at 100 °C, just like water.
  3. 0.90 g of water is 0.050 mol, which is about 3.0 × 10²² molecules.

What happened to the water? Which clue rules out each half of the friend’s claim?

Show the solution

The water turned to invisible water vapour: the same H₂O molecules, now spread through the whole flask instead of sitting in a puddle at the bottom. Clue 1 rules out “lighter”: nothing left the sealed flask, so the mass did not change. Clue 2 rules out “broken up”: the liquid that came back behaves exactly like water, because it is water. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen would not condense on cooling. The molecules never changed; only their spacing did. Clue 3 reminds you how many molecules were wandering around the flask while you couldn’t see them.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

So Democritus was right: there are uncuttable pieces, and we can even count them. But picturing water as a crowd of tiny balls treats each atom as featureless. It cannot tell us what makes an oxygen atom different from a hydrogen atom, or where electric charge comes from. In the next chapter the adventure moves to a laboratory in Cambridge in 1897, where someone is about to discover that atoms are not uncuttable after all.

1

Chapter 1

What makes an atom?

The big questionTable salt contains sodium ions, Na⁺, which have exactly as many electrons as an atom of neon. So why doesn’t salt contain neon?

  1. 1.1Inside an atom
  2. 1.2What identifies an element?
  3. 1.3Same element, different isotope
  4. 1.4Where does charge come from?
  5. 1.5Reading an atom’s identity
  6. 1.6What might explain patterns?

At the end of Chapter 0, Democritus’s uncuttable pieces had been counted. But the people who counted them already knew a secret that would have astonished him: atoms can be cut. They have insides.

Here is a puzzle to carry through this chapter. Gold and mercury sit side by side in the periodic table. Gold is a heavy yellow metal that stays bright for thousands of years. Mercury is a silvery liquid at room temperature that runs about like quicksilver, which is its old name. And yet, deep inside, a mercury nucleus has exactly one more proton than a gold nucleus: 80 instead of 79. One tiny particle separates a wedding ring from a puddle of liquid metal. This chapter opens the atom up, counts what is inside, and finds out which of those counts decides what an atom is.

1.1Inside an atom

Cambridge, 1897

The first crack in the uncuttable atom appeared in a glass tube. At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, J. J. Thomson, a Manchester bookseller’s son who had become head of the laboratory at just 28, pumped nearly all the air out of a tube, sealed a metal plate into each end, and connected them to a high voltage. A ghostly beam streamed from one plate, making the glass glow where it struck. Thomson bent the beam with magnets and with electric charges, and from how much it bent he worked out that it was made of tiny particles with negative charge, far lighter than any atom. It did not matter which metal he used for the plates or which gas was left in the tube: the particles were always the same. So every atom must contain them. These were electrons, and the atom had just been shown to have parts.

Proton, neutron, electron

The three particles that atoms are built from. Charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1. A proton or neutron has nearly 2,000 times the mass of an electron.

Nucleus

The tiny centre of an atom, holding its protons and neutrons, and almost all of its mass.

Today we know every atom is built from three kinds of smaller particle. Protons carry a positive electric charge. Neutrons carry no charge at all. Electrons carry a negative charge, exactly as strong as a proton’s positive one but opposite in sign. Protons and neutrons are packed together in a tiny, dense centre called the nucleus. Electrons occupy the much larger space around it.

But Thomson did not know about the nucleus. He imagined the electrons dotted through a soft ball of positive charge, like currants in a pudding. Finding out how wrong that picture was took a darkened room in Manchester.

Manchester, 1909

Picture a small room with the blinds down. Hans Geiger, a German physicist, and Ernest Marsden, a twenty-year-old student, sit in the dark for half an hour until their eyes adjust. In front of them is a source of alpha particles: small, fast, positively charged bullets shot out by radioactive radium. The bullets are aimed at a sheet of gold foil only about a thousand atoms thick. Beyond the foil is a screen that gives off a tiny flash of light each time an alpha particle hits it, and the two men count the flashes through a microscope, one by one.

Predict first. Remember the mystery box from Chapter 0: this is the same game, with gold atoms in the box and alpha particles for marbles. If each gold atom really were a soft pudding, with its positive charge spread thinly all through it, what would you expect the fast alpha particles to do when they hit the foil? Decide before you read on.

Their professor, Ernest Rutherford, a farmer’s son from New Zealand with a booming voice and a habit of singing hymns, loudly and off-key, as he walked round the lab, expected the bullets to pass through the soft “pudding” atoms of gold with hardly a wobble, and almost all of them did. But about one in several thousand was turned aside by a large angle, and a very few came almost straight back towards the source. Rutherford said it was as surprising as firing a heavy shell at a sheet of tissue paper and having it bounce back at you. He thought about it for nearly two years. In 1911 he gave the only explanation that worked: each gold atom’s positive charge and almost all its mass are crammed into a minute centre, with mostly empty space around it. The pudding was gone. The nucleus had arrived. (If you predicted that nearly all would sail straight through, you were right about the many, as Rutherford was. The surprise was in the few: a soft pudding has nothing hard enough to send anything back.)

The story behind this

The shell that bounced backA student was asked to look for something nobody expected to see. What he found showed that every atom is almost entirely empty space around a tiny, heavy centre.

So almost all of an atom’s mass is in its nucleus, because a proton or a neutron has nearly 2,000 times the mass of an electron. But almost all of an atom’s size comes from its electrons. If an atom were blown up to the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a pea on the pitch, and the rest of the stadium would be the region where its electrons are found.

A grain of salt and a very big atom

Ask an adult to come outside with you to a park or a long, safe pavement. Put one grain of salt on the ground: that is your nucleus. Now walk away from it, counting your steps. For a carbon atom built to this scale, the edge of the atom would be somewhere between about 5 and 15 metres away (roughly seven to twenty big steps), depending on how you measure an atom’s edge. Turn round and look back at the grain you can hardly see. Almost all of the atom’s mass is in that grain. Everything between you and it is the space where the atom’s six electrons are found. That is why most of Geiger and Marsden’s alpha particles flew straight through.

Drawing an atom on a page is a problem, then: draw the nucleus big enough to see and the atom would not fit in the room. So chemists use a different kind of picture.

Counting model

A diagram that shows how many particles of each kind there are. It is not a picture of where they are or how big they are.

The electrons in that drawing are dots scattered around the nucleus. They are not on tracks, and the dots are not where real electrons “are” at some moment. Electrons do not behave like tiny planets, and we will improve this part of the picture as the book goes on. For now, this is a counting model: it is drawn to help you count how many of each particle there are, and nothing more.

Understand itThe nucleus

What is it?

The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. It holds almost all of the atom’s mass but takes up almost none of its space.

Why is it called this?

From Latin nucleus, “kernel”, which comes from a word for a little nut: the hard centre inside a fruit. Rutherford was using the word for the atom’s core by 1912.

What problem did it solve?

Thomson’s “plum pudding” atom could not explain why a few alpha particles bounced back from gold foil. Something small, heavy and positively charged had to be there.

Why does it work?

All of the atom’s positive charge is packed into that minute centre, so an alpha particle that comes very close to it feels a fierce push, strong enough to turn it right round. The rest pass through the empty space.

How does it help?

It explains why atoms are mostly empty space and where their mass comes from, and it gives the picture used for the rest of this book: a nucleus, with electrons around it.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Geiger and Marsden counted flashes from alpha particles fired at gold foil in Manchester in 1909. About one in several thousand was turned aside sharply, which only a tiny, heavy, charged centre can explain.

What it isn’t

Not a sun with electrons going round it like planets. Electrons do not follow tracks at all.

Where does it stop working?

A small solid ball is itself only a model. The nucleus has its own inner structure, which takes nuclear physics to describe.

1.2What identifies an element?

Element

A substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons.

An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. Hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, gold and mercury are all elements, and there are 118 known so far. But what makes two atoms “the same kind”? For a long time nobody could say. Chemists arranged the elements in order of how heavy their atoms were, and a few of them stubbornly seemed to sit in the wrong places.

Manchester, 1913

The answer came from one of Rutherford’s young researchers, Henry Moseley, who was twenty-five. He fired electrons at targets made of different elements, one after another, and measured the X-rays that came off. Each element gave out its own X-ray “note”. When Moseley plotted the square root of each note’s frequency, the points rose in a perfectly even staircase, one step per element, with no wobbles at all. The steps were counting something inside the atom: the positive charge of its nucleus, in other words the number of protons. Moseley’s staircase put every element in its correct place, and where a step was missing, it showed exactly where an undiscovered element must fit.

Atomic number (Z)

The number of protons in an atom’s nucleus. It decides which element the atom is: 1 is hydrogen, 6 is carbon, 8 is oxygen, 79 is gold.

That number is called the atomic number, and it has the symbol Z. It is the answer to the question, and it is simple and absolute: two atoms are the same element if, and only if, they have the same number of protons.

Moseley did not live to see what his staircase became. In 1915, during the First World War, he was killed by a sniper at Gallipoli, aged 27. Many scientists have said that his death was one of the war’s great losses to science.

The story behind this

Henry Moseley’s staircaseA 26-year-old in Manchester found the true order of the elements by measuring X-rays, and counted the missing ones.

Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, whether it is in a pencil, a diamond, a sugar crystal or the carbon dioxide you breathe out. Every atom with 7 protons is nitrogen. Change the number of neutrons, and you still have the same element. Change the number of electrons, and you still have the same element. Change the number of protons, and you have a different element. Add one proton to gold, and you have mercury.

So could you turn mercury into gold, the dream of the alchemists and of Isaac Newton at his furnace, by taking one proton away? In the lab app you can do it with one tap. In the real world, that is not something chemistry can do, and this is why every alchemist failed. Chemical changes, like burning or rusting or cooking, move electrons around and rearrange atoms, but they never change the number of protons in a nucleus. However hot the furnace, however clever the recipe, the nucleus is untouched. Changing that number takes a nuclear process, such as the reactions in the core of a star or in a nuclear reactor. So when you tap that button, you are editing a model, not doing an experiment.

Nuclear physics, though, can do it, and in our own time it has. At CERN, the giant laboratory near Geneva, the Large Hadron Collider smashes lead nuclei together at nearly the speed of light. In May 2025 the team running its ALICE experiment reported that when two lead nuclei only just miss each other, the electric jolt can knock three protons out of one of them. Lead has 82 protons; take away three and you have 79, which is gold. Over the years 2015 to 2018 the collider made gold nuclei this way, about 29 picograms in all (a picogram is a millionth of a millionth of a gram), and each one lasted only a split second before hitting the machine’s walls and breaking apart. Then, in October 2026, a US start-up called Marathon Fusion announced that it had made gold from mercury, using neutrons from fusion reactions: a neutron knocks a neutron out of mercury-198, making mercury-197, which then decays by itself into gold-197. That is a company’s claim, and when this book was written its data had not yet been published or checked by other scientists. Either way, notice what did the work. Not a chemical recipe, but a change to the nucleus.

The story behind this

Mercury into gold, at lastThe alchemists’ dream came true in the twentieth century, but in a way no alchemist imagined, and it turned out that the gold was not the treasure.

The story behind this

The last of the magiciansThe man who explained gravity and light also spent decades as a secret alchemist, chasing the one thing chemistry can never do.

Careful

“Na⁺ has 10 electrons, the same as neon. So it has turned into neon.”

Count the protons instead. A sodium ion still has 11 protons, so it is still sodium, just with a positive charge. Neon has 10 protons. Having the same number of electrons as another element makes two particles similar in some ways, but it never makes them the same element. That is the answer to this chapter’s big question.

Understand itElement

What is it?

A substance made of only one kind of atom: atoms that all have the same number of protons. Carbon, oxygen and gold are elements, and 118 are known so far.

Why is it called this?

From Latin elementum, a first principle or basic part. Where the Latin word itself came from, nobody knows.

What problem did it solve?

For two thousand years people argued about what the basic ingredients of everything were. Elements are the ingredients chemistry cannot split any further, and Moseley’s proton count finally gave an exact test of which is which.

Why does it work?

The number of protons fixes the charge of the nucleus. That fixes how many electrons a neutral atom holds, and the electrons decide how the atom behaves.

How does it help?

Every substance in the world is made of elements joined in different ways, so a list of 118 ingredients describes everything you will ever touch.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Moseley’s X-ray staircase of 1913 rose by one equal step per element, with no wobbles: it was counting the protons.

What it isn’t

Not “an atom with a certain mass” or “an atom with a certain number of electrons”. Isotopes and ions change those, and the element stays the same. Only the protons count.

Where does it stop working?

Chemistry can never turn one element into another, but nuclear processes can, in stars, in reactors, and in machines like the Large Hadron Collider.

1.3Same element, different isotope

Cambridge, 1919

Back in Cambridge, J. J. Thomson had noticed something odd as early as 1913. When he sent a beam of charged neon atoms through magnetic and electric fields, it split into two faint streaks instead of one, as if neon came in two weights. His former assistant Francis Aston returned from war work and built a much sharper machine to settle it, one of the first mass spectrometers. It gives atoms an electric charge, then sends them flying through a magnetic field. The field bends heavier particles less than lighter ones, so the beam splits into separate streams, one for each mass. In 1919 Aston confirmed that neon really is a mixture of two kinds of atom, and went on to show the same for chlorine and many other elements.

Isotopes

Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons.

Mass number (A)

The number of protons plus the number of neutrons in one nucleus. It is always a whole number.

How can one element come in different weights? The protons cannot differ, or it would be a different element. The extra weight belongs to the neutrons. Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. Carbon atoms, for example, can have 6, 7 or 8 neutrons, and all of them are carbon. These versions are called isotopes. We name an isotope by its mass number, the total number of protons and neutrons: carbon-12 has 6 + 6 = 12, carbon-13 has 6 + 7 = 13, and carbon-14 has 6 + 8 = 14.

Isotopes behave almost identically in chemistry, because chemistry is mostly about electrons, and isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons. But their nuclei can be very different. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 last forever. Carbon-14 is radioactive: its nuclei slowly break down, so that half of any sample is gone after about 5,700 years. That is how archaeologists date ancient wood and bone. Adding a neutron in the app does not tell you whether the new nucleus would be stable; that depends on nuclear physics, not on counting.

Average atomic mass

The average mass of an element’s atoms in a natural sample, weighted by how common each isotope is. This is the decimal number printed on most periodic tables.

Most elements found in nature are a mixture of isotopes. Chlorine, for example, is about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37. So the average atomic mass of chlorine is somewhere between 35 and 37. Here is the arithmetic, using the real measured fractions:

0.758 × 35.0 + 0.242 × 37.0 ≈ 26.5 + 9.0 = 35.5

(With the isotopes’ exact masses, 34.969 and 36.966, the answer is 35.45.)

That is why periodic tables give chlorine as 35.45. But notice something odd: no single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.45. Every chlorine atom is either about 35 or about 37. The average describes the crowd, not any member of it, in the same way that the average number of children in a family can be 2.4 even though no family has 0.4 of a child.

This is exactly the kind of picture Aston’s machine drew: one peak for each isotope, with the height of each peak showing how common it is.

An element made of beans

Make your own “element” with two isotopes: mix 75 rajma beans and 25 small brown chickpeas, kala chana (any two clearly different sizes of bean or dal will do; big white chickpeas can weigh about as much as rajma) in a bowl. Predict first: will the average mass of a bean in the bowl be nearer a rajma’s mass or a chickpea’s? A kitchen scale only reads to about a gram, so weigh beans in twenties: weigh 20 rajma and divide by 20; weigh 20 chickpeas and divide by 20. Work out the average just as for chlorine: 0.75 × (one rajma) + 0.25 × (one chickpea). Check it by weighing all 100 and dividing by 100. Then look in the bowl: is any bean an “average bean”? Each one is a rajma or a chickpea, just as each chlorine atom is chlorine-35 or chlorine-37.

Understand itIsotope

What is it?

One of the different versions of the same element. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their atoms have different masses.

Why is it called this?

From Greek isos, “equal”, and topos, “place”: isotopes of an element sit in the same place in the periodic table. The word was suggested to Frederick Soddy in 1913 by Margaret Todd, a Scottish doctor and writer and a friend of his family.

What problem did it solve?

Thomson’s neon beam split in two, and many elements had average masses that were not whole numbers. Isotopes explained both: an element can be a mixture of atoms of different masses.

Why does it work?

Neutrons add mass but no charge, so they change the weight of the nucleus without changing the electrons. Chemistry is mostly about electrons, so isotopes of an element behave almost the same.

How does it help?

It explains averages such as chlorine’s 35.45, and gives tools such as carbon-14 dating of ancient wood and bone.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Aston’s mass spectrometer of 1919 split neon, and then chlorine and many other elements, into one stream for each mass.

What it isn’t

Not a different element, and not necessarily radioactive. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 last forever; only some isotopes, such as carbon-14, break down.

Where does it stop working?

“Almost the same” is only almost. Hydrogen is the big exception: its heavy isotope, deuterium, doubles the atom’s mass, and “heavy water” made from it freezes at about 3.8 °C instead of 0 °C.

1.4Where does charge come from?

Try a little magic before the explanation.

The balloon that sorts salt from pepper

On a dry day, sprinkle a teaspoon of salt and a pinch of ground black pepper on a plate and mix them. Blow up a balloon, tie it, and rub it hard on your hair or a wool jumper for ten seconds. Now hold the balloon a couple of centimetres above the plate and slowly lower it. The pepper jumps up and sticks to the balloon first; bring it lower and some salt follows. Rubbing moved electrons from your hair onto the balloon, giving it a negative charge, and that charge pulls on the specks below. The lighter pepper flakes are lifted first. Now rub a second balloon, hang both from threads so that they dangle side by side, and let them go: they swing apart. Both carry the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other away. Only electrons moved in all this. Your hair, having lost some, is left with a positive charge, which is why it may lift towards the balloon.

Nothing was created when you rubbed that balloon. Electrons were simply moved from one place to another. Each proton has a charge of +1 and each electron a charge of −1, measured in a unit called the elementary charge. Neutrons have no charge. So the overall charge of any particle is just a subtraction:

charge = number of protons − number of electrons

Elementary charge

The size of the charge on one proton (+1) or one electron (−1). It is the smallest amount of charge any free particle has.

Ion

An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge, because its numbers of protons and electrons are not equal.

A sodium atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons, so its charge is 11 − 11 = 0: it is neutral. If it loses one electron, it has 11 protons and 10 electrons, and its charge is +1. A particle with an overall charge is called an ion. This one is written Na⁺, “sodium plus”. An oxygen atom with 8 protons that has gained two extra electrons has 8 − 10 = −2, and is written O²⁻.

Notice what does not change when an ion forms: the nucleus. The protons and neutrons stay exactly where they were. That is why an ion is still the same element.

London, the 1830s

The word “ion” is older than the electron. At the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday, who had started life as a bookbinder’s apprentice, was passing electric currents through all sorts of substances. Solid salt would not carry a current. But when salt was melted, or dissolved in water, a current flowed through it, and new substances appeared at the metal plates where the current went in and out. Something in the liquid was carrying charge from one plate to the other. In 1834 Faraday named these charge-carriers ions, from the Greek for “going”. Sixty years before anyone knew about electrons, he had found their footprints. We now know that in salt water they are Na⁺ ions drifting one way and Cl⁻ ions drifting the other.

Arithmetic lets you write down any charge you like: carbon with 5 electrons, oxygen with 12. But being able to write a particle down does not mean it can exist for long in the real world. Whether an ion survives depends on its surroundings. Na⁺ ions last indefinitely in salt crystals and in seawater; a C⁺ ion can be made in a vacuum chamber but would not last a moment in water. The subtraction tells you the charge. It does not tell you whether the particle is real.

Careful

“The charge of an atom is the number of protons minus the number of neutrons.”

Neutrons have no charge, so they cannot affect the subtraction at all. They change the mass of an atom, not its charge. Charge is always protons minus electrons.

Understand itIon

What is it?

An atom, or a group of atoms, with an electric charge, because it has more or fewer electrons than protons. Na⁺ has lost one electron; O²⁻ has gained two.

Why is it called this?

From the Greek for “going”. Michael Faraday named ions in 1834, on the suggestion of his friend William Whewell, because they travel through a liquid towards the plates where a current goes in and out.

What problem did it solve?

Faraday could not explain how melted or dissolved salt carried an electric current when solid salt could not. Charged particles moving through the liquid were the answer.

Why does it work?

Charge is a simple count: protons minus electrons. Move electrons on or off and the count changes, while the nucleus, and so the element, stays exactly the same.

How does it help?

It explains why salt water carries electricity, why salt is safe to eat although sodium and chlorine are dangerous, and much of what happens inside batteries.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Pass a current through melted or dissolved salt and new substances appear at each plate, just as moving charged particles would make them.

What it isn’t

Not a different element. Na⁺ still has 11 protons, so it is still sodium, even though it has the same number of electrons as neon.

Where does it stop working?

The arithmetic can describe ions that cannot last. A C⁺ ion can be made in a vacuum chamber, but it would not survive a moment in water.

1.5Reading an atom’s identity

You have now met everything the explorers of this chapter found: Thomson’s electrons, Rutherford’s nucleus, Moseley’s proton count, Aston’s isotopes, Faraday’s ions. Chemists have a compact way of writing all of it down at once. Take the element’s symbol, for example O for oxygen, and put three numbers around it, each in its own corner.

The bottom-left number is the atomic number, Z. It is the number of protons, and it is really the same information as the symbol: an O always has 8. The top-left number is the mass number, A, protons plus neutrons. The top-right number is the charge, protons minus electrons, with its sign written after the number. Leave it off when the charge is zero.

So 178O2− means: 8 protons; 17 − 8 = 9 neutrons; and a charge of −2, so 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.

To find the neutrons, subtract the bottom number from the top: N = A − Z. To find the electrons, start from the protons and use the charge: a charge of 2− means two more electrons than protons; a charge of 3+ means three fewer.

The positions of these numbers are an international agreement, kept up to date by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), so that a chemist in Mumbai, Moscow or Montreal reads the symbol in exactly the same way. Getting the corners mixed up is one of the commonest mistakes in chemistry exams, so the labels in Figure 1.5 are worth learning.

Careful

“The periodic table says oxygen is 15.999, so the top-left number for oxygen should be 15.999.”

These are two different kinds of number. The top-left number in a nuclear symbol describes one nucleus, and it is always a whole number because you cannot have part of a proton or neutron. The 15.999 on the periodic table is the average atomic mass for natural oxygen: an average over a mixture of isotopes, measured in units in which the individual masses are not quite whole numbers either.

Make a particle with 8 protons, 9 neutrons and 10 electrons. Before you look at the app’s symbol, write the full nuclear symbol yourself, and explain each number.

An atom has Z = 7 and A = 15. How many neutrons does it have, and which element is it?

Answer at the back of the book

1.6What might explain patterns?

London, 1807

Go back a century, to the basement laboratory of the Royal Institution, where Faraday would later work. Humphry Davy, a woodcarver’s son from Penzance in Cornwall who had become the most famous lecturer in London, passed a powerful electric current through a lump of slightly damp potash. Tiny silvery globules appeared, like drops of mercury; some burst into flame as they broke through the crust. Davy had discovered potassium. His cousin Edmund, who was helping him, later recalled that Davy danced about the room with delight. A few days later he made sodium the same way.

Lithium, sodium and potassium are soft, shiny metals that react with water (sodium and potassium fiercely) and are stored under oil. Chemists noticed long ago that they belong together as a family, and that the same family pattern repeats across the elements. That repeating pattern is what Dmitri Mendeleev, a chemist born in Siberia and teaching in St Petersburg, built his periodic table around in 1869. Something about these atoms must be alike. Their nuclei are very different (3, 11 and 19 protons), so it must be something about their electrons.

The story behind this

The patience game: the story of the periodic tableHow a Russian professor laid out the elements like a card game, left gaps, and dared nature to fill them.
Ionisation energy

The energy needed to pull one electron completely away from an atom. A high value means the electron is held tightly.

The clue comes from measuring how much energy it takes to pull one electron off an atom. This is called the ionisation energy. Figure 1.6 shows it for the first 18 elements.

Shell

A group of electrons with similar energy in an atom. Shells are energy levels, not circular tracks.

The pattern is not a smooth climb. It rises, crashes, rises again, crashes again. The best explanation is that electrons are arranged in groups, called shells, at different energies. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons; the next holds up to 8; for the first 18 elements, the third also fills at 8. Lithium has 2 electrons in the first shell and 1 in the second (written 2, 1). Sodium has 2, 8, 1. Both have a single electron in their outermost shell, farther from the nucleus and more shielded from its pull by the electrons inside it. That lone outer electron is easy to remove, and it explains why the two metals behave so much alike.

The story behind this

Why the table has that strange shapeTwo tall towers, a sunken middle, a strip floating underneath: the shape of the periodic table is a picture of how electrons fill an atom.

Predict first. The rings in the figure above look like tracks, with electrons running round them like trains on a circle line. If you could photograph an electron in a neon atom again and again, would the dots all land on a neat circle?

They would not. Electrons don’t follow paths at all. What we can know is where an electron is likely to be found, and that likelihood makes a cloud: thick in some places, thin in others, fading away with no edge. Each shell is made of one or more of these clouds, and each cloud holds at most two electrons. The first shell is a single round cloud (called 1s). The second shell is a bigger round cloud (2s) plus three dumbbell-shaped clouds (2p) at right angles to each other: 1 + 3 = 4 clouds × 2 electrons = 8, the second shell’s eight. Turn the atom below and see for yourself.

The rings are not wrong: they are a model that keeps the counting right and leaves out the shapes. You will meet the clouds again in the story of why the periodic table has its strange shape: the 2p clouds are why the second row has six columns on the right, and the five d clouds are why the middle of the table is ten columns wide.

What, then, makes a full shell special? You will often hear the answer “atoms want a full shell”. It is time to look at that word properly.

Careful

“Sodium wants to lose its electron to get a full shell, and chlorine wants to gain one.”

The word. “Want” is shorthand. Scientists use it when talking quickly, and your school book may say that atoms gain, lose or share electrons “to get a full outer shell”. It is a handy way to predict what happens. But an atom has no wishes, so the word hides the real reason. Here is the reason.

The real principle. Put a marble in a bowl and it ends up at the bottom and stays there. Not because it wants to be at the bottom, but because getting it out again costs energy that something has to supply. On its way down it gave energy away, as a little heat, which spread out into the bowl and the air. Arrangements of atoms work the same way: the ones that last are the ones lower in energy, because leaving them costs energy. And once the energy has gone out as heat, it spreads through the surroundings and does not come back by itself, for the same reason that a shuffled pack of cards never sorts itself back into order: there are overwhelmingly more spread-out ways than gathered-up ones.

The sodium paradox. If sodium really “wanted” to lose its electron, taking it off would give out energy. It does the opposite. Look at the graph: removing sodium’s outer electron costs about 496 kJ per mole. When chlorine catches that electron it gives back only about 349 kJ. So the swap on its own is uphill: the pair ends up 147 kJ worse off, and if nothing else happened, salt would never form. What makes the whole journey run downhill is what comes next: the new ions pull together into a crystal and release about 787 kJ per mole. You will see that energy account in full in Section 2.5. (In Chapter 2 you can follow this energy account step by step in a moving figure.)

Why full shells look “stable”. A full shell is not magic; it is where the next step gets expensive. Take one electron from sodium (2, 8, 1) and you remove the lonely outer one, which is far out and shielded. Try to take a second, and it must come out of the full shell underneath, much closer to the nucleus: that costs about 4,560 kJ per mole, more than nine times as much. Neon (2, 8) is the mirror image. An extra electron would have to go into a brand-new shell much farther out, where the 10 electrons inside shield it from almost all of the nucleus’s pull, so it would not be held at all: a neon atom cannot keep an extra electron. Full shells mark the places where adding or removing one more electron suddenly costs a great deal of energy. That is all “a full shell is stable” really means.

Careful

“Shells are the circles that electrons travel around on, like planets around the Sun.”

Shell diagrams are a way of counting electrons by energy, and they are useful. But electrons do not follow tracks at all. The truth, which needs quantum physics to describe properly, is that we can only say how likely an electron is to be found in different places. Shell diagrams are a simplified model, and later chapters will show where it needs improving.

Investigation 1.6

Compare neutral lithium and sodium. Write down the pattern they share. Then write one question about them that a counting diagram cannot answer.

Check yourself

Neutral fluorine has 9 electrons and neutral chlorine has 17. Work out their shell counts. What do they have in common?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 1

The three mystery beams

A particle detector picks up three kinds of particle, called X, Y and Z.

  • X has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 10 electrons.
  • Y has 8 protons, 10 neutrons and 8 electrons.
  • Z has 10 protons, 10 neutrons and 10 electrons.

A lab assistant notices that X and Z have the same number of electrons, and that Y and Z have the same mass number. She concludes that at least two of them must be the same element.

Which of X, Y and Z are the same element? Write a full nuclear symbol for each, and explain where the assistant went wrong.

Show the solution

Only the protons decide the element. X and Y both have 8 protons, so both are oxygen. Z has 10 protons, so it is neon.

  • X is 168O2−: oxygen-16 with two extra electrons, an oxide ion.
  • Y is 188O: oxygen-18, a neutral atom of a heavier isotope.
  • Z is 2010Ne: neon-20, a neutral atom.

The assistant matched the wrong counts. Sharing an electron count (X and Z) or a mass number (Y and Z) does not make two particles the same element. Sharing a proton count (X and Y) does.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You can now take any atom or ion and count everything in it. But a single atom on its own is a lonely thing, and almost nothing in the world around you is made of lonely atoms. Water is made of molecules, salt of a crystal of ions, diamond of carbon atoms locked together by the trillion. What holds atoms to each other? In Chapter 2 we go back to Davy’s basement, and to a silvery metal and a poisonous green gas that together make something you sprinkle on your dinner.

2

Chapter 2

How atoms form substances

The big questionSodium is a soft metal that fizzes violently in water. Chlorine is a choking green gas. Together they make the salt you sprinkle on your food. How can two dangerous elements turn into something you eat every day?

  1. 2.1Element, compound or mixture?
  2. 2.2How do charges interact?
  3. 2.3How can atoms share electrons?
  4. 2.4What is a molecule?
  5. 2.5A formula without a molecule
  6. 2.6Why composition is not enough
  7. 2.7Unequal sharing and molecular dipoles

London, 1807

We left Chapter 1 in the basement of the Royal Institution, with Humphry Davy dancing round his laboratory over a few silvery globules of potassium. A few days later he made sodium the same way: a metal so soft you can cut it with a knife, which tarnishes in seconds in air and skates fizzing across water. A few years after that, in 1810, Davy showed that a choking yellow-green gas, first made by the Swedish apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1774, was an element too. He named it chlorine, from the Greek for “pale green”.

Put those two together and something extraordinary happens. Sodium burns in chlorine with a fierce yellow flame, and what is left behind is a white powder you could sprinkle on your chips: table salt. Two dangerous elements become something you eat every day. That is a clue that when atoms join, they become something new.

Look around the room you are in. The walls, the air, a glass of water, the screen or page in front of you: almost nothing is made of single, separate atoms. Atoms are nearly always attached to other atoms. Sometimes a few of them join into a small group; sometimes trillions lock together into a crystal. This chapter is about what holds them together, and why the same handful of elements can make substances as different as water, salt, pencil lead and diamond.

2.1Element, compound or mixture?

Spain, the 1790s

In the 1790s a French chemist called Joseph Proust was working in Spain, where the king paid for a fine laboratory. Proust analysed copper carbonate, a green substance, again and again: some he made himself, some was dug out of the ground. However it had been made, it contained the same elements in exactly the same proportions by mass. He argued that every pure compound has a fixed recipe. The most famous chemist in France, Claude-Louis Berthollet, disagreed, and for several years the two argued politely in print. Proust won. His idea, now called the law of definite proportions, became one of the main clues that matter is made of atoms that join in whole-number ratios.

Chemists now sort every material into three kinds. An element you met in Chapter 1: it contains only one kind of atom. Oxygen gas is an element, even though its atoms travel in pairs, O₂, because both atoms in each pair are oxygen.

Compound

A substance made of two or more elements joined together in a fixed ratio, such as water, H₂O.

A compound contains two or more elements joined together, always in the same fixed proportions, just as Proust found. Water is a compound: every water molecule has exactly two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. Water from the Arabian Sea, from a monsoon puddle or from a laboratory bottle has the same 2 : 1 ratio, and that is why it can be given one formula, H₂O.

Mixture

Two or more substances mingled together but not chemically joined. Their proportions can vary, and they can usually be separated by physical means such as evaporating or filtering.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are simply mingled, not joined. Salt water is a mixture: you can stir in a little salt or a lot, and you can get the salt back by letting the water evaporate. A mixture has no single formula, because its proportions can vary.

Here is a subtle point. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gas contains exactly the same kinds of atoms as water. But it is not water, and it behaves completely differently: it is an invisible gas, and with a spark it explodes. What matters is not just which atoms are present, but how they are joined.

The reverse surprise is just as striking: a compound can be utterly unlike the elements it is made from. Sugar is a sweet white powder, yet it is made of carbon (black, like soot), hydrogen and oxygen (two invisible gases).

Find the carbon in sugar (an adult does this one)

This needs the stove, so an adult does the heating while you watch from a safe distance. Melted sugar sticks to skin and burns very badly, so only the adult handles anything, holding the spoon with tongs or an oven glove. The adult puts half a teaspoon of sugar in an old steel spoon and holds it over a low flame, with a window open. Over a minute or two it melts, turns golden, then brown, and finally black and bubbling, with a sharp burnt smell. The adult holds a cold, dry steel plate above it for a moment and the plate mists over. (A gas flame makes a little water of its own, so for a fair test the adult can first hold the plate over an empty spoon and compare.) Predict first: where do the black stuff and the mist come from? The black solid is mostly carbon and the mist is water: both were locked inside the sugar all along, joined into one compound that looked like neither. (Let the spoon and the black crust cool completely, for at least ten minutes, before anyone touches them.)

Get the salt back

Stir two teaspoons of salt into half a glass of warm tap water until it disappears. The water looks just like plain water, but it is a mixture. Pour a thin layer into a saucer or a dark plate and leave it somewhere warm and still, like a sunny windowsill, for a few days. As the water evaporates, white crusts of salt appear, often as tiny cubes. You have separated a mixture without any chemistry at all. Try the same thing with sugar water and compare what is left.

Understand itCompound

What is it?

A substance made of two or more elements joined together in a fixed ratio. Water, H₂O, is always two hydrogen atoms to one oxygen atom.

Why is it called this?

From Latin componere, “to put together”: a compound is elements put together.

What problem did it solve?

Chemists argued over whether a substance could hold its elements in any proportions. Proust showed that a pure compound always has the same recipe, a key clue that atoms join in whole numbers.

Why does it work?

Atoms join in particular whole-number patterns, so every molecule or crystal of the compound has the same ratio of atoms.

How does it help?

A compound can be given one formula and has fixed properties, so you can predict what a recipe will make, every time.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Proust analysed copper carbonate again and again in the 1790s. Made in the lab or dug from the ground, it held the same elements in exactly the same proportions by mass.

What it isn’t

Not a mixture. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gas contains the same atoms as water, but it is not water: it explodes with a spark.

Where does it stop working?

Some solid compounds, such as certain minerals and metal oxides, have slightly variable ratios. Chemists call them berthollides, after Proust’s rival, who was partly right after all.

Your turn

Explain Compound to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Compare all four samples in the app. For each one, decide: element, compound or mixture? Then explain why oxygen, O₂, is an element even though it is made of molecules.

Is air an element, a compound or a mixture? Give a reason.
