2.2How do charges interact?

Remember the balloon that lifted pepper off a plate in Chapter 1? Everything that holds atoms together comes down to the same rule, one of the four ideas at the start of the book: opposite charges attract, and like charges repel. A proton and an electron pull towards each other. Two electrons push each other apart. So do two protons.

Paris, 1785

How strong is the pull? The first person to measure it was Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, a French army engineer who had spent years building a fort on the Caribbean island of Martinique before turning to physics. He hung a light rod from a very thin wire, with a small charged ball on one end. When he brought another charged ball near it, the rod turned and twisted the wire. The more the wire twisted, the bigger the force, so the twist was a way of weighing a force too small to feel.

Inverse-square law

A rule where a force gets weaker with the square of the distance: twice as far, one quarter of the force; three times as far, one ninth.

By changing the distance between the balls, Coulomb found the rule, now called Coulomb’s law. The pull depends on two things: how big the charges are, and how far apart they are. Bigger charges pull harder. And the force gets weaker very quickly with distance. If you double the distance between two charges, the force does not halve. It drops to a quarter. Triple the distance, and it drops to a ninth. Scientists call this an inverse-square law.

Coulomb’s law is about tiny charged points, and atoms are not points. When two atoms come very close, their electron clouds start to overlap and a powerful push-back sets in, which is why atoms do not collapse into each other. To describe that properly you need quantum physics. But almost every attraction in this book, between ions, between atoms in a molecule, between neighbouring molecules, is at heart this electric pull.

Careful

“If you double the distance, the force halves.”

It is much more dramatic than that. Twice the distance means one quarter of the force, because the distance is squared: 2 × 2 = 4. This is why electric forces between atoms matter enormously at close range and fade quickly further away.

See why the distance is squared

Cut a small square hole, about 1 cm across, in a piece of card. In a dark room, hold the torch of a phone (its light is a tiny point, which is what you want) 5 cm behind the hole, and shine it onto a sheet of squared paper 10 cm from the light. Measure every distance from the light itself, not from the card. Count how many squares the patch of light covers. Now move the paper to 20 cm from the light, keeping the card where it was. Predict first: twice the distance, so twice as many squares? Count them: about four times as many, because the patch has grown twice as wide and twice as tall. The same light is spread over four times the area, so each square gets a quarter as much. Electric pull spreads out from a charge in a similar way, which is why it falls off with the square of the distance.

Investigation 2.2

Hold the distance fixed and change the sign of one charge. What happens to the direction of the force? Then double the distance and predict the new size of the force before you look.

Check yourself

Two opposite charges are 1 unit apart. They are moved to 3 units apart. What fraction of the original attraction is left?

Answer at the back of the book

2.3How can atoms share electrons?

Berkeley, California, 1916

Salt’s ions hold together because they have opposite charges. But what about a hydrogen molecule, H₂, where two identical atoms cling together and neither has a charge? This puzzled chemists until the American chemist Gilbert Newton Lewis, head of chemistry at the University of California in Berkeley, suggested a simple answer in 1916: the two atoms share a pair of electrons. Lewis had been doodling atoms as little cubes with electrons at the corners in his notebooks since 1902. His dots-for-electrons drawings are still used in every chemistry class in the world.

The story behind this

Dots and lines: how atoms hold on to each otherA professor’s doodles of cubes became the shared pair of electrons, the idea at the heart of almost every molecule.
Covalent bond

A link between two atoms that share electrons. Both nuclei are attracted to the shared electrons between them.

Picture two hydrogen atoms floating towards each other. Each has one proton and one electron. As they get close, each electron starts to feel the pull of both protons. The electrons spend much of their time in the space between the two nuclei, and both nuclei are attracted to that shared negative region. This joins the atoms into a molecule of hydrogen, H₂. A link like this, made by shared electrons, is called a covalent bond.

A bond is not a stick or a hook. It is a balance. Pull the two nuclei closer, and the two positive nuclei repel each other more strongly. Pull them further apart, and they lose the shared attraction. In between there is a best distance, where the energy is lowest. For H₂, that distance is 74 picometres (0.074 nanometres).

Predict first. Two hydrogen atoms drift towards each other. Will they keep getting closer until they touch, stop somewhere, or bounce away? Make your guess, then move them with the slider below.

Because bonded atoms sit in an energy dip, pulling them apart always takes energy. To split one mole of H₂ molecules into separate hydrogen atoms takes 436 kilojoules: about enough to bring a litre of water from room temperature to the boil, and then some. This is worth fixing firmly in your head, because everyday life suggests the opposite (snap a stick, and it seems to let something out): breaking a bond never gives out energy; it always costs energy. Energy comes out when bonds form, as the atoms drop into the dip.

Try Let them come together in the figure. The atoms roll down into the dip and rock back and forth, and they only settle at the bottom if the extra energy is carried away, as heat passed to other molecules. That is the whole secret of a bond: it is the bottom of an energy valley. Nothing holds the atoms with a hook. They stay because climbing out would cost 436 kJ for every mole, and nobody is paying.

How can anyone measure a distance of 74 picometres? With light. Molecules vibrate and spin, and they absorb and give out light only at particular colours that match those movements. From those colours, physicists work out how far apart the nuclei are and how much energy it takes to pull them apart. The same measurements have been made for thousands of other bonds, and X-ray maps of crystals show that, in many of them, electrons really do pile up in the regions between bonded atoms, just where Lewis drew his shared pairs.

Careful

“Hydrogen atoms bond because each one wants two electrons to be stable.”

Atoms do not want anything. The bond forms because the arrangement with shared electrons has lower energy than two separate atoms: each electron is attracted to two protons instead of one. Energy has to be put in to break that arrangement. That is the whole story, without any wishing.

Understand itCovalent bond

What is it?

A link between two atoms that share a pair of electrons. Both nuclei are pulled towards the shared electrons between them, and that holds the atoms together.

Why is it called this?

“Co-” means together, and “valence” is chemists’ word for an atom’s power to combine, from Latin valentia, strength. The American chemist Irving Langmuir introduced “covalence” in 1919 for electrons shared between atoms.

What problem did it solve?

Ions explained salt, but not molecules such as H₂, where two identical atoms with no charge cling together. Lewis’s shared pair of 1916 explained how.

Why does it work?

Each shared electron is attracted by two nuclei instead of one, which lowers the energy. Too close and the nuclei repel; too far and the sharing is lost. The bond sits at the distance where the energy is lowest.

How does it help?

It explains how molecules hold together, why breaking a bond always costs energy, and where the energy of a reaction comes from when new bonds form.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

The colours of light that molecules absorb reveal how long and how strong their bonds are: 74 pm and 436 kJ per mole for H₂. X-ray maps of crystals show electrons piled up between bonded atoms.

What it isn’t

Not a stick or a hook, and not two atoms “wanting” to fill their shells. It is a balance of attractions and repulsions.

Where does it stop working?

Real bonds lie on a scale, from equal sharing, through unequal sharing (Section 2.7), to the complete hand-over of electrons that makes ions. The neat sharing picture is one end of that scale.

Your turn

Explain Covalent bond to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Compare H₂, O₂ and H₂O in the app. Sketch which atoms belong to each molecule. Then write down something the formula H₂O does not tell you about a water molecule.

Rewrite this sentence so it is scientifically accurate: “Atoms bond because they want to fill their shells.”

2.4What is a molecule?

Turin, 1811

A hundred years before Lewis, chemists had a puzzle about gases. The French chemist Joseph Gay-Lussac, who once rode a hydrogen balloon seven kilometres up into the sky to sample the air, noticed that gases react in simple volume ratios. Two litres of hydrogen react with one litre of oxygen to make two litres of steam (all measured at the same temperature and pressure). If each atom acted alone, you would expect only one litre of steam.

In northern Italy, a quiet professor from Turin called Amedeo Avogadro, then teaching in the nearby town of Vercelli, who had trained as a lawyer before falling in love with physics, explained it in 1811. Equal volumes of gas contain equal numbers of particles, he said, and hydrogen and oxygen gas are made not of single atoms but of pairs, H₂ and O₂. Then 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O fits the volumes exactly. Almost nobody listened. It took about fifty years before most chemists accepted his idea, and by then Avogadro had died.

Molecule

A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds that acts as a single unit. All the molecules of one substance are identical (apart from tiny differences between isotopes).

What Avogadro had seen was the molecule: a small group of atoms held together by covalent bonds, which travels around as one unit. A water molecule is three atoms; an oxygen molecule is two; a sugar molecule is 45. Every molecule of a given substance is the same.

Subscript

The small lowered number in a formula. It counts atoms of the element just before it, in one molecule or formula unit.

A formula tells you which atoms are in one molecule, and how many. The small number written low after a symbol, called a subscript, counts atoms of that element in one molecule: CO₂ has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms. A big number written in front counts whole molecules: 3 CO₂ means three separate carbon dioxide molecules, with 3 carbon atoms and 6 oxygen atoms between them.

The grouping matters. “3 C and 6 O” lists the atoms, but loses the most important fact: they come as three separate CO₂ molecules, each one a straight line of O=C=O.

Investigation 2.4

Build three water molecules and then three carbon dioxide molecules. Count the atoms in each, but draw them in their groups rather than as one pile.

Check yourself

How many oxygen atoms are in four CO₂ molecules?

Answer at the back of the book

2.5A formula without a molecule

Ionic lattice

A giant, regular, repeating arrangement of positive and negative ions, held together by their attraction in every direction.

Now back to Davy’s two elements, sodium and chlorine. When sodium metal burns in chlorine gas, each sodium atom passes one electron to a chlorine atom. That makes Na⁺ ions and Cl⁻ ions. Opposite charges attract, so the ions pack together. But the attraction works in every direction at once, so each Na⁺ pulls in Cl⁻ ions on all sides, and each Cl⁻ pulls in Na⁺ ions on all sides. The result is not a set of little pairs but a huge, repeating three-dimensional grid of alternating ions: an ionic lattice. A single grain of salt contains roughly 10¹⁸ of them.

Salt is made of cubes

Sprinkle a few grains of ordinary table salt onto a dark plate and look at them through a magnifying glass, or through a phone camera zoomed right in. Many grains are tiny cubes, or broken pieces of cubes, with flat faces and square corners. Now do the same with sugar: its grains are a different, more slanted shape. The square shape of a salt grain is the ionic lattice in the figure below, repeated millions of times in every direction until it is big enough to see.

Leeds and Cambridge, 1913

How do we know the grid is really there? In 1912 the German physicist Max von Laue showed that X-rays passing through a crystal scatter into a pattern of spots. Within months, a father and son in England turned that pattern into a way of seeing atoms. William Henry Bragg was a professor at Leeds; his son William Lawrence Bragg was a young researcher at Cambridge. Together they shone X-rays through crystals of rock salt and worked out the only arrangement that could make the pattern: a regular grid of alternating ions, with every sodium surrounded by six chlorides and every chloride by six sodiums. No sodium was paired with one particular chloride. Some chemists found this very hard to accept: what had happened to the salt molecule? The father and son shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1915. Lawrence was 25, and he is still the youngest physics laureate.

The story behind this

Seeing inside salt: the Braggs and their X-raysA father and son found a way to see where atoms sit, and discovered that salt has no molecules at all.

So in solid salt there is no such thing as “a NaCl molecule”, and no pairs either.

Careful

“Each sodium ion is bonded to the chloride ion that took its electron, so salt is really made of Na–Cl pairs.”

It is a very natural picture, because the story of salt usually begins with one sodium handing one electron to one chlorine. But look at the lattice: each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions, all exactly the same distance away, all pulling equally. Which one is “its” partner? None of them. An ion is held by its charge, not by its history. Here is proof you have already made with your own hands: the salt cubes that grew on your saucer in Section 2.1 formed from ions that were already ions, floating in water. Not one of those sodium ions gave an electron to the chloride beside it, and yet the crystal holds together exactly as well as any other.

Formula unit

The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound. NaCl means 1 Na⁺ for every 1 Cl⁻; MgCl₂ means 1 Mg²⁺ for every 2 Cl⁻.

The formula NaCl tells you the ratio: one sodium ion for every chloride ion, which makes the whole crystal neutral. Chemists call that smallest ratio a formula unit.

Here is the answer Chapter 1 promised. Pulling an electron off a sodium atom costs energy: 496 kJ for every mole of atoms. A chlorine atom capturing that electron gives some energy back, 349 kJ per mole. That still leaves the pair 147 kJ worse off. If ions just floated apart, salt would never form. But when the ions come together into a lattice, all those opposite charges pulling on each other release a great deal of energy: about 787 kJ per mole. So the lattice ends up far lower in energy than the separate atoms. Sodium does not “want” to lose an electron. Losing it costs energy, and the attraction in the crystal pays that cost back several times over.

Predict first. Sodium “wants” to lose an electron, school books often say. If that were true, would pulling the electron off sodium give out energy or cost energy? Decide, then follow the energy one step at a time below.

Watch the ball. It climbs 496 kJ when sodium loses its electron, comes only part of the way back down (349 kJ) when chlorine catches it, and is still 147 kJ uphill. Only the last step, the ions packing together into a crystal, carries it far below where it started: 787 kJ down, 640 kJ below the start overall. Salt forms not because any atom wants anything, but because the finished crystal sits at the bottom of a deep energy valley.

And that also answers the big question about why salt is safe to eat. The ions in salt are not sodium metal or chlorine gas. Na⁺ ions have different numbers of electrons from sodium atoms, so they behave completely differently: they do not react with water at all. Same nuclei, different electrons, different chemistry.

Understand itIonic lattice

What is it?

A giant, regular, repeating grid of positive and negative ions, each held by its neighbours in every direction. In salt, each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻, and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺.

Why is it called this?

A lattice is a criss-cross framework of thin strips with gaps between them, like a garden trellis; the word comes from an old French word for a strip of wood. “Ionic” because it is built from ions.

What problem did it solve?

Chemists expected salt to be made of NaCl molecules, and could not explain why it melts only at a very high temperature, grows as cubes, and carries electricity only when melted or dissolved. A grid of ions explains all three.

Why does it work?

Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. In alternating rows, every ion is surrounded by opposite charges, so the attractions win in every direction and release a great deal of energy: about 787 kJ per mole for salt.

How does it help?

It explains why the formula NaCl gives a ratio and not a molecule, why salt grains are cubes, and why the energy account for salt runs downhill.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

In 1913 the Braggs shone X-rays through rock salt and showed that only a grid of alternating ions, each with six neighbours, could make the pattern of spots.

What it isn’t

Not a collection of Na–Cl pairs. No ion belongs to any one partner.

Where does it stop working?

Real crystals have flaws: missing ions, cracks and rough surfaces. The perfect grid describes the inside of a crystal, not every corner of it.

Your turn

Explain Ionic lattice to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 2.5

Compare sodium chloride with water in the app. Sketch a small repeating patch of the ionic lattice next to a single water molecule, and label what makes them different.

Check yourself

Magnesium chloride is an ionic solid with formula MgCl₂. Magnesium ions have a charge of 2+. What does the 2 in MgCl₂ tell you?

Answer at the back of the book

2.6Why composition is not enough

Paris, 1772

On a sunny day in Paris, a group of chemists gathered round a giant magnifying glass. Among them was Antoine Lavoisier, a wealthy young tax official who spent every spare hour, and much of his fortune, on chemistry. They focused the sunlight onto a diamond sealed inside a glass jar. The diamond grew hot, then simply vanished, and the air in the jar now contained “fixed air”, what we call carbon dioxide. Twenty-five years later, in 1797, the English chemist Smithson Tennant burned weighed amounts of diamond and of charcoal, and showed that equal masses give equal amounts of carbon dioxide. The most precious stone in the world was nothing but carbon, the same stuff as soot.

Diamond and graphite, the grey material in a pencil, are both pure carbon. (Pencil “lead” has no lead in it at all: it is graphite mixed with clay.) Burn a gram of either one in oxygen and you get exactly the same amount of carbon dioxide. So their formula is the same: just C. And yet diamond is the hardest natural material known, while graphite is so soft that it leaves a trail on paper. Graphite even conducts electricity; diamond does not.

Covalent network

A giant structure in which covalent bonds link atoms throughout a whole crystal, with no separate molecules. Diamond is one.

Allotropes

Different forms of the same element, with their atoms joined in different ways. Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon; O₂ and O₃ (ozone) are allotropes of oxygen.

The difference is entirely in how the atoms are connected. In diamond, every carbon atom is joined by covalent bonds to four others, pointing to the corners of a pyramid-like shape called a tetrahedron. The bonds continue in every direction through the whole crystal, making one enormous, rigid covalent network. In graphite, each carbon atom is joined to only three others, in flat sheets of hexagons like chicken wire. The sheets are stacked in layers, and the attraction between layers is weak, so they slide past each other easily. That sliding is what you see when a pencil leaves a mark: thousands of sheets peeling off onto the paper. Much later, X-rays like the Braggs’ showed exactly how differently the carbon atoms are arranged in the two.

You can test the strangest of these differences yourself.

Draw a wire

Do this with an adult nearby. You need a very soft pencil (6B to 8B; an ordinary HB pencil will not work), a 9-volt battery, a small LED (red works best) and some sticky tape. On paper, shade a short, wide strip, about 4 cm long and 1 cm wide, pressing hard and going over it again and again until it is dark and shiny. Hold one terminal of the battery on one end of the strip. Press one leg of the LED firmly onto the other end of the strip, and touch the LED’s other leg to the battery’s other terminal, so that the electricity has to travel along the pencil line. (If it does not light, turn the LED round: it only works one way, with its longer leg towards the battery’s + terminal.) Predict first: can a pencil line carry electricity? It can: the LED glows, faintly, so dim the room to see it, because electrons can travel along graphite’s sheets. Make the strip longer or thinner and the LED dims, or goes out. A diamond line, if you could draw one, would carry nothing, though it is the same element. Never touch the LED’s legs straight onto both battery terminals: without the pencil line to hold the current back, it will burn the LED out. Use only a small battery like this, never the mains.

Different forms of the same element are called allotropes. Oxygen has them too: ordinary oxygen, O₂, which you breathe, and ozone, O₃, a sharp-smelling gas that high in the atmosphere absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet light.

Lavoisier did not live to see any of this. During the French Revolution, tax officials were hated, and in 1794 he was sent to the guillotine. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange is reported to have said that it took only a moment to cut off that head, and a hundred years might not produce another like it.

Investigation 2.6

Select diamond, and compare it with graphite. Write a question about these two materials that the formula C cannot answer.

Check yourself

Can the formula C tell you whether a sample is graphite or diamond? What extra information do you need?

Answer at the back of the book

2.7Unequal sharing and molecular dipoles

Partial charges (δ⁺, δ⁻)

Small charges on atoms in a molecule, caused by electrons being shared unequally. They are fractions of a full charge.

In a hydrogen molecule, both atoms are the same, so the shared electrons are shared equally. But in a water molecule, the oxygen nucleus, with 8 protons, pulls on the shared electrons much more strongly than a hydrogen nucleus with only 1 (even after oxygen’s inner electrons screen off part of that pull). So the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen. The oxygen end becomes slightly negative, written δ⁻ (“delta minus”), and the hydrogen ends slightly positive, δ⁺. These are partial charges: much smaller than the full charge of an ion.

Pasadena, California, 1932

Electronegativity

How strongly an atom in a bond pulls shared electrons towards itself. Fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen are among the strongest.

How hard does each atom pull? In 1932 Linus Pauling, a young chemist at the California Institute of Technology who would later win two Nobel Prizes, one for chemistry and one for peace, worked out a scale by comparing the energies of many different bonds. How strongly an atom pulls shared electrons is called its electronegativity. On the scale that grew from Pauling’s, hydrogen scores 2.20, carbon 2.55, nitrogen 3.04 and oxygen 3.44. The bigger the difference between two bonded atoms, the more unequal the sharing. A bond with unequal sharing is called a polar bond.

Dipole

A molecule (or bond) with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end.

Now the interesting part. Carbon dioxide has two polar bonds too: oxygen (3.44) pulls harder than carbon (2.55). But a CO₂ molecule is perfectly straight, O=C=O, so the two oxygen ends pull in exactly opposite directions and cancel out, like two equally strong children in a tug of war. The molecule as a whole has no positive end and no negative end. Water is bent, with an angle of 104.5° between its bonds, so its two pulls do not cancel. Water has a negative oxygen side and a positive hydrogen side: it is a polar molecule, with a dipole.

So a molecule’s polarity depends on two things at once: its bonds, and its shape. Methane, CH₄, also comes out non-polar: its four slightly polar bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel. Ammonia, NH₃, is a squat pyramid, and its bonds do not cancel.

How do we know? Measuring a molecule’s lopsidedness 20th century

Polar molecules twist to line up in an electric field, and this changes how a substance responds to the field and how its molecules absorb microwaves. The Dutch-born physicist Peter Debye worked out how to turn such measurements into each molecule’s dipole moment, a measure of how lopsided its charge is; the unit is named the debye after him. Water’s is 1.85 debye, ammonia’s 1.47 and hydrogen chloride’s 1.08. Carbon dioxide and methane come out at zero, just as the shapes predict. These same measurements also confirmed the shapes themselves.

Careful

“A thin stream of water bends towards a charged comb, so that proves water molecules are polar.”

It is a lovely demonstration, and you may see it in a textbook. But careful experiments in 2000 showed that the stream bends mainly because the charged comb pulls extra charge onto the water as it flows from the tap, and then attracts that charge. How much a liquid bends depends mostly on how easily charge can flow onto it, not simply on whether its molecules are polar. So the bending stream is not good evidence that water molecules are polar. The real evidence is the dipole-moment measurements described above. It is a good example of why scientists keep re-checking even familiar experiments.

So what can you see at home? Not dipoles themselves, but one of their most important consequences: polar substances mix with polar substances, and non-polar with non-polar.

Fireworks in a glass

Fill a tall glass nearly to the top with water. In a cup, stir three or four drops of food colouring into two tablespoons of cooking oil (the drops will not mix in; they break into little beads). Pour the oil gently onto the water. Predict first: what will the coloured beads do? They sink slowly through the oil. Some rest on top of the water for a little while (give them a few minutes), but when each one breaks through it bursts into a streaming cloud of colour. Food colouring is dye dissolved in water. It mixes into water, whose molecules are polar, but not into oil, whose molecules are almost non-polar. This shows “like mixes with like”; it does not measure a dipole, but it is a real effect of one.

Understand itPolar molecule

What is it?

A molecule with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, because its electrons are shared unequally and its shape does not let the pulls cancel. Water is polar; carbon dioxide is not.

Why is it called this?

From “pole”, the name for each end of a magnet, which comes from the Greek polos, a pivot or axis. A polar molecule has two ends with opposite charges, so it is also called a dipole, “two poles”.

What problem did it solve?

It explained why some substances mix and others refuse, and why molecules with the same kinds of bond can behave so differently: CO₂ and H₂O both have polar bonds, but only water is a polar molecule.

Why does it work?

A more electronegative atom, such as oxygen, pulls shared electrons towards itself, making small partial charges. If the molecule is lopsided, like bent water, the pulls add up; if it is straight or evenly balanced, they cancel.

How does it help?

It predicts what dissolves in what (“like mixes with like”), and helps explain how strongly molecules stick to each other, which Chapter 3 uses to explain boiling points.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Measured dipole moments: water 1.85 debye, ammonia 1.47, carbon dioxide and methane zero, just as their shapes predict.

What it isn’t

Not an ion. The charges are only partial, small fractions of a full charge, and the molecule as a whole is neutral.

Where does it stop working?

Electronegativity is a handy scale, not a single measured thing, and different scales give slightly different numbers. It tells you roughly how unequal the sharing is, not exactly.

Explain Polar molecule to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Ammonia (NH₃) is a pyramid, with the nitrogen at the top. Boron trifluoride (BF₃) is flat, with its three fluorines spread 120° apart. Both have three polar bonds. Which molecule is polar overall, and why?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 2

The case of the three unlabelled jars

A laboratory has three jars whose labels have fallen off. The labels on the floor say water, carbon dioxide and sodium chloride. Here is what the technician finds.

  1. Jar A holds a colourless liquid that boils at 100 °C. Measurements show its molecules have a dipole moment of 1.85 debye.
  2. Jar B holds a white solid at −80 °C, which turns straight into a colourless gas at −78 °C without melting first. Its molecules have polar bonds, but a dipole moment of zero.
  3. Jar C holds hard, white, cube-shaped crystals that melt only at 801 °C. As a solid it does not conduct electricity; dissolved in water, it does.

Which label belongs on each jar? For each one, say what kind of particles it is made of and which clue settles it.

Show the solution
  • Jar A is water. It is made of bent H₂O molecules. The bent shape means the two polar O–H bonds do not cancel, giving a dipole moment (clue 1); and water boils at 100 °C.
  • Jar B is carbon dioxide, frozen (“dry ice”). It is made of straight O=C=O molecules: polar bonds whose pulls cancel exactly, so the dipole moment is zero (clue 2).
  • Jar C is sodium chloride. It is an ionic lattice, not molecules. The very high melting point (clue 3) shows how strong the attractions in the lattice are. It cannot conduct as a solid because the ions are locked in place; dissolved, they are free to move.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

You now know what holds atoms together inside a molecule or a crystal. But one big puzzle remains. When you heat ice, it melts, and then boils, and steam is still water. The bonds inside the H₂O molecules never break. So what does change when a substance melts or boils? Chapter 3 is about the forces between molecules, and the jiggling of heat that fights against them.

3

Chapter 3

Why matter has different states

The big questionWhen water boils in a kettle, bubbles of invisible gas rise through it and escape as steam. What is inside those bubbles, and what actually breaks when water boils?

  1. 3.1One substance, three states
  2. 3.2Temperature and particle motion
  3. 3.3Changing state is not changing identity
  4. 3.4Squeezing a gas
  5. 3.5Where did the solute go?
  6. 3.6Intermolecular forces against thermal motion

Glasgow, Scotland, around 1761

On a cold winter’s day a young professor called Joseph Black set a pan of ice and a pan of ice-cold water side by side in a warm room, and watched two thermometers. The water warmed up steadily, as you would expect. The ice did something strange. Its thermometer sat stuck at the freezing point, hour after hour, while the ice slowly turned to water. Heat was pouring into it from the room, and yet it was getting no warmer. Where was all that heat going?

Black had been born in Bordeaux, in France, the son of a wine merchant from Belfast, and trained as a doctor. He was a quiet, cautious man who hated to publish anything until he was sure, and he lectured to packed rooms of medical students rather than write books. But he trusted his thermometers more than the ideas of his day, and that is what let him see the puzzle at all.

Black’s answer was that melting itself swallows heat: the ice needed energy just to stop being ice. He did not know about molecules, and nor did anyone else in Glasgow. But he had caught the first clue to the question this chapter answers. Ask a few people what is inside the bubbles in boiling water, and some will say “air”, some “oxygen”, and some “hydrogen and oxygen, because the water is splitting up”. Predict first: before you read on, decide what you think is in those bubbles, and keep your answer in mind. By the end of Section 3.3 you will have seen the evidence for yourself. Follow the particles of a substance as it melts, boils and spreads out, and you find that the particles themselves never change. What changes is how far apart they are, how fast they move, and whether the pulls between them can hold them together.

3.1One substance, three states

States of matter

Solid, liquid and gas. The same substance can be in any of them, depending on its temperature and the pressure around it.

Water is the only substance most of us see every day as a solid, a liquid and a gas: ice in the freezer, water in the tap, steam from the kettle. These are the three common states of matter. You can tell them apart without any equipment. A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, but keeps the same volume: a litre of water is a litre whether it is in a bottle or a bowl. A gas spreads out to fill whatever space it is given, and can be squashed into a smaller space.

The particle model explains all three with one picture. In a solid, the particles are packed closely together and each one vibrates about a fixed spot, held there by the attractions of its neighbours. In a liquid, they are still close together, which is why a liquid is hard to squash, but they move around and slide past each other, which is why it flows. In a gas, the particles are far apart compared with their own size and fly about freely, colliding with each other and with the walls.

Two things in that picture are invisible, and both are easy to get wrong. The first is the space between the particles. It is not filled with air, or with anything else: air is itself made of particles, and between those there is nothing at all. The second is the motion in a solid. The molecules in an ice cube are not frozen still; they shiver in place all the time, and the colder the ice, the smaller the shiver.

How much further apart are they in a gas? When water boils at 100 °C and normal pressure, the steam takes up about 1,700 times as much space as the liquid water it came from. A 250 mL cup of water makes roughly 400 litres of steam: enough to fill a bathtub. That enormous swelling is what James Watt and the engineers after him harnessed in steam engines, a few years after Black’s ice experiment and in the same university town.

Careful

“When ice melts, the water molecules melt too, and when water boils, the molecules expand.”

The molecules do not melt, swell or soften, and they do not stop moving when water freezes. Every H₂O molecule in steam is exactly the same size and shape as one in ice. What changes is the space between molecules and how freely they move. Water even shows that a solid is not always more tightly packed than its liquid: ice is slightly less dense than liquid water, because its molecules are held in an open, hexagonal pattern. That is why ice floats.

Watch heat vanish into ice

Put a few ice cubes and a little cold water in a glass, stir, and put a kitchen thermometer in it (or just feel the glass). Keep stirring now and then. As long as there is still ice in the glass, the temperature stays at about 0 °C, even though the room is pouring heat into it. Only when the last of the ice has melted does the water start to warm up. You are watching Joseph Black’s puzzle: the heat is going into pulling the molecules out of their ice pattern, not into making them move faster.

Understand itThe particle model

What is it?

The idea that every substance is made of tiny particles that are always moving and that attract each other. Solid, liquid and gas are the same particles, arranged and moving differently.

Why is it called this?

“Particle” comes from Latin particula, “a little part”. It is called a model because it is a simplified picture built to explain what we observe, not a photograph.

What problem did it solve?

Why does a solid keep its shape, a liquid flow but keep its volume, and a gas fill any space and squash easily? One picture explains all three.

Why does it work?

In a solid, the attractions hold particles in place while they vibrate. In a liquid, they stay close but slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and fly freely. Heating or cooling changes which wins: the motion or the pull.

How does it help?

It predicts what happens when you heat, cool or squeeze things: why ice melts at a fixed temperature, why gases can be squashed, and why steam takes up about 1,700 times the space of the water it came from.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Brownian motion shows the particles jostling (Chapter 0), and the heat that vanishes into melting ice, Joseph Black’s puzzle, is just what pulling particles out of their pattern would need.

What it isn’t

The space between the particles is not filled with air, or with anything else: it is empty. And the particles themselves do not melt, swell or stop moving.

Where does it stop working?

Some materials do not fit three neat states, such as glass, gels and toothpaste, and at very high temperatures matter becomes a fourth state, plasma, as in lightning and the Sun.

Your turn

Explain The particle model to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

3.2Temperature and particle motion

Paris, 1 December 1783

Half of Paris had come to the gardens of the Tuileries Palace. Ten days earlier, two men had floated over the city under a huge paper-and-cloth balloon filled with hot air from a fire, built by the Montgolfier brothers: the first people ever to fly. Now a physicist named Jacques Charles was about to go one better. His balloon was filled not with hot air but with hydrogen, a gas much lighter than air, and he rose into the sky with his engineer Nicolas-Louis Robert, a thermometer and a barometer on board to take measurements. Charles flew for about two hours and came down safely, 36 kilometres away.

Charles spent the following years asking a quieter question: what does heat do to a gas? Warm a gas, he found, and it swells; and every gas he tried swelled by the same fraction for the same warming. To understand why, you need to picture the particles.

The particles in everything around you are always moving. In a gas they are fast. The nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the air of your room are zooming about at an average of roughly 500 metres per second, faster than a passenger jet. They do not get far: each one collides with another molecule billions of times a second.

Temperature

A measure of how hot something is. In a gas it goes up and down with the average energy of the particles’ motion.

What we feel as temperature is connected to this motion. The hotter a gas is, the faster its particles move, on average. Not every particle moves at the same speed; some are always faster and some slower. But warm the gas and the whole crowd speeds up.

Remember the two glasses from Chapter 0, with a drop of food colouring in each? Here is the inference you were reaching for. The water molecules are always moving and jostling the colour’s molecules about, and in the warm glass they move faster, so the colour is shoved outwards sooner. Nobody stirs it: the molecules do the stirring.

Pressure

The push of a gas (or liquid) on each square metre of surface. Measured in pascals (Pa); normal air pressure is about 101,000 Pa, or 101 kPa.

Picture a gas sealed in a strong box. Its particles keep slamming into the walls, and all those tiny collisions add up to a steady push on the walls: the pressure of the gas. Heat the box, and the particles move faster. They hit the walls more often and harder. So the pressure rises, even though the number of particles and the size of the box have not changed. (Let the walls move, as the skin of a balloon can, and instead of the pressure rising, the gas swells: Charles’s discovery.)

To make this rule work, temperature has to be measured from the right starting point, and finding that starting point was its own small adventure. In about 1702 the French physicist Guillaume Amontons noticed that air in a sealed container pushes harder when it is heated. A century later Charles and Joseph Gay-Lussac measured carefully how the volume (and, later, the pressure) of many gases changes with temperature. Plot either one against temperature, and every gas gives a straight line. Follow the lines backwards, and they all point to zero at the same temperature: about −273 °C. In 1848 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a temperature scale that starts right there. Real gases turn to liquid before they get that cold, but the lines still point the way.

Kelvin (K)

A temperature scale that starts at absolute zero (−273.15 °C). Kelvin = degrees Celsius + 273.15.

The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, −273.15 °C, the coldest anything can possibly be, where particle motion is as small as nature allows. A kelvin step is the same size as a degree Celsius, so to convert, you add 273.15. Water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K. Doubling the temperature in kelvin doubles the pressure of a gas in a sealed box. Doubling it in Celsius does not: going from 10 °C to 20 °C is only going from 283 K to 293 K.

The story behind this

How cold can cold get?Thermometers, a frozen guess at the coldest possible cold, and the Scottish scientist who gave us a temperature scale that starts from nothing at all.

A balloon that breathes

Stretch a balloon over the neck of an empty plastic bottle. Stand the bottle in a bowl of hot tap water, or water an adult has mixed from the kettle (hot, but not boiling), for a few minutes, and the balloon slowly lifts and stands up as the air inside warms and swells. Move the bottle into a bowl of ice water, and the balloon sags again. Nothing has gone in or out: the same air molecules are simply moving faster, then slower. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh the bottle and balloon cold and again when warm, wiping the bottle dry each time. Predict first: will the warm one be heavier? (It weighs the same. Faster molecules take up more room, but there are no more of them, and none of them got heavier.)

Understand itTemperature

What does it measure?

How hot something is. In a gas, it measures the average energy of the particles’ motion: the hotter the gas, the faster its particles move on average.

Why is it called this?

From Latin temperatura, “a mixing in the right proportion”, from temperare, to mix or moderate. Galileo and later Boyle used the word for the degree of heat.

What problem did it solve?

“Hot” and “cold” are feelings that differ from person to person. A temperature scale turns them into numbers anyone can check, and the kelvin scale gives a true starting point, absolute zero.

Why does it work?

When a hot thing touches a cold one, energy passes from the faster-moving particles to the slower ones until both are at the same temperature. A thermometer settles at the temperature of whatever it touches, and reads its own.

How does it help?

It lets you predict how gases behave: double the kelvin temperature of a sealed gas and its pressure doubles.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Plot the volume or pressure of a gas against temperature and every gas gives a straight line, all pointing to zero at about −273 °C, the start of the kelvin scale.

What it isn’t

Not the same as heat. A bucket of warm water holds far more energy than a cup of hot tea, enough to melt much more ice, even though the tea is at a higher temperature.

Where does it stop working?

Temperature describes a crowd. A single molecule has a speed, not a temperature, and in any gas some molecules are always faster and some slower.

Your turn

Explain Temperature to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

3.3Changing state is not changing identity

London, May 1800

News had just arrived from Italy that Alessandro Volta had built the first battery, a tall pile of metal discs and salty cardboard that pushed a steady electric current. Within weeks, two Londoners, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, had built their own. They dipped its two wires into water, and bubbles of gas streamed off both of them: hydrogen at one wire, oxygen at the other, with twice as much hydrogen as oxygen. Electricity had torn water apart into two elements.

Change of state

Melting, freezing, boiling (evaporating) or condensing. The substance stays the same; only the arrangement and motion of its particles change.

So could boiling do the same? Is that what is inside the bubbles in a kettle? The answer is no. Inside the bubbles in boiling water is water: water vapour, made of the same H₂O molecules as the liquid. When water boils, the molecules break away from their neighbours and spread out, but each molecule stays whole. Boiling, melting, freezing and condensing are changes of state. They change how molecules are arranged, not what the molecules are.

One small thing about the word “steam”. Look closely at a boiling kettle: right at the spout there is a clear gap, and the white cloud starts a little further out. The clear gap is the real water vapour, and it is invisible, like air. The white cloud is made of tiny droplets of liquid water that have already cooled and condensed. So the bubbles in boiling water are full of something you cannot see at all: water as a gas.

The proof is in any kitchen. When steam from a pan meets a cold lid, drops of liquid form on it. They are water: they look and behave exactly like water. If boiling had split the molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, the steam would be a mixture of two gases that would not turn back into liquid on a cold plate, and that would explode if it met a flame. No amount of ordinary boiling does what Nicholson and Carlisle’s battery did.

Boil water without a flame (an adult does this one)

Hot water can scald, so this one is for an adult to do while you watch. You need a plastic syringe from the chemist (20 mL is ideal, no needle) and a blob of Blu-Tack. The adult pours some water that has just boiled into a cup, sucks up about 10 mL into the syringe, pushes out any air with the nozzle pointing down into the cup, and seals the nozzle firmly with the Blu-Tack. Then, holding the syringe in a cloth, they pull the plunger back hard and hold it. Predict first: with no flame, and water that is cooling down, can it boil?

It can. The water fills with bubbles and froths, as if it were on the stove. (It works best while the water is still very hot, so do it straight away; as it cools you have to pull harder.) Now let the plunger go: the bubbles vanish, back into liquid. At most a tiny bead of air may be left, which was dissolved in the water. Think about what that rules out. Nothing could get in through the sealed nozzle, and the big bubbles disappeared when squeezed, so they were not air. They turned straight back into liquid when squeezed, so they are not hydrogen and oxygen. And no heat was added, so heat did not “break” anything. Pulling the plunger gave the molecules room, and the fastest ones escaped into it, just as in a kettle. Bubbles in boiling water are water.

Intermolecular forces

Attractions between separate molecules. They are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule.

So what does break when water boils? The pulls between molecules. Inside each molecule there are strong covalent bonds. Between neighbouring molecules there are much weaker attractions, called intermolecular forces. Boiling needs only enough energy to overcome the weak ones. This is what Joseph Black’s vanishing heat was doing: pulling molecules away from their neighbours.

The numbers show how different the two changes are. Boiling a mole of water (18 grams) at 100 °C takes about 41 kJ of energy. Breaking all the O–H bonds in that same mole, two per molecule, would take about 926 kJ, more than 20 times as much. (Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen costs less than that, about 286 kJ, because new H–H and O=O bonds form and pay some of it back.) Steam at 100 °C is nowhere near hot enough to do that.

What observation in a kitchen shows that the steam from a kettle is still water?

3.4Squeezing a gas

Oxford, England, 1662

A century before Charles’s balloon, in a house on the High Street in Oxford, Robert Boyle and his brilliant young assistant Robert Hooke were at work. Boyle was the fourteenth child of the Earl of Cork, one of the richest men in Ireland, and he could have lived an idle life. Instead he spent his money on glassware, furnaces and assistants, and argued, against most scholars of his day, that you learn how nature works by doing experiments and writing down exactly what happens, failures included. He and Hooke were busy with the most exciting machine in England: an air pump, which could suck the air out of a glass globe. Boyle was fascinated by what he called “the spring of the air”: squeeze air, and it pushes back, like a spring.

To measure the spring, Boyle used a glass tube bent into the shape of a J, with the short end sealed. He poured mercury into the long open end, trapping a pocket of air in the short end. The more mercury he poured in, the harder it pressed on the trapped air, and the smaller the air pocket became. When he doubled the pressure, the air’s volume halved. When he tripled it, the volume fell to a third. The rule is still called Boyle’s law.

Push the handle of a bicycle pump while blocking the end with your thumb, and you can feel Boyle’s spring of the air. Why does the air push back harder and harder?

Before going on, notice something easy to forget: the air in the pump has mass, like any other matter.

Weigh some air

Find a football or basketball that is soft and needs pumping. Weigh it on a kitchen scale. Predict first: after you pump it up hard, will the scale read more, less or the same? Pump it up and weigh it again. A football pumped up from nearly flat gains about 3 to 5 g; one that was only a little soft gains less, perhaps a gram or two, so you need a scale that shows single grams. All of the extra is air you have squeezed in. Squashing a gas does not make it lighter or heavier; adding more of it does.

The temperature has not changed much, so the molecules are moving at about the same speed as before. But now the same number of molecules is crowded into less space. Each bit of wall gets hit more often. Halve the volume, and the molecules hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles. Double the volume, and the pressure halves. As long as the temperature and the amount of gas stay the same, pressure × volume stays the same.

The story behind this

Air has weight: pumps, tubes and balloonsHow a pump that would not pump, a glass tube of mercury and a race of balloons revealed that air is a crowd of particles pressing on everything.
Ideal gas law

PV = nRT. It links the pressure, volume, amount and kelvin temperature of a gas. It works well for most gases unless they are very squashed or very cold.

Boyle’s squeezing rule and Charles’s warming rule can be combined into one statement, called the ideal gas law: P × V = n × R × T. Here P is pressure, V volume, n the number of moles, T the kelvin temperature, and R is a fixed number, 8.314. You do not need to memorise it now. What matters is what it says: pressure goes up with more particles and higher temperature, and down with more space.

1 mole of gas at 300 K in a 10-litre box:
P = nRT ÷ V = 1 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ 10 = 249 kPa (with V in litres, P comes out in kPa).
In 5 litres: 1 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ 5 = 499 kPa, twice as much.
In 20 litres: 125 kPa, half as much.

The ideal gas law treats molecules as dots that never attract each other. That works because gas molecules are usually far apart. Squeeze a gas hard enough, or cool it enough, and the molecules get close enough for their attractions to matter. Then the gas stops following the rule, and eventually it turns into a liquid. That is how the butane in a lighter is stored as a liquid: squeezed under pressure in its little tank.

Understand itGas pressure

What is it?

The push of a gas on each square metre of the walls around it, made by countless particles hitting the walls. Normal air pressure is about 101 kPa.

Why is it called this?

From Latin pressura, “pressing”, from premere, to press. Scientists began using the word for a push spread over an area in the 1650s, around the time of Boyle’s experiments.

What problem did it solve?

Boyle wanted to explain “the spring of the air”: why squeezed air pushes back harder and harder. Pressure, pictured as particles hitting the walls, explains it.

Why does it work?

Squeeze the same particles into half the space and each bit of wall is hit twice as often, so the pressure doubles. Heat them and they hit harder and more often, so the pressure rises again.

How does it help?

With the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, you can predict the pressure in a tyre, a pressure cooker or a gas cylinder from its volume, the amount of gas and the temperature.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Boyle’s J-shaped tube of 1662: double the pressure of the mercury on a trapped pocket of air, and its volume halves.

What it isn’t

Not something a single particle has. One molecule hitting a wall is a tiny tap; pressure is the steady total of billions upon billions of taps.

Where does it stop working?

Squeeze or cool a gas enough and its particles get close enough to attract each other. Then the simple rule fails and the gas turns into a liquid, like the butane in a lighter.

Your turn

Explain Gas pressure to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 3.4

Hold the temperature at 300 K. Compare 5 L, 10 L and 20 L, and save two results. Multiply pressure by volume for each one. What do you notice?

Check yourself

A gas at constant temperature is squeezed from 12 litres to 4 litres. What happens to its pressure?

3.5Where did the solute go?

Dandi, Gujarat, 6 April 1930

Early in the morning, after a march of 24 days and nearly 390 kilometres from his ashram at Sabarmati, Mahatma Gandhi walked down to the shore at Dandi and picked up a lump of natural salt left by evaporating seawater. It was a small act that shook an empire: the British government of India taxed salt and forbade Indians to make their own. Gandhi chose salt because everyone needed it, and because anyone could see where it came from. The sea is full of it, though you cannot see a single grain.

Stir a spoonful of salt into a glass of water, and in a minute or so the crystals vanish. The water looks exactly as clear as before. Has the salt gone?

Predict first: put a glass of water and a spoonful of salt (in its own little cup) on a kitchen scale together; then stir the salt in and put the empty cup back beside the glass. Will the reading be lighter, heavier or the same?

Solute, solvent, solution

The solute is the substance that dissolves (salt); the solvent is what it dissolves in (water); the mixture is a solution.

Taste it and you know the salt has not gone. It has dissolved: its ions have separated and spread out among the water molecules, too small and too evenly mixed to see. The salt is the solute; the water it dissolves in is the solvent; together they make a solution.

Try it, and the scale reads the same before and after: not one particle has left. The salt is still all there, just spread out too finely to see.

Careful

“The sugar melted in the tea.”

It dissolved; it did not melt. Melting needs heat and involves one substance: sugar melts on its own in a hot pan at about 186 °C and turns into a sticky liquid, which soon starts to brown as it breaks down. Dissolving needs a second substance, and happens even in cold water: the sugar molecules come away from their crystal and spread out among the water molecules. Nor is dissolving a chemical reaction. Every sugar molecule is still a sugar molecule; let the water evaporate slowly and you get your sugar back.

Dissolved particles are so small that they pass straight through filter paper, which easily stops grains of sand. But they are still there, and they can be counted. Dissolve 5.00 g of salt in water, pour it through filter paper, and nothing is caught. Heat the solution gently in a weighed dish until all the water has gone, and 5.00 g of white crystals are left behind: exactly the mass you put in. The salt pans of Gujarat’s coast and the Rann of Kutch do the same thing on a vast scale, with the sun as the heater.

Concentration

How much solute there is in each litre of a solution. Concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of solution.

How much solute is in each bit of a solution is called its concentration. Chemists usually measure it in moles of solute per litre of solution (mol/L). One mole of salt dissolved to make 2 litres of solution has a concentration of 0.50 mol/L. Add water to make 4 litres, and the same one mole is spread through twice the volume, so the concentration halves to 0.25 mol/L. This is called dilution. Every sip is weaker, but the total amount of salt has not changed. You do this every time you make nimbu pani or Rooh Afza: a little concentrated syrup from the bottle goes into a big glass of water. All the syrup is still there, but spread through more water, so each sip is less sweet.

concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of solution

One small detail: the volume that counts is the final volume of the whole solution, not the volume of water you poured in. When you dissolve things, volumes do not always add up exactly, which is why chemists make solutions in special flasks with a single line marking an exact final volume.

Understand itDissolving

What happens?

The particles of a solid such as salt or sugar come away from their crystal and spread out evenly among the water molecules, too small to see. The salt is the solute, the water is the solvent, and together they make a solution.

Why is it called this?

From Latin dissolvere, “to loosen apart”, from solvere, to loosen or untie. The crystal is loosened apart, not destroyed.

What problem did it solve?

Where does salt go when it disappears into water? The answer, that every bit of it is still there, explains how the sea can hold salt you cannot see, and how salt pans get it back.

Why does it work?

Water molecules are polar, so they pull on the charged ions of salt (and on sugar’s slightly charged molecules), surround them and tug them away from the crystal. Their constant motion then spreads them through the whole solution.

How does it help?

It lets you make solutions of any strength and work out their concentration, from a glass of nimbu pani to a hospital drip.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Weigh a glass of water and a spoonful of salt before and after stirring: the scale reads the same. Let the water evaporate and the salt comes back.

What it isn’t

Not melting, which needs heat and only one substance, and not a chemical reaction: every sugar molecule is still a sugar molecule.

Where does it stop working?

Water can hold only so much. Keep adding salt and eventually no more dissolves: about 36 g in 100 g of water at room temperature.

Your turn

Explain Dissolving to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 3.5

Keep the amount of dissolved solute fixed and increase the final volume. Explain what changes and what stays the same.

Check yourself

Bottle A holds 1 litre of salt solution at 0.50 mol/L. Bottle B holds 4 litres at 0.25 mol/L. Which tastes saltier? Which holds more salt altogether?

3.6Intermolecular forces against thermal motion

Here is a puzzle that bothered chemists for a long time. Methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃) and water (H₂O) are all small molecules with almost the same mass: 16, 17 and 18 grams per mole. Each molecule even has exactly 10 electrons. Yet methane boils at −161.5 °C, ammonia at −33.3 °C, and water at +100 °C. Why such huge differences?

Water was the oddest of all. In most families of similar compounds, boiling point rises steadily with molecular size. The compounds of hydrogen with the elements in oxygen’s column of the periodic table boil at about −60 °C (H₂S), −41 °C (H₂Se) and −2 °C (H₂Te). Follow that trend down to the smallest member, water, and you would expect it to boil far below zero. Instead it boils at +100 °C. If water followed the pattern, there would be no rivers, no oceans, no monsoon and no you.

Thermal motion

The constant random movement of particles. The higher the temperature, the more vigorous it is.

Every state of matter is a contest. On one side are the attractions between molecules, pulling them together. On the other side is thermal motion, the jiggling of heat, shaking them apart. A substance boils at the temperature where the jiggling becomes strong enough to tear molecules away from their neighbours. Strong attractions mean a high boiling point.

There are three main kinds of attraction between molecules, from weakest to strongest (for small molecules like these):

Dispersion forces

Weak attractions between all molecules, caused by electrons briefly bunching up on one side. Stronger for bigger molecules with more electrons.

Hydrogen bond

An attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to N, O or F and a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom on a neighbouring molecule. Still far weaker than a covalent bond.

  • Dispersion forces: the electrons in any molecule slosh around, making brief, flickering positive and negative patches that attract the patches on neighbouring molecules. Every molecule has these. Molecules with more electrons and more surface have stronger ones.
  • Dipole attractions: in polar molecules (Section 2.7) the permanent positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of the next.
  • Hydrogen bonds: an especially strong dipole attraction. A hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine is left very positive, and it is pulled towards a lone pair of electrons on an N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule.

The idea of the hydrogen bond grew up in the laboratory of G. N. Lewis at Berkeley, in California, where in 1920 two young chemists, Wendell Latimer and Worth Rodebush, suggested that a hydrogen atom could be shared, weakly, between two neighbouring molecules. Water’s strange boiling point, and ammonia’s and hydrogen fluoride’s, were among the strongest clues that they were right.

Methane is non-polar and has no hydrogen attached to N, O or F, so only weak dispersion forces hold its molecules together: it boils at a very low temperature. Ammonia can form hydrogen bonds, so it boils much higher. Water forms them most of all: each molecule can make up to four, with its two hydrogens and the two lone pairs on its oxygen. So water stays liquid right up to 100 °C. Life on Earth depends on that.

The story behind this

The strange case of waterWhy ice floats, why water boils so late, and the invisible links between water molecules that make life on Earth possible.

Hydrogen bonds sound strong, but remember the scale. Breaking an O–H bond inside a water molecule takes about 463 kJ per mole; a hydrogen bond between molecules is roughly 20 times weaker. That is why boiling separates whole molecules and never breaks them apart.

Predict first: almost every substance shrinks when it freezes, because the particles settle closer together. Water does the opposite: ice floats. Before you turn the model, decide what you think the molecules in ice must be doing to take up more room than the same molecules in liquid water.

Turn the ice until you are looking straight down the channels. Each oxygen is joined to four others, never more, and the four links point to the corners of a tetrahedron, like the legs of a camera tripod with one more leg pointing up. Four links that stiff cannot fold up tightly: they build a honeycomb with holes in it. In the liquid, the links break and re-form all the time (in real water, a hydrogen bond lasts only a few million-millionths of a second), so the honeycomb keeps collapsing and molecules slip into the holes. The same molecules end up closer together. That is why liquid water is denser than ice (about 1.00 g per mL against 0.917), and why ice floats with about nine-tenths of itself under the surface.

This one odd fact matters enormously. Lakes and ponds freeze from the top down, and the floating ice blanket keeps the water underneath liquid all winter, so fish and plants survive. If ice sank, cold lakes would fill up with ice from the bottom.

Careful

“When water boils, the heat breaks the bonds inside the water molecules.”

Boiling overcomes the attractions between molecules: mostly hydrogen bonds in water. The covalent O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact. Steam is made of whole H₂O molecules.

Investigation 3.6

Select water and raise the temperature from 250 K to 420 K. Then compare methane and carbon dioxide at 300 K. Which attraction is being overcome at each change, and which bonds never break?

Check yourself

Carbon dioxide (CO₂, 22 electrons per molecule) and hydrogen (H₂, 2 electrons) are both non-polar gases at room temperature. Solid CO₂ turns to gas at −78.5 °C, but hydrogen boils at −252.9 °C. Why the difference?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 3

The case of the quadrupled pressure

An engineer seals 1.0 mol of methane gas in a steel cylinder closed by a piston, holding 10 litres at 200 K. The pressure gauge reads 166 kPa. Later, the gauge reads 665 kPa: four times as much. A worried colleague says: “The amount of gas must have quadrupled. Either something leaked in, or the methane has broken up into more, smaller molecules.”

  1. The sealed cylinder, piston and all, is weighed before and after. Its mass has not changed at all.
  2. The log shows that the gas was warmed from 200 K to 400 K, and then the piston was pushed in until the gas filled only 5 litres.
  3. A sample of the gas, cooled and analysed afterwards, is still pure methane, CH₄. Methane boils at 112 K, so at 200 K and 400 K it is a gas throughout.

Explain the fourfold rise in pressure without any new molecules. Which clue rules out each of the colleague’s ideas?

Show the solution

Two changes each doubled the pressure. Doubling the kelvin temperature (200 K to 400 K) makes the molecules move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often: pressure × 2 (Charles’s and Amontons’s discovery). Halving the volume (10 L to 5 L) crowds the same molecules into half the space: pressure × 2 again (Boyle’s). Altogether, 166 × 2 × 2 ≈ 665 kPa, exactly what the gauge shows. Clue 1 rules out a leak: nothing was added. Clue 3 rules out breaking up: the molecules are unchanged. The number of molecules stayed at 1.0 mol the whole time.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

In this chapter, molecules moved apart, came together, spread through water and bounced off walls, but they never changed. Every H₂O stayed an H₂O. Real chemistry begins when that stops being true: when bonds break and atoms rearrange into substances that were not there before. For that part of the adventure we go to Paris in the 1770s, to a rich young man with a laboratory full of the finest balances in Europe, who decided to weigh everything.

Change and quantity

What happens when substances turn into new ones: where the atoms go, where the energy goes, how fast it happens, and how chemists count what they cannot see.

Chapter 4

What changes in a reaction?

The big questionA big log burns down to a small heap of ash, so it looks as if matter has vanished. An iron nail left in the rain turns to rust and gets heavier. Where did the wood go, and where did the extra mass on the nail come from?

  1. 4.1What counts as a chemical change?
  2. 4.2Reading a chemical formula
  3. 4.3Where did every atom go?
  4. 4.4What a balanced equation cannot tell us

Paris, 1774

In his private laboratory in Paris, Antoine Lavoisier and his wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, were weighing a glass vessel with a piece of tin sealed inside it. Lavoisier was thirty, trained as a lawyer, and earned his fortune as a partner in the company that collected the king’s taxes; chemistry was what he did before breakfast and after work, and on one whole day each week. He was rich, careful and slightly obsessed. He owned some of the most accurate balances in Europe, and he had come to believe that if you wanted to understand a change, you had to weigh everything, before and after, including the parts you could not see. Marie-Anne kept the notes, and later drew the engravings of his apparatus that chemists still reproduce today.

A hundred years earlier, Robert Boyle (the same Boyle who squeezed air in Chapter 3) had heated tin in a sealed flask, opened it, and found that the tin had become heavier. He thought particles of fire had soaked through the glass and stuck to the metal. Lavoisier repeated the experiment with one small change, and the change was everything. He did not open the vessel before weighing it.

So far, every change in this book has left the particles themselves alone. Ice melted, water boiled, salt dissolved, and the same molecules or ions were there at the end as at the start. Now something new happens. When wood burns, or iron rusts, or a cake bakes, the substances at the end are different substances from the ones you started with. This chapter is about what changes in a chemical reaction, and, just as important, what never does. It is also the chapter where chemistry, thanks largely to Lavoisier, became a science of measuring.

The story behind this

The man who weighed everythingHow a careful Parisian with a very good balance proved that nothing is lost when things burn, and gave oxygen its name.

4.1What counts as a chemical change?

Physical change

A change of state, shape or mixing in which no new substance is made. The particles keep their identity.

Put an ice cube in a glass and wait. It melts into water, which still freezes at 0 °C, still boils at 100 °C, and is still H₂O. Nothing new has been made: the molecules have only moved further apart and started sliding past each other. That is a physical change.

Chemical change (reaction)

A change in which atoms are rearranged into new substances, with new properties. The atoms themselves are kept.

Now leave an iron nail outside through a Mumbai monsoon. A flaky, reddish-brown crust grows on it. The crust is not iron: it is brittle where iron bends, it is not attracted to a magnet the way iron is, and it does not shine. It is rust, a compound of iron, oxygen and hydrogen (mostly a form of iron oxide with water built into it). New substances have appeared, so this is a chemical change, also called a chemical reaction.

At the particle level, the difference is sharp. In a physical change the same molecules end up in a different arrangement. In a chemical change the bonds inside the starting substances break and new bonds form, so the atoms regroup into different particles.

How would you know which kind of change you are looking at, in a real kitchen? Clues like fizzing, a colour change, a smell, or heat given out are hints, but not proof. Sugar dissolving in chai disappears, yet it is still sugar (the tea tastes sweet). A pan of water bubbling on the stove is not making a gas from nothing; it is boiling. The real test is whether the substances at the end have different properties from the ones at the start: a different melting point, a different colour, different behaviour with a magnet or with water. If they do, something new was made.

How do we know? Test the stuff, not the drama 18th century onwards

Chemists decide that a reaction has happened by testing what is there afterwards. Melted ice, refrozen, behaves exactly like the ice you started with: same melting point, same density, same everything. Rust does not: dissolve it in acid and you get a yellow-brown solution of iron ions; heat it strongly with carbon and you can get iron back, but only by another chemical reaction. When the properties are new, the substance is new.

Careful

“The picture changed from H₂ and O₂ to H₂O, so a reaction has happened.”

In the app, choosing a different diagram just shows you a different picture. It is not an experiment. In the real world, a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can sit in a sealed bottle for years without turning into water (you will see why in Chapter 5). A claim that a reaction happened needs evidence that a new substance was formed.

Investigation 4.1

Compare the H₂ and O₂ mixture with water in the app. Count the hydrogen and oxygen atoms in each picture. What is the same? What is different? Then write one real measurement you could make to show that water is a different substance from the mixture.

Understand itChemical reaction

What is it?

A change in which the atoms of the starting substances let go of their old partners and join up in new ways, making new substances with new properties. Rust is not iron; water is not hydrogen and oxygen.

Why is it called this?

From re- (“back, again”) and action: the substances act on each other. English chemists were using “reaction” in this sense by the 1830s.

What problem did it solve?

It separated two very different kinds of change. Melting, dissolving and mixing leave the substances what they were; burning, rusting and cooking make something new. Without that line, nobody could say what had really happened in a pot or a furnace.

Why does it work?

Atoms are held together by bonds. In a reaction some bonds break and new ones form, so the same atoms end up in different particles. The atoms themselves are never changed.

How does it help?

It tells you what to look for. To prove a reaction, test whether a new substance is there afterwards: a new melting point, a new colour that stays, a gas that turns limewater milky.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Testing what is there afterwards. Refrozen ice behaves exactly like the ice you started with; rust does not behave like iron, however you treat it.

What it isn’t

It is not the same as drama. Fizzing, a colour change or warmth are clues, not proof: sugar vanishes into chai and is still sugar, and boiling water bubbles without becoming anything new.

Where does it stop working?

The border can be blurry. When salt dissolves, its ions come apart and get wrapped in water, which is a bit of both. And changes that alter the atoms themselves, inside the nucleus, are nuclear reactions, not chemical ones.

Your turn

Explain Chemical reaction to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

When a fizzy tablet is dropped into water, bubbles appear and the water cools slightly. Is that enough to prove a chemical reaction has happened? What would you need to test?

4.2Reading a chemical formula

Stockholm, 1813

By the early 1800s chemists had a problem of handwriting. John Dalton in Manchester drew each element as a little circle with a pattern inside: a dot for hydrogen, a plain ring for oxygen, a ring with a cross for sulfur. That worked for twenty elements, and became impossible for fifty, and nobody could print it easily. In Stockholm, the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who spent years measuring the masses of elements with fierce precision, proposed something far simpler: use the first letter of each element’s Latin name, adding a second letter when two names begin the same way. H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, C for carbon, Cu for copper (cuprum), Na for sodium (natrium), Fe for iron (ferrum). Two hundred years later, every chemist on Earth writes his letters.

The story behind this

Letters for atoms: the language of chemistryHow chemists stopped drawing secret signs and circles and started writing H₂O, the shorthand every chemist in the world now shares.
Subscript

The small low number in a formula. It counts the atoms of the element just before it, in one particle (or one formula unit).

A chemical formula is a recipe for one particle. H₂O says: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, joined. The small number written low, the subscript, belongs to the atom just before it. No number means one. (Berzelius himself wrote the numbers high, like H²O; the low position became standard later.)

Coefficient

The big number written in front of a formula. It counts how many whole particles there are.

If you want to talk about more than one particle, you put a big number in front, called a coefficient. 3 H₂O means three separate water molecules. Count the atoms by multiplying: 3 × 2 = 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 × 1 = 3 oxygen atoms.

The two numbers do very different jobs. A coefficient changes how much you have. A subscript changes what you have. H₂O is water, which you drink. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a pale liquid that bleaches hair and is used to clean wounds in dilute form; concentrated, it is dangerous. One extra oxygen atom in the recipe, and it is a different substance.

For ionic compounds (Chapter 2), the subscripts give the ratio of ions, and that ratio comes straight from the charges. A crystal as a whole has no overall charge, so the positive and negative charges must cancel. A magnesium ion is Mg²⁺ and a chloride ion is Cl⁻, so you need two chlorides for every magnesium: MgCl₂. Aluminium oxide needs a bit more thought. Al³⁺ and O²⁻ balance when there are two aluminiums (+6) for every three oxides (−6): Al₂O₃.

Careful

“2 H₂O and H₄O₂ are the same thing. They both have four hydrogens and two oxygens.”

They have the same number of atoms, but they say different things about how the atoms are grouped. 2 H₂O is two separate water molecules. H₄O₂ would claim a single molecule with all six atoms joined together, which is not water (and is not a real substance you can buy). The grouping is the chemistry.

Investigation 4.2

Change the number of water molecules from 1 to 3. Watch how the atom counts change. Then try the ion combiner with Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻, and with Al³⁺ and O²⁻. Before you look, predict the formula from the charges.

Check yourself

How many hydrogen atoms are there in 4 NH₃? And what is the formula of the compound made from calcium ions, Ca²⁺, and chloride ions, Cl⁻?

Answer at the back of the book

4.3Where did every atom go?
