But two solutions of the same concentration can behave completely differently: one stings, one does not; one dissolves metal, one goes on your salad. To see why, the adventure moves to a brewery in Copenhagen, a purple cabbage, and the most important trade in chemistry: the passing of a single proton from one molecule to another.

Chapter 7

Acids, bases and passing protons

The big questionKitchen vinegar contains about 0.8 moles of acetic acid in every litre. Hydrochloric acid diluted to a tenth of that concentration is still far more acidic. How can the weaker-looking solution be the stronger acid?

  1. 7.1What makes a solution acidic?
  2. 7.2Strong or concentrated?
  3. 7.3Every step on the pH scale is tenfold
  4. 7.4Titration curves and buffers

Start with a trick. Chop a few leaves of red cabbage, soak them in warm water for ten minutes, and strain off the juice. It is a deep purple. Pour a little into three glasses. Into the first, squeeze some lemon: the purple turns a bright pink-red. Into the second, stir a pinch of baking soda: it turns blue, then green. The third you leave alone, and it stays purple. Nothing was heated, nothing was mixed except kitchen food, and yet the colours changed as if by magic.

If you have ever seen a yellow haldi stain on a white kurta turn red-brown when it was scrubbed with soap, you have already met a detector like this. The cabbage is not magic; it is a detector. Its purple colour comes from molecules called anthocyanins, and their colour depends on how many hydrogen nuclei they are carrying. Lemon juice pushes extra ones onto them; baking soda pulls them off. By the end of this chapter you will know exactly what is being pushed and pulled, and you will be able to read the cabbage like an instrument.

Oxford, 1664

People have used colour detectors like this for a long time. In 1664 the Irish-born scientist Robert Boyle, the fourteenth child of one of the richest men in Ireland, who spent his fortune on laboratories and insisted that every idea be tested by experiment, wrote a book about colours in which he noticed that syrup of violets turns red with sour substances and green with substances such as potash. He used it to sort substances into groups. Later chemists settled on litmus, a purple dye made from lichens, which turns red in acid and blue in its opposite. Your cabbage does the same job with a fuller rainbow.

Acid

A substance that can pass a proton (a hydrogen nucleus, H⁺) to another particle. Acids taste sour and turn litmus red. (Never taste anything in a laboratory.)

Lemon juice, vinegar, tamarind and the acid in your stomach all taste sour, turn blue litmus red, fizz with baking soda and slowly eat into some metals. Chemists call substances like these acids. Their opposites, which feel slippery and taste bitter, like soap or baking soda, are bases. Your own blood sits on a knife edge between the two: its acidity has to stay within a very narrow range (a pH of 7.35 to 7.45, as you will learn to say in Section 7.3), even when your muscles pour acid into it during a sprint. This chapter explains what acids and bases actually are, why some are far fiercer than others, and how a solution can resist being made more acidic.

Base

A substance that can accept a proton from an acid.

Do not let “acid” make you think “danger” and “base” make you think “safe”. The fiercest chemicals in most homes are bases: drain cleaner, caustic soda, and the chuna that goes into paan can all burn skin and eyes. Strong bases are every bit as dangerous as strong acids.

The story behind this

Sour and slippery: what is an acid?For 250 years chemists argued about what makes a thing sour. The answer turned out to be one tiny particle: a bare proton.

7.1What makes a solution acidic?

For a long time nobody knew what all acids had in common. Lavoisier, whom you met weighing everything in Chapter 4, guessed it was oxygen. He even named the gas for it: oxygène comes from Greek words meaning “acid-maker”. It was a reasonable guess, and it was wrong. Around 1810 Humphry Davy, the discoverer of potassium from Chapter 1, showed that the acid in hydrochloric acid, then called muriatic acid, contains hydrogen and chlorine and no oxygen at all. The common ingredient was hydrogen. But plenty of substances contain hydrogen and are not acids (sugar is full of it), so what was special?

Here is the clue. Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is a gas. Dry, it is made of separate HCl molecules, and liquid HCl hardly conducts electricity at all. But bubble the gas into water and something dramatic happens: the solution, now called hydrochloric acid, conducts electricity very well. Charged particles have appeared that were not there before.

Hydronium ion (H₃O⁺)

A water molecule that has accepted an extra proton. More hydronium ions means a more acidic solution.

What happened is a transfer. Each HCl molecule hands its hydrogen nucleus, a bare proton, over to a water molecule. The electrons that used to hold the H to the Cl stay behind on the chlorine. So the chlorine becomes a chloride ion, Cl⁻, and the water molecule, now with an extra proton, becomes H₃O⁺, a hydronium ion.

HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻

Copenhagen and Cambridge, 1923

In 1923, two chemists who were working separately, Johannes Brønsted in Copenhagen and Thomas Lowry in Cambridge, published the same idea within months of each other. An acid is a proton donor, and a base is a proton acceptor. That one sentence is the whole definition. In the reaction above, HCl is the acid and water is the base. The extra hydronium ions are what make a solution acidic: what turns litmus red, reacts with baking soda, and stings a cut. And it is what your cabbage detects: an acid passes protons to the anthocyanin molecules, a base takes them away, and each form of the molecule has a different colour.

The idea also explained something older theories could not: why ammonia, NH₃, which contains no OH, still behaves as a base. In water it takes a proton from a water molecule, making NH₄⁺ and leaving OH⁻ behind. Brønsted and Lowry’s idea is still the one chemists use most every day.

Notice that “proton” here does not mean a proton torn out of a nucleus. A hydrogen atom is just one proton and one electron. Take away the electron and a bare proton is all that is left. The chlorine nucleus, with its 17 protons, does not change at all; nor does any other nucleus. Chapter 1’s rule still holds.

Careful

“A bottle of hydrochloric acid is full of HCl molecules floating in water.”

In ordinary dilute hydrochloric acid, almost none are left. Every HCl molecule has handed its proton to water, so the bottle is full of H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ ions instead. Many people draw whole HCl molecules in the water; it is one of the commonest mistakes in chemistry, and Section 7.2 shows why it matters.

Careful

“An acid loses a proton from inside one of its atoms’ nuclei.”

The proton that moves is the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, which is just a single proton. No nucleus is broken open, and no atom changes element. That would take a nuclear reaction, not an acid in a beaker.

Investigation 7.1

Compare pure water, 0.10 mol/L hydrochloric acid and 0.10 mol/L sodium hydroxide. Which particle becomes more common in the acid? Which becomes more common in the base?

Understand itAcids and bases

What is it?

An acid is a substance that hands protons (bare hydrogen nuclei) to other particles, usually water. A base is a substance that takes them. Lemon juice and vinegar are acids; baking soda, soap and chuna are bases.

Why is it called this?

Acid comes from Latin acidus, “sour”, because the ones people met first tasted sour (never test one by tasting). Base was used by the French chemist Rouelle in 1754 for the substance that gave a salt its solid “base”. Alkali, the old word for a strong base, comes from the Arabic al-qalī, the ashes of saltwort, a plant of salty soils.

What problem did it solve?

For centuries acids were known only by their effects: sour taste, colour changes, metals fizzing. Nobody knew what they had in common; Lavoisier guessed oxygen and was wrong. The proton idea of Brønsted and Lowry in 1923 finally explained them all, and bases with them.

Why does it work?

A hydrogen atom stripped of its electron is a single proton, small and easily passed on. Acids let go of such protons; bases have a spare pair of electrons that one can bond to. Every acid–base reaction is a proton changing hands.

How does it help?

It explains why acids and bases cancel each other out, why your stomach, your blood and the sea care so much about acidity, and how to make, test and handle them safely.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Dry hydrogen chloride hardly conducts electricity, but dissolved in water it conducts well: the protons have moved to the water, making ions.

What it isn’t

It is not “acids are dangerous and bases are mild”. Strong bases such as drain cleaner and caustic soda are just as dangerous as strong acids.

Where does it stop working?

Proton-passing covers almost everything in this book, but chemists also use a wider idea, built on electron pairs, for reactions with no protons at all.

Your turn

Explain Acids and bases to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

When ammonia dissolves in water, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which molecule is the acid (proton donor), and which is the base (proton acceptor)?

Answer at the back of the book

7.2Strong or concentrated?

Uppsala, Sweden, 1884

Five years before his energy barrier of Chapter 5, the young Svante Arrhenius spent months passing electric currents through solutions and measuring how well they conducted. He found that, at the same concentration, hydrochloric acid conducted electricity far better than acetic acid, the acid in vinegar. His explanation was bold: in water, some substances split into charged ions, and some split much more than others. This was the thesis his examiners nearly failed, and the idea that won him the Nobel Prize in 1903.

Here is the answer to this chapter’s big question. Hydrochloric acid and acetic acid both give protons to water, but they do it to very different extents.

Strong acid

An acid that gives up its protons to water almost completely, such as hydrochloric acid.

Weak acid

An acid that gives up its protons to water only partly, so most of its molecules stay whole, such as acetic acid.

In hydrochloric acid, essentially every HCl molecule gives up its proton. Chemists call it a strong acid. Acetic acid, CH₃COOH, is a weak acid: in vinegar, only a few molecules in every thousand have handed over a proton at any moment. The rest stay whole. The transfer goes both ways, molecules giving and taking protons back all the time, and it settles into a balance (the dynamic equilibrium of Chapter 5) in which most acetic acid molecules are intact.

So “strong” and “concentrated” are answers to two different questions. Concentration asks how much acid was dissolved in each litre (Section 6.5). Strength asks how readily the acid’s molecules give up their protons, and that is fixed for each acid: at the same concentration, a strong acid hands over all of them and a weak acid only a small fraction. Think of a classroom: concentration is how many children are in the room; strength is how eager each of them is to put a hand up.

Here is another way to hold it, which will pay off in the case at the end of the chapter. A weak acid keeps most of its protons in the bank, locked up in whole molecules. The hydronium ions are the cash in hand. A pH meter (Section 7.3) counts only the cash. A titration (Section 7.4) counts the whole fortune, bank and all.

Put numbers on it, using measured values. Hydrochloric acid at 0.010 mol/L gives 0.010 mol/L of hydronium ions, because every molecule takes part. Acetic acid at 1.00 mol/L, a hundred times more concentrated, gives only about 0.0042 mol/L of hydronium ions, because only about 0.42% of its molecules take part. The dilute strong acid has more than twice as many hydronium ions per litre as the concentrated weak one. Arrhenius’s meter was really counting those ions; today a pH meter (Section 7.3) measures the hydronium concentration directly, and for 1.00 mol/L acetic acid it reads that same 0.0042 mol/L.

Strong acids are among the most useful chemicals in the world, for making fertilisers, dyes, medicines and metals, and for a long time India had to import them.

Calcutta, 1901

Prafulla Chandra Ray, a chemistry professor at Presidency College in Calcutta (now Kolkata), wanted that to change. He had studied in Edinburgh, came home determined that Indian science should serve India, and lived so simply that he is said to have given much of his salary away. In 1892, with a few hundred rupees, he started a small chemical works, and in 1901 it became the company Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, which grew into one of the first big Indian companies to make medicines and laboratory chemicals, acids among them, in India itself. He is often called the father of Indian chemistry.

The story behind this

The chemist who wanted India to make its ownA teacher in Calcutta discovered a new compound, wrote the history of chemistry in ancient India, started a company in his own rooms, and trained a generation of Indian scientists.

Back to the kitchen. That is why vinegar is safe on your salad. Kitchen vinegar is roughly 0.8 mol/L acetic acid, but it has only about 0.004 mol/L of hydronium ions. Hydrochloric acid at a tenth of vinegar’s concentration would have about 0.08 mol/L, twenty times more, and would be dangerous to drink.

Careful

“If you add enough water to a strong acid it becomes a weak acid.”

Adding water makes an acid more dilute, never weaker. Every HCl molecule still gives up its proton; there are just fewer of them per litre. Strength belongs to the acid itself, so concentrated acetic acid is still a weak acid, and diluted acetic acid is still a weak acid too. (Diluting a weak acid actually lets a slightly bigger fraction of its molecules give up their protons, because the balance shifts, but the solution still ends up less acidic than before.)

Investigation 7.2

Compare 0.010 mol/L hydrochloric acid with 1.00 mol/L acetic acid. Save both, and compare the fraction of molecules that gave up a proton and the concentration of hydronium ions in each.

Check yourself

Sketch or describe two beakers of particles: (A) a concentrated weak acid and (B) a dilute strong acid. How does your drawing show concentration, and how does it show strength?

Answer at the back of the book

7.3Every step on the pH scale is tenfold

Copenhagen, 1909

pH

A number that says how acidic a solution is, by counting the powers of ten in its hydronium concentration. pH 7 is neutral; lower is more acidic; higher is more basic.

At the Carlsberg Laboratory, run by the famous beer company, the Danish chemist Søren Sørensen was studying how proteins and enzymes behave during brewing. He found that they were exquisitely sensitive to acidity, and he needed a simple way to write it down. The trouble was the numbers. Strong acid might have 1 mole of hydronium per litre; pure water has one ten-millionth of a mole per litre, 0.000 000 1 mol/L; a strong base might have a ten-millionth of that, 10⁻¹⁴ mol/L. Writing those out is clumsy, so in 1909 Sørensen invented a shortcut: the pH scale. In the same year, Fritz Haber and Zygmunt Klemensiewicz described the glass electrode, the heart of the pH meters still used today.

The idea is to count powers of ten. Write the hydronium concentration as a power of ten, then take the number on top and drop the minus sign:

0.1 mol/L = 10⁻¹ mol/L → pH 1

0.01 mol/L = 10⁻² mol/L → pH 2

0.001 mol/L = 10⁻³ mol/L → pH 3

0.000 000 1 mol/L = 10⁻⁷ mol/L → pH 7 (pure water at 25 °C)

Three things follow, and all three surprise people.

Lower pH means more acidic. Because of that dropped minus sign, pH 1 has more hydronium than pH 3.

Each step of 1 is a factor of ten. pH 2 has ten times more hydronium than pH 3, and pH 1 has a hundred times more than pH 3. The pH scale is not like a ruler where each centimetre is the same size; it is like the powers-of-ten scale in Chapter 0.

In-between numbers are allowed. Acetic acid at 1.00 mol/L has 0.0042 mol/L of hydronium, which lies between 10⁻³ and 10⁻², so its pH lies between 3 and 2. A calculator gives 2.37. (Mathematicians call this power-counting a logarithm; you do not need the word yet.)

The story behind this

Sørensen’s brewery and the pH scaleA Danish chemist trying to make better beer needed a simple way to say how acidic something is, and invented a scale every school now uses.

Pure water is neutral, pH 7, because water molecules pass protons to each other very slightly: a tiny number become H₃O⁺ and an equal number become OH⁻. Acids push the hydronium concentration up and the pH below 7. Bases mop up hydronium, so the pH rises above 7. Your red cabbage juice is a rough pH meter. It is red around pH 2, pink-purple around pH 4, purple near neutral, blue around pH 8, green by pH 10 and greenish-yellow by pH 12. Notice what it reads: pH, not strength. Lemon juice and vinegar are both weak acids, yet both turn it red, because both have plenty of hydronium for the cabbage to see.

A red cabbage rainbow

Ask an adult to help you make red cabbage juice: chop a quarter of a red cabbage, cover it with warm tap water, leave it for 10 minutes, then strain the purple liquid into a jug. Set out five clear glasses with a little juice in each. Add, one to each glass: a squeeze of lemon juice, a spoonful of white vinegar, nothing (plain juice), a pinch of baking soda, and a bigger spoonful of baking soda. (More baking soda deepens the blue-green but cannot push the pH much past 8, so do not expect yellow. If an adult has washing soda, the laundry powder, they can add a pinch to a sixth glass for a clear green; it stings eyes and skin, so it is theirs to handle.) Before each one goes in, say out loud what colour you expect. Line them up from most acidic to most basic and you have a pH rainbow. Can you guess where milk, sugar water or salt water will land before you test them?

Careful

“pH 2 is twice as acidic as pH 4.”

pH 2 has 10⁻² mol/L of hydronium and pH 4 has 10⁻⁴ mol/L. That is a difference of two powers of ten: 10 × 10 = 100 times more hydronium, not twice as much.

Investigation 7.3

Start with 0.10 mol/L hydrochloric acid and dilute it tenfold, then tenfold again, then again. Before each step, predict the new pH. What happens to the hydronium concentration each time?

Understand itpH

What is it?

A single number that says how acidic or basic a solution is: 7 is neutral, lower is more acidic, higher is more basic. Each step of one means ten times more or less hydronium, the particle that makes a solution acidic.

Why is it called this?

Søren Sørensen invented it in 1909. The H stands for hydrogen. What the p stood for, he never explained, and people still argue: perhaps “power” (Potenz in German, puissance in French), perhaps “potential”, perhaps nothing at all.

What problem did it solve?

Acidity was written as clumsy numbers like 0.000 000 1 moles per litre. Sørensen, studying brewing, needed a quick, easy way to record it. Counting the powers of ten gave one.

Why does it work?

It counts the powers of ten in the hydronium concentration: 10⁻³ mol/L becomes pH 3. A huge range of numbers shrinks to a short, friendly scale.

How does it help?

Gardeners, doctors, swimming-pool cleaners and chemists all use it to keep things in the right range: soil, blood, pool water, a reaction in a flask.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

A pH meter, built on the glass electrode of 1909, measures it directly; indicators like red cabbage juice change colour along the scale.

What it isn’t

It is not an ordinary ruler. pH 2 is not twice as acidic as pH 4; it has a hundred times more hydronium.

Where does it stop working?

The scale is not fenced in at 0 and 14: very concentrated acids can go below 0. And “7 is neutral” is exact only at 25 °C; neutral pure water is a little below 7 when it is warmer.

Your turn

Explain pH to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

You have 1.0 L of a strong acid at pH 2. How much water must you add to raise its pH to 4?

Answer at the back of the book

7.4Titration curves and buffers

Titration

Adding a solution of known concentration, a little at a time, to measure exactly how much of something is in another solution.

How do you find out how much acid is in an unlabelled bottle? French chemists worked out the answer in the decades around 1800, when bleach and soda makers needed to know exactly how strong their solutions were. Around 1791 François Descroizilles built an early graduated tube for adding a liquid little by little, and in 1824 Joseph Gay-Lussac, whom you met in Chapter 6 measuring gas volumes, refined it and gave it its name: the burette. You let the unknown acid react with a base whose concentration you already know, adding the base drop by drop from the burette and measuring the pH as you go. This is a titration. The base used is usually sodium hydroxide, NaOH, which gives OH⁻ ions; each OH⁻ grabs one proton from the acid to make a water molecule.

Equivalence point

The moment in a titration when just enough base has been added to react with all of the acid.

Figure 7.4 shows two titrations, calculated from measured constants. Each flask holds 25 mL of acid at 0.10 mol/L, which is 2.5 thousandths of a mole (2.5 mmol). The burette holds 0.10 mol/L sodium hydroxide, so it takes exactly 25 mL of base to match the acid proton for proton. That point is called the equivalence point.

Predict first: before you look at Figure 7.4, take a pencil and sketch what you think the pH does as the base goes in, from 0 mL to 40 mL. A straight line climbing steadily? Something else? Most people draw a straight line.

Buffer

A mixture of a weak acid and the particle it forms when it gives up a proton (here, acetic acid and acetate). It resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

It is not a straight line. Both curves stay low at first and then shoot up almost vertically near 25 mL. The flat start does not mean nothing is happening: every drop of base is reacting, but there is so much acid left that each drop’s OH⁻ is grabbed at once and the hydronium hardly changes. Only the last few drops find no acid left to react with, so the OH⁻ piles up. But look at the middle of the weak acid’s curve. For a long stretch, adding base barely changes the pH. That stretch is a buffer.

Here is why. Halfway through, half the acetic acid has been turned into acetate ions, CH₃COO⁻, so the flask contains plenty of both. Any OH⁻ you add is grabbed by a whole acetic acid molecule (CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O) before it can pile up. Any extra acid you add is grabbed by an acetate ion. The pH depends on the ratio of acetic acid to acetate, and adding a little of either only nudges that ratio. At exactly halfway, when the two amounts are equal, the pH is 4.74, a number that is fixed by how strong acetic acid is.

The same base, two different destinations. Start with 50 mL of an acetate buffer containing 2.5 mmol of acetic acid and 2.5 mmol of acetate (pH 4.74). Add 10 mL of 0.10 mol/L sodium hydroxide, which is 1.0 mmol of OH⁻.

In the buffer: acetic acid falls to 1.5 mmol and acetate rises to 3.5 mmol. The pH rises from 4.74 to about 5.11, a change of about 0.37.

In 50 mL of pure water instead: the 1.0 mmol of OH⁻ has nothing to react with. The pH jumps from 7.0 to about 12.2.

Boston, 1908

The American physician and chemist Lawrence Henderson wanted to know how blood keeps its acidity so steady. In 1908 he showed that it is a buffer of exactly this kind, built from carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions (the same hydrogencarbonate that is in baking soda), and he wrote down the rule linking the pH to the ratio of the two. It is why a hard sprint, which pours acid into your blood, changes its pH by so little.

A buffer race

You can feel Henderson’s buffer at work with the very same pair of particles. Pour a little red cabbage juice into two glasses and top each up with half a cup of water. Into glass B only, stir a small pinch of baking soda (it turns blue). Now add lemon juice to both glasses, one drop at a time, counting the drops.

Predict first: which glass will turn pink first, and by how much?

Glass A turns pink within a handful of drops. Glass B drifts from blue to purple and then holds its colour stubbornly for dozens more drops, because each drop of acid is being mopped up by hydrogencarbonate. Only when that runs out does it give way and turn pink. A buffer, its capacity, and the end of its capacity, all in one glass.

The story behind this

How your blood stays at 7.4Your muscles pour acid into your blood every time you run, yet its pH hardly moves. A Harvard doctor worked out why.

Careful

“A buffer stops the pH from changing at all.”

A buffer slows the change; it does not stop it. Every bit of base you add uses up some of the weak acid. Once the weak acid runs out, the pH climbs as fast as in plain water. That is exactly what happens near the equivalence point in Figure 7.4. How much a buffer can absorb before it gives way is called its capacity.

A kitchen titration

Put a quarter of a cup of red cabbage juice in a glass and stir in half a teaspoon of baking soda: it turns blue-green. Now add white vinegar one teaspoon at a time, stirring and counting. (It will fizz: that is carbon dioxide.) Write down the colour after each spoonful. For the first few spoonfuls the colour hardly moves, but look at the fizz: every spoonful is reacting, using up some of the soda. Then, when the soda is nearly gone, the colour swings through purple to pink. Repeat with a whole teaspoon of baking soda. Does it take about twice as many spoonfuls? You have just done a titration, with a spoon for a burette and a cabbage for a pH meter.

Investigation 7.4

Step the sodium hydroxide from 0 mL to 12 mL, 24 mL, 26 mL and 40 mL, first for hydrochloric acid and then for acetic acid. Where is the pH most stubborn, and where does one drop change everything?

Understand itBuffer

What is it?

A mixture of a weak acid and the particle it forms when it gives up a proton. It soaks up small amounts of added acid or base, so the pH hardly changes.

Why is it called this?

After the cushioning pads, like the buffers at the end of a railway line, that soften a knock. The French chemists Fernbach and Hubert described the effect as a tampon (a cushion or pad) in 1900; it became Puffer in German and buffer in English.

What problem did it solve?

Living things only work in a narrow range of acidity. Henderson, in 1908, wanted to know how blood stays so steady when the body keeps making acid. Buffers were the answer.

Why does it work?

The weak acid mops up any base that arrives, and its partner particle mops up any acid. Both stay in the solution, ready for the next drop.

How does it help?

It keeps your blood, the oceans and many medicines and foods at a safe, steady pH, and lets chemists hold a reaction at the acidity they need.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Add the same drops of acid to plain cabbage juice and to cabbage juice with a pinch of baking soda: the plain one changes colour almost at once, the buffered one holds out.

What it isn’t

It does not stop the pH from changing at all. It only slows the change.

Where does it stop working?

Every buffer has a limit. Once its weak acid or its partner particle is used up, the pH changes as fast as in plain water. Each buffer also works best near its own particular pH.

Your turn

Explain Buffer to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Check yourself

Why does a mixture of acetic acid and acetate resist a change in pH when a small amount of sodium hydroxide is added?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 7

The two bottles at pH 3

Two unlabelled flasks both read exactly pH 3.00 on a pH meter. One contains hydrochloric acid and the other acetic acid. You take 25 mL from each and titrate it with 0.10 mol/L sodium hydroxide.

  1. Flask A reaches its equivalence point after only 0.25 mL of sodium hydroxide, a few drops.
  2. Flask B needs 14.1 mL of sodium hydroxide to reach its equivalence point.
  3. After 5.0 mL of sodium hydroxide, Flask A reads about pH 12.2 and Flask B about pH 4.5.

Which flask holds which acid? Both have the same pH, so how can one contain about 57 times more acid than the other?

Show the solution

Flask A is hydrochloric acid and Flask B is acetic acid.

Equal pH means equal concentrations of hydronium ions, 10⁻³ = 0.0010 mol/L. It does not mean equal amounts of acid. Hydrochloric acid gives up every proton, so it only needs 0.0010 mol/L of acid to reach pH 3: 25 mL holds 0.025 mmol, matched by 0.25 mL of the base (clue 1). Acetic acid gives up only a small fraction of its protons, so to reach the same hydronium concentration it must be about 0.057 mol/L: 25 mL holds about 1.41 mmol, which needs 14.1 mL of base (clue 2). That is about 57 times more acid, almost all of it hiding as whole molecules that the pH meter cannot see.

Clue 3 shows the difference in action. After 5.0 mL, Flask A’s tiny amount of acid is long gone and the extra OH⁻ sends the pH soaring. In Flask B the base has turned some acetic acid into acetate, making a buffer, so the pH has only crept up to about 4.5.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

In this chapter the thing being passed from particle to particle was a proton. In the next, it is an electron. Back in Chapter 6 you saw Nicholson and Carlisle split water with Volta’s brand-new battery. Next you find out how that battery worked: when zinc metal meets copper ions, electrons jump from one to the other, and if you can make them travel through a wire on the way, you have built a battery.

8

Chapter 8

Electron transfer and electrochemistry

The big questionPut a strip of zinc into blue copper sulfate solution and it gets coated with copper while the liquid warms up. Split the very same chemicals between two beakers joined by a wire, and they can light a bulb. How does a chemical reaction push electricity through a wire?

  1. 8.1When metals and ions trade electrons
  2. 8.2Balancing electrons as well as atoms
  3. 8.3Why doesn’t copper dissolve in zinc sulfate?
  4. 8.4Galvanic cells and recharging

Bologna, Italy, the 1780s

Luigi Galvani was a doctor who taught anatomy at the University of Bologna, a careful, devout man more at home with nerves and muscles than with machines. In his laboratory, often working alongside his wife Lucia, he was dissecting frogs. One day, so the story goes, a frog’s leg twitched when a metal scalpel touched a nerve while an electrical machine was sparking nearby. Galvani spent years on it, and he found that a leg would twitch even with no machine at all, if it was touched by two different metals at once. He published in 1791 and concluded that living things make their own “animal electricity”.

A few hundred kilometres away in Pavia, the physicist Alessandro Volta read Galvani’s work and disagreed. Volta was a restless experimenter who had already discovered methane by poking at the mud of marshes and catching the bubbles, and he trusted instruments more than theories. The electricity, he thought, did not come from the frog. It came from the two metals; the wet frog leg was only a damp path between them. To prove it he left out the frog altogether. He piled up discs of zinc and copper, with cardboard soaked in salt water between each pair, and in 1800 he announced the result: a steady flow of electricity from a stack of metal and wet card. It was the first battery, and in 1801 he was demonstrating it to Napoleon in Paris.

Neither man knew what was really moving. That took another century, and the discovery of the electron. In Chapter 7, acids and bases passed protons from one particle to another. This chapter is about the second great family of reactions, in which the thing passed along is an electron. These reactions rust iron, tarnish silver, burn fuel and release the energy from your food. And because electrons moving through a wire are an electric current, they are how every battery works, from Volta’s pile to the one in a phone.

The story behind this

Frogs’ legs and the first batteryAn argument between two Italian professors about twitching frogs’ legs produced the first battery, and with it the age of electricity.

8.1When metals and ions trade electrons

Here is a piece of chemistry that looks like a magic trick. Take a strip of dull grey zinc and lower it into a beaker of clear blue copper(II) sulfate solution. Within minutes the grey strip starts to blush: a crumbly reddish-brown coat of copper grows over it, as if the metal were turning into a different one before your eyes. The blue colour of the liquid slowly fades. The beaker gets slightly warm. Test the liquid afterwards and you find zinc dissolved in it that was not there before.

Predict first. Where did that copper come from? (a) Some of the zinc turned into copper. (b) It came out of the air. (c) It was in the blue liquid all along. Choose before you read on, and notice the clue you have been given: the blue colour faded.

Nothing magic has happened, and nothing has turned into anything else. The answer is (c). The particle story is a swap. The blue colour comes from copper ions, Cu²⁺, in the water. Each Cu²⁺ ion has 29 protons and only 27 electrons. When one bumps into the surface of the zinc, a zinc atom (30 protons, 30 electrons) hands over two electrons. The zinc atom becomes a Zn²⁺ ion (30 protons, 28 electrons) and drifts off into the water. The copper ion becomes a neutral copper atom (29 protons, 29 electrons) and stays stuck to the strip as metal.

Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s)

The letters in brackets say what state each thing is in: (s) for solid, (aq) for dissolved in water, from aqua.

The words chemists use for this have a history. In Lavoisier’s day, to “oxidise” something meant to combine it with oxygen, as iron does when it rusts. Once the electron was discovered in 1897, chemists saw that what really matters in rusting, burning and this zinc-and-copper swap is the same thing: electrons leaving one substance for another. So the words were widened. Losing electrons is now called oxidation. Gaining electrons is called reduction. They always happen together, because an electron that leaves one particle must go to another; there are no spare electrons floating loose in the water. A reaction like this is a redox reaction: reduction plus oxidation. A memory trick many chemists use is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

Oxidation

Losing electrons. Zinc is oxidised when Zn becomes Zn²⁺.

Reduction

Gaining electrons. Copper ions are reduced when Cu²⁺ becomes Cu.

Redox reaction

A reaction in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Oxidation and reduction always happen together.

If you meet oxidation described as gaining oxygen, that is the same event seen from outside: when magnesium burns, 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO, each magnesium atom gains oxygen by handing it two electrons; the electron version is simply wider, because it also covers swaps like zinc and copper, where no oxygen takes part at all.

The story behind this

Rust, fire and moving electronsRusting nails, burning wood and browning apples turn out to be the same kind of change: electrons moving from one substance to another.
Spectator ions

Ions that are present in a reacting mixture but come out unchanged, like the sulfate ions in copper sulfate solution.

Notice what stays the same. Every nucleus is untouched: zinc stays zinc and copper stays copper, because their proton numbers never change. The alchemists who dreamed of turning cheap metals into precious ones would have been delighted by the copper coat on the zinc, and disappointed to learn that the copper was in the beaker all along. The beaker also contains sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻, but they come out exactly as they went in. Ions that are present but take no part are called spectator ions, and chemists usually leave them out of the equation.

Careful

“The zinc gives the copper two protons, and that turns it into copper.”

Chemical reactions never move protons out of a nucleus. Copper ions are already copper (29 protons); they only lack two electrons. What moves is electrons, from the outside of the zinc atoms to the copper ions. Count the protons before and after and you will find 30 and 29 both times.

Understand itRedox

What is it?

A reaction in which electrons pass from one substance to another. The one that loses electrons is oxidised; the one that gains them is reduced. The two always happen together.

Why is it called this?

Reduction plus oxidation. “Oxidation” comes from oxygen, a name Lavoisier made up in 1777 from Greek words meaning “acid-maker” (he wrongly thought every acid contained it). “Reduction” is from the Latin for “leading back”: heating an ore led the metal back out of it, and the ore got lighter as oxygen left as a gas. Both names are older than the electron, so they mislead a little: oxidation needs no oxygen at all, as zinc and copper show.

What problem did it solve?

Rusting, burning, tarnishing, one metal coating another, and batteries all looked like separate puzzles. Once the electron was found in 1897, chemists saw they are one event: electrons moving from one substance to another.

Why does it work?

When an exchange of electrons gives out energy overall, as zinc meeting copper ions does, the electrons move in that direction and not the other. Every electron one particle loses, another must gain, because there are no spare electrons floating loose in the water.

How does it help?

You can predict which metal will coat which (the reactivity series), balance equations by counting electrons as well as atoms, and understand batteries, rust and how metals are got out of their ores.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Watch and weigh: the zinc wastes away, copper appears and the blue of the copper ions fades. Put the two halves in separate beakers joined by a wire and a salt bridge, and a meter shows the electrons flowing through it, exactly as the half-equations say.

What it isn’t

Not one element turning into another. Every nucleus is untouched: the copper was in the liquid all along as ions, and only electrons moved.

Where does it stop working?

In many reactions electrons are shared rather than handed over completely, as in the covalent bonds of Chapter 2. Chemists still keep redox accounts there, using “oxidation numbers”, but then it is careful bookkeeping, not a picture of whole electrons jumping across.

Your turn

Explain Redox to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Copper out of a blue liquid

You need plenty of old, dull copper, a good handful: tarnished scraps from an old copper vessel, or old wire gone brown (Indian coins are no longer copper). Bright new wire works poorly, because it is the dull coating that dissolves first. Put the copper in a small glass jar with as little white vinegar as will cover it, stir in a teaspoon of salt, and leave it for a day or two with the lid off, swirling now and then. Often you cannot see any colour, but copper ions have gone into the liquid. Now scrub an iron nail clean and bright and stand it in the liquid overnight. Predict first: what will its surface look like?

It comes out with a thin, patchy pinkish-copper coat. (If you see only a dark smudge, the liquid did not get enough copper: add more dull copper and wait another day.) Iron atoms have handed electrons to the copper ions, exactly as the zinc did. For a second race, stand another clean nail in plain salty water beside it: that one rusts instead. Both nails are losing electrons, to copper ions in one jar and to oxygen from the air in the other. (Pour the liquids away afterwards, and wash your hands. Nothing here is for eating.)

Investigation 8.1

Step the reaction forward one group at a time, up to four. For each step, write how many zinc atoms have been oxidised, how many copper ions reduced, and how many electrons have moved. What is the rule linking the three numbers?

Check yourself

In Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which particle is oxidised and which is reduced? How many electrons move for every zinc atom that reacts?

Answer at the back of the book

8.2Balancing electrons as well as atoms

The Royal Institution, London, 1833

Michael Faraday was a blacksmith’s son who left school early and became a bookbinder’s apprentice, reading the science books he was binding. In 1812 a customer gave him tickets to hear Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution. Faraday wrote up his notes, bound them beautifully, sent them to Davy, and soon afterwards got a job as his assistant, washing bottles. By the 1830s he was the most famous experimenter in Britain, and he wanted to know how much chemistry a given amount of electricity could do. He passed electric currents through solutions of different metals’ salts and weighed the metal that formed on the plates.

He found a rule so clean that it surprised everyone. Before you read it, predict: suppose a certain amount of electricity deposits 108 grams of silver. Pass exactly the same amount through a copper solution instead. Will you get more copper, the same, or less?

The answer: the same amount of electricity always produced the same number of “chemical portions” (what he called equivalents) of each substance, but not the same mass, and not the same number of atoms for every metal. In today’s numbers, the charge that deposits about 108 grams of silver deposits only about 32 grams of copper. That is half as many copper atoms as silver atoms. Faraday never knew why. We do: each copper ion needs two electrons to become an atom, while each silver ion needs only one. Faraday’s balance was counting electrons sixty years before anyone discovered them.

Here is the same idea in a beaker. Put a ribbon of magnesium into a solution of silver nitrate, and needles of shiny silver crystals grow on it while the magnesium dissolves. A magnesium atom loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺. But a silver ion, Ag⁺, has a charge of only +1, so it can take only one electron to become a silver atom. Where does the second electron go?

To a second silver ion. For every magnesium atom that reacts, two silver atoms appear:

Mg(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s)

A handy way to see this is to split the reaction into two half-equations, one for each side of the swap, with the electrons written in:

oxidation: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2 e⁻
reduction: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (needed twice: 2 Ag⁺ + 2 e⁻ → 2 Ag)
electrons given = 2, electrons taken = 2, so they cancel when you add the two halves

Half-equation

One half of a redox reaction written on its own, showing the electrons lost (oxidation) or gained (reduction).

The rule is the one from the front of the book, count everything, with one extra thing to count. A balanced redox equation must have the same number of atoms of each element on both sides and the same total electric charge on both sides. Check it: on the left, Mg has charge 0 and two Ag⁺ ions have +2; on the right, Mg²⁺ has +2 and two silver atoms have 0. Both sides total +2.

Try writing it the lazy way, Mg + Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Ag. The atoms balance, one of each. But the charge does not: +1 on the left, +2 on the right. One electron has appeared from nowhere, and electrons, like atoms, are never created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

The same idea works for harder pairs. Aluminium forms Al³⁺ (losing three electrons), and each copper ion takes two. The smallest number that both 3 and 2 go into is 6, so two aluminium atoms give six electrons to three copper ions:

2 Al(s) + 3 Cu²⁺(aq) → 2 Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Cu(s)

Careful

“One magnesium atom splits into two silver atoms.”

Atoms of one element never turn into another in a chemical reaction. Each silver atom was a silver ion in the solution all along; it was waiting for one electron. The magnesium atom supplies two electrons, and so two silver ions become silver metal. (Silver atoms are also more than four times heavier than magnesium atoms, so a magnesium atom could not possibly “split” into two of them.)

Investigation 8.2

Choose Mg + 2 Ag⁺ and step the reaction forward. Compare the number of Mg²⁺ ions made with the number of silver atoms plated. Then switch to 2 Al + 3 Cu²⁺ and predict the numbers before you look.

Check yourself

Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and silver ions are Ag⁺. Write the balanced equation for aluminium metal reacting with silver ions, and check that the charge is the same on both sides.

Answer at the back of the book

8.3Why doesn’t copper dissolve in zinc sulfate?

Alchemists loved to grow glittering crystal “trees” of silver in their flasks, and gave them names like the Tree of Diana. You can grow one with no mystery at all: hang a coil of copper wire in colourless silver nitrate solution, and over an hour a sparkling tree of silver crystals grows on it while the liquid slowly turns blue. Copper is giving electrons to silver ions, and going into solution as blue Cu²⁺.

So try the obvious next experiment. Zinc dropped into copper ions gets coated in copper. What about a piece of copper dropped into colourless zinc sulfate solution? You can write the equation perfectly well:

Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s)

It balances for atoms (one copper, one zinc on each side) and for charge (+2 on each side). And yet, if you try it, nothing happens. Leave the copper there for a day, a week, a month: it stays shiny and the liquid stays colourless. Put the silver from your tree into copper sulfate, and nothing happens either.

This is the lesson of section 4.4 again, now with electrons: a balanced equation tells you what would be conserved if a reaction happened. It does not tell you that the reaction happens. Electron transfer has a direction. Electrons move readily from zinc to copper ions, but not from copper to zinc ions, like water that runs down a staircase but never climbs back up on its own. The reason is the total energy change, which includes pulling atoms out of the solid metal and water molecules gathering round the new ions, not just how tightly a lone atom holds its outer electrons. The forward reaction gives out energy (that is why the beaker warmed up), and running it backwards would need that energy to be put back in.

Reactivity series

A list of metals in order of how readily they give away electrons. A metal will push a lower metal’s ions out of solution, but not a higher one’s.

By testing metals against each other’s ions, every pairing, chemists in the 1800s found one consistent order, with zinc above copper above silver. They lined the metals up in order of how readily they give away electrons, and called it the reactivity series. A metal higher in the series pushes the ions of a lower metal out of solution and coats itself with that metal; a lower metal does nothing to the ions of a higher one. The same order shows up again as the voltage when the metals are made into cells, as you will see next.

Careful

“Copper doesn’t react with zinc sulfate because the equation can’t be balanced.”

It balances perfectly, for atoms and for charge. The reason is energy, not bookkeeping: electrons do not pass from copper to zinc ions on their own, because that would be an uphill move. Balance is necessary for any real reaction, but it never proves one will happen.

Clean silver with aluminium foil (with an adult)

Find a silver spoon, puja item or anklet gone black with tarnish. The black is silver sulfide: silver that has given electrons to sulfur from the air. Aluminium, higher in the series, can push those electrons back. Line a bowl with aluminium foil, shiny side up. Ask an adult to pour in hot water from the kettle, then stir in a tablespoon each of baking soda and salt. Using a wooden spoon or tongs, not fingers (the water is hot), lay the tarnished silver in the water so it touches the foil. Predict first: what will happen to the black, and does it matter whether the silver touches the foil?

Within minutes the black fades and the silver shines: aluminium atoms give up electrons and silver ions take them back. With the silver not touching the foil, very little happens, because the electrons need a path. Keep a window open for the faint smell of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulfide). Don’t use it on “oxidised” jewellery, which is blackened on purpose, or on valuable antiques.

Investigation 8.3

Compare zinc in Cu²⁺ with copper in Zn²⁺. Predict what the model will show for the second before you switch to it. Then explain why a balanced equation was not enough to decide.

Check yourself

Magnesium is above zinc in the reactivity series. What happens if you put magnesium ribbon into zinc sulfate solution? What happens if you put zinc into magnesium sulfate solution?

Answer at the back of the book

8.4Galvanic cells and recharging

King’s College London, 1836

Volta’s pile made electricity, but it was a frustrating thing to use. Within minutes its current faded, because bubbles of hydrogen gas collected on the metal plates and smothered the reaction. John Frederic Daniell, the first professor of chemistry at the new King’s College, was a practical man who had already invented an instrument for measuring the moisture in the air. He wanted a battery that would keep going.

Think about what happens when zinc sits in copper sulfate. The electrons jump straight from zinc atoms to copper ions at the surface of the strip. The energy comes out as a little warmth and then it is gone. Daniell’s idea was to make those same electrons travel somewhere useful on the way.

Galvanic cell

Two halves of a redox reaction in separate containers, joined by a wire and a salt bridge, so that the electrons travel through the wire as an electric current.

He separated the two halves of the reaction. A zinc plate stands in a beaker of zinc sulfate; a copper plate stands in a beaker of copper sulfate. Now the zinc atoms cannot reach any copper ions. Connect the two plates with a wire, though, and the electrons have a road. Zinc atoms give up electrons, which travel through the wire to the copper plate, where copper ions from the solution collect them and become copper metal. Electrons flowing through a wire are an electric current, so a bulb or a small motor in the wire will run. A cell that turns a chemical reaction into electricity like this is called a galvanic cell, after Galvani and his frogs.

Salt bridge

A path of salt solution between the two beakers of a cell. Ions move along it to keep each beaker electrically neutral, completing the circuit.

There is one more part, and it is easy to overlook. As zinc dissolves, the left beaker fills up with extra Zn²⁺ ions, more positive charge than negative. As copper plates out, the right beaker loses Cu²⁺ ions and is left with extra negative sulfate ions. Within a fraction of a second, the build-up of charge would stop the current completely. The fix is a salt bridge: a tube or a strip of paper soaked in a salt solution, such as potassium nitrate, dipped into both beakers. (Daniell’s first cells used a barrier of animal membrane, and later ones a porous clay pot, which do the same job.) Its ions drift to cancel the build-up: nitrate ions (negative) move towards the zinc beaker, potassium ions (positive) towards the copper beaker. Electrons carry the current through the wire; ions carry it through the liquids. Only together do they make a complete loop.

Anode and cathode

The anode is the electrode where oxidation happens; the cathode is where reduction happens. In a cell that makes electricity, the anode is the negative terminal.

The two plates have names. The anode is where oxidation happens (here, zinc), and the cathode is where reduction happens (here, copper). As the cell runs, the zinc plate gets thinner and the copper plate gets thicker. In a cell like this one, the anode is the negative terminal, which surprises many people: isn’t the zinc losing electrons? Each zinc atom that reacts leaves as a Zn²⁺ ion but leaves its two electrons behind in the metal. Electrons collect in the zinc plate faster than anywhere else, which is exactly why they pour out of it along the wire.

Daniell’s two-liquid design gave a steady current for hours, and it went to work at once: Daniell cells powered many of the early electric telegraphs of the 1840s and 1850s, carrying messages along wires across countries. Measured carefully, a Daniell cell with standard solutions gives 1.10 volts: the size of the push the zinc-to-copper electron transfer can give.

Can you run a cell backwards? Yes, if you push. Connect a power supply that pushes harder than the cell does (more than 1.10 V, the other way round) and you can force electrons onto zinc ions to make zinc metal again, and pull them off copper. Using electricity to drive a reaction that would not go on its own is called electrolysis. It was electrolysis that made Humphry Davy famous. Davy was a woodcarver’s son from Penzance in Cornwall who had taught himself chemistry, tried breathing laughing gas in the name of science, and become the most dazzling lecturer in London. In 1807, using a giant version of Volta’s pile, he passed a current through melted potash and watched tiny globules of a new metal burst out and catch fire: potassium. Days later he made sodium the same way. Both had been locked in their compounds so tightly that no ordinary chemistry could free them.

The story behind this

The boy from Penzance who lit up LondonA woodcarver’s son from the edge of England who breathed laughing gas, tore new metals out of rocks with electricity, and made chemistry the most exciting show in London.
Electrolysis

Using electricity from outside to drive a redox reaction that would not happen by itself.

And recharging a phone battery is exactly this idea: the charger pushes the battery’s reaction backwards, storing energy that the battery gives out again later. (The chemistry inside a phone is different from Daniell’s cell, and Chapter 11 looks at it.)

Understand itElectrolysis

What is it?

Using electricity from outside to drive a chemical reaction that would not happen on its own: pushing electrons where they would not go by themselves.

Why is it called this?

Michael Faraday introduced the word in 1834, prompted by the scholar William Whewell. It means “loosening by electricity”, from the Greek lysis, a loosening, because the current pulls a compound apart. The same pair gave us anode and cathode (Greek for “way up” and “way down”) and ion, “one that goes”.

What problem did it solve?

Some elements are locked into their compounds so tightly that no ordinary reaction can free them. Electrolysis prised them out: Humphry Davy made potassium and sodium this way in 1807, and it is still how aluminium, sodium and chlorine are made today.

Why does it work?

A power supply pushes electrons onto one electrode and pulls them off the other, harder than the reaction can push back. Ions drift to the electrode of opposite charge, where they gain or lose electrons and become atoms or molecules again.

How does it help?

It makes metals and gases we could not otherwise get, coats objects with a thin layer of metal (electroplating), and it is exactly what a charger does to a rechargeable battery.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Faraday weighed what the current deposited. In today’s numbers, the same amount of electricity that deposits about 108 g of silver deposits only about 32 g of copper: half as many atoms, because each copper ion needs two electrons and each silver ion one.

What it isn’t

Not the current smashing the compound like a hammer. It delivers electrons one at a time, and the energy goes into moving them uphill.

Where does it stop working?

It costs a great deal of energy: making one kilogram of aluminium takes about 15 units (kilowatt-hours) of electricity, as much as a ceiling fan uses running day and night for more than a week. And what forms at each electrode depends on everything in the beaker; in salty water you get hydrogen, not sodium, because water molecules take the electrons more easily.

Your turn

Explain Electrolysis to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“The electrons travel through the salt bridge to get back to the zinc.”

Free electrons do not travel through water or salt solution. In the wire and the metal plates, current is carried by electrons. In the solutions and the salt bridge, it is carried by ions drifting in opposite directions. The loop is complete, but it is made of two different kinds of traffic.

A lemon battery (with an adult)

You can repeat Volta’s argument with Galvani on the kitchen table. You need three lemons, four pieces of thick copper wire (stripped electrical wire is fine; Indian coins are not copper), three galvanised (zinc-coated) iron nails or screws, four short wires with crocodile clips, and a small red LED. If anyone has a cheap multimeter, borrow it too. Roll each lemon on the table to loosen the juice inside.

Predict first. Push two copper pieces into one lemon, a few centimetres apart, and connect them to the LED or the meter. Will anything happen? Then swap one copper piece for the zinc-coated nail. What changes?

With two coppers, nothing worth measuring (a meter reads close to zero): the same metal on both sides gives no push, however juicy the lemon. With copper and zinc, the meter shows a bit under one volt. The lemon is only the damp path, as Volta said of the frog; the push comes from the two different metals. One lemon is not quite enough for most LEDs, so make two or three lemon cells and join them in a chain, the copper of one to the zinc of the next, and look closely in a dim room (if the LED stays dark, turn it round: it only works one way). Plain iron nails work too, but you need five or six lemons, because iron sits lower than zinc in the reactivity series and gives a smaller push.

Now a harder question. Leave the LED glowing for an hour. What has been used up: the electrons, the lemon, or the zinc? Throw the lemons away afterwards rather than eating them, because some zinc will have dissolved into the juice.

Careful

“A battery is full of electrons, and it goes flat when they are used up.”

Electrons are never used up. Every electron that leaves the zinc goes round the wire, through the LED, and into the copper; the same number come out of one end as go in the other. What gets used up in the lemon is zinc atoms, which go into the juice as Zn²⁺ ions, and hydrogen ions in the juice, which take the electrons at the copper and become hydrogen gas. A battery is a store of chemicals that will react as soon as they are given a path; the electrons are only the go-between. When the chemicals run out, the push stops.

Understand itThe battery

What does it do?

A battery is a store of chemicals that are ready to react, arranged so that the electrons they exchange must travel through a wire, doing useful work on the way.

Why is it called this?

Around 1749 Benjamin Franklin called a row of linked electrical jars a “battery”, probably because it looked like a battery of cannon lined up to fire together. The word fitted Volta’s pile of 1800, a stack of many cells. A single cell like Daniell’s is called galvanic, after Galvani and his frogs, even though Volta showed Galvani was wrong about where the electricity came from.

What problem did it solve?

Before 1800, electricity came only in sudden sparks from friction machines and charged jars. Volta’s pile gave the first steady current, and Daniell’s cell of 1836 kept it steady for hours, enough to run the electric telegraph.

Why does it work?

Two different materials pass electrons on with different ease. Keep them apart, give the electrons a wire and the ions a salt bridge, and the electrons run downhill through the wire, from the material that lets them go to the one that takes them.

How does it help?

Every torch, phone and electric car runs on one. And a cell’s voltage measures how hard one metal pushes electrons onto another: the reactivity series, read off a meter.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Two copper pieces in a lemon give almost no voltage; copper and zinc give nearly a volt. The push comes from the difference between two materials, not from the lemon, just as Volta argued against Galvani.

What it isn’t

Not a tank of electrons that empties. Every electron that leaves goes round the circuit and back in; it is the chemicals, such as zinc atoms and hydrogen ions, that run out.

Where does it stop working?

When a reacting chemical runs out, the push stops. Most cells can’t be reversed. Rechargeable ones can be pushed backwards by a charger, but even they slowly wear out as side reactions trap some of their chemicals.

Your turn

Explain The battery to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.
