Case file 8

The cell that would not light

Riya builds a cell from a magnesium strip in magnesium sulfate solution and a silver strip in silver nitrate solution, in two separate beakers. She joins the strips with wires through a small bulb and an ammeter (a meter that measures current). To keep her solutions pure, she does not join the beakers with anything else.

  1. The bulb never lights. The ammeter reads 0 the whole time.
  2. The metal strips are clean and the solutions are fresh. The wires and the bulb work when tested with a torch battery.
  3. Magnesium is far above silver in the reactivity series: a magnesium ribbon dropped straight into silver nitrate grows silver crystals within a minute or so.
  4. When she dips a strip of filter paper soaked in potassium nitrate solution into both beakers, the bulb glows at once. After an hour, she finds that 0.020 mol of magnesium has dissolved.

Why did nothing happen at first? And how many moles of silver should have formed on the silver strip by the end of the hour?

Show the solution

At first the circuit was not a complete loop. Electrons could travel through the wire, but nothing could carry charge between the two beakers. If even a few magnesium atoms had given up electrons, the magnesium beaker would have gained positive charge and the silver beaker would have been left with extra negative nitrate ions, and that imbalance would instantly have stopped any more electrons from moving. In practice, no measurable current flows at all. Clue 3 shows that the reaction itself is ready to go; clue 2 rules out a broken bulb; clue 4 shows the missing piece was the salt bridge.

Silver: each magnesium atom gives 2 electrons and each silver ion takes 1 (Mg + 2 Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2 Ag), so 0.020 mol of magnesium makes 2 × 0.020 = 0.040 mol of silver, about 4.3 g.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Zinc gives its electrons away more readily than copper, and copper more readily than silver; magnesium more readily still. For metals in water, the full reason is an energy account with several entries. But one entry runs through all of chemistry: how tightly an atom holds its outer electrons. That is written into the shape of the periodic table itself, a table that a Russian chemist laid out like a game of patience, half a century before anyone knew what an electron shell was. Chapter 9 reads it.

9

Chapter 9

The shape of the periodic table

The big questionGoing across a row of the periodic table, each atom has one more proton and one more electron than the last. So why do the atoms get smaller, not bigger?

  1. 9.1Why atoms shrink across a row
  2. 9.2Why removing an electron always costs energy

A rooftop in India, Diwali night

Rockets climb into the dark and burst: crimson, then emerald green, then a gold that crackles, then a deep blue that is the hardest colour of all to make. Every one of those colours was chosen by a chemist. The crimson comes from strontium compounds packed into the shell, the green from barium, the yellow-gold from sodium, the blue from copper. Heat a compound of any one of these metals hot enough and it glows with its own colour, as reliably as a signature.

In the 1850s two friends in Heidelberg turned that signature into an instrument. Robert Bunsen was a tough, kindly chemist who had lost the sight of one eye in a laboratory explosion and carried on regardless; Gustav Kirchhoff was a younger physicist who had worked out the rules of electric circuits while still a student. Bunsen had a burner with an almost colourless flame (the one still named after him), and Kirchhoff passed the light from it through a glass prism. Each element’s glow split into its own pattern of sharp, bright coloured lines, different from every other element’s. In 1860 they found a pair of sky-blue lines that belonged to no known element, and named the new metal caesium, from the Latin for sky-blue. A year later deep red lines gave them rubidium, from the Latin for dark red. Light from a flame had become a way of discovering elements nobody had seen.

Light would keep giving up secrets for the rest of the story. In 1921 an Indian physicist, C. V. Raman, sailing home from England, stared at the deep blue of the Mediterranean and refused to accept the usual explanation that the sea simply reflects the sky. Back in Calcutta he and his students spent years shining light through liquids, and in 1928 they found that a tiny fraction of the scattered light comes out with a slightly different colour, changed by the vibrating molecules it has met. Each kind of molecule changes it in its own way. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for it, the first Asian scientist to win a Nobel Prize in science, and chemists still use his effect to identify substances by the light they scatter.

The story behind this

Where the elements come fromHydrogen from the Big Bang, carbon and oxygen from stars, gold from colliding dead stars: every atom in you has an address in the history of the universe.

By the 1860s chemists knew about sixty elements, and they were drowning in facts about them. Which belonged together, and why?

St Petersburg, 1869

Dmitri Mendeleev was the youngest child of a large family in Tobolsk, in Siberia. His father, a headmaster, went blind; his mother kept the family going by running a glass factory, and when it burned down she took her teenage son thousands of kilometres to St Petersburg so that he could study science. She died soon after he got in. By 1869 he was a professor there, wild-haired and famously impatient, and he was writing a chemistry textbook for his students and needed a sensible order to describe the elements in. He wrote each element’s properties on cards and arranged them, in order of the masses of their atoms, so that elements that behaved alike fell into the same columns. (A famous story says the final arrangement came to him in a dream after days of shuffling the cards like a game of patience. It comes from a friend’s recollection years later, so treat it as a legend.) He did all this without knowing about protons, neutrons or electrons, purely from the way the elements reacted.

His boldest move was to leave gaps. Where the pattern demanded an element nobody had found, he left a space and described what would fill it. Below aluminium, he said, there should be a metal with atoms about 68 times as heavy as hydrogen, a density of about 5.9 grams per cubic centimetre, and a low melting point. In 1875 Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, a largely self-taught French chemist from a family of brandy merchants in Cognac, looking at a zinc ore through exactly the kind of spectroscope Bunsen and Kirchhoff had built, saw two violet lines nobody had seen before. He named the new metal gallium. His first measurement of its density was 4.7. Mendeleev wrote to tell him it should be closer to 5.9; Lecoq purified his sample, measured again, and got 5.9.

The story behind this

The Siberian who left gapsThe youngest child of a Siberian family, carried across Russia by a mother who would not give up on him, who arranged the elements so well that he could describe ones nobody had yet found.

A table that predicts things nobody has yet seen must be catching something real. But what? Mendeleev could not say. The answer came in the next fifty years, from the inside of the atom, and you already know the beginning of it: the gold foil of Chapter 1, the nucleus, and the electrons arranged in shells around it. This chapter uses that to explain two of the table’s patterns: the sizes of atoms, and how tightly they hold their electrons.

The story behind this

The patience game: the story of the periodic tableHow a Russian professor laid out the elements like a card game, left gaps, and dared nature to fill them.

Rainbows from a CD

You can split light into its colours the way Kirchhoff did, using an old CD or DVD instead of a prism. In a darkened room, hold the shiny side of the disc so that it reflects light from a lamp into your eye, and tilt it until you see a band of colours. Try different lights around the house: an old-style bulb, a white LED, a fluorescent tube, a phone screen. Some give a smooth rainbow; others give separate bright stripes of colour with dark gaps between them. If you can, try an orange sodium street lamp at night: older ones give almost nothing but a single strong yellow-orange band, the same yellow that salt gives a flame. (Never look at the Sun, directly or in the disc.) Then, with an adult at the gas stove, ask them to sprinkle a few grains of table salt onto the blue flame while you stand back (the grains crackle and can jump), and look at the flash through your disc: the same yellow as the street lamp. The flash is brief, so it may take a few tries to catch it. That is Bunsen and Kirchhoff’s discovery, in your kitchen.

9.1Why atoms shrink across a row

Manchester, 1913

Mendeleev had ordered the elements by mass, and in a few places that order was wrong. Tellurium atoms are heavier than iodine atoms, yet tellurium clearly belongs in front of iodine. Mendeleev simply swapped them, trusting the chemistry over the masses. In 1913 Henry Moseley, a young physicist working in Rutherford’s laboratory in Manchester, found out why. He fired electrons at targets made of different elements and measured the X-rays that came off. The X-ray frequency rose in a perfectly regular staircase, one step per element, and the steps counted the positive charge on the nucleus: the number of protons. That number, the atomic number, is the true order of the table, and tellurium (52) comes before iodine (53). Moseley was killed two years later, at Gallipoli in the First World War, at the age of 27.

The story behind this

Henry Moseley’s staircaseA 26-year-old in Manchester found the true order of the elements by measuring X-rays, and counted the missing ones.

So the table is built one proton at a time. Across the second row, from lithium to fluorine, every step adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron around it. You might expect each atom to be a little bigger than the one before. Measurements say the opposite. A lithium atom is the largest in the row; a fluorine atom is less than half its width.

How can anyone measure something so small? You cannot put a ruler on an atom, but you can measure the distance between two atoms joined by a bond, by bouncing X-rays off crystals or by studying the light that gases absorb. Half the distance between two bonded atoms of the same element gives a rough size for one atom. The distance changes a little from one compound to another, so chemists average thousands of measurements from many different molecules and crystals. Those averages are the sizes in the next figure.

To see why, think about the electrons as two teams. Lithium has 3 protons and 3 electrons: 2 electrons in the inner shell and 1 in the outer shell. Fluorine has 9 protons and 9 electrons: the same 2 inner electrons, and 7 outer ones. In every atom of row 2 the outer electrons are in the same shell, and the inner shell is the same two electrons.

The outer electrons are pulled inwards by the protons, and pushed outwards by the other electrons (remember from Chapter 2: like charges repel). The two inner electrons sit between the nucleus and the outer shell, so they cancel out a large part of the nucleus’s pull. This is called shielding. Think of the nucleus as a bright lamp and the inner electrons as a screen around it: an outer electron sees the lamp dimmed. (The screen is not a solid wall; it is made of electrons that are themselves moving. But on average it sits between.) Electrons in the same shell are no better placed than each other, so they shield one another only a little.

Shielding

The way inner electrons reduce the pull of the nucleus on outer electrons, by repelling them. Electrons in the same shell shield each other only weakly.

Now take one step across the row, from lithium to beryllium. Every proton pulls on every electron, so the extra proton pulls on each outer electron, not just on “its own”. And the extra electron does not share out the nucleus’s pull more thinly, as if the nucleus had a fixed amount of pull to divide up; it only adds a small push from a neighbour that is no closer to the nucleus. More pull on each outer electron, hardly any more screening: so with every step the outer shell is held in more tightly, and the atoms get smaller.

Going down a column is different. Sodium has one more full shell than lithium, and potassium one more than sodium. Each new shell sits farther out, and has more inner electrons screening it. Electric attraction gets weaker with distance, so the outer electron is held more loosely and the atom is bigger.

Careful

“More electrons always take up more room, so atoms must grow across a row.”

Electrons are not marbles, each needing its own space. The size of an atom is set by how strongly its outer electrons are pulled in. Across a row, the pull wins: the protons added are not cancelled by the electrons added to the same shell.

Predict first: before you open the landscape, guess. If every element’s atom size were a tower standing on its square of the periodic table, where would the tallest towers be: on the left, in the middle, or on the right? And would the towers in the bottom rows be taller or shorter than the ones at the top?

Turn the landscape and you can see the whole of this section at once. Each row after the first begins with a skyscraper on the left, an alkali metal, and the towers step down towards the right, with a few bumps along the way. Every step adds one proton, which pulls the same shells in a little tighter. Then the next row begins with a new, taller skyscraper, because it has a whole new shell. Press Look along the rows and all seven rows line up behind each other: the same downhill slope, again and again. (Row 1, with only hydrogen and helium, is too short to join in.) That repeating shape is what “periodic” means.

Understand itShielding

What is it?

The way an atom’s inner electrons stand between the nucleus and the outer electrons and cancel part of its pull, so an outer electron feels a much weaker tug than the full charge of the nucleus.

Why is it called this?

Because the inner electrons act like a shield, or like a screen in front of a lamp; chemists also call it screening. These are plain everyday words, chosen because the picture works, not technical names with a hidden meaning.

What problem did it solve?

Across a row, atoms gain protons and electrons, so you might expect them to grow; down a column they gain many more protons, so you might expect them to shrink. Measurements say the opposite both times. Shielding explains why.

Why does it work?

Electrons repel each other. Inner electrons spend most of their time between the nucleus and the outer shell, so they push outwards on the outer electrons and cancel much of the protons’ pull. Electrons in the same shell are no closer to the nucleus than each other, so they shield one another only a little.

How does it help?

It explains the sizes of atoms, why ionisation energies rise across a row and fall down a column, and so why metals on the left give electrons away readily while non-metals on the right hold on to them.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Remove lithium’s electrons one by one. The outer one, behind its two-electron shield, costs 520 kJ/mol; the next, with no shield in front of it, costs 7,298.

What it isn’t

Not a fixed amount of pull shared out among the electrons. Every proton pulls on every electron; shielding is the push of the other electrons partly cancelling that pull.

Where does it stop working?

The inner electrons are not a solid wall: they move, and outer electrons spend some of their time close to the nucleus. Exact numbers need quantum mechanics, and the simple picture can’t explain small details such as the dips at boron and oxygen.

Your turn

Explain Shielding to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Orbital

A region around a nucleus where an electron is likely to be found, with a definite shape and energy. Shells are made up of orbitals.

The shell model has done well here. But it is not the end of the story, and you can already see why in Chapter 1’s graph of ionisation energies (Figure 1.7). Across row 2 the line climbs, but with two small dips, at boron and at oxygen. Shells alone cannot explain those. Nor can they explain the sharp coloured lines from Bunsen’s flame: why should sodium glow at one exact yellow and not at every colour? In the 1920s, physicists such as Erwin Schrödinger and Wolfgang Pauli worked out a new kind of mechanics for electrons, quantum mechanics, which answered both questions. Electrons in an atom can have only certain energies, so when they drop from a higher energy to a lower one they give out light of only certain colours. And the electrons in a shell are arranged in smaller groups, described by orbitals. An orbital is not a track: it describes the region where an electron is likely to be found, more like a fuzzy cloud with a particular shape. Some orbitals are round; others have two lobes, like a figure of eight. The dips appear where an electron starts a new kind of orbital (boron) or has to share an orbital with another electron (oxygen). You will meet orbitals properly when you study chemistry further; for now, it is enough to know that shells are a simplified first map.

Investigation 9.1

In the force model, hold the distance fixed and increase the positive charge from +1 to +2. What happens to the pull? Then make the distance smaller. How does this explain why the outer shell moves inwards across a row?

Check yourself

Sodium (2, 8, 1) is much bigger than lithium (2, 1), even though it has 8 more protons. Why?

Answer at the back of the book

9.2Why removing an electron always costs energy

How tightly does an atom hold its outermost electron? The answer is its ionisation energy, which you met in Chapter 1: the energy needed to pull one electron right away from an atom. For every element that has ever been measured, the answer is positive. No neutral atom gives up an electron for free. Even lithium and sodium, the easiest in the first 18 elements, need 520 and 496 kilojoules per mole of atoms.

The trends follow from section 9.1. Across a row, the outer electrons are pulled harder and sit closer, so they are harder to remove: lithium needs 520 kJ/mol, neon needs 2,081. Down a column, the outer electron is farther away and better screened, so it is easier to remove: lithium 520, sodium 496, potassium 419. The pattern in the reactivity series of Chapter 8 has the same roots: metals whose outer electrons are held loosely tend to be the ones that give electrons away readily, although in water other energy changes matter too. It is also why most of the metals in the firework colours come from the left-hand side of the table. A flame is hot enough to lift one of their outer electrons to a higher energy level without tearing it away, and the atom gives out its coloured light as the electron falls back. The colour is set by the size of that drop, which is different for every element.

Predict first: sodium in a flame glows yellow, and nothing else. If an electron can fall from many different heights, why does salt not give a whole rainbow? Make a guess, then press Give it energy a few times and watch where each colour lands.

Think of the levels as the rungs of a ladder with fixed, uneven gaps. An electron can stand on a rung, never between rungs, so it can only fall by the exact height of one gap or another. Each gap gives light of one exact colour. Sodium’s ladder has one gap that gives far brighter visible light than any other, from its 3p level down to its 3s level, and that light is yellow, at 589 nanometres. Most of its other falls give infrared or ultraviolet light, which is real light that our eyes cannot see, and the few that are visible are very faint. That is why salt in a flame glows an almost pure yellow (so do the low-pressure sodium lamps once used on some roads).

Switch to hydrogen and you will see four visible lines, red, blue-green, blue and violet, all from falls that end on hydrogen’s second rung. Switch to A rainbow and you will see the difference that Bunsen and Kirchhoff used. A hot solid, like a bulb’s filament, gives every colour at once. A hot gas of separate atoms gives only its own few colours, as personal as a fingerprint.

Now try removing a second electron from lithium. Lithium’s first electron was alone in the outer shell. Once it has gone, the next one must come from the inner shell, which is much closer to the nucleus and has almost nothing screening it. The energy needed jumps from 520 to 7,298 kJ/mol, about 14 times as much.

Predict first. Sodium’s electrons are arranged 2, 8, 1. Sketch bars for the energy needed to remove its first three electrons, one after another. Where should the big jump come? Then check your idea against lithium (2, 1) below.

Successive ionisation energies

The energies needed to remove an atom’s electrons one after another. A large jump shows that the next electron is in an inner shell.

These successive ionisation energies are some of the strongest evidence that shells are real. For any element, plot the energy needed to remove each electron in turn, and a big jump appears exactly where you run out of outer-shell electrons.

How do we know? Knocking electrons out with light from the 1960s

Ionisation energies are measured by shining very energetic light (ultraviolet or X-rays) on atoms of a gas and measuring how fast the electrons fly out. The light’s energy, minus the electron’s leftover energy of motion, is the energy it took to free that electron. This method, called photoelectron spectroscopy, shows separate groups of electrons with different energies inside every atom: direct evidence for shells, and for the orbitals inside them.

Understand itAn element’s colour signature (its spectrum)

What is it?

The exact set of colours of light that an element gives out when it is heated, or soaks up when light shines through it. Spread out by a prism, it shows as sharp coloured lines that belong to that element alone.

Why is it called this?

Spectrum is Latin for “an appearance” or “an image”. Isaac Newton brought the word into the study of light in the 1670s for the band of colours from a prism. Bunsen and Kirchhoff named two new elements after their spectra: caesium, from the Latin for sky-blue, and rubidium, from the Latin for dark red.

What problem did it solve?

How to tell which elements are present without weighing or reacting anything: in a flame, in a mineral, even in the Sun. Bunsen and Kirchhoff used it to discover two new elements in 1860 and 1861.

Why does it work?

An electron in an atom can have only certain energies. Heat lifts an outer electron to a higher level; when it falls back, the atom gives out exactly the energy of that drop as light of one colour. Each element has its own ladder of levels, so its own set of colours.

How does it help?

Firework makers choose metals for their colours, chemists detect tiny traces of elements, and astronomers read what stars are made of from their light.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

The lines are the same every time, in every laboratory and in starlight: the two yellow lines that salt gives a gas flame sit exactly where two dark lines cross the Sun’s spectrum.

What it isn’t

Not the element burning or being used up. Its electrons are lifted and fall back, again and again, for as long as the atom stays hot.

Where does it stop working?

Shells alone can’t predict the exact colours of most elements: that needed quantum mechanics in the 1920s. And molecules and solids give broad, blurred bands rather than sharp lines, which are much harder to read.

Your turn

Explain An element’s colour signature (its spectrum) to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“Sodium gives off energy when it loses its electron, because it wants a full shell.”

Removing sodium’s outer electron costs 496 kJ/mol; nothing about it gives energy out. Sodium does end up as Na⁺ in salt because of what happens afterwards: the oppositely charged ions pull together into a crystal, which gives out more energy than the ionisation cost (Chapter 2). The energy accounting is what decides, not any wish of the atom.

Predict first: atom size had skyscrapers on the left. If you made the towers show how hard it is to pull an electron away instead, where would the tallest ones go now?

It is the mirror image. Now the noble gases on the far right are the mountain peaks: helium highest of all, at about 2,372 kJ/mol. The alkali metals on the left are the deepest valleys: caesium needs only about 376. Big atoms hold their outer electron loosely, far from the nucleus and behind many shielding electrons; small atoms hold it tightly. Two different measurements, one pattern, and one reason behind both. That is why chemists trust the table.

Understand itIonisation energy

What is it?

The energy needed to pull one electron right away from an atom, usually given per mole of atoms. It measures how tightly an atom holds its outermost electron.

Why is it called this?

An atom that has lost or gained electrons is an ion, a word Michael Faraday introduced in 1834, on William Whewell’s suggestion, from the Greek for “going”, because ions travel towards an electrode. Ionisation is turning an atom into an ion, and the ionisation energy is what that costs.

What problem did it solve?

It turned “how readily does this element give electrons away?” into a number you can measure, and it gave some of the strongest evidence that electrons are arranged in shells.

Why does it work?

The outer electron is pulled in by the protons and pushed out by the other electrons. The closer it sits and the less it is shielded, the more energy it takes to tear it away.

How does it help?

It predicts which atoms let electrons go (metals on the left, with low values) and which hold on (non-metals on the right), and a big jump in successive ionisation energies tells you how many outer electrons an atom has, as in the element with a cliff.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Shine very energetic light on atoms of a gas and measure how fast the electrons fly out. The light’s energy, minus the electron’s leftover energy of motion, is the ionisation energy (photoelectron spectroscopy).

What it isn’t

Not energy given out when an atom gets rid of an electron. It is always a cost: no neutral atom gives up an electron for free, not even sodium.

Where does it stop working?

It describes a lone atom in a gas. For a metal in water or in a crystal, other energy changes join in, which is why the reactivity series is not simply the order of ionisation energies.

Your turn

Explain Ionisation energy to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Be Mendeleev

Make your own “cards” the way Mendeleev did. On small pieces of paper, write the name and atomic number of the first twenty elements, from hydrogen (1) to calcium (20), and on each one note one fact you can look up: metal or non-metal, gas or solid at room temperature, and whether it forms ions with a charge of +1, +2, −1 or none. Shuffle them, then lay them out in order of atomic number, starting a new row each time you reach an element that behaves like one you have already placed. When your columns line up (lithium, sodium and potassium together; fluorine and chlorine together; helium, neon and argon together), you have rebuilt the shape of the periodic table from its chemistry alone.

Investigation 9.2

Draw ionisation as an uphill energy step. Compare a small step (an alkali metal such as lithium) with a big one (a noble gas such as neon). Explain the difference using distance and screening, without using the word “want”.

Check yourself

Lithium’s first ionisation energy is 520 kJ/mol and its second is 7,298 kJ/mol. Explain why the second is so much larger.

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 9

The element with a cliff

A sample of an unknown element X, from row 3 of the periodic table, is turned into a gas and its electrons are removed one at a time. The energies needed are:

Electron removed 1st 2nd 3rd 4th
Energy (kJ/mol) 738 1,451 7,733 10,543

The suspects are sodium (2, 8, 1), magnesium (2, 8, 2) and aluminium (2, 8, 3).

  1. Every value is positive.
  2. The 2nd value is about twice the 1st. The 3rd is more than five times the 2nd.

Which element is X? Which clue decides it, and what does the other clue tell you?

Show the solution

X is magnesium. The cliff comes between the 2nd and 3rd electrons, so X has exactly two electrons in its outer shell before the inner shell is reached: that is 2, 8, 2. Sodium would show its cliff after the 1st electron; aluminium after the 3rd. Clue 1 tells you nothing about which element it is, but it is worth noticing: removing any electron, from any atom or ion, always takes energy.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Right in the middle of row 2 sits carbon: four outer electrons, held neither very loosely nor very tightly, so that it neither gives them away nor takes extra ones easily. Instead, carbon shares. It shares with hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and above all with other carbon atoms, building chains, rings and frameworks of almost endless variety. Chapter 10 is about the chemistry that carbon makes possible, including the chemistry of life.

10

Chapter 10

Carbon chains and the chemistry of life

The big questionPetrol and sugar are both built mostly from carbon and hydrogen. So why does sugar vanish into your chai, while petrol floats on a monsoon puddle in a rainbow film?

  1. 10.1Chains, branches and rings
  2. 10.2The part that does the chemistry
  3. 10.3Longer chains, higher boiling points
  4. 10.4Same formula, different molecule
  5. 10.5Double bonds and locked shapes
  6. 10.6Acids, amines and the links of life

Berlin, February 1828

A 27-year-old chemist named Friedrich Wöhler is heating a white salt called ammonium cyanate, made from nothing more mysterious than minerals and the gases of a laboratory. When he looks at the crystals that form, he finds something that should not be there. They are urea: the same substance that living bodies make and get rid of in urine. Wöhler had trained as a doctor before chemistry pulled him away, and he had spent a year in Stockholm learning from the most famous chemist in Europe. Now he writes, delighted, to that old teacher in Stockholm, Jöns Jacob Berzelius, that he can make urea without needing a kidney, “either of man or dog”.

Why was that exciting? For centuries people had believed that the substances of living things, sugar, oil, urea, the stuff of flesh and wood, could only be made by life itself, by some special “vital force” that ordinary chemistry could never copy. Wöhler’s crystals did not end that belief overnight (the story is slower and messier than that, and you can read it in full), but they were one of the first cracks. Slowly chemists came to see that the molecules of life obey exactly the same rules as everything else in this book. They are special for a different reason: almost all of them are built on a skeleton of carbon.

The story behind this

Life’s chemistry is just chemistryA young chemist accidentally makes a substance from a living body in a flask, and the wall between “living” and “non-living” chemistry starts to crack.

Look at the label on almost anything in a kitchen: sugar, cooking oil, ghee, vinegar, rice, the plastic of the bottle, the soap by the sink. Different as they are, nearly all of them are made of molecules built around carbon. So are the fibres of your clothes, the DNA in your cells and the fuel in a scooter. Of the many millions of compounds that chemists have described, the great majority contain carbon. This episode of our adventure is about why one element can build so much, and about the small groups of atoms that decide what each carbon molecule actually does.

10.1Chains, branches and rings

Utrecht, the Netherlands, 1874

Tetrahedron

A pyramid with four triangular faces. The four bonds of a carbon atom with only single bonds point to its four corners, about 109.5° apart.

In 1874 a 22-year-old chemist called Jacobus van ‘t Hoff, not yet even a doctor of science, published a little pamphlet with a bold idea. He was a doctor’s son from Rotterdam who read poetry and philosophy as eagerly as chemistry, and he believed that a scientist needed imagination as much as a good balance. Some carbon compounds were known to come in two forms that were mirror images of each other, like your left and right hands. That made no sense if a carbon atom’s bonds lay flat on a page, as chemists usually drew them. But it made perfect sense, van ‘t Hoff argued, if the four bonds of a carbon atom pointed to the four corners of a tetrahedron, a little pyramid with a triangle for a base. In Paris, Joseph Le Bel had reached the same idea independently, within months. A famous German chemist, Hermann Kolbe, mocked van ‘t Hoff in print for his flights of fancy. The young man turned out to be right. Decades later X-ray measurements showed the angle between the bonds of such a carbon atom: about 109.5°, exactly a tetrahedron’s angle. And in 1931 the American chemist Linus Pauling, a pharmacist’s son from Oregon who had lost his father at nine and worked his way through college, chopping wood and teaching younger students, used the new quantum physics to explain why carbon’s four bonds point that way. In 1901 van ‘t Hoff received the very first Nobel Prize in Chemistry (for different work), and molecules have been three-dimensional ever since.

The story behind this

Molecules in three dimensionsTwo young chemists, working separately, realise that molecules have shapes in space, and an older professor mocks them for it.

Why four bonds? A carbon atom has 6 electrons: 2 in its inner shell and 4 in its outer one. Those 4 outer electrons let it form four covalent bonds, four shared pairs of electrons (Chapter 2). Count the lines meeting at any carbon atom in a structure, and you will almost always find four.

Organic compound

A compound built around carbon atoms, usually bonded to hydrogen. The name is old: people once thought only living things could make them.

What makes carbon special is that its bonds to other carbon atoms are strong, roughly as strong as its bonds to hydrogen. So carbon atoms can join to each other again and again, forming long chains, chains with branches, and closed rings, with hydrogen atoms (and sometimes oxygen or nitrogen) filling the remaining bonds. Silicon, the element just below carbon in the periodic table, also forms four bonds, but a silicon–silicon bond is only about two-thirds as strong as a carbon–carbon bond, and long silicon chains fall apart easily in air and water. Carbon’s chains don’t.

Alkane

A chain of carbon atoms joined by single bonds, with hydrogen everywhere else. Formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: methane, ethane, propane, butane…

The simplest family is the alkanes: chains of carbon with only hydrogen attached and only single bonds. Methane, CH₄, has one carbon; ethane, C₂H₆, has two; propane has three; butane has four. Each extra carbon brings two more hydrogens, so an alkane with n carbons has 2n + 2 hydrogens.

Turn the 3D model and you will see van ‘t Hoff’s tetrahedra everywhere: at every carbon, the four bonds splay out into space, which is why a “straight” chain is really a zig-zag.

Skeletal formula

A shorthand drawing of a molecule: lines for the carbon skeleton, a carbon at each corner and end, hydrogens on carbon left out.

Drawing every hydrogen gets tiring, so chemists often use a shorthand called a skeletal formula: just the zig-zag lines of the carbon skeleton, with a carbon understood at every corner and every end, and enough hydrogens understood to give each carbon four bonds. Butane becomes a little zig-zag of three lines. You will see these drawings in any chemistry book; now you know how to read them.

Understand itOrganic chemistry

What is it?

The chemistry of compounds built on a skeleton of carbon atoms, usually with hydrogen attached: sugars, oils, plastics, fuels, medicines and the molecules of life.

Why is it called this?

Berzelius named it around 1807 for substances that came from living organisms, because people then believed only life could make them. The name outlived the belief. In chemistry, “organic” does not mean natural or pesticide-free: petrol and plastic are organic compounds.

What problem did it solve?

Millions of different substances seemed to follow no shared rules. Seeing them as carbon skeletons with groups attached turned a jungle into a handful of patterns.

Why does it work?

A carbon atom has four outer electrons, so it forms four bonds, and its bonds to other carbon atoms are strong. So carbon can link to itself again and again in chains, branches and rings, with bonds left over for hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.

How does it help?

Know a molecule’s skeleton and its functional groups, and you can predict how it behaves: whether it mixes with water, how high it boils, whether it is an acid or a base.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

In 1828 Wöhler made urea, a substance of living bodies, from lifeless starting materials, and in 1901 Fischer joined the building blocks of proteins by hand. The molecules of life obey the same rules as everything else.

What it isn’t

Not “made only by living things” any more, and not “healthy” or “natural”. The word describes carbon chemistry, nothing more.

Where does it stop working?

The border is blurry. Carbon dioxide, carbonates and diamond all contain carbon but are usually counted as inorganic, by tradition rather than by any deep rule.

Your turn

Explain Organic chemistry to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 10.1

Compare diamond, water and salt in the app, then look at the 3D carbon structures. In each, which particles are joined by bonds that go on and on, and which are separate little groups?

Check yourself

A straight-chain alkane has 5 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have? Check by counting the bonds each carbon needs.

10.2The part that does the chemistry

Your kitchen, with an orange and a balloon

Here is a trick that looks like magic. Blow up a balloon and tie it. Peel an orange, then hold a piece of peel close to the balloon and squeeze it hard, so that a fine spray of oil from the peel lands on the rubber. Very often, within a few seconds, the balloon bursts. Nothing sharp touched it.

The trick works because of a rule chemists sum up as like dissolves like. The oil in orange peel is mostly a molecule called limonene: a carbon skeleton covered in hydrogen, with no charged ends at all. Balloon rubber is also a long carbon-and-hydrogen molecule. The limonene soaks into the stretched rubber, softens and weakens it, and the balloon pops. Water, whose molecules have slightly charged ends, would do nothing to the balloon at all.

The orange-peel balloon

You need a balloon and an orange (or a lemon). Blow up the balloon, then squeeze a piece of peel, coloured side towards the balloon, so its oil sprays onto the rubber. Try it on a few spots. Then try dripping plain water on another balloon. What does the difference tell you about which molecules dissolve which? (Keep the peel away from your eyes.)

Alkanes and molecules like limonene are rather dull chemically. Their C–C and C–H bonds share electrons almost equally, so the molecules have no positive or negative ends, and they don’t mix with water. That is the answer to half of this chapter’s big question: petrol is a mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, and water molecules stick to each other far more strongly than they stick to petrol, so the two stay apart and the lighter petrol floats on top. (The rainbow colours on a monsoon puddle come from light bouncing off the top and bottom of that very thin film of petrol.)

Now swap one hydrogen on ethane for an oxygen with a hydrogen attached, an –OH group. You get ethanol. The two molecules are almost the same size, yet ethane is a gas that boils at −88.6 °C and ethanol is a liquid that boils at 78.4 °C and mixes with water in any amount.

The difference comes from the O–H bond. Oxygen attracts the shared electrons much more strongly than hydrogen does, so the oxygen end carries a slight negative charge and the hydrogen a slight positive one. That hydrogen can be attracted to an oxygen on a neighbouring molecule: a hydrogen bond, the same kind of attraction that holds water molecules together (Chapter 3). It was Linus Pauling, again, who gave chemists a number scale for how strongly each element pulls on shared electrons, and who made hydrogen bonds a central idea in chemistry; later he used them to work out how protein chains coil and fold. Ethanol molecules hold on to each other, which raises the boiling point, and they hold on to water molecules too, which lets them mix.

The story behind this

The boy who never stopped asking whyA pharmacist’s son from Oregon who worked his way through college became the chemist who explained how atoms hold together, won two Nobel Prizes, and got some big things wrong too.
Functional group

A small group of atoms on a carbon molecule, such as –OH or –COOH, that gives it its typical behaviour.

A small group of atoms like –OH, which gives a molecule its particular behaviour, is called a functional group. It is the part that does the chemistry. The carbon skeleton is the frame; the functional groups are the handles, hooks and switches fixed onto it.

Group Name Example What it does
–OH hydroxyl (alcohols) ethanol hydrogen bonds; mixes with water
–COOH carboxyl (carboxylic acids) ethanoic acid, in vinegar gives away H⁺: a weak acid
–NH₂ amino (amines) in almost every amino acid picks up H⁺: a weak base
C=C double bond (alkenes) ethene holds the molecule flat; can open up to join other molecules

Sugar answers the other half of the big question. A sugar molecule has a carbon skeleton studded with –OH groups, five of them on a glucose molecule, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water all over its surface and dissolves easily into your chai.

Soap is a molecule with a split personality, and that is exactly why it works. One end is a long carbon tail with no charged ends, which mixes with grease; the other end is charged and loves water. The tails bury themselves in a spot of oil, the heads face outwards into the water, and the oil is carried away in tiny wrapped-up droplets.

Oil, water and soap

Half-fill a clear glass jar with water and add a spoonful of cooking oil. Put the lid on and shake hard. Watch: within a minute the oil gathers back into a layer on top. Now add a few drops of washing-up liquid, shake again, and compare. Which molecules are holding on to which?

Then a second test. Drop one sugar-coated sweet (a Gems or similar) into a glass of water and another into a glass of cooking oil. Predict first: which one will lose its colour? The sugar coat, studded with –OH groups, dissolves in the water and the colour runs; in the oil, it hardly changes. (The sweet from the oil glass is still fine to eat once wiped.)

Careful

“Adding an –OH group makes the molecule boil higher just because it makes it heavier.”

Check the masses. Ethane (30 grams per mole) and methanol, CH₃OH (32 grams per mole), weigh almost the same, yet ethane boils at −88.6 °C and methanol at 64.7 °C. The extra mass is tiny; the hydrogen bonding between methanol molecules is what holds them together.

Understand itFunctional group

What is it?

A small group of atoms on a carbon skeleton, such as –OH or –COOH, that gives the molecule its typical behaviour. The skeleton is the frame; the functional group is the part that does the chemistry.

Why is it called this?

Because it decides the molecule’s function: how it reacts and what it mixes with. Molecules with the same group behave alike, whatever the length of their skeleton.

What problem did it solve?

With millions of carbon compounds, learning each one separately is impossible. Learn a dozen groups and you can predict the behaviour of most of them.

Why does it work?

Carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen bonds share electrons almost evenly and do little. Groups containing oxygen or nitrogen share them unevenly, making slightly charged ends that form hydrogen bonds, give away H⁺ or pick it up.

How does it help?

It explains why sugar dissolves in chai but petrol floats on a puddle, why vinegar is sour, why soap lifts grease, and how amino acids link into proteins.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Swap one hydrogen on ethane for –OH: a gas that boils at −88.6 °C becomes ethanol, a liquid that boils at 78.4 °C and mixes with water. Almost the same size; one group changed everything.

What it isn’t

Not just extra weight. Methanol is only slightly heavier than ethane, yet it boils more than 150 °C higher, because of the hydrogen bonds its –OH group makes.

Where does it stop working?

Groups affect their neighbours. The –OH inside vinegar’s –COOH gives up H⁺, while the –OH in ethanol essentially doesn’t, because the C=O next door changes it. A group’s behaviour depends on what it is attached to.

Your turn

Explain Functional group to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 10.2

Compare methane with ammonia and water at the same temperature. All three molecules are about the same size. Predict which will be gases and which liquids, then check, and say which bonds are making the difference.

Check yourself

Methane does not dissolve in water. Methanol, CH₃OH, mixes with water completely. Explain the difference in terms of what the molecules attract.

10.3Longer chains, higher boiling points

Titusville, Pennsylvania, August 1859

On a farm in western Pennsylvania, a man named Edwin Drake and a hired well-driller had spent months boring a hole into the ground, while the locals laughed at “Drake’s folly”. At about 21 metres down, the drill hit oil. It was not the first oil anyone had ever seen, but Drake’s well started an industry. Within a few years refineries were heating crude oil to sort it into its parts, at first for one thing above all: kerosene, a clean-burning fuel for lamps that could replace whale oil.

What the refiners were exploiting is one of the neatest patterns in chemistry. Crude oil is a jumble of alkanes, from tiny ones to long ones. They have no –OH groups, no charged ends, nothing to grab with. You might expect them all to behave alike. Yet the gas in a camping stove is a gas, the petrol in a car is a liquid, and a candle is a solid, and all three are alkanes. What changes is the length of the chain.

Dispersion forces

Weak attractions between all molecules, caused by electrons bunching up for an instant. They are stronger for bigger molecules with more surface in contact.

Even molecules with no permanent charged ends attract each other a little. The electrons in a molecule are always moving, and at any instant they may be slightly bunched on one side, making a fleeting charged end that tugs on the electrons of the next molecule. These flickering attractions are called dispersion forces. Each one is weak, but they add up along the whole length of the molecule. A long chain has more electrons and more surface touching its neighbours than a short one, so long chains cling together more, and it takes a higher temperature to pull them apart into a gas. These are the same flickering attractions, added up over millions of tiny hairs on its toes, that let a gecko hang upside down from your ceiling.

That is how a refinery sorts crude oil. The oil is heated until most of it boils, and the vapour rises up a tall tower that gets cooler towards the top. Each kind of molecule condenses back into liquid at the height where the temperature falls below its boiling point: the long, heavy chains low down, and the short ones higher up. Short chains become gas for cooking, middle ones petrol and kerosene, long ones diesel, lubricating oil and wax. If boiling points did not climb steadily with chain length, as Figure 10.3 shows, the mixture could not be sorted this way.

Careful

“When butane boils, its molecules break apart into carbon and hydrogen.”

No C–C or C–H bond breaks when an alkane boils. Boiling only pulls whole molecules away from their neighbours, overcoming the weak dispersion forces between them; the strong bonds inside each molecule are untouched. The molecules in butane gas are exactly the molecules that were in the liquid, and if you cool the gas they become liquid butane again. Breaking the bonds inside the molecule is a different and far bigger job: that is burning, or what a refinery’s “crackers” do at much higher temperatures with a catalyst.

Understand itDispersion forces

What are they?

Weak attractions between all molecules, even ones with no charged ends, caused by electrons bunching up for an instant on one side of a molecule and tugging on the electrons of the next.

Why are they called this?

The physicist Fritz London named them in 1930, because his quantum theory of them closely resembled the theory of the dispersion of light, the way light spreads into colours. Chemists often call them London forces after him. The name comes from the mathematics, not from anything spreading out.

What problem did they solve?

Why should molecules with no charged ends, like the alkanes or the noble gases, stick together at all? Without some attraction, they could never become liquids or solids.

Why do they work?

Electrons are always moving. At any instant one side of a molecule may have a few more, making a fleeting charged end that pulls the electrons of its neighbour into step. Each tug is tiny, but they add up along the whole length of a molecule.

How do they help?

They explain why longer chains boil higher (so a refinery can sort crude oil), why branched molecules boil lower, why straight-chained ghee is solid while kinked olive oil is runny, and how a gecko walks on a ceiling.

Go deeper how do we know, what they aren’t, where do they stop working
How do we know?

Boiling points climb steadily as each carbon is added to an alkane chain, from methane, a gas, to octane, a liquid, with nothing changing except the length of the chain.

What they aren’t

Not bonds inside the molecule. When butane boils, no bond breaks; whole molecules pull away from their neighbours.

Where do they stop working?

They are the weakest attractions between molecules. Where molecules have permanent charged ends, and above all where they can hydrogen-bond, those stronger forces usually decide the boiling point instead.

Your turn

Explain Dispersion forces to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

The alkane ladder

This one is for looking, not for heating. Many homes hold a ladder of alkanes of different lengths. The LPG cylinder in the kitchen holds mostly propane and butane, 3 and 4 carbons long (just look at it; don’t touch the valve). Baby oil (liquid paraffin) is chains of roughly 15 to 30 or more carbons, many of them branched or bent into rings, so they pack together badly. A paraffin candle is mostly straight chains of roughly 20 to 40. Predict first: which is a gas, which a runny liquid, which a solid, and why in that order? Petroleum jelly (Vaseline) sits in between, because it is a mixture: long waxy chains with oily ones trapped among them. Rub a drop of baby oil and a dab of Vaseline between your fingers and feel the difference that chain length makes.

Investigation 10.3

Step the carbon skeleton from methane up to butane, keeping only hydrogens attached. Watch the dispersion attraction and the boiling point. Predict pentane before you look it up.

Check yourself

Propane boils at −42.1 °C and octane at 125.6 °C. One is sold as a liquid fuel for cars; the other is squeezed into gas cylinders for cooking. Which is which, and why?

Answer at the back of the book

10.4Same formula, different molecule

Germany, the 1820s

Isomers

Different compounds with the same molecular formula but atoms joined in a different order.

Two young chemists who had never met were puzzling over two silver compounds. In Paris and then Giessen, Justus von Liebig studied silver fulminate, a substance so dangerous that it exploded at a touch. Friedrich Wöhler, the man who would later make urea, studied silver cyanate, which was perfectly calm. When their analyses were published side by side, something looked badly wrong: both compounds were made of exactly the same elements, in exactly the same proportions. Each chemist suspected the other of a mistake. They checked, and checked again, and found that both were right. Instead of becoming enemies, they became lifelong friends and partners. In 1830 Berzelius gave the puzzle its name: these were isomers, from Greek words meaning “equal parts”.

The story behind this

Two chemists, two silver saltsTwo young rivals analyse two very different silver salts and get exactly the same answer. Each thinks the other has made a mistake. Neither has.

The answer to the puzzle is that a formula lists the parts, but not how they are put together, any more than the list “four wheels, two seats, one engine” tells you whether you have a car or a rickshaw. Here are two substances with exactly the same formula, C₄H₁₀. Each molecule contains 4 carbons and 10 hydrogens, the same atoms, the same mass. One boils at −0.5 °C, the other at −11.7 °C. In butane the four carbons make a straight chain. In isobutane three carbons hang off a central one.

The butane pair differ for the reason you met in 10.3: a compact, branched molecule has less surface in contact with its neighbours than a stretched-out chain, so its dispersion forces are weaker and it boils lower.

The second pair differ far more. C₂H₆O can be ethanol, with its –OH group, or dimethyl ether, with the oxygen in the middle of the chain and every hydrogen attached to carbon. Ethanol boils at 78.4 °C; dimethyl ether at −24.8 °C, more than 100 °C lower. Without a hydrogen attached to the oxygen, dimethyl ether molecules can’t form hydrogen bonds with each other. Same atoms, different arrangement: a liquid you could pour versus a gas.

Careful

“Butane and isobutane boil at different temperatures, so one of them must be heavier.”

They contain exactly the same atoms, so their molecules have exactly the same mass. Any difference in how they behave must come from their shape and their connections, not their mass.

Understand itIsomers

What are they?

Different substances whose molecules contain exactly the same atoms, joined in a different order or arrangement. Same formula, different molecule.

Why are they called this?

Berzelius named them in 1830 from the Greek isos, “equal”, and meros, “part”: made of equal parts.

What problem did they solve?

Liebig’s explosive silver fulminate and Wöhler’s calm silver cyanate had exactly the same composition, and each chemist assumed the other had made a mistake. Isomers showed both were right: what a molecule is made of is not the whole story.

Why does it work?

A molecule’s behaviour depends on how its atoms are connected and on its shape. Rearranging the same atoms can hide or expose a group that forms hydrogen bonds, or make a molecule more compact so its neighbours grip it less.

How do they help?

They warn you that a formula names only the parts, and they explain why ethanol is a liquid while dimethyl ether, with the same atoms, is a gas. Shape matters just as much in medicines and inside your body.

Go deeper how do we know, what they aren’t, where does the idea stop working
How do we know?

Butane and isobutane, both C₄H₁₀, boil at −0.5 °C and −11.7 °C, and can be separated and bottled as two pure substances.

What they aren’t

Not one molecule heavier than the other. Isomers have exactly the same mass; the differences come from shape and connections.

Where does the idea stop working?

Some arrangements turn into each other all the time, for example by spinning around a single bond, so they can’t be bottled separately, and chemists don’t usually count them as different substances. Only when an arrangement is locked, for example by different connections or by a double bond, do you get two separate substances.

Your turn

Explain Isomers to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 10.4

Compare butane with isobutane, then ethanol with dimethyl ether. Before each switch, predict which one boils higher and give your reason.

Check yourself

Pentane, C₅H₁₂, has three isomers: a straight chain; a chain of four with one branch; and a “cross” shape with four carbons around a central one, almost a ball. Put them in order of boiling point, highest first, and explain.

Answer at the back of the book

10.5Double bonds and locked shapes

A kitchen shelf on a winter morning

Look along a kitchen shelf on a cool morning and you will find a puzzle. The ghee in its jar is solid. The coconut oil may be solid too, if the room is cold enough. But the olive oil and the sunflower oil are runny liquids. All of them are fats, made of the same kinds of atoms in the same kinds of long chains. Why are some solid and some liquid at the same temperature? The answer is a tiny, rigid kink.

Double bond

Two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms. A C=C double bond is shorter and stronger than a single bond, and cannot twist.

Carbon atoms can share two pairs of electrons with each other: a double bond, written C=C. Ethene, C₂H₄, is the simplest example. It has two fewer hydrogens than ethane, because each carbon is now using two of its four bonds on its partner. Molecules with C=C bonds are said to be unsaturated: they hold fewer hydrogens than they could.

A single bond is like an axle: the two ends of ethane spin round it freely, billions of times a second at room temperature. A double bond is different. Its second shared pair sits above and below the line between the two carbons, and it only works while the two ends stay lined up, so twisting one end would break part of the bond. At ordinary temperatures, that doesn’t happen. All six atoms of ethene stay in one flat plane, with the bonds around each carbon about 120° apart.

How do we know a double bond really can’t twist? Because some molecules come in two versions that would turn into each other if it could. But-2-ene is a chain of four carbons with a double bond in the middle. It comes as two separate substances: one with the two end groups on the same side of the double bond, which boils at about 4 °C, and one with them on opposite sides, which boils at about 1 °C. Chemists can bottle them separately. If the double bond could spin, there would be only one substance.

Now back to the shelf. The long chains in fats are mostly alkane-like. In ghee and butter, many of the chains are fully saturated and straight, so they pack together neatly, like pencils in a box, and the fat is solid at room temperature. In olive oil, many chains have a double bond with the two halves of the chain on the same side, which puts a fixed kink in the middle. Kinked chains can’t pack neatly, their dispersion forces are weaker, and the oil stays liquid. Stearic acid, a straight 18-carbon chain, melts at about 69 °C; oleic acid, the same length with one kinked double bond, melts at about 13 °C.

The fridge test

Put a spoonful each of ghee or butter, coconut oil (if you have it) and olive or sunflower oil into three small clean bowls and leave them in the fridge for an hour. Which ones turn hard, which go cloudy, and which stay runny? The more straight, saturated chains a fat has, the more easily its molecules pack together into a solid.

Investigation 10.5

Switch between ethane and ethene in both the flat and the 3D views. Count the hydrogens, measure the angles, and try to rotate one end of each.

Check yourself

Why is a fat whose chains are all straight and saturated more likely to be solid at room temperature than an oil whose chains each have a kinked double bond?

Answer at the back of the book

10.6Acids, amines and the links of life

Berlin, 1901

Seventy-three years after Wöhler’s urea, in the same city, the great German chemist Emil Fischer and his colleague Ernest Fourneau did something that would have astonished the believers in a vital force. They took two molecules of glycine, the simplest of the building blocks of proteins, and joined them by hand into a single molecule. It was the first time anyone had deliberately made the kind of link that holds every protein in every living thing together. Fischer went on to build chains of up to eighteen of these building blocks, and showed that they behaved like the fragments you get by breaking real proteins apart. Fischer was a timber merchant’s son whose father, the family story goes, gave up trying to make a businessman of him and sent him off to study instead. He became the most famous organic chemist of his age: he had already worked out the shapes of the sugars, and won the Nobel Prize in 1902. To understand what he joined, and how, we need two more functional groups.

Carboxyl group

–COOH. The functional group of carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid. It can give an H⁺ to water.

Vinegar is sour because of ethanoic acid (also called acetic acid), CH₃COOH. Its working part is the carboxyl group, –COOH: a carbon with a double-bonded oxygen and an –OH. That hydrogen on the end can be passed to a water molecule as H⁺, so ethanoic acid is an acid, though a weak one: in vinegar, only a small fraction of its molecules give up their H⁺ at any moment (Chapter 7). The neighbouring C=O pulls on the electrons nearby, and once the H⁺ has gone, the leftover negative charge is spread over both oxygens rather than sitting on one. That is why the –OH in a carboxyl group gives up H⁺ while the –OH in ethanol essentially does not.

Amino group

–NH₂. A nitrogen with two hydrogens. Its spare pair of electrons can pick up H⁺, so it acts as a weak base.

The amino group, –NH₂, does the opposite. Its nitrogen has a pair of electrons not used in bonding, which can pick up an H⁺. So amines are weak bases. You can smell this one. The fishy smell of fish is mostly a small amine, trimethylamine, drifting into the air. Squeeze lemon on the fish and the smell fades: the lemon’s acid hands H⁺ to the amine’s spare pair of electrons, turning it into a charged ion that stays dissolved in the juice instead of floating up your nose.

Condensation reaction

A reaction in which two molecules join and a small molecule, usually water, is released.

When a carboxyl group meets an –OH or an –NH₂ on another molecule, the two can join together, and in doing so they release a molecule of water. This is called a condensation reaction. An acid joined to an alcohol makes an ester; many esters smell of fruit, and they are part of what makes a ripe banana or pineapple smell the way it does.

Amino acid

A molecule with both an amino group and a carboxyl group. Twenty kinds are used to build the proteins in living things.

Now the big one, the link Fischer made. An amino acid has a carboxyl group and an amino group on the same molecule. So amino acids can join head to tail: the –COOH of one with the –NH₂ of the next, releasing water each time. The new link, –CO–NH–, is called a peptide bond, and the result can join to another amino acid, and another, and another. A protein is a chain of hundreds or thousands of amino acids made exactly this way, folded into a particular shape. Every enzyme in your body, the keratin in your hair and the haemoglobin in your blood were built like this, one water molecule at a time.

Joining amino acids is one thing; seeing the shape of the finished molecule is another. In Oxford, Dorothy Hodgkin, who had fallen in love with crystals as a ten-year-old growing them at home, spent decades photographing how X-rays scatter off crystals of the molecules of life. She worked out the structure of penicillin in 1945, of vitamin B₁₂ in the 1950s, and in 1969, after thirty-four years of trying, of the protein insulin, much of it while living with painful arthritis in her hands. She won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964.

The chemists who followed Wöhler and Fischer turned these ideas into medicines. In Kolkata in the mid-twentieth century, Asima Chatterjee, one of the first women in India to earn a doctorate in science, who had chosen chemistry against the expectations of her time, spent her working life finding out the structures of molecules from plants used in traditional medicine, and helped develop medicines from them. Every one of those molecules was a carbon skeleton with functional groups attached, obeying exactly the rules in this chapter.

Careful

“When two molecules join to make an ester, some atoms are destroyed, which is why the ester is lighter.”

Every atom is accounted for: C₂H₄O₂ + CH₄O → C₃H₆O₂ + H₂O. In grams per mole, 60.05 + 32.04 = 74.08 + 18.02. The ester is lighter than the two starting molecules combined only because one water molecule’s worth of atoms left as water.

Investigation 10.6

Compare the carboxyl, amino and ester options on a short carbon skeleton. For the condensation, count the C, H and O atoms before and after, and find the water.

Check yourself

Glycine, C₂H₅NO₂, has a mass of 75.07 grams per mole. Two glycine molecules join by a peptide bond. What is the formula of the new molecule, and what is its mass per mole? (Water is 18.02 grams per mole.)

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 10

The case of the two clear liquids

Two unlabelled bottles each hold a few millilitres of a colourless liquid. The label that fell off says only “C₂H₆O”. A chemist runs three tests.

  1. Bottle A boils at 78 °C. Bottle B is barely liquid: it is in a sealed, chilled pressure bottle, and when it is opened at room temperature it hisses away as a gas.
  2. Each sample has exactly the same mass per molecule: 46 grams per mole.
  3. A drop of A mixes completely into water. A drop of liquid B, chilled first, mixes with water only partly.

A friend says the labels must be wrong, because one substance can’t have two boiling points. Who is right? Draw both molecules, and explain all three clues.

Show the solution

Both bottles are correctly labelled C₂H₆O. They are isomers: the same atoms joined differently, just as Liebig’s and Wöhler’s silver salts were.

  • Bottle A is ethanol, CH₃–CH₂–OH. Its oxygen carries a hydrogen, so ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to each other (high boiling point, 78.4 °C) and to water (mixes completely).
  • Bottle B is dimethyl ether, CH₃–O–CH₃. All six hydrogens are on carbon, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other; only weaker attractions hold them, and it boils at −24.8 °C. Its oxygen can still accept a hydrogen bond from water, which is why it mixes partly.

Clue 2 rules out the idea that one is heavier: same formula, same mass. The friend’s mistake is assuming a formula names a single substance. It names only the parts.

What this chapter can’t explain yet

Wöhler’s crystals, van ‘t Hoff’s tetrahedra and Fischer’s peptide bond showed that the molecules of life are built from carbon by ordinary chemistry. But the world is bigger than one molecule at a time. When fuel burns, its carbon ends up in the air and the sea; when you charge a phone, electrons and ions are pushed around inside a battery. The last episode of our adventure brings every idea in this book together on the scale of a whole planet.

11

Chapter 11

Earth, materials and energy

The big questionWhen we burn fuel, where does all the carbon go? And can we store energy for later without burning anything at all?

  1. 11.1The ocean and the carbon dioxide we add
  2. 11.2A battery you can refill

Open a cold bottle of soda water and listen. That hiss is carbon dioxide escaping: the gas was squeezed into the water at the factory, and the moment you release the pressure, some of it bubbles out. Taste the water and it is faintly sharp, a little sour, even though nobody added lemon. Something in that water is a weak acid, and it came from the gas.

Hold on to that bottle, because it is a small model of something enormous. The whole ocean is slowly doing what your soda water did at the factory: taking in carbon dioxide from the air above it.

All through this adventure, ideas have lived in separate episodes: atoms in one, acids in another, batteries in a third. The real world doesn’t sort itself like that. A single flame on a gas stove involves counting atoms, breaking and making bonds, energy barriers, moles, the air and, years later, the sea. This last episode follows two of the biggest pieces of chemistry on our planet, the carbon dioxide we add to the air and the batteries we hope will replace much of our burning, and shows that you already have every idea you need to understand them.

11.1The ocean and the carbon dioxide we add

Mauna Loa, Hawaii, March 1958

High on the side of a volcano in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, more than three thousand metres up and thousands of kilometres from the nearest continent, a young American scientist, not yet thirty, named Charles David Keeling set up an instrument to measure one thing: how much carbon dioxide there is in the air. Other people had measured it before, but their numbers jumped about wildly, because air near towns, fields and forests is always being changed by whatever is nearby. Keeling was a keen hiker and camper who had first taken up measuring carbon dioxide almost by accident, as a young researcher in California, carrying glass flasks into forests and up mountains. He was fussy, in the best way. He built careful instruments, checked them against standard gases again and again, and chose a place where the air had blown across thousands of kilometres of open sea.

His first readings were about 315 parts per million: out of every million molecules of air, about 315 were carbon dioxide. Within a couple of years he noticed two things. The number went up and down with the seasons, a few parts per million each year, as the forests of the northern half of the world drew carbon dioxide in each summer and let it out again each winter: the planet breathing. And underneath the breathing, the number climbed, every single year. The measurements have continued ever since, and the line, now called the Keeling curve, has passed 420 parts per million.

The story behind this

The man who measured the airA young scientist builds an instrument fussy enough to measure the air properly, takes it to the top of a volcano, and finds the planet breathing, and changing.

Where is all that carbon dioxide coming from? When methane, petrol or coal burns, its carbon atoms join with oxygen from the air to make carbon dioxide. None of those atoms disappears (Chapter 4), so all of that carbon ends up somewhere. Some stays in the air, where carbon dioxide traps heat and warms the planet. (The warm ground gives off invisible infrared light. Carbon dioxide molecules absorb some of it and send it off again in every direction, some of it back down, so less heat escapes to space.) Some is taken up by plants. And a large share dissolves into the sea: over the past two centuries, the oceans have absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of the carbon dioxide released by burning fuel.

That sounds like good news, and in one way it is: without the oceans, the air would hold even more carbon dioxide. But dissolving carbon dioxide changes the sea, exactly as it changed your soda water. When CO₂ dissolves, a little of it reacts with water to make carbonic acid, H₂CO₃, a weak acid that can pass an H⁺ to water:

CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

Carbonic acid

H₂CO₃, a weak acid formed when carbon dioxide reacts with water. It gives the slight sharpness to fizzy drinks.

More H⁺ means a lower pH. But seawater has a defence, and you met it in Chapter 7: a buffer. Seawater contains carbonate ions, CO₃²⁻, and most of the new H⁺ ions are picked up by them, turning them into bicarbonate ions, HCO₃⁻:

H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻

Put the two steps together and count everything. For every molecule of carbon dioxide that dissolves and reacts, one carbonate ion is used up and two bicarbonate ions are made:

CO₂ + H₂O + CO₃²⁻ → 2 HCO₃⁻

Buffer

A solution containing particles that take up added H⁺ (or OH⁻), so its pH changes much less than it otherwise would.

The buffer race

Ask an adult to help you make red cabbage indicator: chop a few leaves of red cabbage, cover them with warm tap water, leave them for half an hour, then strain off the purple liquid. Pour equal amounts into two glasses and top each up with the same amount of water (filtered RO drinking water, if you have it, gives the clearest result). Into one glass only, stir the tiniest pinch of baking soda, just enough to turn it blue-green: this is your pretend sea, slightly basic and buffered. The other glass is plain water with no buffer.

Predict first. You are going to blow ten slow breaths through a straw into each glass (blow out only; never suck up the liquid). Which glass will change colour first?

Your breath carries carbon dioxide, made when your body “burns” its food, and in water it makes carbonic acid. The plain glass shifts towards pinkish purple quite quickly; the change is gentle, so judge it against white paper. The pretend sea holds its colour much longer, because its bicarbonate soaks up the H⁺. Keep blowing into it, ten breaths at a time, and slowly it drifts towards purple too: the buffer is being worn down, breath by breath, just as the sea’s carbonate is. For one more link in the chain, an adult can hold an upturned glass a hand’s width above a lit tealight for ten seconds, slide a saucer over its mouth while turning it the right way up, then pour in a little indicator and swirl: burning, too, makes carbon dioxide. That change is small, so look against white paper. (Drink none of it.)

So the buffer works: the sea’s pH has not plunged towards the pH of lemon juice. But a buffer is not free. Every H⁺ it soaks up uses up a carbonate ion, and corals, oysters, sea snails and many tiny plankton build their shells and skeletons out of exactly those ions:

Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ CaCO₃ (shell)

Ocean acidification

The slow fall in the pH of seawater as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air.

With fewer carbonate ions around, it becomes harder for them to build shells, and in places where the water is already low in carbonate, existing shells can start to dissolve. This whole process is called ocean acidification.

A shell in vinegar

Put a clean piece of eggshell (or a small seashell) in a glass and cover it with white vinegar. Watch closely: tiny bubbles form on the shell. Leave it overnight and see how much of the shell is left. Eggshell and seashell are both mostly calcium carbonate, CaCO₃; the acid in vinegar takes away its carbonate as carbon dioxide gas. Vinegar is far, far more acidic than seawater, so this is a dramatic, sped-up picture, not what is happening in the ocean. But the chemistry pulling on the carbonate is the same.

The pH of the surface ocean has fallen from about 8.2 before industry began to about 8.1 today. A tenth of a pH unit sounds tiny. But remember that each step on the pH scale is a factor of ten (Chapter 7):

Change of 0.1 in pH → H⁺ concentration multiplied by 10⁰·¹
10⁰·¹ = 1.26
So there are about 26% more hydrogen ions in surface seawater than before industry. (You will often see “about 30%” quoted, because estimates of the starting pH vary a little.)

Careful

“Ocean acidification means the sea is turning into acid.”

Seawater is still slightly basic: its pH of about 8.1 is above 7, the neutral point. “Acidification” means moving towards acid, not becoming acidic. The worry is not that the sea will burn your skin. It is that the carbonate balance that marine life depends on is shifting faster than it has for a very long time. Nor is it caused by factory waste or acid rain: it is the same carbon dioxide that is in your soda water, simply far more of it.

How do we know the sea is really changing, and not just the air? Keeling’s curve tells us about the air. For the water, scientists needed a second patient watcher. Since 1988, researchers have sailed regularly to a spot in the open ocean north of Hawaii, a station called ALOHA, and sampled the seawater there, month after month. As the carbon dioxide in the air has risen, the dissolved carbon dioxide in the water has risen with it, and the pH has fallen steadily: by a few hundredths of a unit in thirty years. Two long, careful records, one of the air and one of the sea, tell the same story.

Understand itOcean acidification

What is it?

The slow fall in the pH of seawater as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. The sea is still slightly basic, at about pH 8.1; it is moving towards acid, not becoming acid.

Why is it called this?

To acidify is to make more acidic, from the Latin acidus, “sour”. The name describes the direction of change, which is exactly why it can mislead: it does not mean the sea is turning into acid.

What problem does the idea explain?

Scientists knew the sea was soaking up a large share of the carbon dioxide from burning fuel, which sounded like good news. This idea names the hidden cost: the water’s chemistry changes, and shell-building animals find it harder to build.

Why does it happen?

Carbon dioxide reacts with water to make carbonic acid, which releases H⁺. Carbonate ions in seawater mop up most of that H⁺, so the pH falls only a little, but every carbonate that does so is used up: CO₂ + H₂O + CO₃²⁻ → 2 HCO₃⁻.

How does it help?

It explains why corals, oysters and plankton are at risk even though the pH has changed by only about a tenth, and why the carbon dioxide we add to the air matters for the sea as well as for the climate.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does the simple picture stop working
How do we know?

Two long records agree: Keeling’s measurements of carbon dioxide in the air since 1958, and monthly samples of seawater at Station ALOHA since 1988, where dissolved carbon dioxide has risen and the pH has fallen steadily.

What it isn’t

Not caused by factory waste or acid rain, and not the sea becoming sour or harmful to swim in. It is the same carbon dioxide that is in soda water, simply far more of it.

Where does the simple picture stop working?

The sea is not one beaker. Cold water takes up more carbon dioxide, some regions are already low in carbonate, and currents mix the water slowly, so the change is uneven from place to place.

Your turn

Explain Ocean acidification to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 11.1

Use the buffer model in the app. Add base or acid in small steps and watch how little the pH moves while both partners of the buffer are present; then keep going until one partner runs out. How is the sea’s carbonate like the partner that gets used up?

Check yourself

If the surface ocean’s pH fell from 8.1 to 7.8, by what factor would the concentration of H⁺ ions increase?
