11.2A battery you can refill

Oxford, England, 1980

In a laboratory at the University of Oxford, a professor named John Goodenough was hunting for a better material to hold lithium. He was already in his late fifties, an age at which many scientists slow down. As a boy he had struggled badly to learn to read (he was probably dyslexic), and he had served as a weather forecaster in the Second World War before coming to science. He never stopped working: he was still going to his laboratory in his nineties. A few years earlier, Stanley Whittingham, working for the oil company Exxon in the United States, had shown that lithium ions could slip in and out between the layers of a solid and make a working rechargeable cell. But Whittingham’s cells used pure lithium metal, which could catch fire, and they gave only a little over 2 volts. Goodenough reasoned that a metal oxide, built in layers, should hold onto incoming electrons more strongly and so give a higher voltage. His team tried lithium cobalt oxide. It gave about 4 volts.

Five years later in Japan, Akira Yoshino, working for the chemical company Asahi Kasei, took the last dangerous piece away. Instead of lithium metal on the other side, he used a form of carbon that could hold lithium atoms tucked between its layers. The cell no longer contained any bare lithium metal at all, and it was far safer. The first lithium-ion batteries went on sale, made by Sony, in 1991. In 2019 the three men shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Goodenough was 97, the oldest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.

The story behind this

The battery in your pocketThree scientists on three continents, working over fifteen years, built the light, rechargeable battery that powers phones and electric cars.
Lithium-ion cell

A rechargeable cell in which lithium ions move back and forth between layers of graphite and layers of a metal oxide, while electrons travel through the outside circuit.

What did they build? Burning releases energy by moving electrons into lower-energy arrangements, as fuel and oxygen turn into carbon dioxide and water. A battery does something similar with electrons, but without fire and without making carbon dioxide, and a rechargeable battery can do it backwards too. The phone in your hand most likely runs on a lithium-ion cell.

Inside, there are two layered materials, separated by a liquid or gel that lets ions through but not electrons (Chapter 8). On one side is graphite, the same flat sheets of carbon as in a pencil, the very pencil this adventure began with. When the cell is charged, lithium atoms are tucked between those sheets. On the other side is a metal oxide, for example Goodenough’s cobalt oxide, also built in layers with gaps between them.

Picture two books. The graphite is one book, and its sheets are the pages; the lithium atoms are slips of paper tucked between the pages. The metal oxide is a second book. Using the battery slides the slips out of the first book, across, and in between the pages of the second. Charging pushes them back. No page is torn and no slip is lost, which is why it can be done hundreds of times.

When you switch on the phone, the cell discharges. Each lithium atom between the graphite sheets gives up one electron and becomes a lithium ion, Li⁺. The electron cannot cross the separator, so it takes the long way round: out through the wire, through the phone, doing useful work, and in at the other side. Meanwhile the Li⁺ ion travels the short way, straight through the electrolyte, and slips in between the layers of the metal oxide, where it meets the electron again.

Count the charges and you will see why the two paths must go together. Every time an electron leaves one side through the wire, a positive ion leaves the same side through the electrolyte, so neither side builds up a charge. Stop either flow (cut the wire, or block the ions) and the other stops too.

When you charge the phone, the charger does work: it pushes electrons back through the wire to the graphite, and the lithium ions follow them back across the electrolyte into the graphite layers. This is the uphill direction (an electrolytic process, Chapter 8), which is why it needs a power supply. No atoms are made or lost in either direction. The same lithium atoms shuttle back and forth, which is why these cells are sometimes called “rocking-chair” batteries.

Why lithium? Three reasons, all from earlier episodes. It is the lightest metal: a mole of lithium has a mass of only 6.94 g. Each atom gives up exactly one electron, so each 6.94 g of lithium can deliver a whole mole of electrons. And lithium gives up that electron very readily, which makes the voltage of a lithium cell high, about 3.6 to 3.7 volts, compared with about 1.1 volts for the zinc–copper cell in Chapter 8.

Moles of electrons per kilogram of metal:
Lithium: 1000 g ÷ 6.94 g per mole × 1 electron = about 144 moles of electrons
Lead (in a car battery, each atom gives 2 electrons): 1000 g ÷ 207.2 g per mole × 2 = about 9.7 moles of electrons
Lithium can deliver about 15 times as many electrons per kilogram.

A whole cell is much heavier than the lithium inside it (there is graphite, metal oxide, electrolyte, casing and wiring too), so a real lithium-ion battery stores several times more energy per kilogram than a lead–acid battery, not fifteen times. That is still why phones and electric cars use lithium.

Careful

“Charging fills a battery up with electrons from the wall socket, so a full battery is heavier.”

The number of electrons in the cell never changes. For every electron the charger pushes into the graphite side, it pulls one out of the metal oxide side. What charging stores is energy: the lithium and its electrons are pushed back into a higher-energy arrangement, ready to run downhill again. (Batteries do slowly wear out, but not because anything is used up by electrons leaving. Side reactions slowly trap some of the lithium in a thin crust on the graphite, so there is less to shuttle.)

Understand itThe lithium-ion battery

What is it?

A rechargeable cell in which lithium ions shuttle between layers of graphite and layers of a metal oxide, while electrons travel round the outside circuit, through your phone.

Why is it called this?

After the ions that do the shuttling. Lithium was named in 1817 by Berzelius, after his student Arfwedson found it, from the Greek lithos, “stone”, because it was discovered in a mineral, unlike potassium, first found in plant ashes, and sodium, known partly from animal blood.

What problem did it solve?

Earlier rechargeable batteries were heavy for the energy they held, and the first lithium cells used bare lithium metal, which could catch fire. Goodenough’s oxide gave a high voltage, and Yoshino’s carbon removed the bare metal: light, safe, rechargeable power.

Why does it work?

Lithium gives up its single outer electron very readily, and its small ion fits neatly between the layers of both materials. Discharging lets lithium and its electrons run downhill into the metal oxide; charging pushes them back up into the graphite. No atoms are made or lost, so it can be repeated hundreds of times.

How does it help?

It powers phones, laptops and electric cars, and it can store electricity from sunshine and wind for later: energy without burning anything.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Lithium is the lightest metal: a kilogram can deliver about 144 moles of electrons, against about 9.7 for lead. And a lithium-ion cell gives about 3.6 to 3.7 volts, against about 1.1 for the zinc–copper cell.

What it isn’t

Not a tank that fills up with electrons from the wall socket. The number of electrons inside never changes; charging stores energy by pushing the lithium into a higher-energy arrangement.

Where does it stop working?

Side reactions slowly trap some lithium, so capacity fades over the years. Damaged or overheated cells can catch fire. And the lithium and cobalt must be mined, which has costs of its own.

Your turn

Explain The lithium-ion battery to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Investigation 11.2

Step the electron transfers in the cell model forward and count what is conserved at each step: atoms of each kind, total charge, electrons. Then compare the spontaneous direction with the uphill, charging direction.

Check yourself

Why must lithium ions move through the electrolyte at the same time as electrons move through the wire? What would happen if they could not?

Answer at the back of the book

Case file 11

The kilogram of gas

The piped gas in many Mumbai kitchens is mostly methane, CH₄. Suppose a family’s stove burns exactly 1.00 kg of it over a few weeks. This last case needs everything you have learned on the whole journey. Here is what the clues say.

  1. One mole of methane has a mass of 16.04 g. Burning it: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.
  2. Careful measurement shows that the flames produced 2.74 kg of carbon dioxide and 2.25 kg of water vapour: almost 5 kg of products from 1 kg of fuel.
  3. Average bond energies, in kilojoules per mole of bonds: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 799, O–H 463.
  4. A sealed bottle of methane and air can sit on a shelf for years without burning, yet a single spark lights it.
  5. Over the following years, a share of that carbon dioxide dissolves in the sea.

Answer these, and for each one say which of the book’s four big ideas (count everything; opposite charges attract; jiggling against sticking; huge numbers make steady averages) you used.

(a) Where did the extra mass of the products come from? (b) Burning breaks every bond in the methane and oxygen, and breaking bonds always costs energy. So why does the flame give out heat? How much, for the whole kilogram? (c) Why doesn’t the gas burn on its own, and why does one spark set it going? (d) What happens to the sea’s carbonate when the CO₂ dissolves?

Show the solution

(a) From the air. 1.00 kg of methane is 1000 ÷ 16.04 = 62.3 moles. The equation needs 2 moles of O₂ for each mole of CH₄, so the flame took 124.7 moles of oxygen, 3.99 kg, out of the kitchen air. Mass in: 1.00 + 3.99 = 4.99 kg. Mass out: 2.74 + 2.25 = 4.99 kg. Every atom is accounted for. Count everything, using moles: huge numbers.

(b) Making bonds pays back more than breaking them costs. For one mole of methane:

  • Break 4 C–H and 2 O=O: 4 × 413 + 2 × 498 = 2,648 kJ taken in.
  • Make 2 C=O and 4 O–H: 2 × 799 + 4 × 463 = 3,450 kJ given out.
  • Net: 2,648 − 3,450 = −802 kJ per mole, which matches the measured value for methane burning to carbon dioxide and water vapour.

For the whole kilogram: 62.3 × 802 ≈ 50,000 kJ, or 50 megajoules. The new bonds hold their atoms more tightly than the old ones did: opposite charges attract, and the electrons end up in lower-energy positions, closer to the nuclei that pull on them.

(c) An energy barrier. At room temperature, only a tiny fraction of collisions between methane and oxygen molecules are energetic enough to get over the barrier and start breaking bonds. A spark makes a small spot so hot that many collisions there do get over it; the heat they release then keeps the next layer of gas hot enough, and the flame keeps going. Jiggling against sticking.

(d) It gets used up. The CO₂ forms carbonic acid, and most of the H⁺ it releases is taken up by carbonate ions, turning them into bicarbonate. The pH falls only a little, but there is less carbonate left for shell-building animals. Equilibria and buffers: huge numbers make steady averages, together with count everything, since every carbon atom from the gas ends up somewhere.

One last story before the end. The alchemists of the Middle Ages, the people who first set up furnaces and flasks and began the long road to chemistry, dreamed above all of turning lead into gold. Chemistry could never do it: as you now know, a reaction only rearranges electrons, and an element is fixed by the number of protons in its nucleus. Only nuclear physics can change that number. In 2025 scientists at CERN’s ALICE experiment reported that lead nuclei, smashed past each other at almost the speed of light, had sometimes lost three protons and become gold: billions of nuclei in all, adding up to only a tiny fraction of a billionth of a gram. In October 2026 a start-up company, Marathon Fusion, claimed to have made gold from mercury using neutrons from fusion; at the time of writing, no one else has yet checked that claim. The old dream came true, in a way nobody in the Middle Ages could have imagined, and it turned out not to matter much. Chemistry’s real treasure was never gold. It was understanding.

The story behind this

Mercury into gold, at lastThe alchemists’ dream came true in the twentieth century, but in a way no alchemist imagined, and it turned out that the gold was not the treasure.

Where you go from here

You started this adventure with a pencil and a diamond, and a question about how anyone can know what is inside things too small to see. Look how far you have travelled since. You stood with Greek thinkers arguing about whether a pebble could be cut forever. You watched a Manchester schoolteacher weigh things nobody could see, and a young team fire particles at gold foil in a darkened room and find almost all of an atom is empty. You counted protons, weighed molecules by the mole, watched energy run downhill and be pushed uphill, saw Wöhler’s crystals and van ‘t Hoff’s tetrahedra, and followed carbon from a gas flame in a Mumbai kitchen, through Keeling’s air, into the sea. And the graphite in that first pencil turned out to be the same carbon that holds the lithium in the phone in your pocket.

Every person you met in this book began exactly where you are now: with a question, some careful measurements, and a willingness to be wrong for a while. None of them knew all the answers. Many got things wrong before they got them right. What they had was the habit you now have too: asking how do we know?, and not stopping until the evidence answers.

There is so much more still to find. Beyond this book, electrons stop looking like dots and become clouds of probability, described by quantum mechanics. Chemists design new molecules step by step, from medicines to materials for better batteries. And some of the most important open questions in the world, how to capture carbon dioxide, how to store sunlight, how life began, are chemistry questions that nobody has fully answered yet. The adventure does not end here. It just stops being a book and starts being yours.

1817 to today

The families of the table

Johann Döbereiner, Humphry Davy, William Ramsay, Homi Bhabha

Crawford Market, Mumbai, any afternoon

Walk through a big Mumbai market and the periodic table is all around you, though nobody has labelled it. The salt in the spice stalls is sodium and chlorine. The steel tiffin boxes are iron with chromium and nickel. The copper handi in the pot shop, the aluminium pressure cooker, the neon-red shop sign, the paan seller’s tin of chuna, the phone in your pocket with its lithium battery and its tiny speaker magnet: every one of them is a member of a family.

Chemists first noticed the families two hundred years ago. In 1817 Johann Döbereiner, in Jena, saw that some elements came in threes with matching habits. You can read that story in the periodic-table story. Here is the cast list as we know it now, column by column, with where to meet each family yourself.

The alkali metals (column 1)

Lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium. Every one has a single electron alone in its outer shell, and it is held loosely, so these metals hand it over at the slightest chance. They are soft enough to cut with a knife, so reactive that they are stored under oil, and they react with water more fiercely the further down you go: lithium fizzes, sodium skates about, potassium bursts into lilac flame. You will never see the metals themselves at home, but their ions are everywhere: sodium in salt, potassium in bananas and coconut water, lithium in the battery of every phone.

The alkaline earth metals (column 2)

Beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, radium. Two outer electrons, a little more firmly held, so they are tougher and less wild than their neighbours. Calcium is in your bones and teeth, in milk, in the marble of old buildings and in chuna, the slaked lime the paan seller spreads on a leaf (it is strongly alkaline, which is why it must never go near eyes). Magnesium sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule, so every green leaf of palak contains it. Strontium makes the crimson of Diwali rockets, and barium the green.

The transition metals (the sunken middle)

Iron, copper, zinc, chromium, nickel, silver, gold, platinum and their neighbours. These are the hard, shiny, useful metals of everyday life. Their newest electrons go into an inner d room, so their outer surfaces look much alike and they mix happily into alloys. Most steel kitchen vessels in India are stainless steel, iron mixed with chromium and usually some nickel (the best grade, often stamped 18/8, has about 18 percent chromium and 8 percent nickel), the chromium forming an invisible skin that stops rust. Copper carries electricity through the wires in your walls. Zinc coats nails and buckets to protect them. Many transition metals make coloured compounds: the blue of copper sulfate, the green of a copper statue, the reds and yellows of iron in the soil.

The boron group and the carbon group (columns 13 and 14)

Here the family characters start to change as you go down a column, from non-metal at the top to metal at the bottom. In column 13, aluminium is the metal of foil and pressure cookers; indium, below it, is in the clear electrical coating on your phone’s touchscreen. Column 14 begins with carbon, the backbone of every living thing (the whole of Chapter 10), then silicon, which as silicon dioxide makes up the quartz in most sand and glass, and which is the heart of the chips in every computer, then tin and lead, which are plainly metals.

The nitrogen and oxygen families (columns 15 and 16)

Nitrogen makes up 78 percent of the air you breathe; phosphorus, below it, is on the striking strip of every matchbox and in the backbone of your DNA. Oxygen is the most abundant element in your body by mass; sulfur, just below, is behind the sharp smell of cut onions and of hing in the tadka. Same outer electrons, very different looks: a reminder that families share chemistry, not appearance.

The halogens (column 17)

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine. Each is one electron short of a full outer shell, and taking an electron from another atom releases energy, so they are fierce, poisonous and colourful: pale yellow fluorine, yellow-green chlorine, red-brown liquid bromine, nearly black iodine with a purple vapour. Tamed as ions, they are everywhere. Chlorine disinfects city tap water and is the “chlor” in bleach. Fluoride in toothpaste hardens teeth. Most salt sold in India has a little iodine added, because a lack of iodine harms growing children.

The noble gases (column 18)

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon. Full outer shells, so they almost never react: for a century chemists barely noticed them, until William Ramsay’s work in the 1890s (his life story tells it). Neon glows orange-red in signs; argon fills welding torches and old-style light bulbs; helium lifts party balloons.

The lanthanides and actinides (the floating strip)

The lanthanides, once called the rare earths, are fifteen near-twins that chemists took a century to separate. They are hidden inside modern life: neodymium makes the tiny powerful magnets in phone speakers and earphones; a coating containing cerium helps turn the blue light of a white LED bulb into white. The actinides are all radioactive. Uranium fuels nuclear power stations, including India’s first, at Tarapur, about a hundred kilometres north of Mumbai, which started up in 1969. Thorium matters especially to India, which has large reserves of it in the monazite sands of Kerala; Homi Bhabha planned India’s nuclear programme around using it one day.

Careful

“Elements in the same family look the same.”

They share outer electrons, so they share chemical habits: what they combine with and in what ratios. They can look completely different. Fluorine is a gas and iodine is a solid; carbon is a black powder or a diamond while lead is a soft grey metal. Look for the family resemblance in how they react, not in how they look.

A family hunt in the kitchen

With an adult, go through the kitchen and the bathroom and read labels. Make a chart with a column for each family and add every element you can find a sign of: sodium and chlorine in salt, iodine in iodised salt, sodium in baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate), calcium in chuna or calcium tablets, aluminium in foil, iron, chromium and nickel in steel vessels, copper in a copper vessel or wire, fluorine in toothpaste, carbon in sugar. Read and look only: do not open or taste anything that is not ordinary food, and leave chuna and cleaning products closed. Which family turns up most? Which can you not find at all?

When you meet a new element, ask first: which family is it in? That one question tells you more about how it will behave than any other fact you could learn about it.

How to remember the periodic table

Hermann Ebbinghaus, Henry Roediger, Jeffrey Karpicke

A study table at home, the night before a test

It is late, the chapter is open, and the periodic table stares back: 118 boxes, every one with a symbol, a name and a number. The temptation is to read it over and over until it sticks. That is the method most people use, and research on learning suggests it is one of the least effective there is. This story is about better ways, and about something even more useful: how to understand the table so well that you hardly need to memorise it at all.

Step 1: understand before you memorise

A chemist who has forgotten where molybdenum goes can still draw the periodic table, because the shape is not arbitrary. It is the 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 pattern of electron rooms (the table-shape story explains why). If you can draw the skeleton from memory, you already know where every block is and roughly where every element must sit.

So learn the skeleton first, as a drawing, not as a list:

Row 1: one box on the far left, one on the far right (hydrogen and helium).
Rows 2 and 3: two boxes on the left, six on the right, a gap between.
Rows 4 and 5: two on the left, a block of ten in the middle, six on the right: 18.
Rows 6 and 7: the same, plus a strip of fourteen floated underneath: 32.

Then learn the families, because a family tells you more than a name ever will. Column 1 is the soft, violent alkali metals; column 17 the fierce halogens; column 18 the calm noble gases (the families story introduces them all). Once you know that sodium is in column 1, you know a dozen things about it without memorising any of them.

Step 2: memorise strategically

Not all 118 boxes deserve equal effort. Most of the chemistry in this book uses the first twenty elements, plus a handful of famous metals (iron, copper, zinc, silver, gold, mercury, lead) and the halogens bromine and iodine. Learn those well and you can read almost any chemistry you will meet for years. The rest you can always look up, and you will find you remember more of them each time you do.

The first twenty, in order, are hydrogen, helium, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, neon, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, argon, potassium and calcium.

Step 3: use methods that actually work

Psychologists have studied memory for more than a century, since Hermann Ebbinghaus in Germany in the 1880s memorised long lists of nonsense syllables and measured how fast he forgot them. Three findings matter most for you.

Test yourself instead of rereading. In a well-known 2006 experiment, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke in the United States had students study a passage, then either study it again or take a practice test. A week later, the students who had tested themselves remembered much more. The struggle to pull something out of your memory is what makes it stick. Reading the table again feels productive; covering it and trying to write it down actually is.

Space it out. A large review of hundreds of experiments, published in 2006 by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues, found that the same amount of practice spread over several days beats cramming it into one session, often by a lot. Ten minutes a day for a week works better than seventy minutes the night before. Each time you are about to forget something and you pull it back, the memory becomes stronger. This idea is called spaced repetition.

Chunk it. In 1956 the psychologist George Miller pointed out that we hold only a few separate items in mind at once, but each item can be a big “chunk”. Do not learn twenty separate elements; learn four rows of the table, or the families, as chunks.

Step 4: tricks that help the hard parts

For lists that have no logic, like the order of the first twenty, memory tricks really do help.

A mnemonic is a sentence whose words start with the same letters as the things you need to remember. The best ones are the ones you make yourself, because making one is itself a kind of practice, and silly or vivid ones stick best. Here is one we made up for this book, with a Mumbai flavour:

Hungry Hens Like Bel But Can’t Nibble Our Fried Neems; Naughty Monkeys Always Silently Pinch Samosas, Clever Arjun Keeps Calm.

(Bel is the wood-apple fruit; neem leaves are bitter, so a fried neem would indeed be hard to nibble.) Now make a better one of your own.

A memory palace is an older trick. According to a story told by the Roman writer Cicero, the Greek poet Simonides survived the collapse of a banquet hall and could name the dead by remembering where each guest had been sitting. Whether or not that happened, the method works: imagine walking through a place you know well, such as your home, and leave each element at a spot along the way. Hydrogen in a balloon at the front door, helium floating beside it, lithium in the phone on the shoe rack, and so on. To recall them, walk the route again in your mind.

There are also songs. The most famous is “The Elements” by the American musician Tom Lehrer, from 1959, which rattles through the names to a tune by Gilbert and Sullivan. If a tune helps you, make your own: a familiar melody with element names fitted to it can be remarkably sticky.

Careful

“Learning the periodic table means memorising all 118 boxes.”

Chemists do not carry 118 boxes in their heads. They carry the shape, the families and the trends, plus the elements they use most, and they look up the rest. Understanding the pattern is worth far more than reciting it, because the pattern lets you predict, and reciting does not.

Practise here

On the book’s page “The periodic table, inside out” you will find a Practise tab, a memory trainer that quizzes you on symbols, names and positions and brings back the ones you got wrong more often: spaced repetition, done for you. Use it a little every day rather than a lot at once.

A week with the skeleton

Every day for seven days, before you look at anything, take a blank sheet and draw the skeleton of the periodic table from memory: the towers, the sunken middle, the right-hand block, the floating strip. Then fill in as many of the first twenty elements as you can. Only then check against the real table and mark what you got wrong. Keep all seven sheets. On day seven, lay them side by side: you will see your memory grow, and you will have used testing, spacing and chunking all at once.

The aim was never to become a walking list. It is to know the table the way you know your own neighbourhood: not every house number, but where everything is, and how to find the rest.

1871 to today

A map that predicts

Dmitri Mendeleev, Marguerite Perey, Emilio Segrè

A map is useful because it tells you about places you have never been. Look at a map of Maharashtra and, even if you have never visited Nashik, you can guess it is inland, north-east of Mumbai, and higher up. The periodic table is a map of that kind. Its greatest power is not that it lists what we know; it is that it lets you work out what you don’t know.

Mendeleev was the first to play this game. In 1871 he described an undiscovered element he called eka-silicon, the gap below silicon. He predicted atoms about 72 times as heavy as hydrogen and a density of about 5.5 grams per cubic centimetre. When germanium was found in Germany in 1886, its atoms came out at about 72.6 and its density at about 5.3. (His life story, and the story of the periodic table, tell the whole adventure.) Now it is your turn.

How to play

There are three rules, and you already know them all.

  1. Find the family. Elements in the same column have the same outer electrons, so they have the same chemical habits.
  2. Follow the trend down the column. Going down, atoms get bigger, the outer electrons sit further out and are held less tightly, so metals get more reactive and non-metals less so. Melting points, colours and densities usually change step by step.
  3. Expect surprises at the extremes. Very heavy atoms have so many protons that their inner electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, and that changes things. (This is why gold is yellow instead of silvery, an effect of Einstein’s relativity on its electrons.)

Predict first: francium sits at the very bottom of column 1, below caesium. Before you tap its tower, decide: taller than caesium’s, or shorter? Then tap it.

It is slightly shorter: 223 picometres against caesium’s 232. Rule 2 says it should be bigger, so this is rule 3 at work. Calculations suggest that in an atom this heavy, relativity pulls the outer electron in a little closer than the simple trend predicts. Nobody has ever had enough francium to measure its size, so this number comes from those calculations, not from a ruler.

Round one: francium

Paris, 1939

Marguerite Perey had joined Marie Curie’s laboratory as an assistant at nineteen. In 1939, carefully purifying a radioactive substance, she noticed radiation that did not fit any known element. She had found element 87, at the bottom of column 1, and named it francium after her country. In 1962 she became the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences, as a corresponding member.

Here is the puzzle: almost nobody has ever seen francium. Its longest-lived form falls apart with a half-life of about 22 minutes, so there is never more than a trace of it anywhere, and nobody has ever gathered enough to see a lump. So what is it like? Use the map.

Column 1 going down: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, then francium.
Each is softer than the one above, melts at a lower temperature and reacts more violently with water.
Caesium melts at about 28 °C, a warm day in Mumbai.
Prediction: francium is a very soft, silvery metal that would melt on a warm day, and would react explosively with water.

That prediction is almost certainly close to the truth, but no one can test it directly, because a visible piece of francium would heat itself, and break apart, from its own radioactivity. The map is the best description we have.

Round two: astatine

Berkeley, 1940

Emilio Segrè and his colleagues made element 85 in 1940 by firing particles at bismuth, and called it astatine, from the Greek for “unstable”. It sits at the bottom of the halogens, under iodine. Like francium, it is so radioactive that only tiny amounts ever exist.

Column 17 going down: fluorine (pale yellow gas), chlorine (yellow-green gas), bromine (red-brown liquid), iodine (nearly black solid with a purple vapour), then astatine.
The colour gets darker and the element goes from gas to liquid to solid.
Prediction: astatine is a black solid, and it behaves like a weaker version of iodine.

Good chemistry, and mostly right. But this is where rule 3 comes in. Some calculations suggest that if you could ever gather enough astatine to look at, it might behave like a metal, shiny and conducting, not like the other halogens. The bottom of the table is where the simple trends start to bend. Nobody has been able to check.

Careful

“If an element is in the table, someone must have seen it.”

Several elements near the bottom have only ever existed a few atoms at a time, for seconds or less. For those, everything we “know” about how a lump of them would look and behave comes from position in the table and from calculations, not from seeing it. That is not cheating: it is the table doing exactly what Mendeleev built it to do.

Round three: elements that do not exist yet

The table ends at element 118, oganesson, which completes row 7. What would element 119 be?

Use the map. A new row starts with a new s room, so element 119 would sit at the top of a new row 8, in column 1, under francium. It should be an alkali metal with one outer electron. The simple trend says it would be the most violent alkali metal of all. But calculations that include relativity suggest the opposite: its outer electron is pulled in closer than the trend predicts, so it may be less reactive than caesium and francium, more like potassium. That is a prediction about an element no one has made. As this book was written, in 2026, teams in Japan and Russia were trying, or preparing, to make it by smashing nuclei together, so far without success.

Is there an island out there?

Most of the heaviest elements fall apart in seconds or less. But physicists have long predicted that certain combinations of protons and neutrons should be unusually stable, the way full electron shells are. Somewhere beyond the elements we have made, there may be an island of stability, where superheavy nuclei last much longer: minutes, days, perhaps much more. Nobody has reached it yet. The heaviest atoms made so far have too few neutrons to land on it, and whether the island exists, and how long its atoms would last, is still an open question.

Will the table ever end?

Nobody knows. Each new element is harder to make than the last, and the nuclei get less stable. Some calculations suggest that beyond about 170 protons the atom itself would behave very strangely, because the nucleus pulls so hard on its innermost electrons. But no one is close to testing that, and it is quite possible the practical end will come long before. One of the most famous charts in science still has an unwritten edge.

Play the prediction game

Cover the bottom of a printed periodic table with a sheet of paper so you can see only the top three rows. Choose any column. Write down two facts about each element you can see (gas, liquid or solid; metal or not; reactive or calm) and look for the trend. Then predict the next element down: its state at room temperature, whether it is a metal, and whether it is more or less reactive. Uncover it and look it up. Score yourself a point for each prediction that was right. Mendeleev would have scored very well.

The periodic table is not a finished list to learn by heart. It is a tool for thinking, and its most exciting boxes are the ones where you have to reason your way to the answer.

13.8 billion years ago to 2017

Where the elements come from

Cecilia Payne, Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler, Fred Hoyle, Jennifer Johnson

Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1925

Cecilia Payne was twenty-five, an English student who had crossed the Atlantic because women in Cambridge, England, could study science but could not be awarded degrees. At Harvard College Observatory she was given thousands of glass photographs of starlight, each one spread into a spectrum crossed by dark lines: the fingerprints of elements, the same kind Bunsen and Kirchhoff had found in flames (the spectra story tells that part).

Using the new physics of the atom, Payne worked out not just which elements were in the stars, but how much of each. Her answer was astonishing. The stars were not made of roughly the same stuff as the Earth, as everyone assumed. They were overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium, with everything else a light sprinkling. The most senior astronomer in America, Henry Norris Russell, told her the result was “clearly impossible”, and in her thesis she wrote that the huge amount of hydrogen was “almost certainly not real”. A few years later Russell himself reached the same conclusion by another route. Her thesis has since been called one of the most brilliant ever written in astronomy.

She was right. By mass, the ordinary matter of the universe is about three-quarters hydrogen and about a quarter helium. Everything else, all the carbon and oxygen and iron and gold, adds up to around two percent. So where did that come from?

Chapter one of the story: the Big Bang

About 13.8 billion years ago the universe was unimaginably hot and dense, and it was expanding fast. In the first few minutes it was hot enough for protons and neutrons to fuse, but it cooled too quickly to get far. It made hydrogen, helium and a tiny trace of lithium, and then the window closed.

That means something remarkable about you. Most of the atoms in your body are hydrogen (you are mostly water, and each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms). Nearly every one of those hydrogen atoms was made in the first minutes of the universe. The hydrogen in a glass of water from your kitchen tap is about 13.8 billion years old.

Chapter two: the kitchens inside stars

For everything heavier, the universe needed stars. A star is a vast ball of gas squeezing itself under its own weight until the centre is hot enough for nuclei to fuse. Our Sun turns hydrogen into helium and will keep doing so for billions of years.

Bigger stars go further. When their hydrogen runs low, their cores squeeze harder and heat up more, and they fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, then those into neon, magnesium, silicon and sulfur, and finally into iron. Each step releases energy, which keeps the star shining. But iron is the end of the line. Fusing iron into anything heavier costs energy instead of releasing it, so a star cannot live on it.

Pasadena, 1957

How all this works was set out in a single huge paper in 1957, “Synthesis of the Elements in Stars”, by Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle. It is still known by their initials, B²FH. Margaret Burbidge had to fight for her place in astronomy: she once had to pretend to be her husband’s assistant to be allowed to use a famous telescope. The paper explained, step by step, how stars could build almost every element, and Fowler later shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for this kind of work.

Chapter three: explosions

When a very big star’s iron core can no longer hold itself up, it collapses in a fraction of a second and the star blows itself apart in a supernova, briefly outshining a whole galaxy. The explosion flings the carbon, oxygen, silicon and iron the star has made out into space, and in the violent blast it makes some heavier elements too. Another kind of explosion, when a small dead star called a white dwarf is pushed over the edge, makes a great deal of the iron in the universe.

The flung-out gas mixes with the clouds between the stars. New stars, and the planets around them, form from that enriched gas. Our Sun and the Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud that had already been seeded by generations of earlier stars. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.

Hanford and Livingston, 17 August 2017

The heaviest elements, like gold, platinum and uranium, need a flood of neutrons to build, far more than ordinary stars can supply. For a long time nobody was sure where that flood happened. Then, on 17 August 2017, the gravitational-wave detectors of LIGO in the United States and Virgo in Italy felt a faint ripple in space itself. It came from two neutron stars, the collapsed cores of dead stars, so dense that a teaspoon would weigh as much as a mountain, spiralling into each other about 130 million light years away. Telescopes around the world turned to the spot and watched a new kind of glow, called a kilonova. Its light carried the signatures of freshly made heavy elements. LIGO’s own summary estimates the collision threw out somewhere between a thousandth and a hundredth of the mass of our Sun.

So the universe has its own gold factory: colliding dead stars. Remember the transmutation story, where people spent fortunes making a few atoms of gold? Nature makes it in quantities the size of planets, in explosions we can now hear across space. Astronomers still debate how much of the universe’s gold comes from mergers like this and how much from rare kinds of supernova; the honest answer is that both seem to contribute, and nobody yet knows the exact share.

Chapter four: cosmic rays and laboratories

Three light elements, lithium, beryllium and boron, are made largely a stranger way (lithium also comes from the Big Bang and from some dying stars): fast particles called cosmic rays smash into heavier nuclei drifting in space and chip pieces off them. And the newest elements of all were made by people. Almost everything heavier than uranium is made in laboratories, a few atoms at a time, by smashing nuclei together; only tiny natural traces of neptunium and plutonium exist.

The astronomer Jennifer Johnson, at Ohio State University, drew a periodic table in which every box is coloured by where that element comes from: the Big Bang, dying small stars, exploding big stars, exploding white dwarfs, colliding neutron stars, cosmic rays. It is one of the most beautiful versions of the table ever made, and worth looking up.

Careful

“Elements are made in factories and chemistry labs.”

Factories and labs only rearrange atoms into new substances. They do not make new atoms of an element; a chemical reaction never changes a nucleus. Almost every atom on Earth, apart from a few made in nuclear reactors and particle accelerators, was made in the Big Bang or in stars long before the Earth existed, and has been recycled ever since.

Your body’s star map

Write down the four elements that make up most of your body by mass: oxygen (about 65 percent), carbon (about 18), hydrogen (about 10) and nitrogen (about 3). Beside each, write where it was made: hydrogen in the Big Bang; carbon, oxygen and nitrogen inside stars. Then add calcium (bones) and iron (blood): both from stars and their explosions. Finally, if anyone in the family has a gold ring, hold it and say where its atoms were most probably made. You are, quite literally, made of stars.

When you look at the periodic table now, you can see a history in it. The first two boxes are the Big Bang. Most of the rest are the work of stars. The heavy metals at the bottom are the ashes of the most violent events in the universe. And the very last boxes were made by people, in laboratories, a few atoms at a time.

1913 to today

Why the table has that strange shape

Niels Bohr, Charles Janet, Theodor Benfey, Eric Scerri

A classroom wall in Mumbai, any school day

Look at the periodic table on any classroom wall and it is a very odd shape for a chart. It is not a neat rectangle. There are two tall towers on the left, a lower block sunk into the middle, a set of six columns on the right with one lonely box perched at the top corner, and then, strangest of all, two long rows floating underneath the whole thing, as if someone had cut them out and forgotten to glue them back.

None of that is decoration. Every bump and gap is a picture of something real: the way electrons arrange themselves around a nucleus. Once you can read the shape, you can say a surprising amount about any element without having memorised anything.

Step 1: shells have rooms inside them

In Chapter 1 you met electron shells: groups of electrons at roughly the same energy, the first holding up to 2, the second up to 8. By the 1920s physicists, Niels Bohr among them, had found that each shell is itself divided into smaller groups, called sub-shells. They are named with letters left over from the early study of spectra: s, p, d and f.

Think of a shell as a floor of a hotel, and the sub-shells as the rooms on that floor. The rooms come in fixed sizes:

  • an s room has 2 seats
  • a p room has 6 seats
  • a d room has 10 seats
  • an f room has 14 seats

Here is what those rooms actually look like. Each “seat pair” is a cloud where an electron is likely to be found: s rooms are round, p rooms are dumbbells pointing three ways.

The first floor has only an s room (2 seats). The second floor has an s room and a p room (2 + 6 = 8). The third floor has s, p and d (2 + 6 + 10 = 18). The fourth has all four kinds (2 + 6 + 10 + 14 = 32). Electrons fill the cheapest seats first, the ones with the lowest energy, just as water fills the bottom of a jug first.

Step 2: the order of filling builds the rows

Here is the twist that gives the table its shape. The rooms are not filled strictly floor by floor. The 3d room, on the third floor, turns out to be slightly more expensive than the 4s room on the floor above, so electrons fill 4s first and only then go back to 3d. (That simple rule is the one that builds the table, but the full story is subtler: once electrons are actually sitting in 3d, the 3d room ends up slightly lower than 4s, which is why an iron atom loses its 4s electrons first when it becomes an ion. You will meet that later.) In the same way, the 4f room waits until after 6s.

Each new row of the table begins when electrons start a new s room. Count what gets filled before the next s room opens, and you get the length of each row:

Row 1: 1s = 2
Row 2: 2s, 2p = 2 + 6 = 8
Row 3: 3s, 3p = 2 + 6 = 8 (the 3d room waits)
Row 4: 4s, 3d, 4p = 2 + 10 + 6 = 18
Row 5: 5s, 4d, 5p = 2 + 10 + 6 = 18
Row 6: 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p = 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32
Row 7: 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p = 2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32

Sub-shell

A group of electron places within a shell. There are four kinds, called s, p, d and f, holding 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons.

That is the famous sequence 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32, and it adds up to 118, exactly the number of elements known today. The rows are not long or short by accident. They are as long as the rooms that get filled.

Step 3: the four blocks

Now the shape makes sense. Colour each element by the kind of room its newest electron went into, and the table splits into four regions, called blocks:

  • the s-block: the two tall towers on the left (2 columns, because s rooms have 2 seats), plus helium
  • the p-block: the six columns on the right (p rooms have 6 seats)
  • the d-block: the ten columns sunk into the middle, starting only in row 4, because that is when the first d room fills
  • the f-block: fourteen elements in each of rows 6 and 7

And the floating strip? If you put the f-block where it really belongs, inside rows 6 and 7, the table would be 32 columns wide: so long and thin that it would not fit on a classroom wall, and every box would be tiny. So printers cut the f-block out and lay it underneath. It is a convenience, not a separate kind of table. Some books do print the long, 32-column version, and it is worth looking at once: it shows the true shape, without the cut.

Step 4: reading the position

This is where the shape pays off. An element’s position tells you how its outermost electrons are arranged, and those outer electrons decide most of its chemistry.

Take sulfur. It is in row 3, so its outer electrons are on the third floor. It is the fourth column of the p-block, so it has 2 electrons in its 3s room and 4 in its 3p room: 6 outer electrons in all. Oxygen sits directly above it, also with 6 outer electrons, and that is why sulfur and oxygen behave like cousins.

A printed box usually carries four things: the atomic number (the proton count), the symbol, the name, and the relative atomic mass (an average over the element’s isotopes, which is why it is rarely a whole number). The atomic number fixes the position, the position tells you the outer electrons, and the outer electrons tell you the chemistry.

Careful

“The table is just a list of elements sorted by weight.”

It is sorted by atomic number, the number of protons, which is why tellurium (heavier) comes before iodine (lighter). And it is not just a list: it is folded. Each fold, each new row, happens where a new shell of electrons begins. The columns line up elements whose outer electrons match.

Careful

“Elements next to each other in a row are similar.”

Usually the opposite. Neighbours in a row can be wildly different: sodium is a soft metal that fizzes in water, while chlorine, a few places along the same row, is a poisonous green gas. It is the columns that hold families. The exception is the f-block, where the newest electrons tuck into a deep inner room and barely change how the outside of the atom looks, so the fifteen elements from lanthanum to lutetium are so alike that chemists struggled for a century to tell them apart.

A few honest wrinkles

The filling order is a very good rule, not a perfect law. A handful of elements bend it slightly; chromium and copper are the famous ones, each moving one electron from the 4s room into 3d. You do not need the details. What matters is that the rule explains the shape of the whole table, and the exceptions are small.

And there are questions about the table that chemists still argue about today.

  • Where does hydrogen go? It has one electron, like lithium and sodium, so it usually sits on top of the first column. But it is a gas, not a metal, and in some ways it acts like the halogens, which are one electron short of a full shell. Some tables float it above the middle, belonging to no family.
  • Where does helium go? Chemically it is a noble gas, so it sits above neon. But its two electrons fill an s room, which would put it above beryllium.
  • Which elements belong in group 3? Under scandium and yttrium, some tables put lanthanum and actinium, and others put lutetium and lawrencium. A task group set up by IUPAC, the international body that looks after chemical names, published a progress report in 2021. It leaned towards lutetium and lawrencium as a possible compromise but did not settle the matter, and tables still differ.

Beauvais, France, the late 1920s

Some people have redrawn the table to show the electron rooms more honestly. Charles Janet, a French engineer and naturalist, drew a “left-step” table in the late 1920s in which every row ends with a filled s room, so helium sits above beryllium and the blocks line up as perfect steps. In 1964 the chemist Theodor Benfey drew the elements as one continuous spiral, with the d- and f-blocks as bulges. People have also drawn the table as pyramids, flowers and towers. They all hold the same information; the classroom version wins because it is the easiest to print and read.

Build the shape from seats

Take a sheet of squared paper. Starting at the top left, colour 2 squares for row 1 (put the second one far over at the right, where helium goes). For row 2, colour 2 on the left and 6 on the right. Row 3: the same. For row 4, add a block of 10 between them. Row 5: the same. For rows 6 and 7, add 14 more, drawn as a separate strip underneath. Count your squares: you should have 118. You have just drawn the periodic table from nothing but the sizes of the electron rooms.

So the next time you see the table on a wall, read its outline like a map. The towers are s rooms, the sunken middle is d rooms, the right-hand block is p rooms, and the floating strip is the f rooms that would not fit. The shape is the atom’s own floor plan.

NB

Niels Bohr

The goalkeeper who drew the atom's staircase

1885 to 1962The Danish physicist who explained why atoms give out light of only certain colours

Copenhagen, 1885

Niels Bohr was born on 7 October 1885 in Copenhagen, the capital of Denmark. His father was a professor of physiology, and his mother came from a family of bankers and teachers. The house was full of scientists and arguments, and Niels and his younger brother Harald grew up listening to both.

The two brothers were inseparable, and both were very good footballers. Niels played in goal for a Copenhagen university club. Harald was even better: he played for Denmark at the 1908 Olympic Games, and the Danish team won the silver medal. For a while, Harald was the more famous of the two Bohrs. That changed.

Niels was not a fast talker or a quick writer. He thought slowly, out loud, turning a problem over and over, and he rewrote his papers again and again. His mother sometimes wrote out his work as he dictated it. But when he had understood something, he had understood it all the way down.

A problem nobody could solve

In 1912 Bohr went to Manchester to work with Ernest Rutherford, who had just discovered that atoms have a tiny nucleus with electrons around it. But there was a serious problem with that picture. According to the physics of the time, an electron circling a nucleus should give out light continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a tiny fraction of a second. Every atom in the universe should collapse. They obviously do not.

There was a second puzzle too. When you heat hydrogen gas until it glows and split its light with a prism, you do not see a rainbow. You see a few sharp coloured lines, always at exactly the same places. Why only those colours?

The staircase

Copenhagen, 1913

Back in Copenhagen in 1913, Bohr made a bold suggestion. Suppose, he said, an electron in an atom cannot have any amount of energy, only certain fixed amounts, like the steps of a staircase. You can stand on step 2 or step 3, but not on step two-and-a-half. While the electron stays on one step, it gives out no light and does not spiral in. It simply stays.

But when an electron drops from a higher step to a lower one, the energy it loses comes out as a single packet of light. A big drop gives a packet with lots of energy (blue or violet light); a small drop gives less (red light). Because the steps are fixed, the drops are fixed, and so only certain colours can ever come out. Those are hydrogen’s lines.

Bohr calculated the heights of the steps for hydrogen, and the colours his staircase predicted matched the measured lines almost perfectly. He could not fully explain why the staircase existed. That came later, with the new quantum mechanics of the 1920s, which replaced his neat circular orbits with fuzzier clouds. But the central idea, fixed energy levels and light coming out when electrons drop between them, is still at the heart of chemistry. It is why the electron shells of Chapter 2 exist, and why every element has its own fingerprint of colours.

The institute

In 1921 Bohr opened his own institute in Copenhagen, and for the next twenty years it was one of the most exciting places in the world to do physics. Young scientists came from Germany, Russia, Britain, America, Japan and India. They argued, played table tennis, went to the cinema together, and in the space of a few years built quantum mechanics. Bohr won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.

Two medals in a jar

Copenhagen, April 1940

In April 1940, German soldiers occupied Denmark. In Bohr’s institute were two gold Nobel medals that did not belong to Bohr. The German physicists Max von Laue and James Franck had sent them to Copenhagen for safe keeping, because both men opposed the Nazis, and sending gold out of Germany was forbidden. If the soldiers found the medals, with the names engraved on them, von Laue and Franck could be in serious danger.

A Hungarian chemist at the institute, George de Hevesy, had an idea. Burying them might not work; the soldiers could search. So he dissolved them. He put the medals in aqua regia, “royal water”, a fierce mixture of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid that is one of the few things that can dissolve gold. It took a while, but the medals vanished, leaving an orange-coloured liquid in a jar. De Hevesy put the jar on a shelf among all the other bottles of chemicals, and there it stayed, in plain sight, through the whole war. Nobody looked twice at it.

When the war ended, the jar was still there. The gold was taken out of the solution, and the Nobel Foundation used it to make new medals for von Laue and Franck.

That is a perfect piece of chemistry. Dissolving the gold did not destroy a single gold atom. The atoms were simply spread out through the liquid as tiny charged gold particles (ions), invisible but all still there, and a chemist could gather them up again. You can change what gold looks like, or where it is, but by chemistry alone you can never make it stop being gold.

Escape

Bohr’s mother came from a Jewish family, and by 1943 he was in danger himself. In September that year, warned that he was about to be arrested, he and his wife escaped by small boat across the narrow sea to Sweden. Within days he was talking to the Swedish government about helping Denmark’s Jewish people, thousands of whom were ferried across the same stretch of water to safety by ordinary Danes. Soon after, Bohr was flown to Britain, crammed into the bomb bay of an aeroplane.

After the war he worked hard, with mixed success, to persuade world leaders to share knowledge about nuclear energy openly rather than race each other to build weapons. He died in Copenhagen in 1962. Element 107 is called bohrium.

Dissolve it, and get it back

You can repeat de Hevesy’s trick with something much safer than gold. Stir a teaspoon of salt into half a glass of water until it disappears completely. Is the salt gone? Taste a drop on your fingertip: it is still there. Now pour a little of the salt water onto a saucer and leave it on a sunny windowsill for a few days. As the water evaporates, the salt comes back as tiny square crystals. Dissolving hides things; it does not destroy them.

Every time this book talks about energy levels, shells, or why a flame turns a particular colour, it is climbing Bohr’s staircase.

RB

Robert Boyle

The sceptical chymist

1627 to 1691A rich nobleman's son who made chemistry an experimental science

Lismore Castle, Ireland, 1627

Robert Boyle was born into enormous wealth. His father, Richard Boyle, the first Earl of Cork, was one of the richest men in the British Isles, and Robert was the fourteenth of his fifteen children. He grew up in a castle above a river in the south of Ireland, and at the age of eight he was sent to Eton, the famous English school.

You might expect a boy like that to grow up to do nothing much. Instead, Boyle became one of the founders of modern science, and the man who did more than anyone to turn chemistry from a secret craft into an open, experimental subject.

A storm and a promise

At twelve, Boyle was sent on a long tour of Europe with a tutor. In Florence, in 1642, he read about Galileo, who had just died there, and he was fascinated by the new science that tested ideas against the world. Earlier, in Geneva, according to his own later account, a violent thunderstorm in the night terrified him so much that he vowed to live a deeply religious life. He kept that promise. All his life he was devout, and he saw science as a way of understanding God’s creation.

When he came home, his father had died and Ireland and England were at war. Boyle inherited land and money, which meant he never needed a job. He spent his life, and his fortune, on experiments.

Doubt everything, test everything

In the 1600s, most people still learned about matter from very old books. Some followed Aristotle’s four elements: earth, water, air and fire. Others followed the alchemists’ three “principles”: salt, sulfur and mercury. Both groups mostly argued from authority: the great teacher said so, so it must be true.

Boyle thought this was the wrong way round. In 1661 he published a book with a wonderful title: The Sceptical Chymist. It is written as a conversation between friends, and in it Boyle asks awkward questions. How do you know fire breaks things into their “elements”? When you burn wood, what comes out depends on how you burn it. Shouldn’t an element be something you can actually find by experiment, rather than something an ancient author declared?

He did not discover the modern elements. But he insisted that chemistry must rest on experiments, done carefully, described exactly, and repeatable by anyone. He wrote down his methods in such detail that other people could check them, which was unusual at the time. This is the habit at the very heart of science.

The air pump

Oxford, 1659

Boyle hired a brilliant young assistant called Robert Hooke, a clergyman’s son from the Isle of Wight, who was a superb builder of instruments. Together they built an improved air pump: a glass globe from which most of the air could be pumped out.

With it, they could do things no one had seen before. A ringing bell inside the globe grew fainter and fainter as the air was removed, showing that sound needs air to travel. A candle went out. A feather and a coin fell together. And Boyle measured how the pressure of trapped air changes when you squeeze it, finding that if you halve its volume, its pressure doubles. That rule is now called Boyle’s law, and you will meet it in Chapter 3. (Hooke deserves much of the credit for the apparatus; Boyle was always generous in saying so.)

Some of the experiments are hard for us to read about. Like many experimenters of his time, Boyle put small animals in the globe to see what happened when the air was taken away. It helped show that animals need air, but it is not something scientists would do today.

A Royal Society

Boyle belonged to a group of curious people who met to discuss experiments, sometimes called the “Invisible College”. In 1660 it became the Royal Society of London, one of the oldest scientific societies in the world. Its motto, Nullius in verba, roughly means “take nobody’s word for it”. That is Boyle’s whole philosophy in three words.

The other Boyle: still an alchemist

Here is the surprise. The sceptical chymist was also a believer in alchemy.

Boyle was certain, like his younger friend Isaac Newton, that metals could in principle be transformed. He spent years on alchemical experiments, traded secret recipes, and in 1676 published a paper about a special kind of mercury that he thought might “heat up” when mixed with gold. He seems to have believed, near the end of his life, that he had once witnessed lead being turned into gold.

England had an old law, from 1404 in the reign of Henry IV, which made “multiplying” gold and silver by alchemy a crime, because the king feared fake gold would wreck the currency. Historians generally credit Boyle with helping to get that law repealed in 1689. He did not want alchemists punished for trying.

Was this hypocrisy? Not really. Boyle was a man of his time, standing on the line between two worlds. He doubted ancient authorities, but he could not yet know that gold is an element whose atoms no chemical process can change. That knowledge was still more than two hundred years away.

What became of him

Boyle never married. He lived for many years in London with his beloved older sister Katherine, Lady Ranelagh, who was herself a keen thinker, and he built a laboratory in her house. He wrote dozens of books on science and religion and died in 1691, just a week after her.

Squeeze the air

Boyle’s law at your desk. Take a plastic syringe from a medicine kit (no needle). Pull the plunger out halfway, then put your finger firmly over the tip. Push the plunger in. Feel how the air pushes back harder the more you squeeze it. Let go, and the plunger springs back. You have just felt what Boyle and Hooke measured: squash a gas into less space and its pressure rises.

When you read about pressure in Chapter 3, and about Boyle’s colourful violet syrup in Chapter 7, remember the rich man’s son who spent his fortune on teaching the world to doubt, and to check.

MC

Marie Skłodowska Curie

The girl from the secret university

1867 to 1934Discovered polonium and radium; the first person to win two Nobel Prizes

Warsaw, 1870s

Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw in 1867, the youngest of five children. Her parents were both teachers. But Poland at that time did not exist as a free country: Warsaw was ruled by Russia, and Polish children had to be taught in Russian. Polish history and language were forbidden in schools. Maria’s father lost his good teaching job, partly because the Russian authorities distrusted him, and the family became poor.

Maria was brilliant. She finished school at fifteen with a gold medal. But universities in Warsaw did not accept women.

The Flying University

So she and her sister studied in secret. In Warsaw there was a hidden, illegal school known as the Flying University. Its classes met in different people’s homes and kept moving so the authorities would not find them. Teachers taught science, history and Polish to young people, many of them women, who could not study anywhere else.

A deal between sisters

Maria and her older sister Bronisława (Bronya) both dreamed of studying in Paris, where women could go to university. They could not afford it. So they made a deal. Maria would work and send money to Bronya while she studied medicine. Then, once Bronya was a doctor, she would help Maria.

For several years Maria worked as a governess, teaching the children of a rich family in the countryside, sending her money to Paris and studying chemistry and physics from books at night.

A garret in Paris

Paris, 1891

In 1891, aged twenty-four, Maria arrived in Paris and enrolled at the Sorbonne, the University of Paris. She now called herself Marie. She lived in a tiny attic room, so cold in winter that she wore all her clothes to bed, and she sometimes forgot to eat. She came top of her class in physics in 1893 and second in mathematics a year later.

In 1894 she met Pierre Curie, a quiet physicist who had already made important discoveries about crystals and magnets. They talked about science, then about everything. They married in 1895, and for their honeymoon they went touring the countryside by bicycle.

Rays from a rock

In 1896 Henri Becquerel had found that uranium gives off invisible rays all by itself (that story is told in radioactivity). Marie chose these rays for her doctoral research. Using a very sensitive instrument that Pierre and his brother had invented, she measured how strongly different substances gave off rays.

She made a key discovery: the strength of the rays depended only on how much uranium was there, not on what it was combined with. That meant the rays came from inside the atoms themselves. She invented a word for this: radioactivity.

Then something odd. A uranium ore called pitchblende gave off more rays than its uranium could explain. Marie reasoned that it must contain something else, something far more radioactive, in tiny amounts.

The shed

A shed at the School of Physics and Chemistry, Paris, 1898 to 1902

Pierre dropped his own work to join her. In 1898 they announced two new elements. The first they called polonium, after Marie’s homeland, which was not on the map. The second they called radium, from the Latin for “ray”.

But other chemists wanted to see the new elements, not just their rays. So the Curies set out to collect pure radium. They had no proper laboratory, only an old shed with a leaking glass roof, freezing in winter and stifling in summer. Marie stirred boiling vats of pitchblende residue with an iron rod nearly as tall as herself.

It took about four years and tonnes of residue (the exact amount is told differently in different accounts) to produce about a tenth of a gram of radium compound: less than a pinch of salt. At night, Marie later wrote, the little glass tubes of radium glowed faintly in the dark.

Two Nobel Prizes, and a terrible day

In 1903 Marie, Pierre and Becquerel shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Marie was the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize.

In 1906 Pierre was killed in a street accident in Paris: he slipped in the rain and was struck by a horse-drawn cart. Marie was left with two daughters, Irène and Ève. She took over Pierre’s teaching post and became the first woman professor at the Sorbonne. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, for discovering polonium and radium. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

The little Curies

When the First World War began in 1914, Marie saw that X-rays could help surgeons find bullets and broken bones in wounded soldiers. She fitted cars with X-ray equipment and helped set up many more X-ray posts, learned to drive, and went to the front lines herself, often with her teenage daughter Irène. Soldiers called the vans petites Curies, “little Curies”.

The cost

Nobody at the time understood how dangerous radiation is. Marie carried radium in her pockets and kept it in her desk. Over the years her health suffered, and in 1934 she died of a blood illness that was almost certainly caused by long exposure to radiation.

Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive today. They are reported to be kept in lead-lined boxes in a French library, and people who wish to read them must take safety precautions.

In 1935 her daughter Irène and Irène’s husband, Frédéric Joliot-Curie, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making new radioactive elements in the laboratory. The Curie family has won more Nobel Prizes than any other.

When you read about the nucleus and radioactivity in Chapter 1, remember the girl who studied in secret, and the glowing tubes in the leaking shed.

JD

John Dalton

The schoolteacher who weighed the invisible

1766 to 1844A Quaker teacher in Manchester who brought atoms back into science

Eaglesfield, Cumberland, 1766

John Dalton was born in a small thatched cottage in a village in the north of England. His father was a handloom weaver, and the family were Quakers, a Christian group who dressed plainly, refused to swear oaths, and believed in education and simple living. They were poor.

Dalton was a quiet, serious boy who loved numbers. A wealthy Quaker neighbour taught him mathematics and let him read his books. And then, at the age of twelve, Dalton did something that seems astonishing today: he opened his own school and began teaching other children, some of them older than he was. It did not last long, but teaching became his life’s work. For the rest of his life, even when he was famous, he earned his living by teaching.

The weather diary

At fifteen he moved to Kendal to teach at a Quaker school with his brother. There he met John Gough, a blind philosopher who taught him science, and Dalton began a habit that he kept until the day before he died: he wrote down the weather. Every day, for 57 years, he recorded the temperature, the air pressure, the rain and the wind. Historians estimate the diary holds around 200,000 observations.

All that watching of the air led him to wonder what air actually is. Why do oxygen and nitrogen and water vapour stay mixed instead of settling into layers? Why does water vapour behave as if the other gases were not there? These questions about gases led him, slowly, to atoms.

Seeing colours differently

Manchester, 1794

In 1793 Dalton moved to Manchester, a booming city of cotton mills, to teach at a new college. In his first paper to the city’s scientific society, he described something odd about his own eyes.

He had noticed it when he bought his mother a pair of stockings he thought were a sober dark blue, suitable for a Quaker woman. She was startled: they were bright scarlet. (This story is told in several versions, and may have been improved in the retelling.) Dalton tested himself and his brother and found that they both saw colours differently from most people. Pink geranium flowers looked sky-blue to him by day.

He wrote one of the first scientific descriptions of colour blindness. For a long time, the condition was even called “Daltonism”. Dalton guessed that the liquid inside his eyes must be tinted blue, and asked that his eyes be examined after his death. They were, and the liquid was perfectly clear: his guess was wrong. But one eye was kept in a jar. In 1995, scientists extracted DNA from it and found that he lacked the gene for one of the three colour-sensing cells in the eye. Two hundred years after he described himself, his own eye told the rest of the story.

Atoms, with weights

Dalton’s great idea came together between about 1803 and 1808. Philosophers had talked about atoms since ancient Greece, but only as an idea. Dalton made atoms into something chemists could use.

His idea, in plain words:

  1. Every element is made of tiny atoms.
  2. All the atoms of one element are identical, and they are different from the atoms of every other element. Above all, they have different weights.
  3. Atoms cannot be created, destroyed or split in a chemical reaction. They are only rearranged.
  4. Compounds form when atoms of different elements join in small whole numbers: one and one, one and two, two and three.

Point 4 explained something chemists had noticed but could not understand: why substances always combine in fixed proportions. And point 2 meant you could compare atoms by weighing. In 1803 Dalton drew up the first table of relative atomic weights, with hydrogen as 1. Many of his numbers were wrong, because he guessed the wrong formulas (he thought water was HO, one hydrogen and one oxygen), but his method was right, and later chemists corrected the numbers.

He drew each atom as a little circle with a pattern inside: a dot for hydrogen, a plain ring for oxygen. Those symbols were soon replaced by letters, but the idea behind them lasted.

A modest celebrity

Dalton became famous across Europe. He was elected to scientific academies, given a royal medal and a government pension. When he was presented to King William IV, there was a problem: Quakers did not wear the colourful court dress the occasion required. Dalton wore the scarlet robe of an Oxford doctor instead. Since he was colour-blind, it is said, it looked a respectable grey to him.

He never married and lived simply, lodging for decades with a friend’s family, playing bowls every Thursday, and teaching right to the end. When he died in Manchester in 1844, the city gave him a huge public funeral, and tens of thousands of people filed past his coffin. A shy weaver’s son had become the man who made atoms real.

Test colour vision the gentle way

Dalton was colour-blind and never knew it until he was in his twenties. You can explore how colours are seen. Collect objects that are red, green, brown and orange, and ask family members to sort them by colour without saying the names out loud. Then try under a dim lamp, where everyone’s colour vision gets worse. About 1 in 12 boys and men, and far fewer girls and women, see some reds and greens differently: if anyone in your family sorts them differently, they are in good company with Dalton.

When you meet Dalton in Chapter 4, picture a quiet Quaker teacher writing in his weather diary, who turned the ancient guess of atoms into a tool every chemist would use.

HD

Humphry Davy

The boy from Penzance who lit up London

1778 to 1829Poet, showman and discoverer of potassium and sodium

Penzance, Cornwall, the 1780s

At the very bottom tip of England, where the land runs out into the Atlantic, there is a small fishing town called Penzance. Humphry Davy was born there in 1778. His father was a woodcarver who never made much money, and when he died the family was left poor. Humphry was the eldest of five children, and at sixteen he had to earn a living.

He was apprenticed to a local surgeon-apothecary: a kind of village doctor who also mixed medicines. It was not a grand job. But the shop had bottles, scales and books, and Humphry read everything. He taught himself chemistry from Lavoisier’s new book, in French. He also wrote poetry, fished, and wandered the cliffs. All his life he would be two things at once: a poet and a scientist.

The gas that made people laugh

Bristol, 1799

At nineteen Davy got a job at a strange new place in Bristol: the Pneumatic Institution, run by a doctor called Thomas Beddoes. “Pneumatic” means to do with air. Beddoes hoped that breathing newly discovered gases might cure diseases.

Davy’s job was to make the gases and test them. Often he tested them on himself, which was brave and also quite reckless. One of them was nitrous oxide. When Davy breathed it, he felt light-headed and giggly, and the world seemed wonderful. Soon his friends were trying it too, including poets. It got the nickname laughing gas.

Davy also noticed something important: it seemed to take away pain. He wrote in 1800 that it might be used during surgery. Almost nobody followed this up for more than forty years, and in the meantime surgery went on without anything to stop the pain. Today nitrous oxide is still used by dentists and in hospitals.

Careful

“Davy was being sensible about safety.”

He was not, by today’s standards. He breathed several gases that could have killed him, and once nearly did. Modern chemists never test unknown gases on themselves. Davy was lucky, and his luck is not a method.

The most famous lecturer in London

The Royal Institution, London, 1801

In 1801 Davy moved to the Royal Institution in London, a new place built to bring science to the public. He was twenty-two, good-looking and a brilliant speaker, and his lectures became the place to be seen. Carriages blocked the street outside. People who knew no chemistry at all came to watch him make things flash, bang, fizz and change colour, while he explained, in beautiful sentences, what was happening.

Tearing metals out of rocks

The Royal Institution basement, October 1807

In 1800, Alessandro Volta had invented the battery (you meet it in Chapter 8). Davy saw at once what it could do. Electricity could pull compounds apart. If you pass a current through water, it splits into hydrogen and oxygen. What else could it split?

For years, chemists had suspected that potash (a substance made from wood ashes) and soda contained metals, but nothing could break them apart. Davy built enormous batteries in the basement of the Royal Institution, melted some potash, and passed a powerful current through it.

At one wire, tiny shining globules appeared, like quicksilver. Some of them burst into flame the moment they appeared. Davy had discovered potassium, a metal so reactive that it catches fire in water. His cousin Edmund, who was helping him, later wrote that Humphry danced about the room with delight. A few days later he made sodium from soda in the same way.

The next year he used the same trick to find calcium, magnesium, barium and strontium. In about two years, one man had added six new elements to the list.

Why did potash resist every chemist before him? Because potassium gives its electrons away more readily than almost any other metal. Ordinary chemicals cannot force those electrons back onto it, so the metal stays locked up in its compounds. A strong enough battery can push the electrons back by brute force. That is why the most reactive metals were the last to be found, and why they were all found with electricity.

A lamp that saved lives

The coal mines of northern England, 1815
