Coal mines were filled with a dangerous gas called firedamp (mostly methane). Miners needed light to work, but a candle flame could set the gas off in a terrible explosion. In 1815 the mine owners asked Davy for help.

He worked out that a flame cannot pass through a fine metal gauze, because the metal draws away heat so fast that the gas on the other side never gets hot enough to catch fire. So he wrapped the flame of a miner’s lamp in a cylinder of wire gauze. The gas could get in and burn harmlessly inside, but the flame could not get out.

Davy refused to patent the lamp. He wanted it to be free for every mine. (An engineer called George Stephenson designed a similar lamp at almost the same time, and there was a bitter argument about who came first.)

His greatest discovery

Davy once hired a young bookbinder as an assistant, a young man called Michael Faraday. It is often said, though nobody knows if Davy himself said it, that “Davy’s greatest discovery was Michael Faraday”. Faraday became an even greater scientist than his teacher.

That was not always easy for Davy. As he grew older and more famous (he was made a knight, then president of the Royal Society), he became prouder and touchier. When Faraday was proposed for the Royal Society in 1823, Davy, as president, is reported to have opposed it. Great people can be generous and jealous at once.

Davy’s health failed in his late forties, perhaps in part because of all the chemicals he had breathed and handled, though nobody can be sure. He died in Geneva in 1829, aged fifty.

Split water with a battery

Ask an adult to help. You need a 9-volt battery, two pencils sharpened at both ends, a glass of warm water and a teaspoon of salt. Stir the salt into the water. Hold one end of each pencil against a battery terminal (the adult can tape them on), and dip the other ends into the water, not touching each other. Watch the pencil tips: tiny bubbles stream off them. Electricity is pulling the water apart, the same trick Davy used on potash. Do not touch the wet ends to your skin, do not use anything bigger than a 9-volt battery, and pour the water away afterwards.

When you read about electrolysis and the reactivity series in Chapter 8, remember the poor boy from Penzance who first used a battery to tear metals out of the rocks that had hidden them for ever.

MF

Michael Faraday

The bookbinder's apprentice

1791 to 1867Bookbinder who became the greatest experimenter of his age

A bookbinder’s shop, Blandford Street, London, 1805

Michael Faraday was born in 1791 in a poor part of London. His father was a blacksmith who was often too ill to work, and there were days when Michael’s share of food for a whole week was a single loaf of bread. He went to a simple day school long enough to learn reading, writing and arithmetic, and that was the end of his schooling.

At about fourteen he was apprenticed to a bookbinder, a kind man called George Riebau. A bookbinder sews and glues the pages of books into their covers. Faraday did something most apprentices did not: he read the books he was binding. One was an encyclopaedia with a long article on electricity. Another was a chemistry book written for beginners by Jane Marcet, Conversations on Chemistry. He tried the experiments he read about, with whatever bits of glass and wire he could afford.

Four tickets that changed a life

The Royal Institution, London, 1812

In 1812 a customer of the shop gave Faraday tickets to four lectures by the most famous chemist in London, Humphry Davy. Faraday sat high up in the gallery and wrote down everything. Afterwards he copied his notes out neatly, added drawings, and bound them into a book.

His apprenticeship was ending and he dreaded spending his life in trade. So he did something bold: he sent the bound notes to Davy and asked for any job at all in science. Davy was impressed, but had nothing to offer. Then, in early 1813, Davy’s laboratory assistant was dismissed after a fight, and Faraday got the job. He was twenty-one. His work included washing bottles and cleaning the apparatus.

A hard journey

Paris, Florence, Rome, 1813 to 1815

Later in 1813 Davy set off on a long tour of Europe, even though Britain and France were at war (Napoleon gave him special permission). He took Faraday as his assistant. Faraday met famous scientists, saw a volcano, and watched Davy use a great burning lens in Florence to burn a diamond and prove it was made of carbon.

But there was a bitter side. Davy’s valet refused to come, so Faraday was asked to act as a servant too. Davy’s wife, Lady Davy, treated him as one. In letters home he wrote how unhappy this made him. He nearly gave up science and went home. He did not, and the tour gave him an education no university could have.

Naming the words you use

Back in London, Faraday became a brilliant chemist in his own right. In 1825 he discovered benzene, a liquid that turned out to be one of the most important compounds in all of carbon chemistry (Chapter 10).

He was even more famous for his work on electricity. He built the first electric motor (1821) and found how to make electricity from magnets (1831), the idea behind every power station today. And he worked out the rules of what happens when electricity passes through a solution and splits it, which he called electrolysis.

He needed words for the new ideas, and he asked a scholar friend, William Whewell, to help him make them up from Greek. Together, in 1834, they gave us:

  • electrode: the metal or carbon rod where the current goes in or out (from Greek for “electricity” and “road”);
  • anode and cathode: the two electrodes (“the way up” and “the way down”);
  • ion: the charged particle that travels through the liquid (from Greek for “going”, because ions move).

Every time you read ion in this book, you are using a word Faraday and Whewell invented.

The Christmas Lectures

The Royal Institution lecture theatre, Christmas, 1860

Faraday never forgot the boy in the gallery. In 1825 he started lectures at the Royal Institution for young people at Christmas. They still happen every year, and are shown on television in Britain.

His most famous set, given in 1860, was called The Chemical History of a Candle. For six lectures he talked about nothing but a candle, and through it explained almost all of chemistry: melting, burning, the gases in air, the water and carbon dioxide made by a flame, even breathing. He said, roughly, that there was no better door into science than studying a candle.

Watch a candle like Faraday

An adult must light the candle and stay with you; this is for looking only. Put a plain candle in a holder on a plate, away from anything that can burn. Look closely: the little cup of melted wax at the top, the wick drawing liquid wax up, the dark zone near the wick and the bright yellow part above it. Hold a cold metal spoon briefly above the flame (the adult can do this): it gets a black coating of soot, which is unburnt carbon. Then hold a cold dry glass upside down well above the flame for a few seconds: mist forms inside. That is water, made by burning. A candle is a small chemistry factory.

Humble to the end

Faraday became world-famous, but stayed simple and modest. He belonged to a small, strict Christian church and lived quietly with his wife, Sarah, above the Royal Institution. It is often said that he turned down a knighthood and, later, the presidency of the Royal Society, wanting to remain “plain Michael Faraday” to the end. The story about the presidency is well recorded: he was offered it twice. The knighthood story is less certain: he said more than once that he would never accept one, but no record has been found that he was ever offered it.

He worked on almost every great question of his day, but his own teachers had never been professors: they were the books he bound and the man whose lectures he copied. He died in 1867.

When you meet ions and electrolysis in Chapters 2 and 8, remember the apprentice who read the books he was meant to be sewing, and who named the very words you are reading.

RF

Rosalind Franklin

Photo 51

1920 to 1958The X-ray expert whose photograph revealed the shape of DNA

London, 1920

Rosalind Elsie Franklin was born on 25 July 1920 in London, into a well-off Jewish family of bankers and publishers. She was clever, determined and very direct. By fifteen she had decided she wanted to be a scientist. Her father, the family story goes, was not keen at first, but she went to Newnham College, Cambridge, to study chemistry.

During the Second World War she worked on something that sounds ordinary but mattered a great deal: coal. She studied the tiny holes inside coal and charcoal, which affect how well they burn and how well they work in gas masks. That work earned her a doctorate.

Paris and the X-rays

Paris, 1947

After the war she went to work in a government laboratory in Paris, and later said those were some of the happiest years of her life. She learned to speak French, went walking in the mountains, and became an expert in X-ray diffraction: shining X-rays through a material and studying the pattern they make, to work out how its atoms are arranged. (The Dorothy Hodgkin story explains the idea.)

DNA

King’s College London, 1951

In 1951 she moved to King’s College London to study DNA, the molecule that carries genetic instructions in every living cell. Everyone knew it was important, but no one knew its shape.

Things went badly at King’s from the start. Another scientist there, Maurice Wilkins, was already working on DNA, and the two were not told clearly who was in charge of what. They did not get on.

Franklin was extremely careful. Working with her PhD student Raymond Gosling, she found that DNA comes in two forms, depending on how wet it is, and she learned to keep the two apart, which had been confusing everyone. In May 1952 she and Gosling took an X-ray photograph of the wetter form, which was later labelled Photo 51. It shows a striking X-shaped cross of dark smudges. To someone who knew how to read it, that cross shouted one word: helix. From her measurements she could also work out the spacings inside the molecule, and she concluded that the phosphate backbone lay on the outside.

Without her knowledge

In Cambridge, two other scientists, James Watson and Francis Crick, were trying to build a model of DNA from wire and metal plates. In January 1953 Wilkins showed Watson Photo 51, without asking Franklin. Around the same time, a report containing her measurements, written for a committee, was passed to Crick. Franklin did not know that her results were being used.

With her data, Watson and Crick built their famous double helix: two twisted strands with pairs of bases joining them like the rungs of a ladder. It was right, and it is one of the greatest discoveries in the history of science. Their paper was published in April 1953, alongside a paper by Franklin and Gosling with their X-ray evidence. But for many years, few people realised how much the model had depended on her work.

It is fair to add that Watson and Crick did something Franklin had not yet done: they put all the pieces together into a model that explained how DNA can copy itself. And Franklin herself was very close. Her notebooks show she was moving towards the answer. Science is often like that: several people, each holding part of the truth.

What came after

In 1953 Franklin left King’s for Birkbeck College, also in London, and began studying viruses, including the tobacco mosaic virus that attacks plants. With her colleague Aaron Klug she produced some of the most important early pictures of how a virus is built. She was respected and productive, and she was happy in her work.

In 1956 she became seriously ill with cancer. She kept working as long as she could. She died on 16 April 1958. She was 37.

In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize. Nobel Prizes are not awarded to people who have died, so Franklin could not have been included. Aaron Klug, carrying on the virus work they had started together, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1982, and many people, Klug among them, have felt that if she had lived she might well have shared it.

Today, her part in the story is told properly. Schools, research centres and a Mars rover have been named after her.

See a diffraction pattern

On a dark evening, look at a distant street light or a small bright torch through a piece of very fine fabric, such as a thin net curtain, a fine mesh sieve, or the fabric of an umbrella held up close to your eye. Instead of a single point of light you will see a cross or a grid of spots. The regular pattern of threads spreads the light into a regular pattern of spots. Photo 51 was made in the same way: the regular pattern of atoms in DNA spread the X-rays into its famous X.

When this book talks about the giant molecules of life, remember the woman whose photograph showed the world the shape of DNA.

DH

Dorothy Crowfoot Hodgkin

Seeing the shapes of molecules

1910 to 1994The crystal-reader who worked out the shapes of penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin

Cairo, 1910

Dorothy Crowfoot was born on 12 May 1910 in Cairo, Egypt. Her father worked for the education service there and later in Sudan, and both her parents were passionate about archaeology. For much of her childhood, though, Dorothy and her sisters lived in England, looked after by relatives and a nanny, while their parents worked abroad. She saw them for only part of each year.

When she was ten, at a small class in her town, she grew crystals for the first time: alum and copper sulfate, slowly forming in a dish. She loved them. She went home and set up a little laboratory in the attic.

At thirteen she visited her parents in Khartoum, in Sudan, and was shown round a laboratory there that analysed soils and minerals. A chemist gave her a kit for testing minerals, and she brought it home with her.

Asking to join the boys

At her school in Beccles, in the east of England, girls were expected to study domestic science, not chemistry. Dorothy and one other girl asked to be allowed into the boys’ chemistry class, and the school agreed. She went on to study chemistry at Somerville College, Oxford, one of the colleges for women at a time when Oxford’s colleges were separate for men and women.

Reading the dots

Cambridge and Oxford, 1930s

At Oxford, and then at Cambridge with a brilliant and unconventional scientist called J. D. Bernal, she learned a technique called X-ray crystallography. The idea is simple to say and very hard to do. You shine a beam of X-rays through a crystal. The X-rays bounce off the regularly arranged atoms inside and come out as a pattern of dots on a photographic film. The pattern of dots depends on exactly where the atoms are. So if you are clever enough, you can work backwards from the dots to the positions of the atoms, and see the shape of the molecule.

For a small, simple crystal like table salt, this was already being done. For the big, complicated molecules of living things, it seemed almost impossible: thousands of dots, each needing pages of calculations by hand, long before computers.

In 1934, working with Bernal, she took the first X-ray photograph of a crystal of a protein, pepsin, a digestive enzyme. Then she went back to Oxford, where she spent the rest of her career.

Penicillin

Oxford, 1945

During the Second World War, penicillin, the first antibiotic, was saving thousands of lives, but nobody knew the exact structure of its molecule, so nobody could be sure how to make it in a factory. Chemists argued about it. Hodgkin and her team worked it out from the X-ray patterns, finishing in 1945. Part of the molecule was a small, strained ring of four atoms that many chemists had thought unlikely. The X-rays showed it was there.

Next came vitamin B12, which the body needs to make healthy blood. Its molecule is far bigger, with more than ninety atoms (not counting hydrogens) and a single cobalt atom at its heart. With the help of some of the first computers, she solved it in 1956. In 1964 she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, only the third woman to win it, after Marie Curie and her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie.

Thirty-four years of insulin

Her longest puzzle was insulin, the hormone that controls the sugar in your blood, which people with type 1 diabetes need as a medicine. She took her first X-ray photographs of insulin crystals in 1935. It was far too complicated for the methods of the time. She kept at it, improving the methods, training students, waiting for computers to become powerful enough. In 1969, thirty-four years after she started, she and her team finally published its structure.

She did all of this with hands that were often painful. In her late twenties she developed rheumatoid arthritis, which made her joints swollen and stiff, especially her hands and feet. She simply found ways to keep working.

A scientist of the whole world

Hodgkin believed that science belonged to everyone. She travelled widely and helped train crystallographers in many countries, including India and China, where scientists were also working on insulin. She worked for peace, and for scientists on different sides of political divides to keep talking to one another.

She married Thomas Hodgkin, a historian, and they had three children. She died in 1994.

Grow your own crystals

You need salt, warm water from the tap, a clean jar and a saucer. Stir salt into half a glass of warm tap water, a spoonful at a time, until no more will dissolve and a little stays at the bottom. Pour some of the clear liquid onto a saucer (leave the undissolved salt behind) and put the saucer somewhere it will not be disturbed. Over a few days, as the water evaporates, small crystals appear. Look at them with a magnifying glass: many are almost perfect little cubes. Their shape comes from the way sodium and chloride ions stack inside, which is exactly the kind of thing Dorothy Hodgkin learned to read from X-rays.

Whenever this book shows you the shape of a molecule, remember that someone had to see it first, and that for some of the most important molecules in medicine, that someone was Dorothy Hodgkin.

LM

Lise Meitner

A walk in the snow

1878 to 1968The physicist who explained how a uranium nucleus splits in two

Vienna, 1878

Lise Meitner was born in Vienna in November 1878, the third of eight children in a Jewish family (as an adult Lise was baptised a Protestant). Her father was a lawyer who loved chess. As a girl she was fascinated by the colours in a puddle of oil and the way light behaved, and she wanted to understand them.

There was a problem. In Austria at that time, girls were not allowed to go to the kind of school that led to university, and universities did not admit women at all. In 1897 the rules changed, and women were allowed to study. But Lise had missed years of the schooling she needed. So she studied privately, cramming eight years of mathematics, physics, Latin and Greek into two, and in 1901 she passed the university entrance exam. In 1906 she became only the second woman ever to earn a doctorate in physics at the University of Vienna.

The basement

Berlin, 1907

In 1907 she went to Berlin, meaning to stay a short while. She stayed for more than thirty years. She began to work with a young chemist, Otto Hahn, on radioactivity. She was the physicist; he was the chemist. They made an excellent team.

But the head of the chemistry institute did not allow women in his laboratories. So Meitner and Hahn set up their equipment in a former carpentry workshop in the basement, which had its own entrance from the street. She was not supposed to go upstairs where the students worked. When the rule was lifted a couple of years later, she simply carried on.

Slowly, things changed. Together with Hahn she discovered a new element, protactinium, in 1917 and 1918. In 1926 she became a full professor of physics in Berlin, one of the first women in Germany to do so. Physicists in the 1920s talked of her as one of the leading experts on radioactivity in the world. Einstein reportedly called her “the German Marie Curie”.

Escape

In 1933 the Nazis came to power in Germany and began driving Jewish people out of their jobs. Because Meitner was an Austrian citizen, she was protected for a while. But in March 1938 Germany took over Austria, and that protection vanished. She was not allowed to leave the country legally, and it was becoming dangerous to stay.

In July 1938, helped by friends, she slipped across the border into the Netherlands by train, with a small suitcase and very little money. Hahn had given her a diamond ring that had belonged to his mother, to sell if she needed to. She went on to Sweden, where she found a place to work but few colleagues and almost no equipment. She was nearly sixty, and she had lost her home, her laboratory and her work.

The puzzle in the letter

Hahn and his assistant Fritz Strassmann carried on in Berlin. They were firing neutrons at uranium, the heaviest natural element, expecting to make elements slightly heavier or slightly lighter than uranium. But in December 1938 they found something they could not believe: barium. Barium is barely more than half as heavy as uranium. How could you get it by tapping uranium with a neutron? It was like throwing a pebble at a boulder and seeing it break cleanly into two big rocks. Hahn wrote to Meitner: what could it mean?

Kungälv, Sweden, Christmas 1938

Meitner was spending Christmas in a small town on the west coast of Sweden, and her nephew, the physicist Otto Frisch, came to visit. She showed him Hahn’s letter. They went for a walk through the snowy woods to think, Frisch on skis and Meitner on foot (she insisted she could walk just as fast). Somewhere along the way they sat down on a tree trunk and began to calculate on scraps of paper.

They imagined the uranium nucleus not as a hard ball but as a wobbling drop of liquid. Add one more neutron, and the drop starts to wobble and stretch, like a water drop pulled into a peanut shape. If it stretches far enough, the electric push between the two ends, both full of positive protons, drives them apart, and the drop snaps into two smaller drops. One of them could be barium.

Then Meitner worked out how much energy would be released. She remembered that the two pieces together weigh slightly less than the uranium nucleus did. Using Einstein’s famous rule, E = mc², that a tiny amount of mass can turn into a huge amount of energy, she calculated the energy from that missing mass. It matched the energy the flying pieces should have. A single uranium nucleus splitting releases millions of times more energy than a single molecule in any chemical reaction.

Frisch borrowed a word from biology, where a living cell splits in two, and called it fission.

Left out

Within months, scientists everywhere understood that fission could release enormous energy, for power stations, and also for weapons. Meitner was invited to join the British and American project to build an atomic bomb. She refused. She wanted, she said, nothing to do with a bomb.

In 1945, Otto Hahn alone was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (the prize for 1944) for the discovery of fission. Meitner was left out. Historians who have since studied the Nobel committee’s papers believe this was a serious mistake, partly because the committee did not properly understand her contribution as a physicist. She stayed friends with Hahn, but it hurt.

What became of her

Meitner lived to be nearly ninety, and spent her last years in Cambridge, near family. Her nephew wrote the words for her gravestone: “a physicist who never lost her humanity”. In 1997 element 109 was named meitnerium. Only two elements are named after real women: curium, which honours Marie and Pierre Curie together, and meitnerium, the only one named for a woman alone.

Split a drop

Put a few drops of water on a smooth plate or a sheet of baking paper so they form a round bead. Gently drag the bead with the tip of a toothpick and watch it stretch. Pull it into a long peanut shape, then draw the toothpick through the narrow middle. The drop snaps into two rounder drops. This is the picture Meitner and Frisch had in their heads as they walked in the snow: a liquid drop stretching until it splits. (A real nucleus is pushed apart by electric charge, not pulled by a toothpick, but the shape of the idea is the same.)

When this book talks about the nucleus, and about whether one element can really become another, remember the woman on the tree trunk in the snow, doing sums on scraps of paper.

DM

Dmitri Mendeleev

The Siberian who left gaps

1834 to 1907Built the periodic table and dared to predict the missing elements

Tobolsk, Siberia, the 1840s

Dmitri Mendeleev was born in 1834 in Tobolsk, a town in western Siberia. He was the youngest child of a very big family: sources disagree on how many children there were (numbers from fourteen to seventeen are given), but everyone agrees he was the last.

His father, Ivan, was the headmaster of the local school, until he went blind and had to stop working. The family was suddenly poor. His mother, Maria, did something remarkable: she took over a glass factory that belonged to her family, and ran it to keep the children fed. Dmitri grew up around furnaces, sand and molten glass. When he was about thirteen his father died, and not long afterwards the glass factory burned down.

A mother’s journey

Maria was sure her youngest son was gifted. In 1849, when he was fifteen, she set off with him across Russia to find him a university place. They travelled thousands of kilometres, mostly by horse-drawn transport. Moscow University would not take him, because he came from Siberia. So they went on to St Petersburg, where in 1850 he got into a college for training teachers, partly because an old friend of his father worked there.

A few months later his mother died. Dmitri was sixteen, alone and often ill (for a while doctors believed he had a lung disease and not long to live). He kept working. Many years later he dedicated a great book to her, and wrote that she had taught him to seek truth patiently, through work rather than words.

Sixty-three elements and a problem

St Petersburg, February 1869

By the 1860s Mendeleev was a chemistry professor in St Petersburg. He was writing a textbook for his students, and he had a problem: how to organise the chapters. About sixty-three elements were known. In what order should he teach them?

Other chemists had noticed patterns. Some elements came in families, such as lithium, sodium and potassium, which all behave alike. But nobody had found one arrangement that included everything.

Mendeleev wrote each element on a card, with its atomic weight and its main properties, and laid the cards out on a table, moving them about to find the pattern. Lining them up in order of weight, he saw that similar properties came round again and again, like the days of the week. He arranged the cards so that families sat together in columns. This was his periodic table, first published in 1869. (A German chemist, Lothar Meyer, found a very similar arrangement at about the same time.)

Careful

“Mendeleev saw the periodic table in a dream.”

This is a famous story, but it is a legend. It comes from an account written decades later by someone who said Mendeleev had told him so. There is no evidence from 1869 itself. What we do know is that he worked hard on it, with cards, notes and many rough drafts.

The daring part: gaps

Here is what made Mendeleev different. Sometimes the next element by weight did not fit the family pattern. Instead of forcing it in, he left a gap, and said: an element belongs here that nobody has discovered yet.

He went further. From the neighbours of each gap he predicted what the missing element would be like: its atomic weight, how dense it would be, what compounds it would make. He gave them temporary names, such as eka-aluminium (“one below aluminium”).

Paris, 1875

In 1875 a French chemist, Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, found a new metal using a spectroscope and called it gallium. Mendeleev read the report and said: that is my eka-aluminium. But Lecoq’s measured density, about 4.7 grams per cubic centimetre, did not match Mendeleev’s prediction of about 5.9. Mendeleev wrote to say the measurement must be wrong. Lecoq purified his sample and measured again, and got about 5.9. The man who had never seen gallium knew it better than the man holding it.

Then came scandium (1879) and germanium (1886), both matching his predictions closely. After that, nobody laughed at the periodic table.

Build a table with gaps

Take an ordinary pack of cards. Secretly remove two or three cards, say the 7 of hearts and the queen of clubs, and give the rest to a friend. Ask them to lay out the cards in a grid: one row for each suit, numbers in order. Gaps will appear exactly where the missing cards belong, and your friend can tell you what the missing cards must be without ever seeing them. That is exactly what Mendeleev did with elements.

A fiery man

Mendeleev was famous for his temper, his wild hair and beard (he is said to have had it cut only once a year), and his energy. He worked on oil, on agriculture, on weights and measures (he later ran Russia’s office of weights and measures), and much else.

In 1887 he went up alone in a balloon filled with hydrogen to watch a solar eclipse from above the clouds, although he had never flown one by himself before. He landed safely.

He never won a Nobel Prize, though he was nominated and came very close in 1906. Historians think he had made enemies, including a powerful Swedish chemist, Svante Arrhenius, whose ideas Mendeleev had criticised. Nobody can be completely sure. He died in 1907. In 1955 a newly made element, number 101, was named mendelevium in his honour.

When you open the periodic table in Chapters 1 and 9, look for the places where he left gaps, and think of the boy from Siberia whose mother would not give up on him.

HM

Henry Moseley

The young man who counted the elements

1887 to 1915The young physicist who found each element's true number

Weymouth, England, 1887

Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley was born on 23 November 1887, into a family of scientists. His father was a naturalist who had sailed round the world on a famous survey ship, HMS Challenger, collecting sea creatures; his grandfather on his mother’s side was an expert on shells. His father died before Henry was four, and he grew up with his mother and sisters, collecting birds’ eggs, studying animals, and doing very well at school. He won a scholarship to Eton, and then went to Trinity College, Oxford, to study physics.

He was quiet, intense, and extremely hard-working. People who worked with him remembered that he would carry on an experiment through the night, and that he was impatient with anyone who wasted his time.

A puzzle in the periodic table

Manchester, 1913

In 1910 Moseley went to Manchester to work with Ernest Rutherford, who had just discovered the atomic nucleus. By then, the periodic table had been in use for forty years. Mendeleev had arranged the elements roughly in order of their atomic weight, and it worked beautifully. But there were a few awkward places where it did not. Tellurium is heavier than iodine, yet iodine plainly belongs in the column after tellurium, alongside chlorine and bromine. Mendeleev had swapped them, trusting their chemistry over their weight. Nobody could explain why that was allowed.

Some scientists had begun to suspect that the true order was not about weight at all, but about the charge on the nucleus: how many units of positive charge sat at the centre of the atom. But nobody could measure that charge.

Moseley found a way. He knew that when you fire fast electrons at a metal, it gives off X-rays, which are light of extremely high energy, far beyond violet. Each metal gives off X-rays of its own particular energies. Using a crystal to split the X-rays (the trick the Braggs had just invented, see the crystals story), Moseley measured them for one element after another: calcium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc.

The staircase

When he plotted his results in the right way (using the square root of the X-ray frequency), the elements lined up like the steps of a perfectly even staircase. Every step was the same height. Going from one element to the next always added exactly the same amount.

It meant that each element has exactly one more unit of charge on its nucleus than the one before. Hydrogen has 1, helium 2, lithium 3, and so on, all the way up. That number is the atomic number, and Moseley had found a way to measure it directly. It is the true order of the periodic table. It explained the tellurium and iodine puzzle at once: tellurium is number 52 and iodine is number 53, whatever their weights say. (The weights are muddled because of neutrons, which add weight but no charge. That was discovered later.)

Gaps you can count

There was an even more exciting consequence. If every step on the staircase is one element, then you can see exactly where steps are missing. Moseley, and others using his method, could say: between molybdenum (42) and ruthenium (44) there should be an element number 43, and nobody has found it. The same for 61, 72 and 75. No more guessing about how many elements might be hiding. You could count the gaps.

All of them were later filled. Element 72, hafnium, was found in 1923 by scientists in Bohr’s institute in Copenhagen, who searched for it in zirconium ores because the staircase told them where to look. Element 75, rhenium, followed in 1925. Element 43, technetium, turned out not to exist naturally on Earth in any useful amount; it was made artificially in 1937. Element 61, promethium, was finally identified in the 1940s.

The war

Moseley did all of this in about two years. He moved back to Oxford in 1914 to continue, and many people expected that he would one day win a Nobel Prize.

In the summer of 1914 he travelled to Australia for a scientific meeting. While he was there, the First World War began. He came home and, against the advice of people who knew how valuable his work was, joined the army as a signals officer, setting up telephone and telegraph lines. In 1915 he was sent to Gallipoli, in what is now Turkey. On 10 August 1915, during the fighting there, he was killed. He was 27 years old.

Many scientists felt his loss very deeply, Rutherford among them. It is often said that his death made the British government more careful about sending its scientists into battle in later wars, though it is hard to know how much difference it really made.

Find the missing step

Here is Moseley’s idea with coins. Ask someone to make a row of stacks of coins: a stack of 1, then 2, then 3, and so on up to 12, but to secretly leave out one stack and push the others together so there is no gap. Now look at the row. You cannot easily see which is missing just by glancing at the heights. But count the coins in each stack in order (1, 2, 3, 4, 6 …) and the missing number jumps out. Moseley found the “coin count” of every element, and the missing elements jumped out in the same way.

Every time you see an element’s atomic number in this book, the small whole number in the corner of its box in the periodic table, you are using what Henry Moseley found in two years in Manchester.

IN

Isaac Newton

The last of the magicians

1642 to 1727The greatest physicist of his age, who spent thirty years secretly trying to make gold

Woolsthorpe Manor, Lincolnshire, Christmas Day 1642

The baby was so small that, as he later said himself, he could have fitted into a quart pot. Nobody expected him to live. His father, a farmer who could not write his own name, had died three months before he was born. When the boy was three, his mother married again, a much older clergyman, and moved to the next village, leaving her son behind with his grandmother. He did not forgive her for years.

That boy was Isaac Newton, and he grew into one of the strangest and most brilliant people who ever lived. Most people know him for gravity and the falling apple. Very few know that he spent more time on alchemy than on gravity.

A lonely, clever boy

Young Isaac was not a friendly child. He built things instead: a working model of a windmill turned by a mouse running on a wheel, sundials carved into the walls of the house, kites carrying paper lanterns that frightened the neighbours at night. At school in Grantham he lodged with an apothecary, a man who mixed medicines, and it was probably there that he first saw jars of salts and powders and the art of turning one substance into another.

His mother tried to make him a farmer. It was hopeless. Sent to watch the sheep, he read books, and the sheep wandered into the neighbours’ corn. In 1661 he went to Trinity College, Cambridge, at first as a poor student who paid his way partly by working as a servant to richer ones.

Woolsthorpe again, 1665 and 1666

Then the plague came. Cambridge closed, and Newton went home to the farm for nearly two years. Alone, in his early twenties, he worked out the beginnings of calculus, showed that white light is a mixture of all the colours, and began to think that the force pulling an apple down might be the same force holding the Moon in its orbit. (Whether an apple actually fell near him is a story he told in old age. It may be true; it is certainly a good story.)

The secret laboratory

Back in Cambridge, Newton became a professor at 26. And from around 1669, he started something he told almost nobody about. He bought furnaces, glassware, chemicals and old books. He built a small laboratory, with a furnace, beside his rooms at Trinity, and for nearly thirty years he worked there, sometimes for weeks on end with the fire burning day and night.

He was doing alchemy. The alchemists believed metals could be transformed: lead or mercury, purified and “ripened” in the right way, might become gold. Above all they hunted for the philosopher’s stone, a substance said to turn base metals into gold. Newton copied out old alchemical texts by hand, compared them, and wrote his own notes in a secret language of symbols. He even signed some papers with a hidden name: Jeova sanctus unus, “Jehovah the holy one”, which is a Latin anagram of Isaacus Neuutonus.

How much did he write? Historians who have studied his papers estimate about a million words on alchemy: more than he wrote on gravity and light. Almost none of it was published.

Why would the cleverest scientist in Europe spend so long on something that now sounds like magic? Because in the 1600s, nobody yet knew it was impossible. Chemistry and alchemy were not yet separate subjects. Newton was not looking for easy riches. He believed that metals might “grow” and change inside the Earth, and that hidden forces worked inside matter, just as gravity worked between planets. He wanted to find them. In that sense he was asking the right question, what are things made of, and what holds them together?, with the wrong tools.

The dark year

In 1693, Newton became seriously unwell. He could not sleep, he wrote wild, angry letters to friends accusing them of plotting against him, and then he wrote again to apologise. Nobody knows for certain why. He was exhausted, he had worked brutally hard for years, and he had been badly upset by personal troubles.

There is another possibility. Newton heated mercury and lead for hours in his laboratory, and sometimes tasted the substances he made, as chemists of his time often did. In 1979, scientists analysed strands of hair said to be his and reported very high levels of mercury. Some historians think mercury poisoning may have played a part in his illness; others point out that his symptoms do not fit neatly, and that we cannot be completely sure the hair was his. It remains an open question. What is not in doubt is that his laboratory was a dangerous place.

Why the gold never came

Here is the part you can understand better than Newton could.

Gold is an element. Every gold atom has exactly 79 protons in its nucleus; that number is what makes it gold. Mercury has 80, and lead has 82. A chemical reaction, however clever, only rearranges atoms and the electrons on their outside. It never touches the nucleus. Heat, acids, distillation, years of patient furnace work: none of it can take a proton out of a mercury atom. So no chemical recipe could ever turn mercury into gold. Newton was searching for a door that chemistry does not have.

That door does exist. But it took nuclear physics, more than two hundred years later, to open it, and the gold it makes is fantastically expensive. That story is told in the transmutation story, and it reaches all the way to the news of this year.

The Master of the Mint

In 1696 Newton left Cambridge for London to become Warden of the Royal Mint, where England’s coins were made, and later its Master. Many people expected him to treat it as an easy job. Instead he threw himself into it: he oversaw the recoining of the nation’s money, and he chased down forgers with the same fierce persistence he brought to everything else. There is a pleasing twist here. The man who had tried for decades to make gold ended up in charge of the country’s real gold and silver.

He became President of the Royal Society, was knighted, and died in 1727 at the age of 84. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.

Sotheby’s auction room, London, 1936

For two centuries his alchemy papers stayed mostly hidden, an embarrassment to people who wanted Newton to be a pure, modern scientist. In 1936 a huge collection of his papers was sold at auction. The economist John Maynard Keynes bought many of the alchemy papers and read them. Afterwards he wrote that Newton “was not the first of the age of reason. He was the last of the magicians.”

Both halves of Newton are real. He was the man who gave us the laws of motion. And he was the last great alchemist, standing at the exact moment when the old magic was turning into modern science.

Split sunlight into a rainbow

Newton’s most famous experiment at home used a glass prism. You can do a version with a glass of water. On a sunny day, fill a clear, straight-sided glass to the brim and stand it on a windowsill in full sun, with a sheet of white paper on the floor below. Move the paper about until you catch a small band of colours. Newton showed that white light is all of those colours mixed, and that the glass bends each colour by a slightly different amount. No alchemy needed.

When you meet Newton in the opening chapters of this book, remember both of him: the scientist who saw the hidden order in the heavens, and the alchemist who could not see that gold was beyond his reach.

LP

Linus Pauling

The boy who never stopped asking why

1901 to 1994The chemist who explained the chemical bond, and won two Nobel Prizes on his own

Portland, Oregon, 1910

Linus Pauling was born on 28 February 1901 in Portland, Oregon, in the United States. His father, Herman, was a pharmacist who mixed medicines in his own shop. When Linus was nine, his father died suddenly. The family was left with very little money, and Linus grew up quickly. He read everything: the encyclopaedia, books on insects, books on minerals.

When he was about thirteen, a friend showed him a simple chemistry set and did a few experiments with it. Linus was hooked. He borrowed equipment and chemicals from an abandoned smelter near his grandfather’s home and set up a laboratory in his basement. He later said he decided then that he wanted to be a chemist.

He left high school without a diploma, after an argument over a missing history credit, and went straight to Oregon Agricultural College. To pay his way he did whatever work he could find: chopping wood, mopping floors, working in a shipyard and checking the materials for new roads. Because the college was so short of teachers, he was even asked to teach chemistry to younger students while still a student himself. In one of those classes was a young woman called Ava Helen Miller. They married in 1923 and stayed together for fifty-eight years. (His high school finally gave him his diploma in 1962, by which time he had already won a Nobel Prize.)

How do atoms hold together?

Pasadena, California, 1920s

Pauling went to Caltech, in California, to study how atoms are arranged inside crystals by firing X-rays through them. Then he travelled to Europe, to Munich, Copenhagen and Zurich, just as the new quantum mechanics was being invented, and he saw immediately what it could do for chemistry.

Chemists had a simple idea, from Gilbert Lewis, that atoms in a molecule are held together by sharing pairs of electrons. Pauling used quantum mechanics to explain why that works, and to predict the shapes it gives. One of his ideas explains why carbon’s four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, the shape you meet in Chapter 10. In 1939 he put it all together in a book called The Nature of the Chemical Bond. It became one of the most important chemistry books of the century, and it shaped how chemists thought for decades.

He also gave chemists a number for each element called its electronegativity: how strongly its atoms pull on the electrons in a bond. Fluorine pulls hardest; elements like sodium pull weakly. When two atoms with very different pulls share electrons, the sharing is lopsided, and the bond is polar. That idea is behind the polar water molecule in this book, and behind the hydrogen bonds that hold water molecules to each other, which Pauling also helped explain.

A helix on a sheet of paper

Oxford, England, 1948

Pauling next turned to the giant molecules of life: proteins, the long chains that make up hair, muscle and enzymes. Nobody knew how those chains were folded.

There is a well-known story, which Pauling himself told, about how he found the answer. In 1948, while visiting Oxford, he was stuck in bed with a bad cold. Bored, he took a sheet of paper, drew a protein chain on it with the correct bond lengths and angles, and began folding the paper to see how the chain could twist so that its parts held onto each other with hydrogen bonds. He found a spiral, like a spring or a spiral staircase. It took another three years of checking with his colleagues before they published it in 1951, as the alpha helix. It turned out to be right: it is one of the most common shapes in proteins in your body.

In 1954 he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on the chemical bond.

The second prize

Linus and Ava Helen were both deeply worried about nuclear weapons. In the 1950s, countries were testing atomic bombs in the open air, and radioactive dust was spreading round the world. Pauling gathered the signatures of thousands of scientists on a petition calling for the tests to end, gave talks everywhere, and was attacked for it: for a while the American government would not let him have a passport. In 1963 a treaty banning nuclear tests in the air came into force, and Pauling was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1962. He is still the only person to have won two Nobel Prizes on his own, without sharing either.

Getting it wrong

Pauling was brilliant, but he was not always right, and the honest story includes his mistakes.

In early 1953 he was racing to work out the structure of DNA. He published a model with three twisted strands, a triple helix. It was wrong: it even had a basic chemical error, putting acid groups in a place where they could not have held together. A few weeks later, James Watson and Francis Crick in Cambridge published the correct double helix, built partly on Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray photographs, which Pauling had never seen.

Later in life, Pauling became convinced that very large doses of vitamin C could prevent colds and help treat cancer. He wrote best-selling books about it. Careful medical trials since then have not supported his biggest claims. Being a great scientist in one area did not make him right in another, and doctors who tested his ideas properly found that the evidence was not there.

That is worth remembering. In science, it does not matter how famous you are. What matters is what the evidence shows.

Fold a helix

Take a long strip of paper, about 3 cm wide (cut along the long side of a sheet). Draw a zigzag line along it, like a chain of bonds. Now wind the strip loosely round a pencil or a marker, at a slant, so it makes a spiral, then slide the pencil out. Notice how, in a helix, each turn sits just above the one before. In a real alpha helix, each turn is held to the next by hydrogen bonds, which is what Pauling was looking for as he folded his paper in bed.

When you read about why water’s molecules stick together, or why carbon’s bonds point the way they do, you are reading Linus Pauling’s chemistry.

PR

Prafulla Chandra Ray

The chemist who wanted India to make its own

1861 to 1944The teacher who founded modern chemistry in India, and its first chemical company

Raruli, Bengal, 1861

Prafulla Chandra Ray was born on 2 August 1861 in the village of Raruli-Katipara in Bengal (today in Bangladesh). His father was a landowner who loved books and had a large library. Prafulla read history, science and the lives of great people, and he decided early that he wanted to be useful to his country.

He studied in Calcutta, and in 1882 he won a scholarship to the University of Edinburgh in Scotland. He studied chemistry there for six years and earned a doctorate in 1887. Even then he was thinking about India. As a student in Edinburgh he wrote an essay criticising British rule in India, which was a bold thing to do.

A teacher on less pay

Presidency College, Calcutta, 1889

When he came home, Ray found it hard to get a job. Eventually, in 1889, he became a lecturer in chemistry at Presidency College in Calcutta. He was paid much less than British teachers doing the same work, simply because he was Indian. He objected, but he did the job anyway, and he did it brilliantly.

His students loved him. He taught chemistry with stories, jokes and demonstrations, and he expected his students to think for themselves. He was called Acharya, “teacher”, a title of great respect. Among the people he taught or trained were some of India’s greatest scientists, including the physicists Meghnad Saha and Satyendra Nath Bose (the “boson” is named after Bose).

A new compound

In 1896, working with mercury and nitric acid in his laboratory, Ray made a yellow crystalline compound that nobody had described before: mercurous nitrite. Chemists had thought such compounds would be too unstable to make. He went on to study many other nitrites, publishing paper after paper, and became so well known for them that the English chemist Henry Armstrong is said to have called him “the Master of Nitrites”.

A company in his rooms

Ray noticed something that troubled him. India had plenty of raw materials, but almost every medicine and laboratory chemical in the country had to be bought from Europe. Indians were trained as clerks and officials, not as makers. He wanted India to make things for itself.

So, in 1892, with very little money (a few hundred rupees; accounts differ on the exact sum), he started making medicines and chemicals in his own rented house in Calcutta, working in the evenings. It was hard going, and for a while it nearly failed. But it grew, and in 1901 it became a proper company: Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works, one of the first modern chemical companies in India. It made medicines, laboratory chemicals and household products, and it still exists today.

The history of chemistry in India

Ray was also fascinated by the past. He studied ancient Sanskrit texts about metals, medicines and alchemy, and in 1902 he published the first volume of A History of Hindu Chemistry. It showed that people in ancient and medieval India had known a great deal of practical chemistry: how to extract and purify metals, make alloys, prepare medicines from minerals, and distil liquids. Some of these texts, like European alchemy, chased the dream of turning base metals into gold. Others recorded careful, real chemistry.

A simple life

Ray never married. He lived in a single room at the university’s science college, wore plain clothes, and spent very little on himself. It is widely said that he gave most of his salary away, to the university, to students who could not afford their fees, and to good causes, though exact amounts are hard to pin down. When floods and famines struck Bengal, as they did in 1921 and 1922, he organised relief work, collecting money and supplies and sending volunteers, many of them students.

He kept teaching into his late seventies, and died in Calcutta on 16 June 1944.

Ray believed that science was not just something to admire in other countries, but something every country could do for itself, with its own people, in its own laboratories. When this book talks about acids, and the chemistry that turns raw materials into useful things, remember the Acharya who started a chemical company in his own rooms.

JP

Joseph Priestley

The minister who invented fizzy water

1733 to 1804A preacher and teacher who discovered oxygen but never believed in it

Birstall, Yorkshire, 1733

Joseph Priestley was the son of a cloth-maker in the north of England. His mother died when he was six, and he was brought up partly by an aunt. He was a sickly boy with a bad stammer, and he could not go to Oxford or Cambridge, because those universities only admitted members of the Church of England, and his family were “Dissenters”, Protestants who would not join it.

So Priestley taught himself. By his twenties he could read Latin, Greek, French, Italian, German and Hebrew, and he became a minister and a teacher. He wrote about grammar, history, religion, politics, electricity and education. Science was, at first, something he did in his spare time.

The brewery next door

Leeds, 1767

In Leeds, Priestley lived next to a brewery. Above the great vats of fermenting beer hung a layer of invisible gas, the same “fixed air” we now call carbon dioxide. It was heavier than air, it put out candles, and mice could not live in it.

Priestley began to play with it. He found that if he held a bowl of water above a vat for a while, some of the gas dissolved in the water, giving it a pleasant sharp, fizzy taste. Later he worked out a neater method, making the gas from chalk and acid and bubbling it through water. In 1772 he published a little pamphlet on how to do it.

He had invented soda water. He thought it might be a cure for scurvy on long sea voyages (it was not), and he never made money from it. A few years later a jeweller called Johann Jacob Schweppe built a business on carbonated water, and the name Schweppes is still on bottles today.

A gas that made a candle blaze

Priestley became fascinated by “airs”, as gases were then called. He discovered or studied around ten new ones, among them the gas we call ammonia and the one that later became laughing gas. He made great use of a clever trick: collecting gases over mercury instead of water, so that gases that dissolve in water could be caught too.

Calne, Wiltshire, 1 August 1774

Using a large lens, Priestley focused sunlight onto a red powder, the “calx” of mercury. A gas came out. He put a candle in it, and the candle burned with an astonishingly bright flame. He put a mouse in a sealed jar of it, and the mouse lived much longer than it would have in the same amount of ordinary air. He even breathed a little of it himself and wrote that his chest felt “peculiarly light and easy” for some time afterwards.

He had found oxygen. But he did not call it that. Priestley believed in the old theory of phlogiston: the idea that things burn by giving off an invisible substance. He reasoned that this new air must contain no phlogiston at all, so it could soak up a great deal of it, and things burned fiercely in it. He called it “dephlogisticated air”.

Later that year, in Paris, he described his experiment over dinner to Antoine Lavoisier. Lavoisier repeated it, measured everything, and realised what Priestley had missed: burning is not losing phlogiston but joining with this gas. Lavoisier named it oxygen. Priestley never accepted the new explanation, defending phlogiston for the rest of his life.

Mint and a mouse

Priestley also made a beautiful discovery about plants. He found that if a candle burned out in a closed jar, the air in it was “injured”: a mouse could not live in it. But if he put a sprig of mint in that jar and waited some days, the air was “restored”, and a candle could burn in it again. Plants, he realised, repair the air that burning and breathing use up. Later scientists, especially the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz, showed that plants only do this in light. Priestley had glimpsed photosynthesis.

The riots

Priestley was an honest, kind and stubborn man, and his opinions made enemies. He supported the American and French revolutions and argued for religious freedom and for people’s right to disagree with the government.

Birmingham, 14 July 1791

On the second anniversary of the storming of the Bastille, a mob in Birmingham, stirred up partly by Priestley’s political enemies, attacked the homes and chapels of Dissenters. Priestley’s house was burned, together with his laboratory, his library and years of notes. He and his family escaped, warned just in time.

He never felt safe in England again. In 1794, aged sixty-one, he sailed to America and settled in Northumberland, Pennsylvania, where he built a new laboratory and kept experimenting until he died in 1804. He knew some of the American founders, including Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin.

Watch fizz being made

Priestley’s “fixed air” is carbon dioxide, and you can make some in the kitchen. Put a teaspoon of baking soda into a glass and pour in a little vinegar. The bubbles are carbon dioxide. Now light nothing, and taste nothing: just watch, and listen to the fizz. If an adult opens a bottle of soda water beside it, you are seeing the same gas, dissolved under pressure and escaping. That is Priestley’s invention, in every fizzy drink on Earth.

When you read about Lavoisier and the discovery of oxygen in Chapter 4, remember the stammering minister who found the gas first, and was generous enough to describe his experiment to the man who would prove his theory wrong.

CR

C. V. Raman

Why is the sea blue?

1888 to 1970The accountant who did physics at night, and found a new secret in scattered light

Tiruchirappalli, South India, 1888

Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman was born on 7 November 1888 near Tiruchirappalli, in what is now Tamil Nadu. His father taught mathematics and physics, and the house was full of books. Raman was a remarkable student. He finished school at eleven, went to Presidency College in Madras (now Chennai), and graduated at sixteen, top of his class, with a gold medal in physics. While still a student he published a research paper about light in a British scientific journal.

In those days there were very few jobs for scientists in India. So Raman took a competitive exam for the government’s finance service, came first, and in 1907 became an assistant accountant-general in Calcutta (now Kolkata). He was eighteen.

Physics after office hours

Calcutta, 1907

Not long after he arrived, Raman noticed a sign on a building on Bowbazar Street: the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science. It had laboratory equipment but very few people using it. He walked in and asked if he could do experiments there.

For the next ten years, Raman lived two lives. By day he was a government accountant. In the early mornings and in the evenings, he was a physicist, working in the Association’s laboratory, studying sound and vibration: why violins and Indian drums like the tabla and mridangam make the beautiful sounds they do. He published paper after paper. In 1917 he finally left the finance service, taking a large cut in pay, to become a professor of physics at the University of Calcutta.

A question on a ship

The Mediterranean Sea, 1921

In 1921 Raman sailed to Britain for a conference. On the voyage he looked down at the deep blue Mediterranean Sea and asked himself a question. Why is it blue?

The usual answer was that the sea is blue because it reflects the blue sky. Raman was not satisfied. He had a small Nicol prism with him, a crystal that can block light reflected off a surface at a slant, and he used it on deck to cut out the reflected skylight. The sea still looked blue. So the colour had to come from the water itself. He suggested that light is scattered by the water molecules, just as sunlight is scattered by air molecules to make the sky blue. (We now know that water’s colour also comes from the way it soaks up a little red light, but Raman’s question started him on a long journey.)

Back in Calcutta, he and his students began to study how light is scattered by all kinds of liquids and gases.

A new colour

Calcutta, February 1928

When light hits molecules and bounces off in a new direction, it almost always keeps exactly the same colour. Blue light comes out blue; green comes out green. But Raman and his colleague K. S. Krishnan noticed that a tiny fraction of the scattered light, perhaps one part in a million or less, came out a slightly different colour.

They used sunlight focused through a telescope lens, and coloured filters, and later a mercury lamp, and looked very carefully. The extra colours were real. On 28 February 1928 Raman announced the discovery. Today, 28 February is celebrated in India as National Science Day.

What was happening? Think of a ball bouncing off a drum. Usually it bounces back with the same energy. But occasionally it sets the drum vibrating, and comes back with a little less energy, having given some away. Light does the same with molecules. Every molecule vibrates in its own particular ways, so it takes away its own particular amounts of energy, and the scattered light comes out shifted by exactly those amounts. The shifted colours are a fingerprint of the molecule.

This is the Raman effect. Today, Raman instruments are used everywhere: to identify chemicals without touching them, to check medicines for fakes, to study paintings without damaging them, and even on Mars rovers to study rocks.

The prize

In 1930 Raman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics, the first Asian scientist to win a Nobel Prize in a science. There is a well-known story that he was so sure he would win that he booked his ship tickets to Sweden months before the announcement. It is often told, but it is hard to know whether it is quite true.

He went on to lead the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore (now Bengaluru), and in 1948 he founded his own research institute there, the Raman Research Institute, where he worked until he died in 1970. He spent much of his later life studying the colours of flowers, gemstones and crystals. He loved diamonds, and built up a large collection to study.

Make a sunset in a glass

You need a clear glass of water, a few drops of milk and a torch, and a dark room. Stir three or four drops of milk into the water. Shine the torch through the side of the glass and look at the glass from the side: the water has a faint bluish glow. Now look through the glass straight towards the torch: the light coming through looks yellowish or orange. The tiny drops of fat in the milk scatter blue light sideways more than red, just as air scatters sunlight to make the blue sky and the orange sunset. Raman spent his life studying scattered light like this, and he found something hidden in it that no one had noticed before.

When this book talks about light and the colours that molecules and atoms give out, remember the young accountant who walked into a laboratory on Bowbazar Street and asked if he could do some experiments.

WR

William Ramsay

The man who found a missing column

1852 to 1916Discovered the noble gases, an entire family of elements hiding in the air

Glasgow, 1850s and 1860s

William Ramsay was born in Glasgow in 1852. His family were engineers and scientists: his father was a civil engineer, one uncle was a famous geologist, and his grandfather had been a chemical manufacturer. William loved languages, music and mathematics as a boy, and it is said that he first became interested in chemistry while reading about how gunpowder is made. By his mid-teens he was studying at the University of Glasgow, and he went on to study chemistry in Germany.

He became a professor in Bristol, then at University College London. He was known as a superb experimenter with glass: he could blow and shape fine glass apparatus himself.

A puzzle about nitrogen

Cambridge and London, 1892 to 1894

The story begins with somebody else. Lord Rayleigh was a physicist who was measuring the densities of gases very, very precisely. He made nitrogen in two different ways. One way was to take air and remove the oxygen, water and carbon dioxide. The other was to make nitrogen from chemicals such as ammonia.

The two samples should have been identical. They were not. The nitrogen from air was heavier, by about half a percent. A litre of it weighed about 1.257 grams; a litre of the chemical nitrogen about 1.251 grams. A tiny difference, but Rayleigh was a careful man and it never went away.

Rayleigh published a letter asking if anybody could explain it. Ramsay offered to help. Each worked on it separately, in close touch. Their guess: the nitrogen from air was not pure nitrogen. Something else, something heavier, was hiding in it.

Argon, the lazy one

Ramsay passed nitrogen from air over hot magnesium, again and again, which slowly removes nitrogen by turning it into a solid. At the end, a small amount of gas remained that would not react with anything. Its spectrum (the pattern of coloured lines it gives off when electricity passes through it; see spectra) matched no known element.

In 1894 Rayleigh and Ramsay announced a new element. They called it argon, from the Greek for “lazy” or “idle”, because it refused to react. It makes up nearly 1% of air. People had been breathing it for ever, and chemists had been weighing it along with their nitrogen for over a century without knowing it was there. (In fact Henry Cavendish, in 1785, had noticed a small bubble of air that would not react, but nobody followed it up.)

Helium, from the Sun to Earth

In 1868 astronomers had seen a yellow line in the spectrum of the Sun that matched no element on Earth, and named the unknown element helium, after the Greek for “Sun”. In 1895 Ramsay dissolved a uranium mineral in acid and collected the gas it released. He found in it the very same yellow line. Helium was not only in the Sun: it was here, trapped in rocks.

A whole new family

Now Ramsay had two unreactive gases that did not fit anywhere in Mendeleev’s periodic table. He made a bold guess: they belonged to a whole new family, a new column, and there should be more members to find.

University College London, 1898

With his young assistant Morris Travers, Ramsay cooled air until it turned into a liquid, then let it boil off slowly, collecting each gas as it came away. In 1898, in just a few weeks, they found three more:

  • neon (“new”), which glows a brilliant red-orange in a tube with electricity (the first “neon signs”);
  • krypton (“hidden”);
  • xenon (“stranger”).

Travers later recalled the moment they first saw neon’s crimson glow. The whole column of what we now call the noble gases was complete, except for radon, which others found among radioactive elements and which Ramsay helped to study.

In 1904 Ramsay won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry and Rayleigh the Nobel Prize in Physics, in the same year. Ramsay is one of very few scientists to have discovered a whole group of the periodic table.

Mendeleev had at first doubted argon. In the end he accepted the new column, and it fitted his table beautifully: it slotted in between the halogens and the alkali metals.

India

Ramsay also has a link to India. In about 1900 he travelled there to advise on plans for a new research institute that the industrialist Jamsetji Tata hoped to found. His advice helped decide where it should go: Bangalore. The Indian Institute of Science opened there in 1909. (Accounts differ about how much influence his report had, but his visit is well recorded.)

Find the lazy gas in your room

You cannot see argon, smell it or taste it, but it is all around you. Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and nearly 1% argon (0.93%, to be more exact). Measure the room you are sitting in with a tape measure, or estimate it. Multiply length × width × height in metres to get cubic metres, and multiply by 1,000 to get litres. Then find 0.93% of that. For a classroom 10 m by 8 m by 3 m: 240 cubic metres is 240,000 litres of air, and about 2,200 litres of it is argon, enough to fill more than ten bathtubs. Every breath you take is nearly one hundredth argon, and it comes out again unchanged.

He died in 1916. When you look at the last column of the periodic table in Chapter 9, the lazy gases that hardly react with anything, remember the half percent of extra weight that a careful man refused to ignore.

ER

Ernest Rutherford

The boy from the potato field

1871 to 1937The farm boy from New Zealand who found the nucleus and turned one element into another

Brightwater, New Zealand, 1871

Ernest Rutherford was born on 30 August 1871 near Nelson, at the top of New Zealand’s South Island, the fourth of twelve children. His father was a wheelwright and flax-miller; his mother was a schoolteacher. There was not much money, but there were a lot of books, and young Ernest was the kind of boy who took clocks apart to see how they worked and built model water wheels in the creek.

He won scholarships at every step: to Nelson College, then to Canterbury College in Christchurch, where he did his first real experiments in a cold, draughty basement, building detectors for radio waves only a few years after they had been discovered. In 1895 he won a scholarship to study at Cambridge, on the other side of the world.

There is a famous story about that moment. The telegram arrived while he was digging potatoes in his family’s garden, and he threw down his spade and said, “That’s the last potato I’ll ever dig.” It is a lovely story, and it is told everywhere, but nobody wrote it down at the time, so treat it as a family legend rather than a fact.

The colonial in Cambridge

At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Rutherford worked under J. J. Thomson, the man who would discover the electron. Some of the English students looked down on the loud young man from the colonies. It did not last. Within a few years Rutherford was famous for one thing above all: he could design simple, clever experiments that went straight to the heart of a question.

Radioactivity had just been discovered, and Rutherford threw himself into it. He found that the rays coming out of uranium were of at least two kinds, and he gave them the names we still use: alpha and beta.

Montreal, and the shock of transmutation

Montreal, Canada, 1901

In 1898 Rutherford became a professor at McGill University in Montreal. There he teamed up with a young English chemist, Frederick Soddy. Together they studied thorium, a radioactive element, and noticed something that seemed impossible: as it gave off radiation, a small amount of thorium was slowly becoming a different element.

For more than two thousand years, alchemists had dreamed of changing one element into another. Serious scientists had decided it could not be done. Now here it was, happening on its own, inside a lump of rock. Soddy later remembered blurting out, “Rutherford, this is transmutation!” and Rutherford snapping back, “For Mike’s sake, Soddy, don’t call it transmutation. They’ll have our heads off as alchemists.” (This is Soddy’s own memory, told many years later, so the exact words may have drifted.)

In 1908 Rutherford won the Nobel Prize. He was a physicist through and through, and he rather looked down on chemistry, so he was amused to find it was the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He joked that he had seen many transformations in his work, but none as quick as his own, from physicist to chemist.

Manchester and the gold foil

Manchester, 1909

By then he had moved to Manchester. He asked his assistant Hans Geiger and a twenty-year-old student, Ernest Marsden, to fire alpha particles at a sheet of gold foil thinner than a leaf, and to count where they went by watching for tiny flashes of light in a darkened room. Almost all of them flew straight through. But about one in every eight thousand bounced back.

Rutherford said it was as if you fired a large shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you. In 1911 he worked out what it meant: almost all the mass of an atom is packed into a tiny, positively charged centre, the nucleus, with the electrons spread out around it, far away. An atom is mostly empty space. Chapter 1 tells this story in full, and you can fire the alpha particles yourself in its figure.

The first person to change an element on purpose

In 1919, just before he went back to Cambridge to run the Cavendish Laboratory, Rutherford did something no alchemist had ever managed. He fired alpha particles into nitrogen gas and found hydrogen nuclei (protons) flying out. A few of the nitrogen nuclei had been hit so hard that they changed. Later work by his colleague Patrick Blackett showed exactly what happened: the alpha particle sticks to the nitrogen nucleus, a proton is knocked out, and what is left is a nucleus of oxygen.

So the first deliberate transmutation in history did not turn lead into gold. It turned nitrogen into oxygen, a handful of atoms at a time. It was worth nothing in money and everything in understanding.

The Crocodile

Rutherford was a big man with a big voice. His students said he sang “Onward, Christian Soldiers” loudly and badly as he walked round the laboratory, and there are stories (perhaps exaggerated) that his booming voice disturbed the delicate instruments. The Russian physicist Pyotr Kapitsa, who worked for him in Cambridge, nicknamed him “the Crocodile”. A crocodile was carved on the wall of the laboratory Kapitsa built there, and you can still see it.

He could be gruff, but he was generous with his students, and he had a gift for picking good people and good problems. A remarkable number of the people who trained or worked with him went on to win Nobel Prizes of their own, among them Niels Bohr, Frederick Soddy, James Chadwick (who found the neutron), and John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton (who split the atom with a machine in 1932).

What became of him

Rutherford became Lord Rutherford of Nelson, named after the town near where he grew up. He died in 1937 and was buried in Westminster Abbey in London, close to Isaac Newton. Element 104 is called rutherfordium in his honour, and his face is on New Zealand’s hundred-dollar note.

Find a hidden shape without looking

This is how Rutherford “saw” the nucleus: by throwing things at it and watching how they bounced. Ask someone to put a small object (a book, a lunchbox, a box of tea) under a large tray or a sheet of cardboard, so you cannot see it. Kneel at the edge and roll marbles under the tray from different directions. Watch where they come out. Some roll straight through; some bounce off at angles. After twenty or thirty rolls, try to sketch the hidden object’s shape and size. Then lift the tray and check. You were doing a scattering experiment.

Whenever you read about the nucleus, or about one element turning into another, you are standing on the potato field in Brightwater, with the boy who threw down his spade.

CS

Carl Wilhelm Scheele

The pharmacist who found everything first

1742 to 1786A Swedish apothecary who discovered oxygen, chlorine and many other substances

Stralsund, on the Baltic coast, 1742

Carl Wilhelm Scheele was the seventh of eleven children of a merchant in Stralsund, a town that then belonged to Sweden. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a pharmacist in Gothenburg. A pharmacy, or apothecary shop, was where medicines were made by hand from plants, minerals, acids and salts. To a boy who loved chemistry, it was a treasure house.

Scheele read every chemistry book in the shop, and at night, after work, he repeated the experiments in them. He never went to university. All his life he worked in pharmacies, and in the back rooms, with simple equipment and very little money, he became one of the greatest discoverers in the history of chemistry.

A list of discoveries

Scheele’s list is astonishing. He was the first to identify or prepare many substances, including:

  • the gas we now call chlorine, a greenish-yellow gas (he did not realise it was an element; Humphry Davy showed that later);
  • acids from fruit and from milk, among them the acid of lemons (citric acid), of sour milk (lactic acid) and of apples (malic acid);
  • glycerol, which is in soap and many foods;
  • and important early work on manganese, barium, molybdenum and tungsten.

He also found that silver salts darken in light, especially violet light, a discovery that photography would later depend on. And a bright green pigment he invented, “Scheele’s green”, became fashionable for wallpaper and paint. Sadly, it contained arsenic, and in damp rooms it could make people ill. Scheele did not know that would happen.

Fire air

Uppsala, around 1771 to 1772

Scheele wanted to know what air is made of. He heated several different substances, among them a red powder made from mercury and a black mineral of manganese, and collected the gas that came off. A candle burned in it with dazzling brightness. He called it “fire air”, because fire loved it. He also found that ordinary air contains some of this fire air and some “foul air” in which nothing will burn: oxygen and nitrogen, in today’s words.

His notebooks suggest he did these experiments around 1771 or 1772, two or three years before Joseph Priestley found the same gas in England in 1774. But Scheele’s book, Chemical Observations and Experiments on Air and Fire, was held up at the printer, and did not appear until 1777. By then Priestley had published, and Lavoisier had named the gas oxygen and explained burning.

So who discovered oxygen? Historians usually say Scheele found it first, Priestley published first, and Lavoisier understood it first. Science is often like that: a discovery is made by several people, each adding a piece.

A dangerous habit

Scheele had one habit that every chemist since has learned not to copy. In his day, chemists described substances by their colour, their smell, and their taste, and Scheele recorded the taste of many of the chemicals he made, including some that we now know are poisonous. He also worked for years with arsenic, mercury and lead, and breathed fumes in a small, poorly ventilated room.

He died in 1786, at only 43. Nobody knows the exact cause. Many historians think years of exposure to toxic chemicals damaged his health; others think he also had an illness unrelated to his work. Either way, it is a lesson that every chemistry lab in the world now teaches on the first day: you never taste a chemical in a laboratory, and you never sniff one directly. In this book the only things you ever taste are ordinary food.

A quiet, happy life
