Scheele was offered jobs as a professor in Berlin and in England, but he turned them down. He preferred his own pharmacy in the small Swedish town of Köping, where he could work in peace. He was elected to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences while still a pharmacist’s assistant, which was a very unusual honour. Just days before he died, he married the widow of the pharmacist whose shop he had taken over, so that she would inherit his business.

The acids in your fruit bowl

Scheele was the first to pull citric acid out of lemons and malic acid out of apples. You can taste the difference between them, because these are ordinary foods. Taste a tiny piece of lemon, then a slice of sour green apple, then a sweet ripe apple. The sharpness you notice comes mostly from the acids Scheele discovered. Now notice that a ripe apple tastes less sharp: as fruit ripens, the amount of acid falls and the amount of sugar rises.

When you read in Chapter 2 about how the elements were found one by one, remember the young apprentice reading by candlelight in a Swedish pharmacy, who found more of chemistry’s secrets than almost anyone, and did it all from a shop.

1839 to 1974

Lucky accidents, and the people who noticed

Charles Goodyear, Alexander Fleming, Roy Plunkett, Spencer Silver, Art Fry

There is a saying, usually credited to the French scientist Louis Pasteur: “chance favours only the prepared mind.” Here are five discoveries that began as accidents, and the people who were prepared enough to notice.

Massachusetts, 1839

Rubber that behaves

Natural rubber, from the sap of rubber trees, was a nuisance in the 1830s. In summer it went soft and sticky; in winter it cracked. Charles Goodyear, an American inventor who was often deeply in debt, spent years mixing rubber with everything he could think of.

According to his own account, in 1839 he dropped some rubber mixed with sulfur onto a hot stove. Instead of melting, it charred like leather and stayed firm and springy. (The details come from Goodyear himself and may have been tidied up in the telling.) Heat had made sulfur atoms form bridges between the long rubber molecules, tying them together like the rungs of a ladder. The process was later called vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. Every car tyre depends on it.

London, 1928

The mould that killed germs

Alexander Fleming, a Scottish doctor, came back from a holiday to find that a dish of bacteria he had left on his bench had grown a fuzzy patch of mould. Around the mould there was a clear ring where the bacteria had died. Something from the mould was killing them.

Fleming called the substance penicillin. He could not make enough of it to use as a medicine, and for about ten years not much happened. Then, around 1940, a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain worked out how to purify it, and the first patients were treated. Penicillin has since saved an enormous number of lives.

New Jersey, 1938

The gas cylinder that went quiet

Roy Plunkett, a young chemist at the DuPont company, was working with a gas for refrigerators. One morning a cylinder that should have been full of gas would not let any out, though it still weighed as much as a full one. Instead of throwing it away, Plunkett had it sawn open. Inside was a white, waxy, slippery powder. The gas molecules had joined together into long chains, all by themselves.

The new material was incredibly slippery and almost nothing reacted with it. It was named Teflon, and today it coats non-stick frying pans.

Minnesota, 1968 and 1974

The glue that did not stick properly

Spencer Silver, a chemist at the company 3M, was trying to make a very strong glue. He made a very weak one instead: it stuck, but peeled off easily and could be stuck again. For years nobody knew what to do with it. Then his colleague Art Fry, who sang in a church choir, was annoyed that his paper bookmarks kept falling out of his hymn book. He remembered Silver’s glue. The result, after more years of work, was the sticky note.

Careful

“Saccharin was found by a chemist licking his fingers, so tasting things is how discoveries get made.”

It is true that in 1879 a chemist named Constantin Fahlberg noticed his bread tasted sweet after a day in the laboratory, traced it to a chemical on his hands, and so found the sweetener saccharin. But many chemists in history poisoned themselves by tasting and smelling unknown substances. Never taste anything from an experiment. Fahlberg was lucky, and lucky is not a method.

What they had in common

None of these people was simply lucky. Goodyear had spent years on rubber. Fleming knew exactly what a clear ring around a mould meant. Plunkett weighed his cylinder instead of assuming it was empty. Each had a prepared mind: they knew enough to recognise that something strange was also something important.

Make a slime that changes

Mix two tablespoons of cornflour with about one tablespoon of water in a bowl. Poke it hard and fast: it feels solid. Let your finger sink in slowly: it flows like a liquid. Nobody planned this; it is just how the starch grains in water behave. Write down what you notice, like a scientist, before reading about it.

about 300 to 1700

Two thousand years of trying to make gold

Zosimos of Panopolis, Jabir ibn Hayyan, Abu Bakr al-Razi, Paracelsus, Hennig Brand

Alexandria, Egypt, about the year 300

Picture a workshop in the great city of Alexandria, on the coast of Egypt. Furnaces glow. Clay pots bubble. A man called Zosimos, from the town of Panopolis, is writing down everything he knows about how to change one metal into another. He describes stills for boiling liquids and catching their vapour, and he writes about a woman he calls Mary the Jewess, who seems to have invented some of this equipment before him. Very little is known about Mary for certain, but a cooking method is still named after her: the bain-marie, a bowl set over hot water.

This was the beginning of alchemy, and for about the next fourteen hundred years some of the cleverest people in the world tried to do the same thing: turn cheap metals such as lead into gold.

Why it seemed possible

The idea was not silly at the time. Metals look alike: shiny, heavy, able to melt and be hammered. Copper mixed with zinc turns a golden colour. Ores dug from the ground change completely in a furnace. If dull rock can become bright metal, why shouldn’t one metal become another? Many alchemists believed metals slowly “ripened” underground, the way fruit ripens, and that gold was the ripest of all. Perhaps, with the right substance, you could speed the ripening up. They called that imagined substance the philosopher’s stone.

The Arabic chemists

When the Roman world faded, the work moved to Baghdad and the other great cities of the Islamic world. A large collection of books is credited to Jabir ibn Hayyan, who may have lived in the 700s. Historians argue about who really wrote them: some of the books were probably written by many different people over a long time and put under his famous name. Whoever wrote them, they describe careful laboratory work: purifying substances, crystallising them, and sorting them into groups.

A little later, in the late 800s and early 900s, the Persian doctor Abu Bakr al-Razi sorted substances into families, such as minerals, salts and spirits, and described his apparatus so clearly that you could rebuild it. He used distillation, the trick of boiling a liquid and cooling its vapour to collect something purer.

You still speak a little of their language every day. Alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kīmiyā, and chemistry comes from that. Alcohol and alkali are Arabic words too.

Paracelsus and the medicine-makers

In the 1500s a loud, quarrelsome Swiss doctor who called himself Paracelsus told alchemists to stop chasing gold and make medicines instead. He was rude to almost everyone, and some of his ideas were badly wrong, but he pushed alchemy towards chemistry: making useful substances and testing what they did.

Hamburg, 1669

Now for one of the strangest discoveries ever made. Hennig Brand, a merchant in Hamburg, was sure the secret of gold was hidden in human urine. It is yellow, after all. So he collected a great deal of it (stories say dozens of buckets, though nobody knows the exact amount), left it to stand for days, and boiled it down.

He did not get gold. At the bottom of his apparatus he got a white, waxy substance that glowed in the dark with a ghostly green light. It caught fire by itself in air. Brand had discovered phosphorus, from the Greek for “light-bringer”. It is usually called the first element whose discoverer we know by name. The elements known before it, such as gold, iron, copper and sulfur, had been in use since ancient times, and nobody knows who first found them.

The secret alchemists

Alchemy did not end when modern science began. Robert Boyle, one of the founders of modern chemistry, practised alchemy all his life and hoped to see a metal transformed. Isaac Newton, the greatest scientist of his age, wrote more than a million words about alchemy, much of it in secret notebooks. Both men are in this book, and both have their own stories.

Why it could never work

Here is the answer the alchemists could not have known. Gold is an element: every gold atom has exactly 79 protons in its nucleus, and that number is what makes it gold. Lead has 82, and mercury has 80.

Chemistry, everything you do with fire, acids, stills and furnaces, only moves the electrons on the outside of atoms. It rearranges atoms into new partners. It never touches the nucleus in the middle. So no chemical reaction, however clever, can turn lead into gold. To change the number of protons, you have to break into the nucleus itself, and that takes energies millions of times greater than any furnace.

Careful

“So the alchemists were just foolish.”

They were not. They had no way of knowing atoms existed, let alone nuclei. And while chasing gold they invented the tools of the laboratory: stills, flasks, furnaces, water baths, and the habit of writing down exactly what they did. They discovered acids, purified salts and found new elements. Modern chemistry grew out of their workshops.

Watch distillation happen

Ask an adult to pour a mug of very hot tap water. Hold a cold plate (straight from the fridge is best) a few centimetres above the mug for half a minute, then look underneath. Water vapour rising from the mug has cooled on the plate and turned back into drops of liquid. That is the heart of distillation, the trick al-Razi and the alchemists used to purify liquids. Don’t use boiling water from a kettle, and keep your hand away from the steam.

The alchemists’ dream did eventually come true, in a way none of them could have imagined, inside particle accelerators and nuclear reactors. That is the story of transmutation.

1865

The snake that bit its own tail

August Kekulé, Michael Faraday, Kathleen Lonsdale

London, 1825

The puzzle began with Michael Faraday. In 1825 he found a new liquid in the oily leftovers of a lighting gas made by heating whale and fish oil, which a London company delivered in metal cylinders. It smelled sweet and caught fire easily. He measured carefully what it was made of, and his numbers, read with what we know today, mean it has equal numbers of carbon and hydrogen atoms. We now write it C₆H₆ and call it benzene.

Here was the trouble. By the 1850s chemists had learned that every carbon atom forms four bonds and every hydrogen atom forms one. A chain of six carbons, like the ones in petrol, needs fourteen hydrogens to use up all those bonds. Benzene had only six. How could six carbons and six hydrogens fit together so that every carbon had its four bonds? And why was benzene so stable, when other molecules short of hydrogen reacted eagerly?

Ghent, Belgium, 1865

August Kekulé, a German chemist teaching in Ghent, had already helped work out that carbon makes four bonds and that carbon atoms can link into chains. In 1865 he proposed something new: the six carbons of benzene join into a ring, a closed hexagon, each carbon holding one hydrogen. To give each carbon four bonds, he suggested the ring had double and single bonds alternating around it.

It was a brilliant idea, and it explained a huge number of facts about benzene and the many substances made from it, including Perkin’s dyes.

The daydream

Twenty-five years later, in 1890, chemists held a great celebration in Berlin for the anniversary of Kekulé’s ring. In his speech, Kekulé told a story. He said he had been dozing by the fire, and saw rows of atoms dancing and twisting like snakes. Then one snake seized its own tail and whirled before his eyes, and he woke with the idea of a ring.

It is a wonderful story, and it is famous all over the world. But it is Kekulé’s own account, told a quarter of a century later at a party in his honour. Some historians think he embellished it, or invented it to make a point about imagination. We cannot know for sure.

Careful

“So the discovery came from a dream.”

Even if the dream happened exactly as he said, it came after years of hard thinking about how carbon atoms join. A dream does not hand you an answer you have not prepared for. Kekulé himself is reported to have ended his speech by telling chemists to dream, but to test their dreams before publishing them.

Seeing the ring

For decades the ring was a brilliant guess that fitted the facts. Then, in 1929, the Irish-born crystallographer Kathleen Lonsdale used X-rays on a crystal of a benzene compound and showed that the ring really is flat and hexagonal. She also found that all six bonds around the ring are the same length. That doesn’t fit Kekulé’s picture of alternating single and double bonds exactly. The modern picture is that the shared electrons are spread evenly around the whole ring, which is why chemists often draw benzene as a hexagon with a circle inside. That evenly spread cloud of electrons is also what makes benzene so stable.

Build a benzene ring

Take six paper clips (the carbons) and link them into a closed ring. Hook one small elastic band or a scrap of paper (a hydrogen) onto the outside of each. Now try to make a straight chain of six clips with only six “hydrogens” so that every clip has four connections: you will find you cannot do it without closing the loop or doubling up connections. That was Kekulé’s puzzle.

1856

The boy who made the world purple

William Henry Perkin, August Wilhelm von Hofmann

East London, Easter holiday, 1856

William Perkin was eighteen, and he had turned part of his family’s house in East London into a laboratory. In term time he was the assistant of a famous German chemist, August Wilhelm von Hofmann, at the Royal College of Chemistry. Over the Easter holiday he carried on experimenting at home.

Hofmann had set him a dream of a problem. Malaria was killing huge numbers of people across the British Empire, including in India. The only medicine, quinine, came from the bark of the cinchona tree, which grew in South America and was expensive and scarce. Could a chemist make quinine in a flask, from something cheap?

The cheap starting point

The cheapest raw material around was coal tar, the black, smelly waste left over when coal was heated to make gas for street lamps. Chemists had found that coal tar contained useful substances. Perkin took one of them, aniline, and treated it with a strong chemical that pulls hydrogen away, hoping to build quinine.

He did not get quinine. Nobody could have, with what was known in 1856: quinine’s structure was far too complicated, and it was not made in a laboratory until 1944. What Perkin got was a black, tarry sludge at the bottom of his flask.

Looking twice

Most people would have thrown it away. Perkin washed the flask out with alcohol, and the alcohol turned a brilliant purple.

He tested the purple on silk. It stuck. It did not wash out, and it did not fade quickly in sunlight. Purple had always been the colour of emperors, because the old purple dye came from sea snails, thousands of them for a scrap of cloth. Perkin had made purple from coal waste.

The gamble

His teacher thought he was throwing away a scientific career. Perkin patented his dye anyway, left college, and, with money from his father and help from his brother, built a factory near London. He was still a teenager. Making it work was hard: they had to work out how to produce aniline by the barrel rather than by the spoonful, and how to fix the dye onto cotton as well as silk.

The colour became known by the French name mauve, and in the late 1850s mauve became the most fashionable colour in Europe. Queen Victoria wore mauve to her daughter’s wedding in 1858. Magazines joked about “mauve measles” because the colour was everywhere.

What came next

Perkin’s dye, later called mauveine, was the first of the coal-tar dyes, and the first artificial dye to become a worldwide success. Within a few years chemists had made magenta, new blues, greens and blacks, all from coal tar. The great chemical companies of Germany and Switzerland began as dye makers. And the skills they learned, building complicated molecules step by step, led straight to synthetic medicines. So in a roundabout way Perkin did help the fight against disease: just not the way he planned.

Perkin made his fortune, sold the factory at 36 and went back to pure research for the rest of his life. He was knighted in 1906, fifty years after that Easter holiday.

Dye with turmeric

You need a spoonful of turmeric powder, a cup of hot tap water (ask an adult), and a strip of white cotton cloth, such as an old handkerchief. Stir the turmeric into the water, drop in the cloth for ten minutes, then rinse it in cold water. It stays bright yellow. Now dab one corner with a little baking soda dissolved in water: turmeric is also an indicator, and it turns red-brown where it meets something basic. Turmeric stains hands and clothes, so wear old clothes and work on a plate.

The lesson to take from Perkin is not “accidents make you rich”. It is that he noticed. Lots of people had made black sludge. He looked at it twice.

1901 to today

Mercury into gold, at last

Ernest Rutherford, Frederick Soddy, Glenn Seaborg, the ALICE team at CERN

Montreal, Canada, 1901

In a basement laboratory at McGill University, two young scientists were puzzling over a radioactive substance called thorium. One was Ernest Rutherford, a farmer’s son from New Zealand. The other was Frederick Soddy, a chemist from England. Thorium kept giving off a gas, and when Soddy tested the gas he realised it was not thorium at all. It was a different element. The thorium atoms were turning, all by themselves, into atoms of something else.

Soddy said many years later that he burst out, “Rutherford, this is transmutation!”, and that Rutherford answered something like, “For goodness’ sake, Soddy, don’t call it transmutation. They’ll have our heads off as alchemists.” We only have Soddy’s memory of the exact words, but the worry was real. Transmutation, changing one element into another, was the alchemists’ word, and serious scientists had spent two hundred years laughing at it.

Yet here it was, happening on their bench.

What makes gold gold

To understand the rest of this story you need one fact. What decides which element an atom is? Not its colour, not its weight, not its electrons. It is the number of protons in its nucleus.

Gold: 79 protons. Mercury: 80 protons. Lead: 82 protons.
To turn mercury into gold, you must take away exactly one proton from each nucleus.

Chemistry cannot do this, because chemistry only rearranges the electrons on the outside. To change the proton number you have to break into the nucleus, which is tiny, extremely tightly held together, and guarded by a powerful electric push against anything with a charge.

The first deliberate transmutation

Manchester, 1919

Radioactive atoms transmute themselves. Could a person make it happen on purpose? In 1919 Rutherford fired fast alpha particles, from a radioactive source, through nitrogen gas. Once in a long while an alpha particle hit a nitrogen nucleus squarely and stuck, and a proton flew out. The nitrogen nucleus became an oxygen nucleus. For the first time, a human being had deliberately turned one element into another. It was not gold, and it was only a handful of atoms, but the door was open.

Gold from mercury, 1941

Then came the neutron (found in 1932), a particle with no electric charge. Because it has no charge, nothing pushes it away, and it can slip into a nucleus easily. In 1941, at Harvard, the physicists Rubby Sherr, Kenneth Bainbridge and Herbert Anderson fired neutrons at mercury and made gold. There was a catch: the gold atoms they made were radioactive kinds that broke down within days. Nobody could have worn it as a ring.

In 1980 the American chemist Glenn Seaborg, who discovered several of the heaviest elements, used a particle accelerator in California to knock protons and neutrons off bismuth (83 protons) and leave gold behind. He made only a tiny number of atoms, and the electricity and machinery cost vastly more than the gold was worth.

The biggest machine in the world

CERN, near Geneva, 2025

The Large Hadron Collider is a ring 27 kilometres round, buried under the border between France and Switzerland. It smashes together nuclei of lead travelling at almost the speed of light. In May 2025 the scientists of its ALICE experiment announced something surprising (published in the journal Physical Review C).

Sometimes two lead nuclei do not hit each other at all. They whizz past very close. Each carries such an intense electric field that, as they pass, a burst of light energy can knock a few particles out of the other nucleus. If exactly three protons are knocked out, lead (82) becomes gold (79).

The ALICE team worked out that in the years 2015 to 2018 the collider had made about 86 billion gold nuclei this way. That sounds like a lot. Add them up, though, and they weigh about 29 picograms: 29 millionths of a millionth of a gram. A single grain of rice is roughly 700 million times heavier. And each gold nucleus lasted only a tiny fraction of a second before it hit the machine’s walls and broke apart.

A claim from a fusion company

Now we come to the news. A company in the United States called Marathon Fusion works on nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun. In 2025 its scientists published a proposal based on computer calculations. Future fusion power plants will release enormous numbers of fast neutrons. If those neutrons struck a kind of mercury called mercury-198, they could knock a neutron out, leaving mercury-197. Mercury-197 is unstable. Over a couple of days its nucleus captures one of its own inner electrons; inside the nucleus that electron and a proton turn into a neutron, so 80 protons become 79. The result is gold-197, the ordinary, stable gold of rings and coins. Their calculations suggested a big fusion plant might make a few tonnes of gold a year as a by-product. That was a model on a computer, not a working machine.

On 21 October 2026 the company announced online that it had actually made gold from mercury, beating CERN’s record “by a factor of 10”. As this book was written, that claim had not been checked by other scientists. That does not mean it is false. It means we do not know yet.

Careful

“If a company says it did something, it did it.”

In science a claim becomes knowledge only when others can check it. Scientists would want to see a detailed paper, reviewed by experts who did not do the work, showing exactly how much gold was made and how it was measured, and ideally an independent laboratory confirming it. Until then, a sensible scientist says: “Interesting, and unconfirmed.”

The real treasure

Isaac Newton spent years of secret work trying to transmute metals. He would have been astonished to learn that it can be done, and perhaps more astonished to learn why it was impossible for him: the change happens deep in the nucleus, at energies no furnace could reach.

Even if fusion gold becomes real, the gold is not the most precious thing in this story. Rutherford and Soddy learned what an element is. That understanding gave us nuclear medicine, carbon dating, smoke detectors and power from the atom. The alchemists were searching for gold. What they and their successors actually found was knowledge, and that turned out to be worth far more.

about 450 BCE to 1908

Can you cut forever? The long argument about atoms

Leucippus, Democritus, Kanada, John Dalton

Abdera, a Greek town on the coast of Thrace, about 450 BCE

Imagine you have a piece of cheese and a very sharp knife. Cut it in half. Cut one half in half again. Keep going. The pieces get smaller and smaller, until they are too small to see. Can you keep going for ever, or is there a smallest piece of cheese that cannot be cut?

About two and a half thousand years ago, a Greek thinker called Leucippus and his student Democritus gave an answer. You cannot cut for ever, they said. In the end you reach tiny pieces that are solid all the way through and cannot be divided. They called them atomos, which means “uncuttable”, and that is where our word atom comes from. Everything, they said, is made of atoms moving through empty space. Sweet things are made of smooth round atoms, sour things of sharp, jagged ones. Water flows because its atoms are slippery.

This was a remarkable guess. But it was only a guess. Democritus had no way to test it, and the most famous philosopher of the next generation, Aristotle, did not believe it. Aristotle taught that matter is continuous, like an endless smooth jelly, and that everything is made of four elements: earth, water, air and fire. Aristotle’s ideas were taught in schools for nearly two thousand years. Atoms were mostly forgotten.

Far away, the same idea

Greece was not the only place where people wondered about this. In India, the philosopher Kanada, founder of the Vaisheshika school, also taught that matter is made of tiny, eternal, indivisible particles, which he called paramanu. Nobody knows exactly when Kanada lived; scholars’ guesses range over several centuries before the Common Era. His particles combined in pairs and threes to make bigger things, an idea that sounds surprisingly modern. Like Democritus, though, Kanada was reasoning, not measuring.

Step 1: why a guess is not enough

Here is the important difference between philosophy and science. A philosopher can say “matter is made of atoms” and argue for it beautifully. A scientist has to ask: if that is true, what should I be able to measure? Only when an idea predicts something you can check does it start to become science.

For atoms, that took until about 1800, and it came from weighing.

Manchester, England, 1803

John Dalton was the son of a poor weaver. He started teaching at a village school when he was twelve years old, the same age you are now. Later he taught mathematics and science in Manchester, and in his spare time he studied the weather, kept a daily weather diary for 57 years, and discovered that he and his brother were colour-blind (it is still sometimes called Daltonism).

Dalton was puzzling over gases, and over a strange regularity that chemists had found when substances combine.

Step 2: the clue in the numbers

When elements combine to make compounds, they always do so in fixed proportions by mass. Water is always about 1 gram of hydrogen for every 8 grams of oxygen, no matter where the water comes from. And when two elements can make more than one compound, the amounts come in simple whole-number ratios. Carbon makes two gases with oxygen: in one, 12 grams of carbon combine with 16 grams of oxygen; in the other, the same 12 grams of carbon combine with 32 grams of oxygen. Exactly twice as much. Never 1.7 times, never 2.3 times.

Why whole numbers? Dalton saw the answer. If each element is made of identical atoms, all with the same mass, and compounds form when atoms join in small whole numbers, then the masses must come in simple ratios. One carbon atom with one oxygen atom makes one gas (we now call it carbon monoxide); one carbon atom with two oxygen atoms makes the other (carbon dioxide). Twice the oxygen atoms, twice the mass of oxygen.

Step 3: Dalton’s atomic theory

In 1808 Dalton published his ideas in a book called A New System of Chemical Philosophy. In simple words:

  1. Every element is made of tiny atoms.
  2. All the atoms of one element are identical, with the same mass. Atoms of different elements have different masses.
  3. Atoms are not created or destroyed in chemical reactions; they just rearrange.
  4. Compounds form when atoms of different elements join in small whole numbers.

He drew each kind of atom as a little circle with its own mark, and made the first table of relative atomic masses, with hydrogen as 1. Some of his numbers were wrong, because he guessed some formulas wrong (he thought water was HO, one hydrogen to one oxygen), but the idea was right, and it gave chemists a way to reason about things they could not see.

Careful

“Dalton proved that atoms exist.”

Not quite. Dalton showed that atoms were a very good way to explain the numbers chemists measured. Many scientists used atoms as a handy bookkeeping idea but doubted they were real objects. Some famous chemists, such as Wilhelm Ostwald, argued against real atoms until the early 1900s. They changed their minds only after Jean Perrin’s measurements of Brownian motion, around 1908, showed that atoms behave exactly like real, countable particles.

Step 4: what we know now

Two of Dalton’s ideas needed improving later, which is exactly how science is supposed to work. Atoms can be cut: they are made of protons, neutrons and electrons, as you will see in Chapter 1. And atoms of the same element are not all identical in mass: they come as isotopes. But his central idea, that chemistry is atoms rearranging in whole numbers, is the foundation of everything in this book.

Cut it as small as you can

Take a sugar cube and crush it with the back of a spoon into the finest powder you can. Look at a pinch of it under a magnifying glass, or with your phone camera zoomed in. Every grain is still a sugar crystal with flat faces. Now stir a spoonful of the powder into warm water until it disappears. Taste a drop: the sugar is still there, in pieces far too small to see. Where would Democritus say the cutting stops? (The answer, in this case, is a single sugar molecule, about a millionth of a millimetre across.)

Democritus asked the right question; Dalton found a way to test it. It took two thousand years to get from one to the other, and another hundred years before the last doubters were convinced.

1897

The particle in the glowing tube

William Crookes, J. J. Thomson

The Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, 1897

In the late 1800s, one of the most fashionable toys in science was a glass tube with almost all the air pumped out of it. Push a metal wire into each end, connect them to a high voltage, and something eerie happens. A glow appears. Rays seem to stream from the negative wire, which was called the cathode, and where they hit the glass at the far end, the glass shines a ghostly green. Nobody could see the rays themselves, so they were simply called cathode rays.

The English scientist William Crookes built beautiful versions of these tubes. He put a little metal cross in the path of the rays, and it cast a sharp shadow on the glowing glass, so the rays travelled in straight lines. He put a tiny paddle wheel inside, and the rays made it turn, as if they were pushing on it. But what were they? German scientists mostly thought they were a kind of light, a wave. British scientists mostly thought they were a stream of tiny particles. The argument went on for years.

Step 1: a question you can test

Joseph John Thomson, known to everyone as J. J., was the head of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge. He decided to settle it with a simple test. Light is not pushed sideways by electric charges or by magnets. Charged particles are. So: can you bend cathode rays?

Magnets bent them easily; that was already known. Electric charges were harder, because earlier experimenters had failed to make the rays bend near charged metal plates. Thomson guessed why: there was still too much gas in their tubes, and the gas was spoiling the experiment. With better pumps, he got a much emptier tube, put two metal plates inside, charged one positive and one negative, and watched. The glowing spot on the end of the tube moved, towards the positive plate.

Things that are pulled towards positive charge must be negative. Cathode rays, Thomson concluded, are streams of tiny, negatively charged particles.

Step 2: weighing something you cannot see

Then Thomson did something brilliant. By bending the rays with a magnet one way and an electric field the other way, and adjusting the two until they cancelled out, he could work out the ratio of the particles’ charge to their mass. He could not find either one separately, but he could find how much charge each particle carried for its weight.

The answer was astonishing. For its mass, each particle carried an enormous charge: over a thousand times more charge for its mass than a charged hydrogen atom in a solution (the lightest charged thing anyone knew). If the charge was about the same size, then these particles were more than a thousand times lighter than the lightest atom. Today we know the exact figure: a hydrogen atom has about 1,836 times the mass of one of these particles.

And here is the most important part. Thomson got exactly the same particles whatever metal he used for the wires and whatever gas was left in the tube. Aluminium, iron, platinum; air, hydrogen, carbon dioxide: the particles were always identical. So they must be a part of every atom.

Step 3: the atom is not uncuttable after all

For two thousand years, “atom” had meant “the thing that cannot be cut”. Thomson had just found a piece of one. The particle was soon given a name that another physicist, George Johnstone Stoney, had suggested years earlier for the smallest unit of electric charge: the electron.

On 30 April 1897, Thomson announced his results at the Royal Institution in London. Some of the audience thought he was joking. He was not. He had found the first subatomic particle, and he won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906.

Step 4: a first model, and why it was wrong

If atoms contain tiny negative electrons, but atoms themselves are neutral, there must be positive charge in there somewhere to balance them. Thomson suggested the atom was a ball of spread-out positive charge with electrons dotted through it, like raisins in a pudding. It became known as the plum pudding model.

It was a sensible guess, and it was wrong. Twelve years later, one of Thomson’s former students, Ernest Rutherford, would fire particles at gold foil and find that the positive charge is not spread out at all. But that is the next story.

Careful

“Electrons are tiny balls that orbit the atom.”

Thomson’s experiment showed that electrons have charge and mass, so in that experiment they behave like particles. But later work showed they also behave like waves, and inside atoms they do not follow tracks at all. The best description we have says where an electron is likely to be found, not where it is. “Particle” is a useful word for electrons, as long as you do not picture a tiny marble.

Pile up some electrons

Rub a balloon on your hair or a wool jumper, then hold it near some small torn bits of tissue paper, or near a friend’s hair. The rubbing moves electrons from one thing to the other, so the balloon ends up with extra electrons: a negative charge. That is the same particle Thomson found, piled up by the trillion on a balloon’s surface.

Every time you switch on a light, electrons are moving through the wire. Every chemical reaction in this book is, at heart, electrons rearranging. They were found because a scientist asked a simple question about a mysterious glow, and then designed an experiment clever enough to answer it.

1913 to 1932

Same element, different weight

Frederick Soddy, Margaret Todd, Francis Aston, James Chadwick, Irène Joliot-Curie

Glasgow, Scotland, 1913

By 1913, chemists studying radioactive substances had a problem. They had found dozens of “new” radioactive substances, far more than there were spaces for in the periodic table. Stranger still, some of them could not be separated from each other by any chemical method at all. One substance from thorium behaved exactly like lead: same reactions, same compounds, same everything. Yet it had a different mass from ordinary lead.

Frederick Soddy, a chemist in Glasgow, decided to stop fighting the facts. Perhaps, he said, these really are the same element. They sit in the same place in the periodic table, but their atoms have different masses. He needed a name for atoms like that. At a dinner party at his father-in-law’s house, he explained the idea to a family friend, Margaret Todd, a Scottish doctor and writer. She suggested a word from Greek: isos, “equal”, and topos, “place”. Same place: isotope.

Step 1: the puzzle in a simple form

If two atoms are the same element, they have the same number of protons (you will meet that idea properly in Chapter 1). But in 1913 nobody knew about protons as separate particles yet, let alone what else might be in a nucleus. So the question was: what can make two atoms of the same element weigh different amounts?

Step 2: sorting atoms by weight

At about the same time, J. J. Thomson in Cambridge sent a beam of charged neon atoms through electric and magnetic fields, and saw two traces on his photographic plate instead of one: most of the neon landed at mass 20, but a little landed at 22. Neon, it seemed, was a mixture.

His assistant Francis Aston took up the idea after the First World War and built a much more precise instrument, the first mass spectrometer (he called it a mass spectrograph), in 1919. It sorts atoms by mass the way a strong wind sorts a handful of thrown objects: light ones are blown further off course than heavy ones. Aston found isotopes in one element after another. Chlorine, for example, turned out to be about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1922.

Step 3: the missing particle

There was still a gap in the explanation. A helium nucleus has twice the charge of a hydrogen nucleus, but about four times the mass. Carbon has six times the charge but twelve times the mass. Something in the nucleus was adding mass without adding charge.

As early as 1920, Rutherford guessed that the nucleus might contain a neutral particle, about as heavy as a proton. But how do you catch something with no charge? Charged particles leave tracks, bend in magnets, and make flashes on screens. A neutral particle does none of that. It slips through everything without a trace.

Step 4: the race of 1932

In 1930 two German physicists, Walther Bothe and Herbert Becker, found that the metal beryllium, when hit by alpha particles, gave off a strange, very penetrating radiation. In Paris, Irène Joliot-Curie (Marie Curie’s daughter) and her husband Frédéric Joliot showed in January 1932 that this radiation could knock protons out of paraffin wax at high speed. They thought it was a powerful kind of light, gamma rays.

In Cambridge, Rutherford’s colleague James Chadwick read their paper and did not believe the explanation. Light hitting a proton should not be able to knock it out that fast. But a particle as heavy as the proton could, just as one snooker ball can send another flying. Chadwick worked almost day and night for about two weeks, measuring how the mystery radiation knocked atoms of different masses. In February 1932 he announced it: the radiation was a stream of neutral particles with almost exactly the mass of a proton. The neutron had been found. Chadwick won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935.

Step 5: everything fits

Now the puzzle of isotopes has a simple answer:

  1. The number of protons decides the element. Chlorine always has 17.
  2. The number of neutrons can vary. Chlorine-35 has 17 protons and 18 neutrons; chlorine-37 has 17 protons and 20 neutrons.
  3. Neutrons have no charge, so they do not change how the atom behaves chemically (that is mostly about electrons). They only change its mass, and sometimes how stable its nucleus is.

That is why Soddy could not separate his “lead” from ordinary lead: chemically they were the same element, just with different numbers of neutrons.

Careful

“Heavier isotopes are a different element.”

No: an isotope is the same element with a different number of neutrons. Heavy water, made with the hydrogen isotope deuterium (one proton and one neutron), is still water: it looks the same and freezes and boils at almost the same temperatures. It is about 11% denser, which is why an ice cube of heavy water sinks in ordinary water.

A mixture you can average

Put 3 large spoons and 1 small spoon into a bag. Weigh each kind on a kitchen scale, then weigh all four together and divide by 4. That average is like chlorine’s 35.45: a real, useful number, even though not one spoon in the bag has that mass.

Isotopes turned out to be useful everywhere: carbon-14 for dating ancient bones, uranium-235 for nuclear power, and harmless heavy isotopes for tracing where atoms go inside living things.

1909 to 1911

The shell that bounced back

Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger, Ernest Marsden

The University of Manchester, 1909

Ernest Rutherford grew up on a farm in New Zealand, one of twelve children. By 1909 he was a famous physicist in Manchester, and he already had a Nobel Prize for his work on radioactivity. His favourite tool was the alpha particle: a tiny, fast, positively charged bullet shot out by radioactive substances such as radium. (We now know an alpha particle is the nucleus of a helium atom.) Rutherford liked to fire alpha particles at things and see what happened.

His assistant, Hans Geiger, had a promising young student, Ernest Marsden, who was twenty years old and needed a project. Rutherford suggested one, more or less to keep him busy: fire alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil, and see whether any of them bounce off at a big angle.

Nobody expected him to find any. According to the best idea of the time, Thomson’s “plum pudding” atom, the positive charge in an atom was spread out thinly, like dough. A fast alpha particle should punch straight through, perhaps wobbling slightly. It was like firing bullets at a cloud of mist.

Step 1: counting flashes in the dark

There were no electronic detectors yet. To see an alpha particle, you let it hit a small screen coated with zinc sulfide. Where it hits, there is a tiny flash of light, a scintillation, too faint to see in daylight. So Geiger and Marsden sat in a completely dark room for half an hour to let their eyes adjust, then peered through a microscope at the screen and counted flashes, one by one, for minutes at a time. It was slow, tiring work, and you could only do it accurately for a short time before your eyes tired.

Most of the flashes came where they expected: almost straight through the foil. But then Marsden moved the screen round to the same side as the source, and kept seeing flashes. Some alpha particles were coming back.

Step 2: “as if you fired a shell at tissue paper”

Only a very few bounced back: for thin gold foil, roughly one in many thousands. But that they bounced back at all was shocking. Rutherford said later that it was the most incredible thing that had ever happened to him, “almost as incredible as if you fired a fifteen-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.”

A heavy, fast alpha particle can only be turned right round by something even heavier and very strongly charged. A thinly spread cloud of charge could never do it. So the positive charge, and most of the mass, must be packed into something tiny.

Step 3: Rutherford’s new atom

Rutherford spent nearly two years working out the mathematics. If all the positive charge sat in a minute point at the centre of each atom, he calculated how many alpha particles should be turned through each angle. Geiger and Marsden then checked his predictions with more painstaking counting, publishing their results in 1913. They matched.

In 1911 Rutherford published his new picture of the atom:

  1. Almost all the mass of an atom, and all its positive charge, are concentrated in a tiny centre. By 1912 he was calling it the nucleus, from the Latin word for a small nut or kernel.
  2. The electrons are spread out around it, far away.
  3. Between them is mostly empty space.

How tiny is tiny? A gold atom is about 0.29 nanometres across. Its nucleus is about 20,000 times smaller across. If a gold atom were the size of a cricket ground, its nucleus would be about the size of a small pea on the centre of the pitch, yet it would hold more than 99.9% of the atom’s mass.

Step 4: why most particles go straight through

Now the result makes sense. An alpha particle flying through the foil passes through thousands of atoms, but each atom is almost all empty space with a tiny nucleus in the middle. Most of the time the alpha particle never comes anywhere near a nucleus, so it sails straight through. Only on the rare occasions when it heads almost straight at one does the enormous push between two positive charges turn it sharply, or send it back.

Careful

“If atoms are mostly empty space, why can’t I push my hand through the table?”

Because “empty” here means “empty of nuclei”, not “empty of everything”. The space is filled by the atoms’ electrons, and when the electrons of your hand come close to the electrons of the table, they push each other apart very strongly. An alpha particle is a tiny, fast nucleus; your hand is a crowd of atoms with their own electrons on the outside.

Find the hidden nail

This is a model of Rutherford’s idea, not of the real sizes. Prop a large tray or a sheet of stiff cardboard on four books, so marbles can roll underneath. Ask someone to hide a few heavy objects (a mug, a small jar) under it, without telling you where. Roll marbles under the tray from one side, many times, along different lines, and watch where they come out. Most roll straight through. A few hit something and bounce off at an angle. From the bounces alone, try to work out where the hidden objects are. You have just done, in a small way, what Geiger and Marsden did with gold.

The nucleus explained the mass of atoms. It also raised a new puzzle: if the electrons are spread out around a positive nucleus, why don’t they fall straight into it? Answering that took a young Danish physicist, Niels Bohr, and a whole new kind of physics.

1913 to 1926

Why electrons don't fall in

Johann Balmer, Niels Bohr, Erwin Schrödinger

Manchester and Copenhagen, 1912 to 1913

When Rutherford found the nucleus, he created a terrible problem. According to the physics everyone trusted, a negative electron moving around a positive nucleus should give off light continuously, lose energy, and spiral inwards. Calculations said it should crash into the nucleus in far less than a millionth of a second. Every atom in the universe should have collapsed long ago. Yet here we are, made of atoms that have lasted billions of years.

In 1912 a young Danish physicist, Niels Bohr, came to work with Rutherford in Manchester. He was twenty-six, softly spoken, and known for thinking aloud in long, careful sentences. He was not willing to throw away the nucleus, because the gold-foil evidence was too strong. So he did something braver: he decided that the old physics must be wrong for things as small as atoms.

Step 1: a clue hidden in light

Bohr found his clue in a pattern that had puzzled people for decades. If you make hydrogen gas glow with electricity and pass its light through a prism, you do not get a smooth rainbow. You get just a few sharp, bright coloured lines: a red one, a blue-green one, and two violet ones, at exactly the same places every time.

In 1885 a Swiss schoolteacher, Johann Balmer, had found a simple formula that gave the positions of hydrogen’s lines exactly, though nobody knew why it worked. When Bohr saw Balmer’s formula, he later said, everything became clear to him.

Step 2: the staircase idea

Bohr’s idea, published in 1913, was this. An electron in an atom cannot have just any energy. It can only have certain fixed amounts, like standing on the steps of a staircase but never between steps. These allowed energies are called energy levels. While an electron stays on one step, it gives off no light at all, so it does not spiral in. That rescued Rutherford’s atom.

But an electron can jump between steps. When it drops from a higher step to a lower one, the difference in energy comes out as a tiny flash of light of one exact colour. Big drop: more energy, bluer light. Small drop: less energy, redder light. Because the steps are always at the same heights, the colours are always the same. Hydrogen’s red line is an electron dropping from the third step to the second; the blue-green line is a drop from the fourth step to the second.

Using his staircase, Bohr calculated the positions of hydrogen’s lines from scratch, and they matched Balmer’s measurements almost perfectly. The word quantum, meaning a fixed amount, became the name for this new kind of physics. Bohr won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922.

Step 3: from steps to shells

Chemists soon used Bohr’s idea to explain the periodic table. Electrons in bigger atoms fill the steps from the bottom up, in groups called shells: the first shell holds up to 2 electrons, the next up to 8, and so on. This is the shell picture you meet in Chapter 1, and it explains why lithium and sodium, each with one electron alone in its outermost shell, behave so alike.

Step 4: the model improves again

Bohr’s atom worked beautifully for hydrogen but struggled with bigger atoms, and it still pictured electrons circling like little planets. In the 1920s, physicists including Louis de Broglie and Erwin Schrödinger found that electrons also behave like waves. In 1926 Schrödinger wrote an equation that describes them, and its answers are not tracks at all. They are clouds: maps of where an electron is likely to be found. These clouds are called orbitals. Some are round, some are shaped like dumb-bells, and some are more complicated still.

Bohr’s steps survived this upgrade: electrons still have only certain allowed energies. What changed was the picture of where they are. That is a perfect example of how science improves its models: the useful part stays, and the part that was wrong is replaced by something better.

Careful

“Electrons orbit the nucleus like planets around the Sun.”

This is the most famous picture of the atom, and it is wrong in an important way. Electrons do not follow paths. The rings in shell diagrams are a way of grouping electrons by energy. The best picture we have, the orbital, says where an electron is likely to be, not where it is going.

See the lines yourself

Look at the reflection of a light in the shiny underside of an old CD or DVD (the tiny grooves split light into colours). An ordinary old-style bulb or daylight gives a smooth rainbow. A fluorescent tube or a street lamp with an orange glow often gives separate bright lines instead, because the light comes from glowing atoms of particular elements, each with its own staircase.

So the reason you are not collapsing right now is a quantum one: the electrons in your atoms are standing on the lowest steps they can reach, and there is no lower step to fall to.

1896 to 1949

Atoms that change

Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie, Pierre Curie, Ernest Rutherford, Frederick Soddy, Harriet Brooks, Willard Libby

Paris, February 1896

Henri Becquerel came from a family of physicists who studied things that glow. Early in 1896, the whole scientific world was excited about X-rays, discovered a few weeks before, and Becquerel wondered whether glowing minerals might give off X-rays too. His idea was to put crystals of a uranium salt in sunlight, so that they would glow, then lay them on a photographic plate wrapped in thick black paper. If the plate darkened, something had passed through the paper.

It did darken. But then Paris had a run of cloudy days. Becquerel put his wrapped plates and uranium crystals away in a drawer to wait for sunshine. On 1 March, for reasons of his own, he developed the plates anyway, expecting nothing. They were strongly fogged, with the shapes of the crystals clearly visible. The uranium had not needed sunlight at all. It was giving off some invisible radiation all by itself, all the time, in the dark.

Step 1: a young scientist picks up the trail

Marie Skłodowska had grown up in Warsaw, in a Poland ruled by Russia, where women could not go to university. She studied in secret, worked as a governess to save money, and moved to Paris, where she studied physics and mathematics and married the physicist Pierre Curie. For her doctoral research she chose Becquerel’s mysterious rays.

She measured the rays with an electrical instrument Pierre and his brother had invented, and found two crucial things. First, the strength of the rays depended only on how much uranium was present, not on what it was combined with or whether it was hot or cold. So the rays came from inside the uranium atoms themselves. Second, a uranium ore called pitchblende gave off more radiation than its uranium could explain. Something even more powerful was hidden in it. She invented a word for this property: radioactivity.

Step 2: hunting in a shed

Marie and Pierre set out to find the hidden substances. They worked in a leaky, freezing shed, grinding, dissolving and boiling down tonnes of pitchblende waste, a bit at a time, following the radioactivity wherever it went. In July 1898 they announced a new element and named it polonium, after Marie’s homeland, which did not then exist as a country on the map. In December 1898 they announced a second, radium, which glows faintly in the dark. It took Marie years more work to collect a tenth of a gram of pure radium compound.

Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 with Pierre and Becquerel, and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911 on her own. She is still the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Step 3: the atom transforms

In Montreal, Ernest Rutherford and the chemist Frederick Soddy studied radioactive thorium in 1901 and 1902. Working with them, Rutherford’s student Harriet Brooks, one of Canada’s first women nuclear physicists, helped show that the “emanation” thorium and radium gave off was a radioactive gas. Rutherford and Soddy found that radioactive atoms were turning into atoms of different elements. Soddy later remembered saying, in amazement, “Rutherford, this is transmutation!”: the old alchemists’ dream of changing one element into another, happening by itself.

For more than a century chemistry had rested on the idea that elements never change. In chemical reactions, that is still true. But inside an unstable nucleus, a radioactive atom can throw out particles and become a different element.

Step 4: the half-life, step by step

Radioactive atoms do not all break down at once. Each one has a fixed chance of breaking down in any given time, a bit like a coin toss. For a large crowd of atoms, that gives a beautifully steady rule: after a certain time, half of them have broken down. That time is the half-life.

Half-life with carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years)
Start: 100% of the carbon-14.
After 5,730 years: 50%.
After 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years: half of 50% = 25%.
After 3 × 5,730 = 17,190 years: 12.5%.
It never quite reaches zero; it keeps halving.

Step 5: a clock in every living thing

In 1949 the American chemist Willard Libby turned this into a clock. A little of the carbon in the air is radioactive carbon-14, made high in the atmosphere. Plants take it in, animals eat plants, and so every living thing has the same small share of carbon-14. When it dies, it stops taking in new carbon, and its carbon-14 starts to halve every 5,730 years. Measure how much is left, and you know how long ago it died. If a piece of ancient wood has a quarter of the carbon-14 of living wood, it died about 11,460 years ago. Libby won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960, and his method is used to date everything from Egyptian mummies to cave paintings.

Careful

“After two half-lives, everything is gone.”

Half and half again is a quarter, not zero. After two half-lives, a quarter is left. Radioactive substances fade away more and more slowly, never quite vanishing.

The coin half-life

Take 32 coins and put them all in a box. Shake, then tip them out: remove every coin that lands heads up. Count what is left, write it down, and put the rest back. Repeat. Each shake is one “half-life”. Roughly half disappear each time: 32, about 16, about 8, about 4… With real atoms there are so many that the halving is almost perfectly smooth.

Radioactivity came at a cost. Nobody yet knew how dangerous it was. Marie Curie carried tubes of radium in her pockets and died in 1934 of a blood disease almost certainly caused by her years of exposure; her notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead-lined boxes. Yet her work also saved lives: radium became one of the first treatments for cancer, and during the First World War she set up mobile X-ray units to help surgeons find bullets and broken bones, and drove them to the front herself.

1859 to 1895

Fingerprints of light

Robert Bunsen, Gustav Kirchhoff, Jules Janssen, Norman Lockyer, William Ramsay

Heidelberg, Germany, 1859

Think of Diwali night. A rocket bursts into deep red, then a shower of green, then a sparkle of brilliant gold. Those colours are not paint. Each one is made by a different element, glowing with its own particular light: strontium for red, barium for green, copper compounds for blue, sodium for that bright yellow-orange. The people who make fireworks learned this by trial and error. The reason it works was discovered by two friends in a German university town.

Robert Bunsen was a chemist who had helped design a new gas burner with a clean, almost invisible blue flame (you may meet a Bunsen burner in a school laboratory). Bunsen liked to hold a bit of a substance in the flame on a wire and watch its colour. Lithium gives crimson, potassium a soft lilac, sodium a strong yellow. This is called a flame test. But colours can be confusing to the eye: a little sodium drowns out almost anything else.

His friend Gustav Kirchhoff, a physicist, suggested a better way to look. Pass the coloured light through a prism, which spreads light out into its separate colours. Together they built an instrument for it, the spectroscope.

Step 1: light in lines

What they saw changed science. A hot glowing solid, like the filament in an old bulb, gives a smooth rainbow with every colour. But a glowing gas or vapour of an element gives only a few sharp, bright lines of particular colours, always in the same places for the same element. Sodium gives a close pair of yellow lines. Lithium gives a red line. Every element has its own pattern, as unique as a fingerprint.

(Why the lines? Nobody knew for another fifty years. The answer, from Niels Bohr in 1913, is that electrons in each kind of atom can only jump between certain energy steps, and each jump gives out light of one exact colour.)

Step 2: finding elements nobody had seen

Bunsen and Kirchhoff realised they now had a detective’s tool. If a sample glowed with a line that matched no known element, it must contain a new one.

In 1860 they boiled down an enormous amount of mineral water from a spa town, tens of thousands of litres of it, and looked at the glow of what was left. There were two bright blue lines that belonged to no known element. They named the new element caesium, from the Latin for sky blue. The next year, in a mineral, they found two deep red lines and named that element rubidium, from the Latin for dark red. Two new elements, found by their colours before anyone had held a pure piece of either.

Step 3: reading the Sun

Kirchhoff went further. Decades earlier, the glass-maker Joseph von Fraunhofer had noticed that sunlight, spread into a rainbow, is crossed by hundreds of thin dark lines. Kirchhoff showed that a cooler gas absorbs exactly the same colours that it gives off when hot. So the dark lines in sunlight are fingerprints of elements in the Sun’s outer layers, absorbing light from the hotter Sun beneath. Sodium’s dark pair sat exactly where sodium’s bright yellow pair would be. For the first time, people could tell what a star is made of, without ever going there.

Guntur, India, 18 August 1868

On that day, a total eclipse of the Sun crossed India. The French astronomer Jules Janssen set up his spectroscope at Guntur, in what is now Andhra Pradesh, and studied the glowing gas leaping off the edge of the darkened Sun. He saw a bright yellow line close to sodium’s, but not quite in the same place. The English astronomer Norman Lockyer saw the same line from England two months later, without needing an eclipse.

No known element on Earth made that line. Lockyer concluded it came from a new element, found so far only in the Sun, and named it after the Greek word for the Sun, helios: helium. Many chemists were doubtful. An element nobody could put in a bottle?

They had to wait twenty-seven years. In 1895 William Ramsay in London dissolved a uranium mineral in acid, collected the gas that came off, and looked at its glow. There was the yellow line. Helium had been found on Earth, after first being discovered 150 million kilometres away.

Step 4: why this matters

  1. Every element gives out and absorbs light of its own particular colours.
  2. So light carries information about the atoms that made it.
  3. That lets us identify elements in tiny amounts, in the lab, in fireworks, in street lamps, and in stars millions of millions of kilometres away.

Spot it in the kitchen

Next time an adult is cooking on a gas stove and a pan of salted water boils over, watch the flame where the water lands: the blue flame flashes bright yellow-orange. That is sodium from the salt, giving off its fingerprint colour. (Just watch: don’t put anything into a flame yourself.) You can also see the same yellow in the old orange street lamps, which are filled with sodium vapour.

The next time you watch fireworks, you are watching a spectroscope experiment in the sky. Every colour is an element announcing itself.

1913 to 1914

Henry Moseley's staircase

Henry Moseley, Antonius van den Broek, Ernest Rutherford

Manchester, 1913

Henry Moseley was 25 when he set up his strangest experiment. He was working in Ernest Rutherford’s laboratory in Manchester, the same place where, a few years earlier, alpha particles had bounced back off gold foil and revealed the nucleus. Rutherford’s team now knew that every atom had a tiny positive centre. But how much positive charge did each nucleus carry, and did it have anything to do with the periodic table?

A Dutch lawyer who did physics as a hobby, Antonius van den Broek, had made a bold guess: perhaps an element’s position in the table, its place number counting from hydrogen, was simply the charge on its nucleus. Hydrogen 1, helium 2, lithium 3. It was a beautiful idea, but nobody had any way to test it. Moseley found one.

A toy railway of elements

Moseley built a long glass tube with the air pumped out. Inside it sat a little trolley that could carry samples of different metals, one after another, into the path of a beam of fast electrons. When electrons slam into a metal, the metal gives off X-rays, invisible light with very short waves. Each metal gives off its own particular X-rays, like a bell ringing its own note.

He measured those notes, one element at a time: calcium, titanium, vanadium, chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, and on through dozens more. And when he plotted them in the right way (taking the square root of each X-ray’s frequency) the points did not scatter. They climbed in a perfectly even staircase: one equal step from each element to the next.

What the steps were counting

Atomic weights do not go up in equal steps; they jump about. But Moseley’s steps were perfectly regular. Something inside every atom increased by exactly one from each element to the next, and the X-rays came from electrons being pulled on by the nucleus. The only sensible conclusion was that the nucleus’s positive charge goes up by one each time. Van den Broek’s guess was right.

That whole number, the charge on the nucleus, is the atomic number. Today we know it is simply the number of protons. It is what makes an element the element it is.

Step by step: why this settled everything

  1. The true order. Mendeleev had arranged elements by weight, but had been forced to put a few elements out of weight order to keep families together, most famously tellurium before iodine. (Argon and potassium, found later, turned out to be the same kind of puzzle.) Moseley’s staircase showed these choices were right. Tellurium is 52 and iodine 53, even though tellurium is slightly heavier (127.6 against 126.9). Order by protons, and the puzzles vanish.
  2. Counting the missing. Because the steps were even, a missing step meant a missing element. Moseley could see exactly where gaps were between aluminium (13) and gold (79): elements 43, 61, 72 and 75 had not been found. All four were found later (hafnium, 72, in 1923; rhenium, 75, in 1925; technetium, 43, and promethium, 61, only after they were made in laboratories).
  3. No room for impostors. Before Moseley, people sometimes announced “new elements” that were really mixtures. After him, any claim could be tested: what is its atomic number? If there is no empty step for it, it is not new.

Careful

“Atomic number and mass number are the same thing.”

They are different counts. The atomic number counts protons only, and it decides the element: every carbon atom has 6. The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, so it can be different for different atoms of the same element: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have atomic number 6.

The war

In August 1914, the First World War began. Moseley, by then working in Oxford, could have stayed in his laboratory. He chose to join the army, as a signals officer. On 10 August 1915, at Gallipoli in Turkey, he was killed by a sniper’s bullet. He was 27.

Many scientists believed he would soon have won a Nobel Prize. It is often said that the loss of Moseley helped persuade Britain to keep its scientists out of front-line fighting in later wars, though historians debate how much difference it made.

Today

Every periodic table in the world, including the one on the cover of this book, is arranged by Moseley’s numbers. When you read that an element “is” its number of protons, you are reading the conclusion of an experiment done with a toy-sized railway inside a glass tube, by a young man who had only two more years to live.

1902 to 1939

Dots and lines: how atoms hold on to each other

Gilbert Newton Lewis, Irving Langmuir, Linus Pauling

Harvard University, 1902

Chemists in 1900 drew molecules with little lines between the atoms, H–O–H for water, and they were very good at it. They knew which atoms joined to which, and how many lines each kind of atom liked to have: one for hydrogen, two for oxygen, four for carbon. But nobody could say what a line actually was. A bond was a mystery written as a dash.

The electron had been discovered only five years earlier. A young American chemist, Gilbert Newton Lewis, began wondering whether electrons might be the answer. In 1902, while preparing a lecture, he sketched atoms as little cubes, with electrons sitting at the corners. A cube has eight corners. Many atoms seemed to end up, when they combined, with eight outer electrons around them. Could a bond be two atoms sharing corners?

He put the sketches in a drawer, and did not publish them for fourteen years.

The shared pair

Berkeley, California, 1916

By 1916 Lewis was a famous professor at Berkeley, and he finally published his idea, improved. A chemical bond, he proposed, is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. Each line in H–O–H stands for two electrons that belong to both atoms at once.

He invented a way of drawing it that you will still see in school books today: the element symbol, with dots around it for the outer electrons. Hydrogen has one outer electron; oxygen has six. Draw water and you see two shared pairs, one between oxygen and each hydrogen, plus two pairs that belong to oxygen alone.

A few years later another American, Irving Langmuir, spread Lewis’s ideas widely and gave a name to sharing bonds: covalent, meaning “sharing strength”. He also popularised the “octet”, the eight outer electrons that Lewis had first drawn on his cubes.

Why does sharing hold atoms together?

Here is the part that matters most, because it is where people start saying atoms “want” to share. They do not want anything. The real reason is electric attraction.

  1. Every nucleus is positive; every electron is negative. Opposite charges pull on each other.
  2. A pair of electrons sitting between two nuclei is pulled by both of them at once, and pulls back on both. It acts like glue between them, held in place by two attractions instead of one.
  3. The nuclei also repel each other, and so do the electrons. If the atoms come too close, the repulsion wins.
  4. The bond length is the balance point, where attraction and repulsion together give the lowest energy. For two hydrogen atoms it is 74 picometres apart.
  5. Pulling the atoms apart takes energy, because you have to work against that attraction. For a mole of hydrogen molecules it takes about 436 kilojoules. That is why breaking bonds always costs energy, an idea that comes back in Chapter 5.

Careful

“Atoms share electrons because they want a full outer shell of eight.”

The “eight” is a useful pattern for many atoms of the lighter elements, and Lewis’s drawings work beautifully for them. But it is a pattern, not a reason. The reason is that shared electrons between two nuclei lower the energy of the whole system, through electric attraction. And plenty of stable molecules break the eight rule.

Pauling makes it scientific

Pasadena, California, 1930s

Lewis’s picture was a sketch. To turn it into science that could calculate, chemists needed the new quantum physics of the 1920s. The person who did more than anyone to bring the two together was Linus Pauling, a young chemist at Caltech who as a boy had collected insects and minerals in Oregon.

Pauling explained why carbon makes four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, why some bonds are shared unequally (his scale of electronegativity, in another story), and how to predict bond lengths and energies. In 1939 he collected it all in a book, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, which became one of the most influential science books of the century. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1954, and later a second Nobel, for Peace, for his campaign against nuclear weapons testing. He is still the only person to have won two Nobel Prizes on his own, not shared with anyone else.

Lines, dots and real molecules

So when you see a line between two atoms in this book, read it as Lewis taught: two shared electrons, held between two nuclei by electric attraction. A double line is two shared pairs; a triple line, three. More shared pairs pull the atoms closer and hold them tighter: the C=C double bond is shorter and stronger than C–C, and the N≡N triple bond in nitrogen gas is one of the strongest bonds there is, which is why nitrogen in the air is so hard to make react.

Build molecules you can hold

Use soft sweets (jelly sweets or marshmallows) for atoms and toothpicks for bonds. Use one colour for hydrogen and another for oxygen and carbon. Build water: an oxygen with two hydrogens, bent, not straight. Build methane: a carbon with four hydrogens, as far apart from each other as they can go. (Hint: it is not a flat cross; try making the four hydrogens point to the corners of a pyramid with a triangular base.) Each toothpick is one shared pair of electrons. Eat the molecules afterwards.

1827 to 1909

The dance that proved atoms are real

Robert Brown, Albert Einstein, Marian Smoluchowski, Jean Perrin

London, summer 1827

The Scottish botanist Robert Brown was studying how plants make seeds. He put pollen grains from a wildflower into a drop of water and looked at them under his microscope. Inside the pollen were much smaller particles, and when they spilled out into the water, they would not keep still. They jittered and wandered, this way and that, never stopping, never settling.

The obvious explanation was that they were alive: tiny swimming creatures, perhaps, or some “vital force” in the pollen. Brown was a careful scientist, so he tested it. He tried pollen that had been dried for a century in a museum. He tried powdered glass, ground-up rock, and even dust from a fragment of the ancient Egyptian Sphinx. Everything that was small enough jiggled in exactly the same restless way. So it could not be life. But then what was it? Brown had no idea. Nobody did, for almost eighty years. The jiggling was named after him: Brownian motion.

(People sometimes say that the Roman poet Lucretius described the same thing two thousand years ago, in dust dancing in a sunbeam. He did describe the dancing dust, and he guessed it was caused by invisible atoms, but the dust in a sunbeam is mostly tossed about by air currents. It is a lovely passage, but it is not quite the same effect.)

Bern, Switzerland, 1905

In 1905 a 26-year-old clerk in the Swiss patent office, Albert Einstein, published several papers that changed physics. One of them was about Brownian motion, although at first he was not even sure that was the right name for what he was describing.

His idea was this. A grain floating in water is being struck by water molecules from every side, all the time. If molecules were infinitely small and infinitely many, the hits from every side would balance perfectly and the grain would sit still. But if water really is made of separate molecules, then at any instant, just by chance, a few more will hit one side than the other. The grain gets a tiny shove. A moment later, a shove in a different direction. Added up, these random shoves make the grain wander, exactly as Brown saw.

Einstein did more than explain it. He worked out how far a grain should wander in a given time, and showed that the answer depends on how big and how numerous the molecules are. In other words: watch the grains carefully enough, and you can count the molecules. A year later the Polish physicist Marian Smoluchowski reached the same conclusion independently.

Step 1: why a big grain is pushed around by tiny molecules

Imagine a huge beach ball being pushed about by a crowd of people who cannot see it. Each person who bumps it gives a tiny nudge. If the crowd is enormous and evenly spread, the nudges cancel and the ball barely moves. If the crowd is made of separate people, there will always be moments when more of them happen to push from the left than from the right, and the ball rolls a little to the right.

A grain of about a thousandth of a millimetre is struck by water molecules more than ten million million million times every second. That number is so big that the pushes almost cancel. Almost. The tiny leftover imbalance, changing every instant, is what makes the grain dance.

Paris, 1908 to 1909

Einstein’s prediction needed testing, and the French physicist Jean Perrin set out to do it. He made thousands of tiny, identical spheres of gamboge, a yellow resin used in paint, which took months of patient work separating them by size in a centrifuge. Then he watched individual grains under his microscope, marking their positions every 30 seconds on squared paper and joining the dots. The pictures he published look like the scribbles of a tired child: zig-zag after zig-zag, never repeating.

Perrin measured how far the grains wandered, used Einstein’s mathematics, and worked out how many molecules there are in a mole. Then he did it again in completely different ways: by how the grains settled into layers in a tall tube, by how they rotated, and more. All the methods gave nearly the same number. It was close to the value we know today, about 6 × 10²³, which Perrin suggested naming after Avogadro.

That agreement settled one of the longest arguments in science. Even the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, who had spent years insisting atoms were just a convenient idea, admitted around 1909 that the evidence had convinced him. Perrin won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1926.

Step 2: what this means for you

Every time you see a box of jiggling particles in this book, remember that it is not just a guess. A botanist saw the effect, a patent clerk explained it, and a physicist measured it so carefully that it revealed the number of molecules in a gulp of water.

Careful

“The grains move because they are alive, or because the water is flowing.”

Brown ruled out life by trying dead and non-living specks; the motion was the same. And it is not a current: neighbouring grains move in completely different directions at the same moment, which a flowing current could never do.

Watch the dance yourself

You will need help for this one, and a microscope if your school has one. Add a tiny drop of whole milk to a drop of water on a glass slide and look at it at high magnification. The fat droplets in milk are small enough to show Brownian motion: they shiver and wander without stopping. (Without a microscope, you can see a related effect: shine a torch beam across a dark room and watch the dust. That dancing is mostly air currents, as with Lucretius, but it gives you the feeling.)

So the dance that puzzled Brown for the rest of his life turned out to be the most direct evidence there is that the world is made of molecules. You cannot see them, but you can watch them push.

1772 to 2010

Pencils, diamonds and footballs

Antoine Lavoisier, Smithson Tennant, Harry Kroto, Richard Smalley, Robert Curl, Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov

Paris, 1772

On a summer day in 1772, in a garden in Paris, a crowd gathered to watch a diamond disappear. Antoine Lavoisier and his colleagues had set up an enormous magnifying glass, a giant burning lens, to focus sunlight onto a small diamond. As the spot of light grew blinding, the diamond slowly vanished. Many people believed diamonds could not be destroyed by fire. They were wrong.

When the scientists repeated the experiment inside a sealed glass jar, they found that the diamond turned into a gas: the same “fixed air” that charcoal makes when it burns, which we now call carbon dioxide. A precious stone and a lump of charcoal seemed to share something. But what?

Same mass, same gas

London, 1797

Twenty-five years later an English chemist, Smithson Tennant, settled it with a careful measurement. He burned diamond and he burned charcoal, weighed each carefully, and measured the carbon dioxide each one made. Equal masses of diamond and of charcoal produced exactly the same amount of carbon dioxide. There was only one possible conclusion: diamond is pure carbon. So is the graphite in a pencil.
