That is one of the most surprising facts in all of chemistry. A diamond is the hardest natural substance known, transparent, sparkling, and it does not conduct electricity. Graphite is so soft it rubs off onto paper, it is grey and shiny, it feels slippery, and it does conduct electricity. Same atoms. Completely different substances.

Same atoms, different arrangement

The difference, as the X-ray crystallographers of the twentieth century confirmed, is entirely in how the carbon atoms are joined.

  1. In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four others, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. The bonds run in every direction through the whole crystal, so a diamond is one giant molecule with no weak places. To scratch it you would have to break strong carbon–carbon bonds, which is why almost nothing can.
  2. In graphite, every carbon atom is bonded to only three others, in flat sheets of hexagons like chicken wire. Within a sheet the bonds are very strong. But the sheets are held to each other only by weak attractions, 0.335 nanometres apart, so they slide over each other easily. When you draw with a pencil, sheets of graphite slide off and stick to the paper.
  3. Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon uses only three of its four outer electrons for bonds; the fourth is free to wander along the sheet. In diamond all four are locked in bonds.

Different forms of the same element are called allotropes. Oxygen has them too: the O₂ we breathe and ozone, O₃, which protects us from ultraviolet light.

The name graphite comes from the Greek word for “to write”, given in 1789. People had been writing with it for over two hundred years before that, ever since a huge deposit of unusually pure graphite was found in Borrowdale, in the north of England, in the 1500s.

A football made of carbon

Houston, Texas, 1985

For two hundred years chemists believed carbon came in just those two pure forms. Then, in 1985, three scientists, Harry Kroto from England and Richard Smalley and Robert Curl from Texas, were blasting graphite with a laser to study the kinds of carbon molecules that might exist in space. Again and again their instruments showed a very stable molecule with exactly 60 carbon atoms.

What shape could hold 60 carbon atoms with no loose ends? They built paper models, and the answer turned out to be the pattern on a football: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, curved into a hollow ball. They named it buckminsterfullerene, after the American architect Richard Buckminster Fuller, whose famous geodesic domes have the same kind of pattern. Most people just call it a buckyball. The three won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996.

A single sheet

Manchester, 2004

The newest chapter began with a roll of sticky tape. In Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov liked to spend Friday evenings trying odd experiments. They pressed sticky tape onto graphite, peeled it off, then stuck the tape to itself and peeled again, splitting the flakes thinner and thinner. Eventually they had flakes just one atom thick: a single sheet of graphite, called graphene.

Graphene turned out to be astonishing: about one atom thick, yet much stronger for its weight than steel, and an excellent conductor of electricity. Geim and Novoselov won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2010. You make a little graphene, tangled up with thicker flakes, every time you draw with a pencil.

Careful

“Diamonds last forever because carbon cannot burn.”

Diamond is carbon, and carbon burns, as Lavoisier showed with his lens. Diamond lasts in everyday life because at room temperature its strong bonds need a great deal of energy to break, so the reaction with oxygen is far too slow to notice. Heated hot enough in air, a diamond burns away to carbon dioxide.

Feel the sheets slide

Scribble hard with a soft pencil (2B or softer) on a scrap of paper until you have a thick, shiny grey patch. Rub it with your fingertip. It feels smooth and slippery: you are feeling sheets of carbon atoms sliding over each other. This is why powdered graphite is used to make stiff locks turn smoothly. Then think of a diamond, made of the very same atoms, which can cut glass.

1912 to 1964

Seeing inside salt: the Braggs and their X-rays

Max von Laue, William Henry Bragg, William Lawrence Bragg, Kathleen Lonsdale, Dorothy Hodgkin, Rosalind Franklin

Munich, 1912

Look at grains of table salt under a magnifying glass and you will see tiny cubes. Sugar grains are little slanted blocks. Snowflakes have six arms. Crystals have flat faces and sharp angles, and for centuries people guessed that this outer shape came from some inner order: atoms stacked in regular rows, like oranges on a market stall. But atoms are far too small to see. How could anyone check?

In 1912 a German physicist, Max von Laue, had an idea. X-rays had been discovered in 1895, and some scientists suspected they were a kind of light with extremely short waves, perhaps about as short as the spacing between atoms. If so, the rows of atoms in a crystal might scatter X-rays the way the fine grooves on a CD split light into rainbow colours. Two of his colleagues shone X-rays through a crystal onto a photographic plate. When they developed it, they found a beautiful pattern of spots. The crystal really was a regular grid of atoms, and X-rays could read it.

A father and son

Leeds and Cambridge, 1913

Laue’s spots were hard to interpret. The puzzle was solved in England by a father and son working together: William Henry Bragg, a professor in Leeds, and his son William Lawrence Bragg, a 22-year-old student at Cambridge.

The son had the key insight while walking along the river in Cambridge. Think of the layers of atoms in a crystal as a stack of very thin mirrors. X-rays bouncing off one layer and off the next layer down travel slightly different distances. At most angles the bounced waves cancel out. But at certain special angles, the extra distance is exactly a whole number of wavelengths, the waves line up, and you get a strong reflection. Measure those angles, and you can calculate how far apart the layers are.

His father built a new instrument, the X-ray spectrometer, to measure the angles precisely. Together they turned it on crystals of ordinary salt, sodium chloride.

Salt has no molecules

What they found surprised many chemists. There were no NaCl molecules in salt at all. Instead, sodium and chlorine took turns, in every direction, in a vast cubic grid: every sodium surrounded by six chlorines, every chlorine surrounded by six sodiums. No sodium belonged to any one chlorine. The formula NaCl did not describe a molecule. It described a ratio: one sodium for every chlorine in the whole crystal.

Not everyone liked this. Years later, in 1927, a senior English chemist, Henry Armstrong, complained that the idea that salt had no molecules went against common sense. But the X-rays did not care about common sense. They showed the same grid every time.

In 1915 father and son shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. Lawrence Bragg was 25, and he is still the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize in Physics. He heard the news while serving as a soldier in France during the First World War.

How X-ray crystallography works, step by step

  1. Grow a crystal: a solid where the atoms or molecules repeat in a regular pattern, over and over, millions of times in every direction.
  2. Shine X-rays at it. Their waves are about the same size as the spacing between atoms, a fraction of a nanometre.
  3. The rows of atoms scatter the X-rays into a pattern of spots. Where the spots fall depends on how the atoms are spaced; how bright they are depends on what kind of atoms they are.
  4. Work backwards from the pattern to the arrangement that must have made it. For salt this was a puzzle of a few hours. For a protein with thousands of atoms it can take years.

Women who read the spots

X-ray crystallography became one of the great tools of the twentieth century, and some of its greatest masters were women at a time when science was hard for women to enter.

Kathleen Lonsdale, who had trained with the elder Bragg in London, showed in 1929 that the ring of six carbon atoms in benzene compounds is flat, settling an argument that had run for sixty years. Dorothy Hodgkin worked out the structures of penicillin, of vitamin B₁₂, and, after 35 years of effort, of insulin, the hormone that people with diabetes need. She won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1964. And Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray photographs of DNA, taken in London in 1952, were crucial evidence for its famous double-helix shape.

Grow your own salt crystals

Ask an adult for a cup of warm tap water. Stir in salt a teaspoon at a time until no more will dissolve. Pour a little of the clear liquid (not the undissolved salt at the bottom) into a saucer and leave it somewhere still and dry for a few days. As the water evaporates, salt crystals grow. Look at them through a magnifying glass. The cubes you see are the giant, visible version of the Braggs’ grid: their shape comes from the way the ions stack.

Every diagram of a crystal in this book, salt, diamond, graphite, ice, rests on the Braggs’ simple idea: layers of atoms act like mirrors for X-rays, and the angles tell you where the atoms are.

about 450 BCE to 2016

From four elements to 118

Empedocles, Robert Boyle, Antoine Lavoisier, Humphry Davy

Sicily, about 450 BCE

Watch a log burn. Smoke rises into the air, sap hisses out as water, flames dance, and grey ash is left behind on the ground. To the Greek thinker Empedocles, living in Sicily about 2,500 years ago, this looked like a clue to everything. Perhaps the log had been made of four basic ingredients all along, earth, air, fire and water, and burning simply let them go.

That idea was taken up by Aristotle and lasted, in one form or another, for about two thousand years. It was wrong, but it was not stupid. It was an honest attempt to explain the endless variety of the world from a few simple things. That hope, that a few ingredients make everything, turned out to be right. Only the ingredients were wrong.

The alchemists’ long experiment

For centuries, alchemists in the Islamic world, in India, in China and in Europe heated, dissolved, distilled and mixed every substance they could find. Many were hoping to turn lead into gold, which cannot be done by chemistry. But along the way they invented much of the equipment chemists still use, and they discovered new substances: strong acids, alcohol, new salts. They piled up an enormous amount of practical knowledge, without a clear idea of what an element really was.

Boyle asks a better question

Oxford, 1661

In 1661 the Irish-born scientist Robert Boyle published a book with a wonderful title, The Sceptical Chymist. “Sceptical” means doubting, and Boyle doubted the four elements. Show me, he said in effect, that you can actually split gold into earth, air, fire and water. Nobody could.

Boyle suggested that an element should be something real you can find by experiment: a substance that cannot be broken down into anything simpler. It was a new kind of definition, based on what you can do in a laboratory rather than on philosophy.

Lavoisier’s list

Paris, 1789

A little over a century later, Antoine Lavoisier put Boyle’s idea to work. In his great textbook of 1789 he listed 33 “simple substances”, things that no one had managed to break down. Many are on the modern list: oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, sulfur, phosphorus, carbon, and metals such as iron, copper, zinc, gold and mercury.

But look closely and you find some surprises. Lavoisier’s list included light and caloric, which he thought was a weightless fluid that carried heat. And it included lime, magnesia and silica, which are not elements at all. Lavoisier had simply not found a way to split them yet. He said so himself: they were simple as far as we know. That honesty is what made the list scientific: it could be corrected.

Davy and the dancing globules

London, October 1807

Correction came with a new tool: electricity. In 1800 Alessandro Volta had invented the battery, and soon chemists were passing electric currents through everything. At the Royal Institution in London, a young chemist named Humphry Davy built one of the most powerful batteries in the world and turned it on potash, a substance people had used for centuries to make soap and glass, and which Lavoisier had suspected might not be simple.

As the current flowed through slightly moist potash, tiny silvery beads appeared, some bursting into flame. Davy had found a new metal, potassium. His cousin Edmund, who was working with him, later told Davy’s brother that Davy bounded about the room in delight. A few days later he did the same with soda and found sodium. In the next year came calcium, magnesium, strontium and barium. Some of the “simple” substances on Lavoisier’s list were metals combined with oxygen, and electricity could pull them apart.

Element, compound or mixture: step by step

By now chemists had three clear words, the same ones you use in Chapter 2.

  1. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom: all the atoms have the same number of protons. Oxygen gas, gold and diamond are elements.
  2. A compound is a substance made of two or more elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Water is always two hydrogens for every oxygen. A compound is a new substance with new properties: sodium is a metal that bursts into flame in water, chlorine is a poisonous green gas, but sodium chloride is the salt on your table.
  3. A mixture is two or more substances simply mingled together, in any proportions, each keeping its own properties. Salt water, air and a fruit salad are mixtures. You can usually separate a mixture by physical means: filtering, evaporating, picking pieces out.

Careful

“Oxygen gas, O₂, is a compound because it is made of molecules.”

Molecules can be elements. O₂ contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element, even though the atoms come in pairs. A compound needs at least two different elements joined together.

Unmix a mixture

Mix a teaspoon of salt with a teaspoon of ground black pepper on a plate. Now separate them, without picking. Here is one way: rub an inflated balloon on your hair or a wool jumper and hold it a centimetre above the plate. The pepper, which is lighter, jumps up and sticks to the balloon; most of the salt stays behind. (Another way: stir the mixture into water. Salt dissolves, pepper floats. Pour off the water and leave it in a sunny place to dry, and the salt comes back.) You cannot do this with a compound. No balloon will pull the sodium out of salt.

The list today

The number of known elements grew steadily: about 30 by 1800, 63 when Mendeleev made his table in 1869, 92 natural elements up to uranium by the 1940s, and then a new kind of discovery. Scientists began making elements that are not found in nature, by smashing nuclei together. The 118th, oganesson, was named in 2016. Some of the newest elements last less than a thousandth of a second before they fall apart.

Every one of them follows Boyle’s rule. It cannot be broken down by chemistry into anything simpler, and every atom of it has the same number of protons.

1643 to 1804

Air has weight: pumps, tubes and balloons

Evangelista Torricelli, Robert Boyle, Robert Hooke, Jacques Charles, Joseph Gay-Lussac

Florence, 1643

The well-diggers and fountain-builders of Italy had a problem that nobody could explain. A suction pump, the kind you work with a handle, could lift water up a pipe, but only so far. Past about ten metres the water simply stopped rising, however hard the pump worked. The great Galileo had puzzled over it before his death in 1642. His young pupil, Evangelista Torricelli, had an idea that sounded almost silly: perhaps the pump was not pulling the water up at all. Perhaps the air outside, pressing down on the water in the well, was pushing it up, and ten metres of water was simply as much as the weight of the air could hold.

If that was right, a heavier liquid should rise less. Mercury is about 13.6 times as heavy as water. So Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury, put his thumb over the end, turned it upside down into a dish of mercury and let go. The mercury dropped, and then stopped, leaving a column about 76 centimetres tall and an empty space at the top of the tube. About ten and a third metres divided by 13.6 is about 76 centimetres. The air really did have weight, and it was holding the mercury up.

Torricelli wrote, beautifully, that “we live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air”. That ocean presses on you all the time. At sea level it pushes on every square centimetre of your skin with the weight of about one kilogram, and on every square metre with the weight of about ten tonnes. You do not feel it because it pushes equally from every side, inside and out. That push is called pressure.

Oxford, 1662

Twenty years later, in England, Robert Boyle and his brilliant assistant Robert Hooke built an air pump that could suck most of the air out of a glass globe. They watched a ringing bell go quiet inside it, and a candle go out. Then Boyle tried something simple and careful. He took a long glass tube bent into a J, sealed at the short end, and poured mercury into the long end. A pocket of air was trapped in the short arm. The more mercury he poured in, the harder it pressed on the trapped air, and the smaller the air pocket became.

When he doubled the pressure, the air squeezed into half the space. When he tripled it, a third. Pressure times volume stayed the same. This is Boyle’s law, and it was one of the first times anyone had found a precise mathematical rule hiding inside the behaviour of an ordinary substance.

Step 1: why squeezing raises the pressure

Today we can explain what Boyle could only measure. A gas is a crowd of tiny particles flying about and bouncing off the walls. Every bounce is a tiny push. Pressure is all those pushes added up.

Squeeze the same particles into half the space and they are packed twice as closely. Each bit of wall gets hit twice as often. Twice the hits means twice the pressure.

Paris, 1783

Then came the balloons. In the summer and autumn of 1783 France went balloon-mad. The Montgolfier brothers, paper-makers, discovered that a big bag of hot air would float, and on 21 November 1783 two men rose over Paris under a Montgolfier balloon, the first people ever to fly. Just ten days later the scientist Jacques Charles went up in a different kind of balloon, filled with hydrogen, the lightest gas of all. A huge crowd watched it rise from the Tuileries gardens.

Charles was interested in more than flying. He noticed that gases expand when they are warmed, and by about 1787 he had found that different gases all expand by the same fraction for each degree of warming. He never published it. In 1802 Joseph Gay-Lussac measured it carefully and published it, generously giving Charles the credit. Two years later Gay-Lussac went up in a balloon himself, to a height of about 7,000 metres, higher than anyone had been, to collect samples of thin, freezing air. (They turned out to contain the same mixture of gases as the air at the ground.)

Step 2: why warming raises the pressure

Warm a gas and its particles move faster. Faster particles hit the walls harder and more often. If the gas is in a sealed, rigid box, the pressure goes up. If the gas is in a stretchy balloon, the balloon swells until the pressure inside matches the air outside again.

The rule only works neatly if you measure temperature from absolute zero, in kelvin, not in degrees Celsius. (The story of how anyone found absolute zero is told in How cold can cold get?)

Step 3: putting it all together

Over the next century these separate rules were joined into one: the ideal gas law. For a fixed amount of gas, pressure goes up when you squeeze it smaller, goes up when you warm it, and goes up when you add more gas. In symbols chemists write it as PV = nRT, but in words it is just those three ideas at once.

A syringe with your thumb over the end.
Pull the plunger out to 20 mL of trapped air, then push it in to 10 mL. Half the space: the pressure inside doubles.
Push it further, to 5 mL: half again, so the pressure is now four times what it was.
That is why it gets harder and harder to push.

It is called “ideal” because it pretends the particles are tiny points that never attract each other. Real gases follow it very closely in everyday conditions, and stop following it when you squeeze them very hard or cool them until they are about to turn into liquid.

Careful

“When you squeeze a gas, the particles get smaller.”

The particles stay exactly the same size. Only the empty space between them shrinks. That is why gases are so easy to squeeze and liquids, whose particles are already touching, are not.

The upside-down glass

Over a sink, fill a glass right to the brim with water. Slide a piece of stiff card over the top so there is no air bubble, hold the card in place, and turn the glass upside down. Take your hand away from the card. The water stays in. The air pushing up on the card is far stronger than the weight of the water pushing down: remember, it could hold up ten metres of water.

A balloon in the freezer

Blow up a balloon, tie it, and measure round its middle with a piece of string. Put it in the freezer for half an hour and measure again. Then let it warm up. The particles inside slow down in the cold and push less hard, so the balloon shrinks; as they warm, it grows back. Nothing got in or out.

Every time this book talks about gases, from boiling water to car tyres to the air in a diver’s tank, it is standing on the shoulders of a pump that would not pump, a tube of mercury, and a sky full of balloons.

1833 to 1903

Charged travellers: Faraday's ions and Arrhenius's risky idea

Michael Faraday, William Whewell, Svante Arrhenius

London, 1833

Michael Faraday left school at 13 to work for a bookbinder. He read the books he was binding, especially the science ones, and taught himself so well that he got a job washing bottles for Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution. Twenty years later he was one of the greatest experimenters in the world.

In the early 1830s Faraday was studying something puzzling. Dry salt does not carry electricity. Pure water hardly carries it. But dissolve salt in water, dip in two metal plates connected to a battery, and a current flows. At the plates, new substances appear: gas bubbles at one, other chemicals at the other. Something in the liquid was carrying electric charge from one plate to the other. What?

Naming the travellers

Faraday did not know what these charge-carriers were, but he needed words to describe his experiments. He wrote to a friend, the scholar William Whewell at Cambridge, who was brilliant at inventing scientific words from Greek. Together they settled on a new vocabulary that every chemist still uses:

  • ion, from the Greek for “going” or “traveller”, for whatever carries the charge through the liquid;
  • anode (“the way up”) and cathode (“the way down”) for the two plates;
  • electrode for any plate, electrolyte for the liquid that carries current, and electrolysis for splitting substances with electricity.

Faraday also found exact rules. The amount of substance produced at a plate was always in proportion to the amount of electricity that passed. Electricity seemed to come in fixed portions, as if it too were made of particles. That hint pointed towards the electron, sixty years before anyone found it.

The student who said the unthinkable

Uppsala, Sweden, 1884

Fifty years later, a young Swede named Svante Arrhenius was measuring how well different salt solutions conduct electricity. His results led him to a startling idea: when salt dissolves in water, it splits up on its own into charged pieces, even when no electric current is flowing at all. Sodium chloride does not wait for a battery to pull it apart. As soon as it dissolves, it is already Na⁺ and Cl⁻, drifting separately through the water.

Most chemists thought this was nonsense. Sodium is a metal that bursts into flame in water, and chlorine is a poisonous gas. How could a glass of salty water be full of free sodium and chlorine? Arrhenius’s thesis was given the lowest passing grade his university could award. He very nearly failed.

The answer to the objection is the key to the whole idea, and you already know it from Chapter 1: an ion is not the same as an atom. Na⁺ has one electron fewer than a sodium atom, and that makes all the difference. It does not react with water the way sodium metal does. Cl⁻ has one electron more than a chlorine atom, and it is not a poisonous gas. They are different particles with different behaviour.

A few scientists, especially Wilhelm Ostwald, then a professor in Riga, took Arrhenius seriously and tested his ideas. The evidence piled up. In 1903, nineteen years after nearly failing, Arrhenius won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for exactly the idea that had almost sunk him.

Ions, step by step

  1. An ion is an atom (or group of atoms) with a charge, because it has gained or lost electrons. Lose electrons and you are positive; gain electrons and you are negative. The nucleus never changes.
  2. Positive ions are called cations and negative ions anions. (Cations travel towards the cathode, anions towards the anode: Faraday and Whewell’s words again.)
  3. In a solid salt crystal, ions are locked in place, so they cannot carry charge. That is why dry salt does not conduct.
  4. Dissolve the salt (or melt it), and the ions can move. Push them with a battery and positive ions drift one way, negative ions the other: an electric current made of moving atoms.
  5. Some ions are groups of atoms that stay together and carry a charge as a team: sulfate, SO₄²⁻; hydroxide, OH⁻; ammonium, NH₄⁺.

Careful

“Salt water conducts electricity because electrons swim through it.”

In metal wires, current is carried by electrons. In salt water, it is carried by ions, whole charged atoms moving through the liquid. The electrons stay at the plates, where they are handed on to or taken from the ions.

Salt that disappears and comes back

Stir a teaspoon of salt into half a glass of warm tap water until it vanishes. The salt has not gone: the ions have spread out among the water molecules, too small to see. Pour a little onto a dark plate and leave it somewhere warm and dry for a day or two. As the water evaporates, the ions find each other again and lock back together. Look at the white crust with a magnifying glass, or your phone’s camera zoomed in: you should see tiny cubes, the shape of the sodium chloride lattice.

Every time this book writes a charge on a symbol, Na⁺ or O²⁻, it is using Faraday’s word and Arrhenius’s idea: atoms that carry electricity by having one or two electrons too few, or too many.

1738 to 1877

A storm of tiny billiard balls

Daniel Bernoulli, Rudolf Clausius, James Clerk Maxwell, Ludwig Boltzmann

Basel, 1738

Look at the air in your room. It seems perfectly still. Now imagine being told that it is a howling storm: countless tiny particles hurtling about faster than a passenger jet, smashing into each other billions of times every second, and drumming on your skin, the walls and the pages of this book without a moment’s rest. That is what the kinetic theory of gases says. “Kinetic” comes from the Greek word for motion.

The first person to take the idea seriously was the Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli. In a book published in 1738 he imagined a gas as a swarm of tiny particles flying about in a closed cylinder and bouncing off a piston. He showed, with mathematics, that their bombardment would push on the piston, and that squeezing the gas into a smaller space would make the push stronger in exactly the way Boyle had measured. It was a brilliant explanation. Almost nobody paid attention. For another hundred years most scientists thought heat was an invisible fluid called “caloric”, and many doubted that atoms existed at all.

Step 1: pressure is a drumming of particles

Think of hailstones on a tin roof. Each stone makes a tiny bang; thousands of them make a steady roar. A gas does the same to its container. Each particle that hits the wall gives it a tiny push; trillions upon trillions of them make a steady pressure. Bernoulli’s picture explains both of Boyle’s discoveries at once: squeeze the gas and the hits come more often; heat it and they come faster and harder.

Zürich, Aberdeen and Vienna, the 1850s to the 1870s

The idea came back to life in the 1850s, when scientists had finally accepted that heat is a kind of motion. The German physicist Rudolf Clausius worked out how far a particle travels before it bumps into another. In 1859 a young Scottish physicist, James Clerk Maxwell, made the crucial step. He realised that the particles in a gas cannot all be moving at the same speed. They are constantly colliding, swapping speed like players in a giant game of billiards, so at any moment some are slow, most are middling and a few are very fast. Maxwell worked out exactly how the speeds are spread out, using mathematics alone, decades before anyone could measure a single molecule.

In Vienna, Ludwig Boltzmann took Maxwell’s ideas much further. He showed how the everyday laws of heat, which engineers used to design steam engines, could all come from the averaged-out behaviour of enormous numbers of particles. His equations are some of the most beautiful in physics. But many powerful scientists of his day, including the chemist Wilhelm Ostwald, still refused to believe atoms were real, and Boltzmann spent years defending them. He died in 1906, only a few years before the experiments of Jean Perrin convinced the doubters that he had been right all along.

Step 2: how fast is fast?

Using Maxwell’s mathematics we can work out the speed of molecules. In the air of a warm room the nitrogen molecules move, on average, at about 480 metres every second. That is roughly 1,700 kilometres an hour: about twice the cruising speed of a passenger jet. Oxygen molecules are a little heavier and a little slower; water vapour molecules, which are lighter, are faster.

How often does an air molecule bump into another one?
In ordinary air, a nitrogen molecule travels only about 70 nanometres (70 billionths of a metre) between collisions.
At about 480 metres a second, that means about 7 thousand million collisions every second, for every molecule.

Careful

“If air molecules move faster than a jet, a smell should cross a room instantly.”

Each molecule is fast, but it never gets far before crashing into another one and shooting off in a new direction. Its path is a hopeless zig-zag. A perfume molecule released on one side of a still room would take a very long time to wander to the other side on its own; in real rooms, gentle air currents carry smells much faster than the zig-zagging alone could.

Step 3: temperature is average motion

Here is the deepest idea in the story. Temperature is a measure of how much energy of motion the particles have, on average. Hotter means the particles are jiggling and flying faster. Colder means slower. At absolute zero they would have the least motion possible.

Because the energy of motion depends on the square of the speed, doubling the kelvin temperature does not double the speed. It multiplies it by about 1.4 (the square root of 2). And at any temperature there is always a spread: a few fast particles, many middling ones, a few slow ones. That spread matters later in this book: it is why a few particles are always energetic enough to escape from a liquid as vapour, or to get over the energy barrier of a chemical reaction.

Hot water and cold water

Fill one clear glass with cold water from the fridge and another with warm water from the tap. Let them stand for a minute so the water is still. Then, at the same moment, add one drop of food colouring to each, without stirring. Watch for a few minutes. In the warm water the colour spreads much faster, because its molecules are jiggling faster and jostle the colour about more quickly.

None of the scientists in this story could see a single molecule. They imagined one, did the mathematics carefully, and found that it explained pressure, heat and temperature. Then the experiments caught up and proved them right. When this book shows you a box of bouncing particles, you are looking at Bernoulli’s, Maxwell’s and Boltzmann’s storm.

1817 to 2016

The patience game: the story of the periodic table

Johann Döbereiner, John Newlands, Lothar Meyer, Dmitri Mendeleev, William Ramsay, Henry Moseley

St Petersburg, February 1869

Dmitri Mendeleev had a problem, and it was a textbook. He was a chemistry professor in St Petersburg, and he was writing a book for his students called The Principles of Chemistry. He had finished the chapters on a few familiar elements, and now he had to decide what came next. About 63 elements were known, and they looked like a hopeless jumble: gases and metals, soft and hard, some that burst into flame in water and some that sat quietly for centuries. In what order could you possibly teach them?

Mendeleev was not the first person to wonder. The answer he found, and the daring way he used it, became the most famous chart in all of science. But the story starts fifty years earlier.

The first clues: families of three

In 1817, and again in 1829, a German chemist named Johann Döbereiner noticed something odd about certain elements that behave alike. Calcium, strontium and barium are all whitish metals that react with water in similar ways. When Döbereiner looked at their atomic weights, the middle one sat almost exactly halfway between the other two.

Calcium 40.1 and barium 137.3: halfway between is (40.1 + 137.3) ÷ 2 ≈ 88.7. Strontium is 87.6.
Chlorine 35.5 and iodine 126.9: halfway is about 81.2. Bromine is 79.9.
Lithium 6.9 and potassium 39.1: halfway is about 23.0. Sodium is 23.0.

He called these families triads. Was it coincidence? It happened too often for that. Something was ordering the elements, but nobody could see what.

The chemist who was laughed at

In 1865 an English chemist, John Newlands, tried something bolder. He lined up all the known elements in order of atomic weight and noticed that similar elements seemed to turn up every eighth place, like the notes of a musical scale: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do again. He called it the Law of Octaves.

When he presented it to the Chemical Society in London in 1866, one member asked him, with a straight face, whether he had ever tried arranging the elements in alphabetical order, since that might give patterns too. The Society refused to publish his paper. Newlands was partly right and partly wrong: his pattern worked for the lighter elements and broke down for the heavier ones, and he left no room for elements nobody had found yet. More than twenty years later the Royal Society gave him a medal for it.

The patience game

Now back to Mendeleev. He wrote the name of each element on a card, with its atomic weight and its main properties: what it combined with, and in what proportions. Then, the story goes, he laid the cards out on a table again and again, like the card game called patience (or solitaire), looking for the arrangement where everything fitted.

Careful

“Mendeleev saw the whole periodic table in a dream.”

This story was told by one of his friends years afterwards, and Mendeleev himself never seems to have described it that way. Historians treat it as a legend. What we do know is that he worked on the problem for weeks, with notes and drafts covered in crossings-out that still survive.

On 17 February 1869, by the Russian calendar of the time (1 March by ours), he wrote out his first table. He put elements in order of atomic weight, but in rows and columns so that families lined up: lithium, sodium and potassium together; fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine together. And then he did two bold things that nobody before him had dared.

Two bold moves

First, he left gaps. Where the next element by weight did not fit the family pattern, Mendeleev did not force it in. He left a blank and said, in effect: an element belongs here that nobody has found yet. Below aluminium he left a gap and called the missing element eka-aluminium (“one beyond aluminium”). There were other gaps below boron and below silicon.

Second, he predicted. From its neighbours in the table, he forecast what each missing element would be like: its atomic weight, how dense it would be, what it would combine with.

Nature answers

In 1875 a French chemist, Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, spotted a new violet line in the light from a zinc ore and tracked down a new metal. He named it gallium, after France (Gallia in Latin). It was Mendeleev’s eka-aluminium. There was one disagreement: Lecoq measured its density as 4.7, and Mendeleev had predicted about 5.9. Mendeleev wrote to him suggesting that his sample was impure. Lecoq purified it, measured again, and got 5.9. A man in St Petersburg had corrected a measurement on a metal he had never seen.

Then came scandium in 1879, matching eka-boron, and germanium in 1886, matching eka-silicon almost perfectly: Mendeleev had predicted an atomic weight of about 72 and a density of about 5.5; germanium turned out to be 72.6 and about 5.3. After that, chemists everywhere took the table seriously.

A whole family nobody expected

Even Mendeleev’s table had a surprise coming. In 1894, Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay found that nitrogen taken from the air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made by chemical reactions. The difference was tiny, but they did not ignore it. Hidden in the air was a new gas that reacted with nothing at all: argon, from the Greek for “lazy”. Within four years Ramsay had also found helium on Earth, and then, with Morris Travers, neon, krypton and xenon. They formed a completely new column, the noble gases, and slotted neatly onto the end of every row. The table bent to fit them without breaking: the sign of a good model.

The last puzzle: the wrong order

There was one awkward thing. In a few places Mendeleev had to put elements slightly out of order of weight to keep the families together. Tellurium (127.6) is heavier than iodine (126.9), but tellurium clearly belongs with oxygen and sulfur, and iodine with chlorine and bromine. So he swapped them and guessed that tellurium’s weight had been measured wrongly. It hadn’t. The real explanation waited until 1913, when the young physicist Henry Moseley showed that the true order is not by weight at all, but by the number of protons in the nucleus: the atomic number. Tellurium has 52 protons, iodine 53. The swap was right all along.

Reading the table, step by step

Here is how to read the chart that grew out of all this.

  1. Each box is one element, in order of atomic number: hydrogen 1, helium 2, lithium 3, and so on.
  2. A row is a period. Each new row starts when the atoms begin filling a new shell of electrons. So the rows get longer as you go down.
  3. A column is a family, called a group. Atoms in the same column have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they behave alike: lithium, sodium and potassium in the first column; fluorine, chlorine and bromine in the next-to-last; the noble gases at the far right.
  4. Metals are on the left and in the middle; non-metals on the right. A staircase line separates them.

The table today

The table now holds 118 elements. The last four were named in 2016: nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson. In 1955, scientists at Berkeley named element 101 mendelevium, in honour of the man who laid out the cards.

A patience game of your own

Take twelve cards or slips of paper. On each write one of these, with its atomic weight: lithium 6.9, sodium 23.0, potassium 39.1 (soft metals that fizz in water); fluorine 19.0, chlorine 35.5, bromine 79.9 (sharp-smelling, poisonous non-metals); beryllium 9.0, magnesium 24.3, calcium 40.1 (harder metals); oxygen 16.0, sulfur 32.1, selenium 79.0. Shuffle them, then lay them out in order of weight in rows so that each family forms a column. You have just rebuilt a corner of Mendeleev’s table.

Every time you look at the periodic table in this book, remember that it began as a set of cards on a professor’s desk, and that its greatest strength was the blank spaces where the professor admitted what he did not know.

1912 to 1932

Who pulls harder? The story of polar molecules

Peter Debye, Linus Pauling

A kitchen, any day

Pour a spoonful of cooking oil into a glass of water and stir as hard as you like. The moment you stop, the oil gathers into drops and floats to the top. Sugar disappears into water without a trace; oil never does. Water and oil are both clear liquids made of small molecules. Why do they refuse to mix?

The answer lies in a tug-of-war that happens inside every bond, and two scientists, a Dutch physicist and an American chemist, learned how to measure it.

An unfair tug-of-war

A bond, as Lewis taught, is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. But sharing is not always equal. Some atoms pull on shared electrons more strongly than others, because their nucleus has more positive charge acting on the outer electrons, or because those electrons sit closer to it.

When the pull is unequal, the shared electrons spend more of their time near the stronger atom. That end of the bond becomes slightly negative, and the other end slightly positive. Chemists write these “slightly” charges with the Greek letter delta: δ⁻ and δ⁺. A bond like this is called polar, because it has two ends, like the poles of a magnet.

Debye measures the pull

Zürich and Utrecht, 1912

In 1912 the Dutch physicist Peter Debye worked out how molecules with a positive end and a negative end, which he called dipoles (“two poles”), would behave between electrically charged plates. They would tend to turn and line up, and that would change how much electric charge the plates could store. By measuring that change for different gases and liquids, and how it varied with temperature, he could calculate how strongly each molecule was polarised.

His method gave numbers. Water’s dipole is large. Carbon dioxide’s is zero, even though each C=O bond in it is polar: the molecule is straight, so the two pulls point in opposite directions and cancel. Methane’s is zero too, because its four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel perfectly. The unit chemists use for dipoles is named after him: the debye. Water’s is about 1.85 debye. Debye won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1936.

Pauling’s scale

Pasadena, California, 1932

Debye had measured whole molecules. Linus Pauling wanted a number for each atom: how hard does it pull shared electrons? In 1932 he worked one out by comparing bond energies. If a bond between two different atoms is stronger than you would expect from the average of the two similar bonds, the extra strength comes from the unequal sharing. From those differences he built a scale he called electronegativity.

Some values on Pauling’s scale (modern figures):
fluorine 3.98 (the strongest pull of all), oxygen 3.44, nitrogen 3.04, chlorine 3.16,
carbon 2.55, hydrogen 2.20, sodium 0.93.

The bigger the difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. Oxygen and hydrogen differ by 1.24, so O–H bonds are strongly polar. Carbon and hydrogen differ by only 0.35, so C–H bonds are nearly even. Sodium and chlorine differ by more than 2, so much that sodium’s electron goes over to chlorine almost completely: that is an ionic bond. Polar bonds sit in the middle of a smooth range from perfectly even sharing to complete transfer.

Polar molecules, step by step

  1. Look at each bond. Is one atom much more electronegative than the other? Then the bond is polar, with δ⁻ on the stronger-pulling atom.
  2. Look at the shape. Draw an arrow along each polar bond, pointing to the δ⁻ end.
  3. Add up the arrows. If they cancel (as in straight CO₂ or tetrahedral CH₄), the molecule is non-polar overall. If they do not cancel (as in bent H₂O or pyramid-shaped NH₃), the molecule is polar: it has a positive side and a negative side.

Back to oil and water

Water molecules are strongly polar. The positive hydrogen side of one molecule is attracted to the negative oxygen side of its neighbours, so water molecules cling tightly to each other. Oil molecules are long chains of carbon and hydrogen, with nearly even C–H bonds: almost non-polar. When you stir oil into water, the water molecules simply hold on to each other and squeeze the oil out. “Like dissolves like”: polar dissolves polar, non-polar dissolves non-polar.

Careful

“You can prove water is polar by holding a charged comb next to a thin stream from the tap: the stream bends.”

The stream does bend, and it is a lovely thing to watch. But careful experiments (published in 2000) showed the bending comes mostly from electric charge that flows onto the stream from the tap, not from the water molecules turning. The real evidence that water is polar comes from measurements like Debye’s.

Oil, water and soap

Half fill a clear jar with water, add a few spoonfuls of cooking oil and a drop of food colouring, put the lid on tightly and shake. Watch the oil separate again. Now add a squirt of washing-up liquid and shake once more. Soap molecules have a polar head, which sits happily in water, and a long non-polar tail, which sits happily in oil. They wrap around tiny oil droplets and let them spread through the water. That is how soap washes grease off your plate.

1593 to 1848

How cold can cold get?

Galileo Galilei, Daniel Fahrenheit, Anders Celsius, Guillaume Amontons, William Thomson (Lord Kelvin)

Padua, around 1593

Hot and cold seem like the simplest things in the world. You can feel them. But try this: put one hand in cold water and the other in hot water for a minute, then put both into the same bowl of lukewarm water. One hand says “warm”, the other says “cold”. Your skin is a terrible thermometer. For most of history nobody could measure how hot something was, only how hot it felt.

Around 1593 Galileo built a gadget called a thermoscope: a glass bulb of air on top of a thin tube dipped in water. When the air in the bulb warmed it expanded and pushed the water down; when it cooled the water rose. It showed changes in hotness, but it had no numbers, and it also wobbled with the weather, because the open water was being pushed by the air outside.

Step 1: putting numbers on hotness

The trick that turned a thermoscope into a thermometer was to choose fixed points: things that always happen at the same hotness, so that everyone’s thermometer could agree. In 1724 the instrument-maker Daniel Fahrenheit, working in Amsterdam, published his scale, using sealed glass tubes of mercury that were far more reliable than anything before. In 1742 the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed a scale with 100 steps between the freezing and boiling points of water. Oddly, he put the boiling point at 0 and freezing at 100; within a few years others turned it the right way up, and that is the Celsius scale used in India today.

Careful

“40 °C is twice as hot as 20 °C.”

It is not, and the reason is the heart of this story. The zero of the Celsius scale is just where water happens to freeze. It is not “no heat at all”. Doubling a Celsius number does not double anything real, in the same way that doubling the floor number of a building does not double its height above the basement.

Step 2: a gas points to the coldest possible cold

Around 1702 the French scientist Guillaume Amontons noticed something strange about air trapped in a sealed container. As he cooled it, its pressure dropped steadily, by the same amount for every degree. He wondered: if you kept cooling, the pressure would keep falling, and at some temperature it would reach zero. A gas cannot push less than not at all. So that temperature must be the coldest there can possibly be.

Over the next century, more careful measurements by Charles, Gay-Lussac and others showed the same thing for every gas they tried. Draw the straight lines of pressure against temperature, extend them backwards into the cold, and they all meet at zero pressure at the same place: about −273 °C. Today we know the exact value: −273.15 °C. It is called absolute zero.

What happens there? Temperature, it turns out, is a measure of how vigorously particles are moving. At absolute zero they would have the very least motion that the laws of physics allow. You cannot go colder than that, for the same reason you cannot be shorter than zero centimetres.

Glasgow, 1848

In 1848 a 24-year-old professor at Glasgow University, William Thomson, proposed a temperature scale that starts at absolute zero itself. Thomson was a prodigy: he had started at university aged ten. Much later, Queen Victoria made him a lord, and he took his title from the River Kelvin that flows past the university, becoming Lord Kelvin. His scale is now called the kelvin scale, and its unit is the kelvin, written K (with no degree sign).

Step 3: converting between Celsius and kelvin

The steps on the kelvin scale are exactly the same size as Celsius degrees. Only the starting point moves. So converting is just adding:

kelvin = degrees Celsius + 273.15
Water freezes: 0 °C = 273.15 K.
A warm Mumbai afternoon: 30 °C = 303.15 K.
Water boils: 100 °C = 373.15 K.
Absolute zero: −273.15 °C = 0 K.

Now try the “twice as hot” question again, in kelvin. 20 °C is 293 K and 40 °C is 313 K. So 40 °C has only about 7% more of the jiggling we call temperature than 20 °C, not twice as much. To be truly twice as hot as a 20 °C room, in the physicist’s sense, something would have to be at 586 K: about 313 °C, hotter than a kitchen oven.

This is why every gas law in this book uses kelvin. When a gas’s kelvin temperature doubles, its particles have twice as much energy of motion, and if it is sealed in a rigid box, its pressure doubles too. That simple doubling only works if you count from the true zero.

Step 4: the race towards zero

Can anyone actually get to absolute zero? Scientists have been racing towards it for over a century. In 1908 the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes turned helium into a liquid at about 4 K, and a few years later discovered that some metals lose all electrical resistance when that cold. Today laboratories can cool clouds of atoms to less than a billionth of a kelvin above absolute zero. But the laws of physics say you can never quite reach it: each step closer gets harder than the last. Even deep space is not that cold: the faint glow left over from the Big Bang keeps it at about 2.7 K.

A thermometer’s fixed point

If you have a kitchen thermometer, fill a glass with plenty of crushed ice and a little cold water, stir, and wait a few minutes. It should read very close to 0 °C. Add more ice, wait, and read it again: still 0 °C. While ice and water are both present, the temperature stays put, which is exactly why melting ice was chosen as a fixed point. (If your thermometer reads 1 or 2 degrees off, you have just calibrated it.)

So whenever you see a temperature in kelvin in this book, remember what the number means: how far you are above the stillest possible state of matter, counted in steps the size of a Celsius degree.

1611 to 1920

The strange case of water

Johannes Kepler, Wendell Latimer, Worth Rodebush, Linus Pauling

Prague, winter 1610

On a snowy day in Prague, the astronomer Johannes Kepler was crossing a bridge when a snowflake landed on his coat. He noticed, as people had before him, that it had six points. Every snowflake he looked at had six. Why six, and never five or eight? He wrote a little book about it as a New Year’s present for a friend, published in 1611, and guessed that it had something to do with how tiny particles pack together. He could not go further. Nobody knew what water was made of.

It took three more centuries to understand Kepler’s snowflakes. The answer turned out to explain far more than snow: why ice floats, why lakes freeze from the top down, why water boils at such a high temperature, and why you sweat on a hot Mumbai afternoon.

Step 1: water is an odd liquid

By most of chemistry’s rules, water should be a gas at room temperature. Look at its relatives. Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, has molecules shaped just like water’s but heavier, and it boils at about −60 °C. Methane, CH₄, with almost the same mass as water, boils at −161 °C. Yet water, with a light little molecule of three atoms, does not boil until 100 °C. Something is holding water molecules to each other unusually tightly.

And then there is ice. Almost every substance shrinks when it freezes: its particles pack more neatly as a solid than as a liquid, so the solid sinks in its own liquid. Water does the opposite. Ice takes up about 9% more space than the water it came from. That is why ice floats, why a full bottle of water in the freezer cracks, and why pipes burst in cold countries.

Berkeley, California, 1920

The explanation came from the laboratory of the great chemist G. N. Lewis, the man who first drew bonds as shared pairs of electrons. In 1920 two young chemists working there, Wendell Latimer and Worth Rodebush, suggested that a hydrogen atom could be held between two oxygen atoms at once: firmly bonded to one, and weakly attracted to the other. This weak link between molecules came to be called the hydrogen bond. In the 1930s Linus Pauling made the idea famous and showed how much of chemistry and biology depends on it.

Step 2: where the hydrogen bond comes from

In a water molecule, the oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons towards itself harder than the hydrogen atoms do. That leaves the oxygen slightly negative and each hydrogen slightly positive. The molecule is also bent, like a boomerang, so the two slightly positive hydrogens are on one side and the slightly negative oxygen on the other.

Now put lots of water molecules together. The slightly positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the slightly negative oxygen of the next. Opposite charges attract: that is all a hydrogen bond is. It is much weaker than the real bonds inside a water molecule, about twenty times weaker, but every water molecule can make several of them, and together they hold the liquid tightly.

That is why water boils so late. To turn water into steam you have to pull every molecule away from its neighbours, breaking all those hydrogen bonds. The O–H bonds inside each molecule do not break at all: steam is still H₂O.

Step 3: why ice floats

When water freezes, each molecule settles into a position where it makes four hydrogen bonds with four neighbours, arranged in a very regular, open pattern of six-sided rings. The rings hold the molecules slightly further apart than they are in the jostling liquid. More space between molecules means the same mass fills a bigger volume, so ice is less dense than water, and it floats. Those six-sided rings are also the reason every snowflake has six points: Kepler’s puzzle, solved.

How much of an ice cube is underwater?
Ice has a density of about 0.917 grams per millilitre; liquid water about 1.000.
A floating object sinks until it pushes aside its own weight of water.
So the fraction underwater is 0.917 ÷ 1.000 ≈ 0.92: about nine-tenths of an ice cube, or an iceberg, is below the surface.

This one strange property matters enormously. When a lake freezes in winter, the ice forms on top and floats there, like a lid, keeping the water underneath liquid. Fish and plants survive the winter below. If ice sank, lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up.

Step 4: why sweat cools you

Breaking hydrogen bonds takes energy. When sweat evaporates from your skin, the water molecules that escape carry that energy away with them, taking it from your body, and you cool down. Evaporating about a litre of sweat takes roughly 2.4 million joules: as much energy as it takes to warm 7 litres of water from room temperature to boiling. On a humid monsoon day the air is already so full of water vapour that sweat evaporates slowly, which is why humid heat feels so much stickier and harder to bear than dry heat.

Careful

“Boiling breaks water molecules apart into hydrogen and oxygen.”

Boiling only breaks the weak hydrogen bonds between molecules. The molecules themselves stay whole. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen is a completely different, chemical change, which needs electricity or a great deal of heat.

Ice that grows

Fill a small plastic cup (not glass) exactly to a line you draw with a marker, about two-thirds full. Put it in the freezer overnight. In the morning the ice will stand clearly above your line, often with a little bump in the middle. Water expanded as it froze: the hydrogen bonds pushed the molecules into their open six-sided pattern.

A floating paper clip

Fill a bowl with water. Lay a small square of tissue paper flat on the surface and gently place a dry metal paper clip on it. As the tissue soaks and sinks, the paper clip is often left floating, resting on the skin of the water. Hydrogen bonds pulling the surface molecules together make that skin. Add a drop of washing-up liquid at the edge and watch what happens.

So water, the most ordinary substance in your life, is one of the strangest in all of chemistry. Its weak little hydrogen bonds decide whether lakes freeze, whether you can cool down on a hot day, and why every snowflake that ever fell has had six points.

1823 to 1889

Why the match needs striking

Johann Döbereiner, Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Svante Arrhenius

Jena, Germany, 1823

The chemist Johann Döbereiner lets a stream of hydrogen gas flow over a small piece of spongy platinum metal. Nobody has lit a match. Yet within moments the platinum begins to glow red, and the hydrogen bursts into flame. Döbereiner turns the trick into a gadget: a glass jar that makes hydrogen, a nozzle and a pinch of platinum. Press a lever and you have fire. “Döbereiner’s lamp” was sold by the thousands as a lighter for pipes and candles, decades before cheap matches. But nobody understood how it worked. The platinum was not burning, and it was not used up. It just sat there and made the reaction happen.

The puzzle of things that do not happen

Here is a stranger puzzle. Hydrogen and oxygen react violently: Chapter 4 showed that a spark makes them explode. And yet you can mix them in a jar at room temperature and leave them for years, and almost nothing happens. This page is the same. Paper and oxygen react to give carbon dioxide and water and a great deal of heat; that is what burning is. You are surrounded by oxygen. So why doesn’t this book burst into flame?

Berzelius gives it a name

In 1835 Jöns Jacob Berzelius, collecting together several strange cases like Döbereiner’s lamp, gave the effect a name: catalysis, from a Greek word meaning “loosening”. A catalyst is a substance that makes a reaction go faster without being used up itself. Berzelius could name it, but he could not explain it. The explanation needed a new idea about why reactions happen at all.

Arrhenius and the hill

Uppsala and Stockholm, Sweden, 1889

The Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius (the same man who had explained ions in water a few years earlier) noticed that the speed of many reactions rises steeply with temperature, much more steeply than you would expect if it simply depended on how often particles collide. In 1889 he suggested the reason. For molecules to react, they must hit each other hard enough. Only collisions with more than a certain minimum energy can stretch and break the old bonds so that new ones can form. That minimum is called the activation energy.

Step 1: picture a hill

Think of a ball resting in a valley, with a deeper valley on the other side of a hill. The ball would be lower, and more settled, in the far valley: that is the products, lower in energy than the reactants. But to get there, the ball must first be pushed up the hill. The top of the hill is the barrier. A gentle nudge just rolls the ball back. Only a hard enough push gets it over.

That is why the book does not burn. Most oxygen molecules hitting the paper are not moving fast enough to get over the barrier. A match is a way of giving a few molecules enough energy to get over; once the burning starts, the heat it releases pushes neighbouring molecules over too, and the fire spreads.

Step 2: why temperature matters so much

In any gas or liquid, molecules have a spread of energies: most are fairly slow, a few are fast. Only the fast few can get over the barrier. Warm things up, and the whole spread shifts: the number of molecules fast enough to get over rises sharply. A useful rule of thumb for many reactions near room temperature is that ten degrees warmer roughly doubles the speed.

Why food lasts longer in the fridge. The chemistry that spoils food runs, as a rough rule, about twice as fast for every 10 °C warmer.
From a 4 °C fridge to a 24 °C kitchen is 20 degrees: two doublings, 2 × 2 = 4 times faster.
To a 44 °C Mumbai rooftop in May: four doublings, 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times faster.
(This is only a rule of thumb; real reactions vary.)

Step 3: what a catalyst does

A catalyst does not push the ball harder. It opens a different path, a lower pass through the hills. With a lower barrier, many more molecules have enough energy to get across, so the reaction runs much faster. On Döbereiner’s platinum, hydrogen and oxygen molecules stick to the metal surface, where their bonds are loosened, and they react easily there. The platinum comes out unchanged, ready for the next molecules.

Two things a catalyst does not do. It does not change where the valleys are: the products end up with exactly the same energy, with or without it. And it lowers the hill in both directions, so it speeds up the backward reaction too. Chapter 5 explains why that means a catalyst cannot change how far a reaction goes, only how fast it gets there.

Life’s catalysts

Your body is full of catalysts called enzymes: large protein molecules, each shaped to speed up one particular reaction. An enzyme in your blood called carbonic anhydrase helps carbon dioxide react with water more than a million times faster than it would on its own. Without enzymes, digesting a meal would take years. Cars carry catalysts too: the catalytic converter, coated with tiny amounts of platinum, palladium and rhodium, turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

Careful

“A catalyst gives the reaction extra energy.”

It gives no energy at all. It provides a route that needs less. That is why it is not used up: it is a guide, not a fuel.

Two experiments with heat and enzymes

Glowsticks. Snap two identical glowsticks to start them (do not cut them open). Put one in a glass of warm tap water and one in a glass of ice water. After a minute, compare them in a dark room. The warm one glows brighter, because its light-making reaction runs faster; it will also run out sooner. The cold one glows dimly but for longer.

Pineapple jelly. With an adult, make two small bowls of jelly from gelatin powder. Stir pieces of fresh pineapple into one and pieces of tinned pineapple into the other, and put both in the fridge. The bowl with tinned pineapple sets; the one with fresh pineapple stays runny. Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that cuts up the gelatin’s protein chains. Tinned pineapple has been heated, which destroys the enzyme’s delicate shape.

So the next time you strike a match, remember the hill: the match is not the energy of the fire, it is the push that gets the first few molecules over the top.

1783 to 1850

Heat is motion

Antoine Lavoisier, Pierre-Simon Laplace, Count Rumford, James Prescott Joule

Paris, winter 1782

A guinea pig sits in a small wire cage. Around the cage is a jacket packed with crushed ice, and around that, another jacket of ice to keep out the warmth of the room. Antoine Lavoisier and the mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace are waiting to see how much ice the little animal’s body heat will melt. It sounds like a strange way to spend a winter, but they are asking one of the deepest questions in science: what is heat?

Heat as a fluid

In the 1700s most scientists believed that heat was an invisible, weightless fluid called caloric. Hot things were full of it; cold things had less. Caloric flowed from hot to cold the way water flows downhill, which is why your chai cools down and the air around it warms up. Lavoisier even listed caloric among the chemical elements.

The caloric idea explained a lot, and Lavoisier and Laplace’s ice machine, the first calorimeter (heat-measurer), was built to measure it. The melted ice dripped out and was weighed: the more ice melted, the more heat had been given off. They found that the guinea pig, over a few hours, melted about as much ice as burning a small amount of charcoal producing the same amount of carbon dioxide. Their conclusion was beautiful and correct: breathing is a slow, gentle kind of burning. Your body “burns” food with oxygen, and that is where your warmth comes from.

The cannon that never ran out of heat

The army arsenal in Munich, 1798

An American-born soldier and inventor, Benjamin Thompson, who had become Count Rumford in Bavaria, was in charge of making cannons. A cannon barrel was made by spinning a solid metal casting against a sharp drill. Rumford noticed how hot the metal became. So he tried an experiment: he used a deliberately blunt drill, turned by horses, with the cannon sitting in a box of water. After about two and a half hours, the water boiled. The watching crowd was astonished: water boiling without any fire.

What struck Rumford was that the heat never ran out. As long as the horses kept turning, heat kept coming. If heat were a fluid stored inside the metal, surely it would eventually be used up. Instead it seemed to be made by the motion. Rumford suggested that heat is not a substance at all, but a kind of motion.

Joule’s paddle wheel

Salford, near Manchester, 1840s

The person who proved it was James Prescott Joule, the son of a wealthy brewer, who did his experiments at home. His most famous apparatus was a paddle wheel inside a container of water. A weight hanging on a string slowly fell, turning the paddles, which churned the water. Joule measured the temperature of the water with a thermometer so precise it could detect a few hundredths of a degree.

The water warmed up, very slightly. And always by the same amount for the same falling weight. A falling weight is motion; warmer water is heat; and there was a fixed exchange rate between them. In 1850 Joule published his best value: the energy of 772 pounds falling one foot raises one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. In today’s units, it takes about 4,200 joules to warm a kilogram of water by one degree Celsius. The unit of energy, the joule, is named after him.

There is a famous story that Joule took a thermometer on his honeymoon in the Alps to test whether the water at the bottom of a waterfall was warmer than at the top. The physicist William Thomson said he met Joule there, thermometer in hand. Whether or not he measured anything, he was right in principle: the water at the bottom of a 100-metre waterfall should be warmer by only about a quarter of a degree, far too little to notice with your fingers.

Step 1: what energy is

Energy is the capacity to make things happen: to move, to warm, to light, to push. It comes in many forms. A falling weight has energy of motion. A stretched spring has stored energy. Chemicals have energy stored in the way their atoms are arranged. Heat is energy too: the energy of particles jiggling.

The great discovery of the 1840s, made by Joule and several others at about the same time, is called the conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed. It only changes from one form to another. The horses’ muscles became the drill’s motion became jiggling metal atoms became boiling water.

Step 2: what heat really is

Now we can say what caloric really was. When something is hot, its particles are jiggling fast. When you put a hot cup in cold air, the fast-jiggling particles of the cup bump into slower air molecules and speed them up, and slow down themselves. That flow of jiggling from hot to cold is heat. There is no fluid. There is only motion, passed on by collisions.

How much energy to make a cup of chai? Warming 250 g of water from 25 °C to 100 °C:
Each gram needs about 4.18 joules for each degree. The water warms by 75 degrees.
Energy = 250 × 4.18 × 75 ≈ 78,000 joules, or 78 kilojoules.
Compare Joule’s falling weight: to warm a kilogram of water by just one degree, a kilogram weight would have to fall about 427 metres, higher than most skyscrapers.

Step 3: chemical reactions and heat

When a reaction gives energy out to its surroundings, they warm up: the reaction is exothermic (“heat out”). Burning gas, a hand-warmer and your own breathing are exothermic. When a reaction takes energy in from its surroundings, they cool down: it is endothermic (“heat in”). An instant cold pack is endothermic. In both cases, Joule’s rule holds: whatever energy the chemicals lose, the surroundings gain, and the other way round. Chapter 5 shows where that energy comes from: the breaking and making of bonds.

Careful

“Cold is a thing that flows into your hand when you touch ice.”

There is no such thing as “cold” flowing. Energy flows out of your warm hand into the ice. Your hand loses jiggling, so it feels cold. Heat always flows from hotter to colder, never the other way by itself.

A rubber band thermometer and a cooling fizz

Take a thick rubber band, hold it against your top lip (which is very sensitive to temperature), and stretch it quickly: it feels warm. Hold it stretched for a few seconds, then let it go back quickly while touching your lip: it feels cool. Stretching does work on the rubber, and some of that work becomes heat. Then, with a kitchen thermometer, measure the temperature of a few tablespoons of vinegar in a cup, stir in a teaspoon of baking soda, and measure again as it fizzes: the temperature drops by a few degrees. That reaction is endothermic: it takes energy from the liquid around it.

From a guinea pig in ice to a paddle wheel in a brewery, the answer was the same: heat is motion, and energy is never lost. Every energy diagram in this book is an account book that Joule would have recognised.

1799 to 1884

The lakes of Egypt and the balance that never stops

Claude-Louis Berthollet, Cato Guldberg, Peter Waage, Henry Le Châtelier

The Natron Lakes, west of the Nile, 1799

In 1798 Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Egypt, and he brought along not only soldiers but more than a hundred scientists, engineers and artists. One of them was Claude-Louis Berthollet, one of the best chemists in France. In the desert west of the Nile he visited a string of salty lakes, still called the Natron Lakes today, and saw something that puzzled him: a white crust of soda (sodium carbonate, used for centuries to make glass and soap, and by the ancient Egyptians to preserve mummies) forming around their shores.

What puzzled him was this. In the laboratory, everyone knew a reliable reaction: mix soda with calcium chloride and you get chalky calcium carbonate and common salt. It went one way, and only one way, or so chemists thought. But around these lakes there was plenty of common salt and plenty of limestone (calcium carbonate) in the rock. And there, in the desert, soda was being made from them. The laboratory reaction seemed to be running backwards.

Berthollet’s big idea

Berthollet’s explanation was bold. Chemists of his time believed each substance had a fixed “preference” for others, so a reaction always went the same way. Berthollet argued instead that reactions can go both ways, and that which way they actually go depends on the conditions, especially how much of each substance is around. In the lakes there was a huge amount of salt, enough to push the reaction backwards. He published his ideas in 1803. Geologists today think the full story of how those lakes make soda is more complicated, but Berthollet’s central insight, that chemical reactions are reversible, was right, and it changed chemistry.

The Norwegians who did the sums

Christiania (now Oslo), 1864

Sixty years later, two Norwegian chemists who were also brothers-in-law, Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage, turned Berthollet’s idea into mathematics. They measured how far reactions went with different amounts of chemicals, and reasoned about how fast they must run forwards and backwards, and found a simple rule: the more crowded a substance is, the faster it reacts, because its particles meet their partners more often. Put a forward reaction and a backward reaction in the same container, each speeding up or slowing down with how much of its starting material is present, and something remarkable happens.

Step 1: the escalator picture

Imagine two escalators between the ground floor and the first floor of a shopping mall, one going up and one going down. Lots of people start on the ground floor, and nobody upstairs. At first, crowds ride up and hardly anyone rides down. But as people collect upstairs, more of them wander onto the down escalator. Eventually the number riding up each minute equals the number riding down. From then on, the number of people on each floor stays the same, even though people never stop moving.

That is a dynamic equilibrium: two opposite changes happening at the same rate, so the totals stop changing while the particles keep on changing. The word “equilibrium” means balance; “dynamic” means it is a moving balance, not a stopped one.

Step 2: unequal amounts, equal rates

Here is the part people often get wrong. At equilibrium, the rates are equal, but the amounts usually are not.

In Chapter 5’s made-up reaction, each A turns into B at a rate set by 2 (per second), and each B turns back at a rate set by 1.
For the two rates to match, there must be twice as much B as A: 2 × (amount of A) = 1 × (amount of B).
Starting with 10 units of A, it settles at about 3.33 units of A and 6.67 units of B.
Check the rates: 2 × 3.33 = 6.67 and 1 × 6.67 = 6.67. Equal. The amounts are not.

Step 3: push it, and it pushes back

Paris, 1884

The French chemist Henry Le Châtelier noticed a pattern in how equilibrium mixtures respond when you disturb them. Add more of one ingredient, and the mixture shifts to use some of it up. Take a product away, and the mixture shifts to make more. Squeeze a mixture of gases, and it shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules. Warm it, and it shifts in the direction that absorbs heat.

This pattern, Le Châtelier’s principle, is not because the mixture “wants” to resist you. It follows from the rates. Add more A, and the forward reaction speeds up (more A particles bumping into each other), while the backward one has not changed yet. So more A turns into B than the other way, until the two rates match again. Chapter 5’s live figure lets you watch it happen.

Careful

“At equilibrium, the reaction has stopped.”

It looks stopped, because the amounts stay the same. But both reactions are still going, at equal speeds. Chemists proved it in the twentieth century by adding a few atoms of a slightly heavier isotope to a mixture already at equilibrium: soon the heavy atoms turned up in both the reactants and the products, which could only happen if the reactions were still running both ways.

A fizzy-drink equilibrium

In a sealed bottle of soda water, carbon dioxide gas above the liquid and carbon dioxide dissolved in it are in equilibrium: molecules leave the water and dissolve back at equal rates. Open the bottle and you remove the gas above, so the balance shifts: dissolved gas comes out as bubbles. Try it with two unopened bottles, one from the fridge and one that has sat in a warm room for a few hours. Open them slowly over a sink, with an adult. The warm one fizzes much more, because less gas can stay dissolved in warm water: warming shifts the balance towards the gas.

Berthollet’s lakes, Guldberg and Waage’s sums and Le Châtelier’s rule all say the same thing: most chemical change is a two-way street, and the traffic never stops. In the story of Fritz Haber, a chemist uses exactly these ideas to feed half the world.

1898 to 1913

Bread from air

William Crookes, Fritz Haber, Robert Le Rossignol, Carl Bosch, Alwin Mittasch, Clara Immerwahr

Bristol, England, 1898

A famous scientist, Sir William Crookes, stands up to give the most important speech of the year to Britain’s scientists, and he gives them a fright. The world’s population is growing fast, he says, and so is its hunger for wheat. Wheat needs nitrogen, and the soil runs out of it. The farms of Europe and America are being kept going with nitrogen dug out of the ground on the other side of the world: piles of seabird droppings, called guano, from islands off Peru, and a salty mineral, Chile saltpetre, from the Atacama desert. Those supplies, Crookes warns, will run out within a few decades. Unless chemists find another source, the world faces hunger.

Then he points out something maddening. Every breath you take is about four-fifths nitrogen. There is unimaginably more of it in the air than any farm could ever need. The problem is that plants cannot use it.

Why air nitrogen is so hard to use

Nitrogen in the air is made of N₂ molecules: two nitrogen atoms joined by a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. Plants (and you) need nitrogen to build proteins and DNA, but only in forms where that triple bond has already been broken, such as ammonia, NH₃, or the nitrates made from it. A few bacteria, and lightning, can break the bond. Humans could not, at least not cheaply.

The table-top in Karlsruhe

Karlsruhe, Germany, 1909

The German chemist Fritz Haber decided to try the most direct route of all: join nitrogen straight onto hydrogen.

N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃

That double arrow is the whole difficulty. The reaction is reversible: ammonia breaks back down into nitrogen and hydrogen as well as forming. Haber used everything the equilibrium story teaches. The forward reaction turns four gas molecules into two, so squeezing the gases hard pushes the balance towards ammonia: Haber worked at about 200 times normal air pressure. The forward reaction also gives out heat, so a cooler mixture gives more ammonia at equilibrium; but a cooler mixture reacts too slowly to be useful. So he compromised on a few hundred degrees, and added a catalyst (the rare metal osmium) to make the reaction fast enough. He also kept removing the ammonia as it formed, so the mixture kept making more.

With his assistant Robert Le Rossignol, a young Englishman who was brilliant at building high-pressure equipment, Haber built a machine about the size of a kitchen table. In July 1909 it produced a slow, steady trickle of liquid ammonia from air and hydrogen, and it kept on running.

From table-top to factory

A table-top machine is not a factory. The chemical company BASF gave the job to an engineer, Carl Bosch, who had to solve problems nobody had faced before. Hot hydrogen at enormous pressure soaked into steel and made it brittle, so the first reactors cracked; Bosch designed a steel tube with a soft-iron lining to protect it. Osmium was far too rare, so his colleague Alwin Mittasch tested thousands of possible catalysts, in many thousands of experiments, and settled on a cheap one based on iron.
