In 1913 the first factory opened at Oppau. The Haber–Bosch process, as it is called, had begun.

Step 1: why it matters so much

Today the world makes well over a hundred million tonnes of ammonia every year, most of it turned into fertiliser. In India, much of it becomes urea, the white granules scattered on fields of rice and wheat. Researchers estimate that about half the people alive today are fed by crops grown with fertiliser from this one reaction, and that roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your own body first passed through a Haber–Bosch factory. Chemistry, quite literally, made bread from air.

Step 2: the chemistry, step by step

  1. Nitrogen comes from the air; hydrogen today comes mostly from natural gas.
  2. The gases are squeezed to a couple of hundred times atmospheric pressure, because four molecules (N₂ + 3 H₂) become two (2 NH₃): squeezing favours fewer molecules.
  3. They are heated to about 400 to 450 °C: hot enough to be fast, not so hot that the balance swings back to nitrogen and hydrogen.
  4. An iron catalyst lowers the energy hill so the reaction is quick.
  5. The ammonia is cooled until it turns liquid and is taken away; the leftover gases go round again.

The other side of the story

Fritz Haber’s story does not end happily, and it would not be honest to pretend it does. When the First World War began in 1914, Haber put his skills to work for Germany’s army. He led the development of poison gas, and on 22 April 1915, near the town of Ypres in Belgium, chlorine gas was released against enemy soldiers for the first time. Thousands were killed or injured. Haber’s wife, Clara Immerwahr, was herself a talented chemist, the first woman to earn a doctorate at the University of Breslau, and she is said to have opposed his work on gas. She died just days after that first attack, a tragedy historians still write about.

Haber received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for making ammonia, and many scientists protested. In 1933, after the Nazis came to power and ordered him to dismiss his Jewish staff, he resigned from his own institute; he had been born Jewish himself. He left Germany and died the following year in Switzerland.

Haber’s life shows something worth remembering. Chemistry is knowledge, and knowledge can be used to feed people or to hurt them. The same man did both. What science is used for is always a choice made by people, and that is why scientists, and everyone else, have to care about how it is used.

Careful

“The Haber process turns all the nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia.”

It cannot: the reaction is an equilibrium, so at any moment some ammonia is breaking down again. In one pass through the reactor only a modest fraction becomes ammonia. That is why the factory takes the ammonia out and sends the unreacted gases round again and again.

Nitrogen you can see

Plants show you when they are short of nitrogen: their older leaves turn pale yellow. If you have two pots of the same small plant (or can sprout two pots of mung beans), water one with plain water and the other with water containing a tiny pinch of houseplant fertiliser (follow the packet, ask an adult, and wash your hands afterwards). Over two or three weeks, compare the colour and growth. The nitrogen in that fertiliser was almost certainly pulled out of the air by the reaction in this story.

The next time you eat a chapati, think of the triple bond in N₂, Haber’s table-top, and Bosch’s giant reactors: some of the nitrogen in that wheat was air not so long ago.

AL

Antoine and Marie-Anne Lavoisier

The man who weighed everything

1743 to 1794The tax collector who weighed everything, and the artist who recorded it

Paris, 1774

In his laboratory in Paris, a tax official spends his early mornings and his evenings doing something odd for a rich man: weighing things. Antoine Lavoisier owns the finest balances in Europe, accurate enough to notice a few hundredths of a gram, and he uses them on everything. Beside him works his wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier. She keeps the laboratory notebooks, draws the apparatus so well that her pictures are still printed in history books, and learns English so she can read what chemists in Britain are writing. Together they are about to overturn the most popular idea in chemistry.

The puzzle of burning

When wood burns, most of it seems to disappear: a heavy log becomes a little grey ash. So the chemists of the 1700s had a sensible-sounding explanation. Anything that can burn, they said, contains a fiery substance called phlogiston (from the Greek for “burned”). Burning is phlogiston escaping into the air. Wood is full of it, so wood burns well and leaves a light ash behind. Air can only soak up so much phlogiston, which is why a candle in a closed jar goes out.

It was a clever theory, and it explained a lot. But there was an awkward fact. When metals are heated in air, they slowly turn into a powdery crust that chemists called a calx (we would say an oxide). And the calx weighs more than the metal did. If phlogiston was leaving, why did the metal get heavier? Some chemists suggested phlogiston must have negative weight. Lavoisier thought that was nonsense. He suspected something was not leaving at all, but arriving, from the air.

Two discoveries of the same gas

The answer was found by two other men, at almost the same time, without knowing about each other. In Sweden, the pharmacist Carl Wilhelm Scheele heated several substances and collected a gas in which a candle burned brilliantly. He called it “fire air”. He found it first, around 1771 or 1772, but his book about it was delayed at the printer and only came out in 1777.

In England, the minister and chemist Joseph Priestley used a large magnifying lens to focus sunlight onto the red calx of mercury, on 1 August 1774. A gas came off. A candle in it burned with a dazzling flame, and a mouse sealed in a jar of it stayed lively far longer than in ordinary air. Priestley, a firm believer in phlogiston, called it “dephlogisticated air”: air with no phlogiston in it, so hungry for more that things burned fiercely.

That autumn Priestley visited Paris and told Lavoisier about his experiment over dinner. Lavoisier understood at once what Priestley had missed.

The sealed-vessel experiments

Lavoisier repeated the work with his balances, and he did one thing that made all the difference: he kept everything sealed. In one famous experiment he heated mercury in a closed flask connected to a measured volume of air, for twelve days. A red crust slowly grew on the mercury, and the air shrank by about a sixth. The air that was left would not let a candle burn or a mouse breathe. Then he heated the red crust strongly on its own, and out came almost exactly the amount of gas the air had lost: Priestley’s gas.

So burning and rusting are not something leaving. They are something joining: a part of the air combining with the metal. Lavoisier named that part oxygen in 1777. (He chose a Greek name meaning “acid-maker”, because he thought every acid contained it. That part turned out to be wrong, as you will find in Chapter 7, but the name stuck.) Combustion, burning, is a substance combining rapidly with oxygen.

Step 1: why weighing settles the argument

Here is the reasoning, slowly. Suppose you burn 2.4 grams of magnesium ribbon in air. It flares white and leaves a white powder.

Phlogiston says: the magnesium loses its phlogiston, so the powder should weigh less than 2.4 g.
The balance says: the white powder weighs about 4.0 g. It got heavier, by about 1.6 g.
Where did 1.6 g come from? From the air: 1.6 g of oxygen joined the magnesium to make magnesium oxide.
Check with atoms: 2.4 g of magnesium is 0.1 mol; it joins 0.1 mol of oxygen atoms, 1.6 g; together 4.0 g.

And the burning log? It gets lighter only because most of what it turns into, carbon dioxide and water vapour, are gases that float away. Burn it in a sealed container and weigh the whole thing, and the total does not change.

Step 2: the law

In 1789 Lavoisier published his great book, the Elementary Treatise of Chemistry. In it he set out the idea that runs through every chapter of this one: in a chemical change, matter is neither created nor destroyed. The total mass after a reaction is the same as the total mass before. We call this the conservation of mass. Today we can say why it is true: chemical reactions only rearrange atoms, and every atom that goes in comes out.

Careful

“Burning destroys things, so burning must lose mass.”

Burning changes things into new substances, often gases you cannot see. If you catch everything, gases included, the total mass stays the same. A candle seems to vanish only because its wax becomes carbon dioxide and water vapour that drift away.

The bag that does not get lighter

You need a zip-lock sandwich bag, a teaspoon of baking soda, a few tablespoons of vinegar and a kitchen scale. Wrap the baking soda in a small piece of tissue and put it in one corner of the bag. Pour the vinegar into the other corner, keeping them apart, squeeze out most of the air and seal the bag firmly. Weigh the bag. Now tip it so the vinegar soaks the tissue: the mixture fizzes and the bag puffs up with carbon dioxide. Weigh it again: the same. Finally open the bag, let the gas escape and weigh once more: now it is lighter, because the gas has left. Lavoisier’s whole argument, on your kitchen table. (Use small amounts so the bag does not burst.)

A sad ending

Lavoisier’s day job was collecting taxes for the king, as a member of a private company called the General Farm, which was hated by ordinary people. During the French Revolution the tax collectors were arrested, and on 8 May 1794 Lavoisier was executed by guillotine, aged 50. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange is said to have remarked that it took only a moment to cut off that head, and a hundred years might not produce another like it. Marie-Anne survived, lost almost everything, and spent years afterwards making sure her husband’s work was published and remembered.

Every time this book asks you to count the atoms on both sides of an equation, you are using the idea the Lavoisiers proved with their balance: nothing is lost, it only changes partners.

1808 to 1813

Letters for atoms: the language of chemistry

John Dalton, Jöns Jacob Berzelius

Stockholm, 1813

Imagine trying to write down a recipe in which every ingredient has a different secret picture, and every cook uses different pictures. That was chemistry for most of its history. Then, in 1813, a Swedish chemist named Jöns Jacob Berzelius suggested something so simple that it seems obvious now: use letters. This is the story of how chemistry got its alphabet.

Secret signs

The alchemists of the Middle Ages, who hoped to turn ordinary metals into gold, wrote with symbols borrowed from astronomy. Gold was a circle with a dot in the middle, the sign of the Sun. Silver was a crescent Moon. Mercury, the liquid metal, shared its sign with the planet Mercury. Many of these signs were meant to be mysterious. Alchemists often wanted to keep their methods secret, and a recipe nobody else can read is a recipe nobody else can steal.

That was fine for secrets, and hopeless for science. Science only works when other people can read exactly what you did and repeat it.

Dalton’s circles

In 1808 John Dalton, the Manchester schoolteacher who brought back the idea of atoms, drew each element as a little circle with its own marking. Hydrogen was a circle with a dot in the centre. Oxygen was a plain empty circle. Carbon was a circle filled in black. Nitrogen had a line down the middle. To show a compound, he put circles side by side, so water was a dotted circle next to an empty one.

It was a big step: for the first time, a symbol meant one atom. But Dalton’s circles were hard to print, easy to confuse, and impossible to type. Imagine writing out sugar, which has 45 atoms, as 45 little circles.

Berzelius’s letters

Berzelius was one of the most careful chemists who ever lived. Over about ten years he analysed some two thousand compounds and worked out the relative weights of the elements far more accurately than anyone before. He needed a quick way to write what he found, and in 1813 he proposed one: use the first letter of each element’s name, in capitals, adding a second small letter when two elements start with the same letter.

He used the elements’ Latin names, which every educated European could read. That is why some symbols puzzle English speakers today:

SymbolElementLatin name
Nasodiumnatrium
Kpotassiumkalium
Feironferrum
Cucoppercuprum
Agsilverargentum
Augoldaurum
Pbleadplumbum (which also gives us the word “plumber”, because pipes were once made of lead)
Hgmercuryhydrargyrum, “liquid silver”

To show how many atoms of each kind a compound contained, Berzelius wrote a small number after the symbol. He wrote it raised up, like H²O; later the custom changed to writing it low, H₂O, which is how the whole world writes it today. Dalton never liked the letters, and kept drawing his circles. But the letters won, because anyone can write them with a pen, print them in a book or type them on a keyboard.

Step 1: reading a chemical formula

A chemical formula is a list of the atoms in one molecule (or, for a crystal like salt, the ratio of atoms). Read it like this:

H₂O: two hydrogen atoms (the small 2 belongs to the H just before it) and one oxygen atom (no number means 1).
CO₂: one carbon, two oxygens.
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (table sugar): 12 carbons, 22 hydrogens, 11 oxygens: 45 atoms in every molecule.
Mg(OH)₂: brackets group atoms together, and the 2 after the bracket doubles everything inside. So: 1 magnesium, 2 oxygens, 2 hydrogens.

Step 2: the big number in front

A number written full-size in front of a formula counts whole molecules. 3 CO₂ means three separate carbon dioxide molecules: 3 carbons and 6 oxygens in all. That is completely different from changing the small number inside: CO₂ is carbon dioxide, which you breathe out; CO is carbon monoxide, a poison. The small numbers say what the substance is. The big number says how many of it you have.

Step 3: sentences made of formulas

Put formulas together with a plus sign and an arrow and you have a chemical equation, a sentence describing a reaction:

2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O

Read it aloud: “two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule react to make two water molecules.” Count the atoms on each side: 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens on the left, 4 hydrogens and 2 oxygens on the right. Lavoisier’s law, that nothing is lost, becomes a rule you can check with your finger: every kind of atom must balance.

Careful

“To balance an equation, I can change H₂O into H₂O₂.”

Never change the small numbers. H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a completely different substance. You may only change the big numbers in front, which decide how many molecules take part.

Spell with the elements

Find a periodic table (there is one on the cover of this book) and try to spell words using only element symbols. “Bacon” works: Ba, C, O, N. So does “Amar”: Am (americium) and Ar (argon). Which names in your family can you spell? Which letters of the alphabet never appear in any symbol? (There are two: J and Q. Try spelling “jam” or “queen”.)

Every formula and equation in this book is written in Berzelius’s alphabet: a language shared by every chemist on Earth, in every country, which a twelve-year-old in Mumbai and a professor in Stockholm can read in exactly the same way.

1773 to 2019

How big is Avogadro's number?

Benjamin Franklin, Josef Loschmidt, Jean Perrin, Robert Millikan

Clapham Common, London, 1773

On a windy day the American inventor Benjamin Franklin, who was living in London, carried a little cruet of oil down to a pond on Clapham Common. The wind was whipping up small waves. He poured out no more than a teaspoon of oil onto the water, and watched something remarkable happen. The oil spread, and spread, and kept spreading, until it covered about half an acre of the pond: roughly the area of eight tennis courts. Where it had spread, the waves went flat, “as smooth as a looking glass”, he wrote.

Franklin did not do the sum that was hiding in his experiment. More than a hundred years later, the English physicist Lord Rayleigh did it, with his own careful measurements of oil on water. It is the first clue in our story.

Step 1: how thin can oil get?

If a teaspoon of oil spreads into a film, the film’s thickness is just its volume divided by its area. Let us do it with Franklin’s numbers.

A teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres = 0.000 005 cubic metres (5 × 10⁻⁶ m³).
Half an acre is about 2,000 square metres.
Thickness = volume ÷ area = 5 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 2,000 ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁹ m, about 2.5 nanometres.

The oil cannot spread any thinner than a single layer of its molecules. So an oil molecule can be no more than about 2.5 nanometres long: two and a half millionths of a millimetre. For the first time, a kitchen-sized experiment had put a ceiling on the size of a molecule.

Step 2: from size to number

If you know roughly how big a molecule is, you can estimate how many there are in a given amount. In 1865 the Austrian scientist Josef Loschmidt did exactly that for the molecules in air, using measurements of how fast gases spread and how much they shrink when turned into liquid. His answer for the number in a mole was rough, but it was in the right neighbourhood. For the first time, somebody had put an actual number on the invisible.

Step 3: many roads, one answer

The real proof came early in the twentieth century, when scientists found completely different ways of measuring the same number, and they all agreed.

  • Jiggling grains (around 1908). Jean Perrin in Paris watched tiny grains of resin bobbing about in water, shoved this way and that by invisible water molecules. From how far they wandered, using a formula that Albert Einstein had worked out in 1905, he could work out how many molecules there must be in a mole. He got roughly 6 to 7 × 10²³.
  • Charge (1909 onwards). The American physicist Robert Millikan measured the electric charge on a single electron by watching tiny oil droplets float between charged metal plates. Chemists already knew how much charge it takes to deposit one mole of silver in electrolysis: about 96,485 units, called coulombs. Divide the charge for a mole by the charge for one electron, and you get the number of electrons in a mole:

96,485 ÷ 0.000 000 000 000 000 000 160 2 (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs per electron)
= 6.022 × 10²³

  • Crystals (from the 1910s). X-rays could measure the exact spacing between atoms in a crystal. Knowing the spacing, you can count how many atoms fit in a given lump.

Perrin listed more than a dozen independent methods, and they all landed near the same value. That, more than anything, convinced the last doubters that atoms were real. Perrin proposed calling the number after Amedeo Avogadro, and in 1926 he won the Nobel Prize for this work.

Step 4: the most perfect sphere in the world

In the 2000s, scientists from many countries joined a project to measure the number better than ever before. They made spheres of almost pure silicon-28, each with a mass of about 1 kilogram and a diameter of about 9.4 centimetres, polished so perfectly that if one were the size of the Earth, its highest mountain would be only a few metres tall. They measured each sphere’s size with lasers and the spacing of its atoms with X-rays, then simply counted: about 2 × 10²⁵ atoms in each sphere.

Their measurements were so good that in 2019 the world agreed to stop measuring and fix the number exactly:

Avogadro’s constant = 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ per mole, exactly

Step 5: feeling the size of it

Here is the honest truth: nobody can picture 6 × 10²³. But you can compare it with other huge things, and feel your way.

A glass of water and the oceans. A 250 mL glass of water holds about 8 × 10²⁴ water molecules. All the oceans on Earth together hold about 5 × 10²¹ glassfuls of water.
So one glass of water contains more than 1,500 times as many molecules as there are glasses of water in all the oceans.

Marbles. If you had a mole of marbles, each 1 centimetre across, and spread them evenly over the whole surface of the Earth, land and sea, they would make a layer nearly a kilometre deep.

Sand. One careful estimate puts the number of grains of sand on all of Earth’s beaches at around 7 or 8 × 10¹⁸. A mole is about 80,000 times more than that.

And yet a mole of water is about 18 grams: one gulp. Your gulp holds more molecules than there are sand grains on all the world’s beaches, many thousands of times over. That tells you, more vividly than any number, how tiny a molecule is.

Careful

“Avogadro’s number is just a very big number that someone chose.”

It is two things at once. Since 2019 its exact value is fixed by agreement, like the number of centimetres in a metre. But that value was not picked out of the air: it was chosen to match more than a century of measurements, so that a mole of carbon-12 atoms still has a mass of 12 grams (to within a tiny fraction of a millionth). The mole story shows why that matching matters.

Measure a molecule-thin layer, almost

Ask an adult to help. Fill a large, clean baking tray with water and sprinkle a very light dusting of ground black pepper over the surface. Dip the tip of a toothpick in a drop of washing-up liquid or cooking oil and touch it to the centre. Watch how far the pepper races away from such a tiny amount. Thin films spread enormously, which is exactly what let Franklin, and later Rayleigh, use them to measure molecules.

So when this book writes 6.022 × 10²³, remember a teaspoon of oil on a windy pond, a dozen different experiments all agreeing, and a silicon sphere polished almost perfectly round. That is how we know.

1811 to 1860

The forgotten idea: Avogadro, and the congress that found him again

Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, John Dalton, Amedeo Avogadro, Stanislao Cannizzaro, Lothar Meyer

Paris, 1808

Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac liked gases, and he liked measuring them. (He also liked danger: a few years earlier he had gone up alone in a hydrogen balloon to about 7,000 metres, higher than anyone had flown, to collect air samples.) Back on the ground, he noticed something strange about how gases react.

Mix hydrogen and oxygen and spark them, and they always combine in a neat ratio by volume: 2 litres of hydrogen to 1 litre of oxygen. Nitrogen and hydrogen make ammonia in the ratio 1 litre to 3. And the steam that comes out also has a simple volume: 2 litres of hydrogen plus 1 litre of oxygen give 2 litres of steam (measured hot, at the same pressure). Whole numbers, every time. Why should gases care about whole numbers?

Step 1: the puzzle with the volumes

John Dalton, in England, had just argued that elements are made of atoms. You might think he would be delighted by Gay-Lussac’s whole numbers. He was not. He thought the result was impossible, and here is why.

If a litre of hydrogen contains some number of hydrogen atoms, and a litre of oxygen contains the same number of oxygen atoms, then 2 litres of hydrogen and 1 litre of oxygen should make 1 litre of water particles (each made from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom). But the experiment gave 2 litres of steam. To get twice as many water particles as there were oxygen atoms, every oxygen atom would have to split in half. And atoms, by definition, cannot be split. Dalton decided Gay-Lussac’s measurements must be wrong. They were not.

Vercelli, near Turin, 1811

Amedeo Avogadro had trained as a lawyer, like his father, before falling in love with physics. In 1811 he was teaching natural philosophy at a college in the small town of Vercelli (he later became a professor in Turin). He read both men’s work and saw a way out that neither had seen. He made two bold guesses.

Guess one: equal volumes of any gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of particles. (This is Avogadro’s hypothesis.)

Guess two: the particles of hydrogen gas and oxygen gas are not single atoms. Each is a pair of atoms stuck together: what we now write as H₂ and O₂.

Step 2: why the guesses solve the puzzle

Let us walk through it with small numbers, pretending each litre holds just 10 particles.

2 litres of hydrogen = 20 particles of H₂ = 40 hydrogen atoms
1 litre of oxygen = 10 particles of O₂ = 20 oxygen atoms
Each water molecule, H₂O, needs 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
40 hydrogen atoms and 20 oxygen atoms make exactly 20 water molecules.
20 particles of steam take up 2 litres. That is exactly what Gay-Lussac measured.

No atom splits. What splits is the pair: each O₂ molecule breaks into two O atoms, and each goes into a different water molecule. Avogadro had invented the word for the pairs too, more or less: he called them “constituent molecules”. Today we write the reaction as 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, and its numbers, 2 : 1 : 2, are exactly the volumes Gay-Lussac saw.

Step 3: fifty years of silence

Avogadro published his idea in 1811. It was correct, and it explained the measurements perfectly. And for half a century, almost everyone ignored it.

Why? Partly because it sounded wrong to the chemists of the day. Many of them believed that atoms of the same element repel each other, so two hydrogen atoms could never stick together into H₂. Partly because Avogadro wrote in a cautious, mathematical way, far from the big laboratories of Paris and London. And partly because without his idea, chemists could not agree on the formula of anything. Was water HO or H₂O? Different books gave different answers, and the same formula could mean different substances in different countries. In 1861 the chemist August Kekulé printed a list of nineteen different formulas that people had proposed for acetic acid, the acid in vinegar.

Avogadro died in 1856. He never knew that he had been right.

Karlsruhe, Germany, September 1860

The confusion became so bad that about 140 chemists from all over Europe met in the town of Karlsruhe for the first international chemistry conference, to try to agree on what atoms and molecules even were. For three days they argued, and they did not agree.

But one of them, the Italian chemist Stanislao Cannizzaro, had written a short pamphlet two years earlier. It showed, clearly and simply, how Avogadro’s forgotten hypothesis sorted out everything: how to work out the true formulas of gases, and from them the true relative masses of atoms. As the meeting broke up, a friend of Cannizzaro’s handed out copies.

A young German chemist named Lothar Meyer put one in his pocket and read it on the journey home. He later wrote that it was as if the scales fell from his eyes: suddenly everything was clear. Within a few years, with Cannizzaro’s corrected atomic masses, Meyer and the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev were each building tables of the elements that would become the periodic table.

Step 4: what the idea gives us today

Avogadro’s hypothesis is why we know H₂ and O₂ are pairs. It is why chemists could finally agree on formulas like H₂O and CO₂, and so on atomic masses. And because equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of particles, it led straight to the idea of a fixed number of particles for counting: the mole. The enormous number in a mole is named in his honour, though Avogadro himself never knew how big it was. That number has a story of its own.

Careful

“Avogadro worked out Avogadro’s number.”

He did not. Avogadro only said that the number of particles in a given volume of gas is the same for every gas. How many particles that actually is was first estimated by Josef Loschmidt in 1865, nine years after Avogadro died, and the name “Avogadro’s number” was suggested by Jean Perrin around 1909.

A volume puzzle with balloons

Ask an adult to help. Put two level teaspoons of baking soda into a balloon using a funnel. Pour some vinegar into an empty plastic bottle, stretch the balloon over its neck, then lift the balloon so the powder falls in. The fizzing makes a gas, carbon dioxide, which fills the balloon. Try again with twice the vinegar and twice the soda: does the balloon get about twice as big? Gases from reactions come in amounts you can measure by volume, just as Gay-Lussac found.

So the next time you see Avogadro’s name in this book, remember a patient Italian professor who solved a puzzle in 1811, and a pamphlet read on a train in 1860 that finally made the world listen.

1971

How strong is your sharbat? Concentration, step by step

Dilip Mahalanabis

A refugee camp at Bangaon, West Bengal, 1971

In 1971, during the war that created Bangladesh, millions of people fled across the border into India. In the crowded camps near the border, cholera broke out. Cholera kills by draining water and salt out of the body through terrible diarrhoea. The usual treatment was a drip of salt solution straight into a vein, but there were far too few drips, needles and nurses for so many sick people.

A young Indian doctor, Dilip Mahalanabis, decided to try something that had only just been tested in hospitals: a drink. Not any drink, but water with salt and sugar dissolved in it in exactly the right amounts, so that the gut could soak up the water. Families could give it to their own children with a cup. In his camp, the share of cholera patients who died is reported to have fallen from around 30 in every 100, as in camps without enough treatment, to fewer than 4 in every 100. That drink, oral rehydration solution or ORS, has since saved tens of millions of lives around the world. And the secret of it is one word: concentration.

Step 1: strong and weak

You already know what concentration means; you just may not have the word yet. A glass of sharbat made with lots of syrup is “strong”. With a splash of syrup and a lot of water, it is “weak”. The syrup is the solute (the thing dissolved) and the water is the solvent (the thing it dissolves in).

But “strong” and “weak” are not good enough for a doctor. Too little salt in ORS and it does not work; too much, and it can pull water the wrong way and make things worse. You need a number.

Step 2: how much in each litre

The trick is to ask how much solute there is in each litre of the finished drink. That number does not depend on how big the jug is.

2 spoons of syrup in 1 litre: 2 spoons per litre.
4 spoons of syrup in 2 litres: still 2 spoons per litre. Same strength, more drink.
2 spoons of syrup in 2 litres: 1 spoon per litre. Half the strength.

Chemists do exactly the same, but instead of spoons they count moles of particles. Concentration is written in moles per litre, mol/L:

concentration = amount of solute (in moles) ÷ volume of solution (in litres)

Step 3: a real recipe

The World Health Organization’s ORS recipe for one litre of water includes 2.6 grams of table salt (sodium chloride) and 13.5 grams of glucose. Let us turn those into concentrations.

Salt, NaCl, has a molar mass of about 58.4 g per mole.
2.6 g ÷ 58.4 g/mol ≈ 0.045 mol in 1 litre, so 0.045 mol/L of salt.
Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has a molar mass of about 180 g per mole.
13.5 g ÷ 180 g/mol ≈ 0.075 mol in 1 litre, so 0.075 mol/L of glucose.

(The full recipe also contains a little potassium chloride and sodium citrate, which bring the total sodium up to about 0.075 mol/L, matched to the glucose. The match is the clever part: the gut takes up sodium and glucose together, and water follows them in.)

Please do not mix medicines at home: ORS comes in ready-made packets for a reason. But now you can read the packet like a chemist.

Step 4: watering down, without losing anything

What happens when you add more water? The number of solute particles does not change. They just spread through more liquid. This is dilution.

Start: 0.5 mol of salt in 1 litre: 0.5 mol/L.
Add water until the total is 2 litres. Still 0.5 mol of salt.
New concentration = 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 mol/L. Double the volume, half the concentration.

Notice the word “total”. The volume in the rule is the volume of the finished solution, not the volume of water you poured in. If you dissolve a lot of sugar, the solution takes up more room than the water did.

Careful

“If I pour half the sharbat into another glass, each glass is half as strong.”

No: each glass is exactly as strong as the jug. Pouring some away removes solute and solvent in the same proportion, so the amount per litre stays the same. What changes is the total amount of syrup in each glass. Concentration is about “how crowded”, not “how much altogether”.

Step 5: some concentrations from real life

Seawater: about 0.46 mol of salt per litre (around 27 grams of sodium chloride in each litre).
Your blood: about 0.14 mol of sodium ions per litre.
Two teaspoons of sugar (about 8 g) in a 250 mL cup of chai: about 0.09 mol/L of sugar.

That last one explains why seawater is no use for quenching thirst: it is more than three times as salty as your blood, so drinking it makes your body lose water to get rid of the extra salt.

A dilution staircase

You need five clear glasses, water and food colouring (or strong tea). Put a few drops of colouring in the first glass with 100 mL of water. Pour half of it (50 mL) into the second glass and add 50 mL of water. Pour half of that into the third glass and add 50 mL of water, and so on. Each glass is half as concentrated as the one before. Line them up against a white sheet of paper. Can you still see colour in the fifth glass? It is 16 times more dilute than the first.

So when this book talks about 0.10 mol/L of an acid, picture a jug with a recipe on it: so many moles of particles, crowded into each litre. That one number told a doctor in 1971 exactly how much salt and sugar a drink needed to save a life.

1808 to 2019

The mole, step by step

John Dalton, Wilhelm Ostwald, Jean Perrin

A market street in Mumbai, any morning

Walk through any market and you will see three different ways of counting. The egg seller counts eggs, but in dozens: nobody asks for “fourteen eggs and a bit”. The stationery shop sells paper by the ream, 500 sheets at a time, and nobody counts the sheets. And the rice seller does not count at all. You ask for a kilo, the grains go on the scale, and in a few seconds you have about fifty thousand grains of rice without anyone counting a single one.

That last trick, counting by weighing, is the whole secret of the mole. Chemists had to learn it, because the things they needed to count were far smaller than rice and far, far more numerous. This is the story of how they did it, one step at a time.

Step 1: the problem

By the early 1800s chemists had discovered something wonderful: substances combine in fixed proportions, because atoms combine in small whole numbers. Two hydrogen atoms join one oxygen atom to make water. One carbon atom joins two oxygen atoms to make carbon dioxide. Chemistry happens atom by atom.

But nobody could pick up an atom. In the laboratory you can only weigh things. So the question became: if a recipe says “two hydrogens for every oxygen”, how many grams of hydrogen and how many grams of oxygen do you need? To answer that, you have to know how heavy each kind of atom is, at least compared with the others.

Step 2: weighing atoms against each other

In 1808 an English schoolteacher, John Dalton, published one of the first tables of relative atomic weights. He could not weigh a single atom, but he could compare. If 1 gram of hydrogen combines with 8 grams of oxygen to make water, and each water molecule has two hydrogens for every oxygen, then one oxygen atom must weigh about 16 times as much as one hydrogen atom. (Dalton himself got water’s formula wrong and put oxygen at 7, but his method was right, and later chemists fixed the numbers.)

Repeat that kind of reasoning for every element and you get a list of relative atomic masses: how heavy each atom is compared with the others. Roughly: hydrogen 1, carbon 12, oxygen 16, sodium 23, chlorine 35.5. These numbers have no units. They are comparisons, like saying an elephant is about 70 times as heavy as a person.

Step 3: the trick that makes counting possible

Here is the clever part. Imagine a jar of big glass marbles, each weighing 16 grams, and a jar of small beads, each weighing 1 gram. You want the same number of marbles as beads, but you only have a kitchen scale.

Weigh out 16 g of marbles: that is 1 marble. Weigh out 1 g of beads: that is 1 bead.
Weigh out 1,600 g of marbles: 100 marbles. Weigh out 100 g of beads: 100 beads.
Whatever you choose, if the masses are in the ratio 16 : 1, the numbers are equal.

Atoms work exactly the same way. An oxygen atom is 16 times heavier than a hydrogen atom. So 16 grams of oxygen and 1 gram of hydrogen contain the same number of atoms. So do 12 grams of carbon, 23 grams of sodium and 35.5 grams of chlorine. Take any element, weigh out its relative atomic mass in grams, and you always get the same number of atoms. You do not even need to know what that number is.

That fixed number of atoms is so useful that it needed a name. In the 1890s the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald gave it one: the Mol, from Molekül, molecule. In English it became the mole. A mole is simply that number of things, just as a dozen is twelve things.

Step 4: but how many is it?

For a long time, nobody knew. Chemists used moles happily for decades while having only a rough idea of how many atoms were in one. Think about how odd that is: it is like buying eggs by the dozen without knowing that a dozen is twelve. It worked because, for chemistry, what matters is that the number is the same for every substance.

The first estimate came in 1865 from an Austrian schoolteacher-turned-physicist, Josef Loschmidt, who worked out roughly how big air molecules must be from how gases behave. His answer was in the right range, astonishingly, but rough. Then, around 1909, Jean Perrin in Paris measured the number several independent ways, including by watching tiny grains jiggle in water, and every method gave nearly the same answer. Perrin proposed naming it after Amedeo Avogadro, whose ideas about gases had made all of this possible. Today it is called Avogadro’s constant, and since 2019 it is not measured at all but fixed by definition:

1 mole = 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ things

Step 5: feeling how big that is

Written out in full, that is 602,214,076,000,000,000,000,000. Numbers this big slide straight past the imagination, so here are two ways to get a grip on it.

If you counted one thing every second, day and night, without stopping, counting to one mole would take about 19 thousand million million years: more than a million times the age of the universe.

A grain of rice has a mass of about 0.02 grams. A mole of rice grains would weigh about 12 thousand million million tonnes (1.2 × 10¹⁶ tonnes). The whole world grows roughly 500 million tonnes of rice a year, so growing one mole of rice would take every rice farmer on Earth tens of millions of years.

And yet a mole of water molecules is only 18 grams: a single gulp. That is how small molecules are.

Step 6: using moles, with your hand held

The mass of one mole of a substance is its molar mass, in grams per mole. For an element it is the relative atomic mass in grams; for a molecule you add up its atoms. Water, H₂O, is 1 + 1 + 16 = 18 grams per mole.

How many moles in 9 grams of water?
Each mole is 18 g. 9 g is half of 18 g. So 9 g is 0.5 moles.
As a rule: moles = grams ÷ molar mass = 9 ÷ 18 = 0.5 mol.

How many sugar molecules in a 4-gram teaspoon of sugar?
Sugar (sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) has a molar mass of about 342 g per mole.
Moles = 4 ÷ 342 ≈ 0.0117 mol.
Molecules = 0.0117 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 7 × 10²¹: about seven thousand million million million molecules in one teaspoon.

Understand itMole

What is it?

A counting unit, like a dozen, but holding 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ things. One mole of any substance weighs its formula’s mass in grams.

Why is it called this?

From the German Mol, coined by Wilhelm Ostwald in the 1890s as a short form of Molekül, molecule. Nothing to do with the animal.

What problem did it solve?

Chemists needed to count atoms to follow a recipe, but they could only weigh things. The mole turns weighing into counting.

Why does it work?

Because atoms of different elements have masses in fixed ratios, equal numbers of atoms always have masses in those same ratios. So weighing out each element’s relative mass in grams always gives the same number of atoms.

How does it help?

It lets you go from a recipe in particles (2 H₂ + O₂) to a recipe in grams that you can weigh out on a scale.

Go deeper how do we know, what it isn’t, where does it stop working
How do we know?

Perrin and others measured the number in completely different ways, and all the answers agreed. Since 2019 the number is fixed by definition.

What it isn’t

It is not a mass, like a kilogram. It is a number, like a dozen.

Where does it stop working?

It is a tool for enormous numbers of tiny things. For anything you can count by eye, just count.

Your turn

Explain Mole to a friend in one sentence, in your own words. Then compare it with the book’s.

Careful

“A mole is an amount of mass, like a kilogram.”

It is not. A mole is a number of things, like a dozen. A dozen eggs and a dozen elephants are both twelve, but they do not weigh the same. A mole of hydrogen atoms has a mass of 1 gram; a mole of gold atoms has a mass of 197 grams. Same number, very different weights.

Careful

“A mole of oxygen is 16 grams.”

It depends what you are counting. A mole of oxygen atoms is 16 g. But oxygen gas is made of O₂ molecules, and a mole of O₂ molecules is 32 g, because each molecule contains two atoms. Chemists always say what they are counting, and so should you.

Count rice by weighing it

You need a kitchen scale and some uncooked rice. Count out exactly 100 grains and weigh them (a sensitive scale helps; if yours only reads to the nearest gram, weigh 200 or 500 grains). Now weigh a cupful of rice. Divide the cup’s mass by the mass of one grain to find how many grains are in the cup, without counting them. Then count a small part of the cup to check. You have just done what chemists do with moles.

So the next time you see “1 mole” in this book, translate it in your head: six hundred thousand million million million of something, which conveniently weighs its formula’s mass in grams. It is the chemist’s dozen, and it is the bridge between the invisible world of atoms and the kitchen scale on the bench.

1808 to 1961

How do you weigh an atom?

John Dalton, Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Jean Servais Stas

Manchester, 1803

John Dalton was a quiet Quaker schoolteacher who kept a weather diary every single day for over fifty years. He was also colour-blind (the condition was called “Daltonism” after him, because he was the first to describe it scientifically). And in his notebooks in Manchester, around 1803, he did something nobody had dared try. He started to make a list of how heavy atoms are.

He could not weigh one. Nobody could, and nobody would be able to for a long time. So Dalton asked a cleverer question: not “how heavy is an atom?” but “how heavy is one kind of atom compared with another?”

Step 1: comparing, not weighing

Think of a see-saw. You do not need to know anyone’s weight in kilograms to discover that your father is about twice as heavy as you: if he sits half as far from the middle as you do, the see-saw balances. Comparing is often easier than measuring.

Dalton chose the lightest thing he knew, the hydrogen atom, and called its weight 1. Then he looked at compounds. If 1 gram of hydrogen combines with 8 grams of oxygen to make water, and water has one oxygen atom for every two hydrogen atoms, then:

Pretend the sample holds just 10 oxygen atoms. Then it holds 20 hydrogen atoms (two for every oxygen).
20 hydrogen atoms weigh 1 gram, so each hydrogen atom weighs 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05 g (pretend grams).
10 oxygen atoms weigh 8 grams, so each oxygen atom weighs 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 g.
0.8 ÷ 0.05 = 16. One oxygen atom is 16 times as heavy as one hydrogen atom, whatever the real number of atoms is.

Dalton himself thought water was HO, one of each, so he wrote oxygen as 7 (his measurements were also a little off). The method was brilliant; the formulas were the problem. It took Avogadro’s idea, and the congress at Karlsruhe in 1860, before chemists agreed on formulas and so on the right numbers.

Step 2: arguing about the starting point

If everything is a comparison, you have to choose something to compare with, and chemists argued about this for 150 years.

  • Dalton said hydrogen = 1.
  • Berzelius, the great Swedish chemist who measured more atomic weights more carefully than anyone of his time, said oxygen = 100, because oxygen combines with almost everything, which made the measurements easier.
  • Later chemists, led by the Belgian Jean Servais Stas, whose measurements were famously precise, settled on oxygen = 16, which kept hydrogen close to 1.

Then a new problem appeared. In the 1920s and 1930s physicists discovered that natural oxygen is a mixture of isotopes. Physicists began using one isotope, oxygen-16, as exactly 16; chemists kept using natural oxygen as 16. The two scales differed by about 3 parts in 10,000: tiny, but enough to cause confusion.

In 1961 both sides agreed on a new standard that everybody could use: one atom of carbon-12 counts as exactly 12. The unit this defines is called the unified atomic mass unit, written u, because it unified the two scales. One u is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Step 3: so what does an atom actually weigh?

Once Avogadro’s constant was known, chemists could finally turn comparisons into real masses.

One mole of hydrogen atoms has a mass of about 1.008 g, and contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
Mass of one hydrogen atom = 1.008 ÷ (6.022 × 10²³) ≈ 1.67 × 10⁻²⁴ g.

That is 0.000 000 000 000 000 000 000 001 67 grams. A grain of sugar has more than a hundred million million million times that mass.

Step 4: why the numbers are not whole

Look at a periodic table and you see numbers like chlorine 35.45 and copper 63.55. If atoms are built from protons and neutrons, each with a mass close to 1 u, why are these not whole numbers? There are two reasons, one big and one small.

The big reason: mixtures. Natural chlorine is about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37. The periodic table gives the average for the natural mixture, which is 35.45, even though no single chlorine atom has that mass. (See the weighted averages tool for how the average is worked out.)

The small reason: binding. Even a single isotope is not exactly a whole number, except carbon-12, which is 12 by definition. When protons and neutrons pull together into a nucleus, a little mass is turned into energy and given off, following Einstein’s famous E = mc². So a nucleus weighs slightly less than the particles it is made from. For carbon-12, the difference is a little under 1%.

Careful

“The relative atomic mass of oxygen is 16 grams.”

Relative atomic mass has no units: it is a comparison, like “16 times as heavy as a hydrogen atom” (more precisely, 16 twelfths of a carbon-12 atom). The grams come in when you take a mole of atoms: a mole of oxygen atoms has a mass of 16 grams.

A see-saw for comparing masses

Make a balance from a ruler resting on a pencil. Put a coin at one end and see how many paper clips (or dried beans) you need at the same distance on the other end to balance it. You have just found the coin’s mass relative to a paper clip, without knowing either mass in grams. Choose a different “standard” object and every number changes, but the comparisons stay true. That is exactly the argument chemists had for 150 years.

Every relative atomic mass in this book, every molar mass, every “18 grams of water”, rests on Dalton’s simple idea: if you cannot weigh one, compare.

1664 to 1923

Sour and slippery: what is an acid?

Robert Boyle, Antoine Lavoisier, Humphry Davy, Svante Arrhenius, Johannes Brønsted, Thomas Lowry

London, the 1660s

Robert Boyle had a favourite trick, and it involved flowers. He would crush violets, soak them, and make a deep purple syrup. Then he added a few drops of different liquids. Vinegar, lemon juice and “spirit of salt” turned the purple syrup red. Other liquids, made from wood ash or lime, turned it green. In 1664 he wrote about it in a book on colours, and he noticed something important: the colour change sorted liquids into two families, no matter where they came from.

People had known the first family for thousands of years. They tasted sour (the Latin word acidus means sour), they fizzed when poured on chalk, and they could eat away metals. The second family felt slippery, like soap, and could cancel out the first. We now call them acids and bases. Boyle had found a way to tell them apart without tasting them: an indicator, a dye that changes colour.

This is the story of how it took two and a half centuries to work out what an acid actually is.

The colour detectives

Boyle was not the first to use plant colours. A purple dye called litmus, made from lichens (crusty growths that cover rocks and tree bark), had been used by dyers for centuries. Litmus turns red in acids and blue in bases, and litmus paper is still in school labs today. Red cabbage, hibiscus flowers, beetroot and even turmeric all contain natural indicators. They work because their colour molecules change shape slightly when an acid or a base gives or takes a tiny particle, which you will meet at the end of this story.

But knowing how to spot an acid is not the same as knowing what one is. That puzzle had several wrong answers first.

Wrong answer 1: oxygen makes acids

In the 1770s Antoine Lavoisier, the great French chemist, burned sulfur, phosphorus and carbon in air and dissolved the products in water. Every time, he got an acid. He concluded that the element he had been studying must be the secret ingredient of all acids, so he named it oxygène, from Greek words meaning “acid-maker”. It was a brilliant guess. It was also wrong, and the name stuck anyway: every time you say “oxygen”, you are repeating Lavoisier’s mistake.

Wrong answer, corrected

In 1810 the young English chemist Humphry Davy took one of the strongest acids known, muriatic acid (we call it hydrochloric acid, HCl), and tried as hard as he could to find oxygen in it. There was none. The greenish gas everyone thought was an oxygen compound turned out to be a new element, which Davy named chlorine. So acids did not need oxygen. But they all contained something else: hydrogen. A few decades later, the German chemist Justus von Liebig suggested that the key was hydrogen that could be swapped for a metal.

Closer: the Swede with the risky idea

In the 1880s a Swedish student named Svante Arrhenius proposed that when an acid dissolves in water, it breaks up into ions, and that every acid releases the same kind of ion: a hydrogen ion, H⁺. Bases, he said, release hydroxide ions, OH⁻, and when the two meet they make water. His examiners were unimpressed and gave his thesis nearly the lowest pass. Twenty years later, in 1903, the same ideas won him the Nobel Prize.

Arrhenius’s idea explained a lot. But it had a hole in it. Ammonia, NH₃, is clearly a base: it turns litmus blue and cancels acids. Yet it contains no OH at all. How can it release hydroxide?

The answer: passing a proton

In 1923 two chemists working separately, Johannes Brønsted in Copenhagen and Thomas Lowry in Cambridge, published the same idea within months of each other. Forget what the substance contains, they said. Look at what it does.

Let’s go through it step by step.

Step 1: what an H⁺ really is

A hydrogen atom is one proton and one electron. Take the electron away and what is left is a bare proton: the smallest, most concentrated speck of positive charge in chemistry. That is all “H⁺” is.

Step 2: an acid gives away a proton

When hydrogen chloride meets water, the proton leaves the chlorine and jumps onto a water molecule. The electrons it shared with the chlorine stay behind.

HCl + H₂O → Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺

The water, now carrying an extra proton, becomes a hydronium ion, H₃O⁺. The chlorine, keeping the electrons, becomes a chloride ion, Cl⁻. Count the charges: zero on the left, (−1) + (+1) = 0 on the right. Nothing was created or lost; one proton simply moved house.

Step 3: a base takes a proton

A base is anything that accepts a proton. Ammonia does it beautifully:

NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

Ammonia takes a proton from water, leaving OH⁻ behind. So ammonia makes hydroxide without containing any. The hole in Arrhenius’s idea is closed.

Step 4: water can play both parts

Look again at the two equations. In the first, water took a proton, so it acted as a base. In the second, water gave a proton, so it acted as an acid. Whether something is an acid or a base depends on its partner. Chemistry is full of relationships like this, the way the same person can be a teacher in one room and a student in another.

Careful

“Acids are dangerous and bases are safe.”

Both families include gentle and fierce members. Lemon juice and vinegar are acids you eat; the acid in a car battery can burn skin. Baking soda is a mild base; oven cleaner and drain cleaner are strong bases that can blind. What matters is how strong and how concentrated a substance is, not which family it belongs to.

Back to the colour detectives

Now you can see what Boyle’s violets were doing. Indicator molecules are themselves weak acids. When there are plenty of spare protons around, they hold onto one and have one colour; when protons are scarce, they lose it and their shape and colour change. The colour is a message from the molecules about how many protons are around.

Make a red cabbage rainbow

Ask an adult to help. Chop a few leaves of red cabbage into small pieces, put them in a jug and cover them with hot water from the tap. Squash them with a spoon, wait ten minutes, then strain off the purple juice. That juice is your indicator. Pour a little into several clear glasses. Add a spoonful of vinegar to one, lemon juice to another, plain water to a third, and a spoonful of baking soda dissolved in water to a fourth. Watch the colours: pink and red for acids, purple for neutral, blue and green for bases. Do not taste any of it, and do not mix in cleaning products.

From Boyle’s violets to Brønsted and Lowry’s proton, the story of acids is the story of a question that kept getting a better answer. In Chapter 7 you will use that answer to understand strong and weak acids, and the pH scale that measures them.

1780s to 1836

Frogs' legs and the first battery

Luigi Galvani, Alessandro Volta, John Frederic Daniell

Bologna, Italy, the 1780s

In his laboratory at the University of Bologna, the doctor and anatomy professor Luigi Galvani was studying how nerves make muscles move, and his favourite subjects were frogs. One day (the details vary in different tellings) he touched the nerve of a dissected frog’s leg with a metal instrument while a machine nearby was making electric sparks, and the dead leg kicked.

Galvani spent years on it. He found that a leg would twitch even with no spark machine at all, if he touched it with two different metals joined together, say a brass hook and an iron railing. In 1791 he published his conclusion: animals make their own electricity, stored in their muscles and nerves. He called it “animal electricity”, and Europe went wild for it.

The professor who disagreed

About two hundred kilometres away in Pavia, the physics professor Alessandro Volta read Galvani’s work, repeated it, and became suspicious. Why did it need two different metals? Perhaps, Volta argued, the electricity was not coming from the frog at all. Perhaps it was coming from the metals, and the frog’s leg was simply a very sensitive detector, twitching whenever a current passed through it.

The two men argued for years, politely but stubbornly. And both were partly right: nerves really do work by electricity, as later scientists showed. But Volta’s hunch about the metals led somewhere much bigger.

The pile

To prove his point, Volta needed to make electricity from metals with no animal involved. He stacked up discs: a disc of zinc, a disc of copper (or silver), a piece of cardboard soaked in salt water, then zinc, copper, wet cardboard again, and so on, dozens of layers high. When he touched the top and bottom of the stack at the same time, he felt a tingle, and it kept coming. This was the voltaic pile, the first battery that could give a steady flow of electricity. He described it in a letter to the Royal Society in London in March 1800.

The news spread astonishingly fast. Within weeks, in London, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle built a pile and used it to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. In 1801 Volta demonstrated his pile in Paris to Napoleon Bonaparte, who was so impressed he gave him a medal and later made him a count. And every time you say “volt”, you are saying Volta’s name.

Let’s see what was really going on inside the pile, step by step.

Step 1: two metals, two different grips

Some metals give up their outer electrons more readily than others. Zinc gives them up more readily than copper (Chapter 8 explains how chemists know). So if zinc and copper are connected and both touch a salty liquid, electrons tend to leave the zinc, which dissolves a little as Zn²⁺ ions, and arrive at the copper side.

Step 2: the long way round

If the two metals touch directly, the electrons hop straight across and the energy just warms things up a tiny bit. The trick of a battery is to give the electrons only one route: through a wire, outside the cell. On the way, they can light a bulb, buzz a buzzer or twitch a frog’s leg.

Step 3: closing the loop

Electrons cannot pile up on one side forever. As they leave the zinc, the liquid around it gains positive ions; as they arrive at the copper, the liquid there would build up negative charge. Something has to keep both sides balanced, or the flow would stop almost instantly. In Volta’s pile, the salty cardboard did the job: ions moving through the liquid carried charge one way while electrons travelled the other way through the wire. A battery always has two paths: electrons through the wire, ions through the liquid.

Step 4: stacking up

One zinc-copper pair gives a push of about one volt. Stack many pairs on top of each other, so the electrons go through one after another, and the pushes add up. Volta’s tall piles gave dozens of volts. Today’s batteries do the same: a 9-volt battery is six small cells stacked inside one box.

The battery that didn’t fade

Volta’s pile had a frustrating problem: its current faded within an hour or so as bubbles of hydrogen formed on the copper and blocked it. In 1836 the London chemist John Frederic Daniell fixed it. He put the copper in a solution of copper sulfate and the zinc in weak sulfuric acid (later versions used zinc sulfate), and kept the two liquids apart with a barrier that let ions through but stopped the liquids mixing: at first a tube made from an ox’s gullet, and later a pot of unglazed, porous clay. Instead of making hydrogen, the copper side now grew a fresh coat of copper metal as Cu²⁺ ions picked up the arriving electrons. The Daniell cell gave a steady push of about 1.1 volts for hours.

Daniell cells powered the electric telegraphs that, from the 1840s, sent messages along wires across countries and later under oceans. In school labs today the porous pot is often replaced by a strip of paper soaked in salt solution, called a salt bridge. It does the same job: it lets ions flow between the two sides, so the electrons can keep flowing through the wire.

Careful

“A battery stores electricity, the way a bottle stores water.”

A battery stores chemicals that are ready to react. The electricity is made as the reaction happens, which is why a battery goes flat when its chemicals are used up. A flat battery is not empty of electrons: it has the same number as a full one. It has simply run out of the reaction that pushes them round.

Make a lemon battery (with an adult)

You need two or three lemons, the same number of zinc-coated (galvanised) nails or screws, the same number of strips of copper (copper wire, or a copper-coated coin), some wire with crocodile clips, and a small red LED. Push one nail and one piece of copper into each lemon, a few centimetres apart, not touching. Each lemon makes a cell of a little under 1 volt. Join the lemons in a chain: the copper of one to the nail of the next. Connect the free copper and the free nail at the ends to the LED’s two legs (if it does not light, swap the legs round). Turn off the lights: the LED should glow faintly. You have rebuilt Volta’s pile. Afterwards, throw the lemons away; do not eat them.

From a twitching frog to the telegraph in about fifty years: Galvani and Volta’s argument turned out to be one of the most useful arguments in history. Chapter 8 opens Daniell’s cell up and follows every electron through it.

1908 to 1916

How your blood stays at 7.4

Lawrence Henderson, Karl Albert Hasselbalch

A school sports day, the 100-metre race

The starter’s whistle goes and you sprint. For ten seconds your leg muscles burn energy faster than your blood can bring them oxygen, and they switch to a quick, messy back-up: they turn sugar into lactic acid. Acid floods out of the muscles and into your bloodstream. You cross the line, gasping.

And here is the strange thing: the pH of your blood has barely changed. Healthy blood stays between about 7.35 and 7.45, almost always. Below about 7.35 or above about 7.45, doctors start to worry, and much further outside that range your cells cannot work properly. A difference of 0.1 in pH is only a 26% change in hydronium, but your body defends that tiny window fiercely. How?

The doctor who did the arithmetic

At the start of the 1900s, Lawrence Henderson, a young doctor and chemist at Harvard University, was puzzled by exactly this. Blood was clearly being flooded with acids all the time, from muscles, from digestion, from carbon dioxide made in every cell, yet its acidity hardly budged. In 1908 he worked out the chemistry of the main reason, and wrote down an equation for it. In 1916 a Danish doctor, Karl Albert Hasselbalch, rewrote Henderson’s equation in terms of the new pH scale, and it has carried both their names ever since. What they had described is called a buffer.

Step 1: a team of two

A buffer is a solution containing two partners: a weak acid, which can give away a proton, and its matching base, which can take one. In blood the main pair is carbonic acid, H₂CO₃, and the hydrogencarbonate ion, HCO₃⁻ (the same ion that is in baking soda). The two are the same particle with and without one proton.

Step 2: when acid arrives, the base catches it

When lactic acid releases extra protons into your blood, hydrogencarbonate ions grab them:

H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃

The protons are not destroyed (nothing in chemistry is), but they are locked up inside weak carbonic acid, which keeps hold of most of them. So the hydronium in the blood rises only a little.

Step 3: when base arrives, the acid steps in

If something removes protons or adds a base, the carbonic acid gives up some of its protons to replace them. Either way, the pair absorbs the change.

Step 4: why the pH barely moves

The pH of a buffer depends mainly on the ratio of the two partners, not on how much of each there is. In blood there is about 20 times as much hydrogencarbonate as carbonic acid, and that ratio is what sets the pH at 7.4. A small splash of acid turns a little hydrogencarbonate into carbonic acid, so the ratio changes a little, and the pH changes only a little.

Here is the difference a buffer makes, using the made-up example from Chapter 7:

Add 1.0 millimole of sodium hydroxide (10 mL of a 0.10 mol/L solution) to 50 mL of pure water: the pH jumps from 7.0 to about 12.2.
Add the same amount to 50 mL of an acetic acid / acetate buffer (2.5 millimoles of each): the pH moves from 4.74 to about 5.11.
Same base, same volume. Without a buffer the pH leaps by five units; with one, it shifts by less than half a unit.

Step 5: your body has helpers

The carbonic acid in blood has a clever escape route. It breaks down into carbon dioxide and water, and your lungs breathe the carbon dioxide out:

H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂

That is one reason you breathe so hard after a sprint: getting rid of carbon dioxide gets rid of acid. Over hours and days, your kidneys help too, removing extra acid in urine and making new hydrogencarbonate. Lungs and kidneys keep refilling the buffer so it never runs out.

Careful

“A buffer stops the pH from changing at all.”

It only slows the change down. Every bit of acid added uses up some of the base partner. Add enough and the base runs out; then the pH falls as fast as in plain water. How much a buffer can take before it gives way is called its capacity.

Buffers everywhere

Once you know to look for them, buffers are everywhere. The oceans are buffered by carbonate and hydrogencarbonate, which is why they are absorbing carbon dioxide without turning sour overnight (Chapter 11 tells that story). Shampoo, eye drops, many medicines and the solutions used in hospitals are buffered so they stay gentle. Even milk has buffers in it.

Watch a buffer hold out

You need red cabbage indicator (see Sour and slippery: what is an acid?), two clear glasses, vinegar, a teaspoon and baking soda. Fill both glasses with the same amount of indicator. Stir half a teaspoon of baking soda into one; it turns blue-green. Now add vinegar to both, a few drops at a time, counting the drops. The plain glass turns pink almost at once. The baking soda glass fizzes and holds out for many more drops before it changes. The hydrogencarbonate in baking soda is catching the acid’s protons, just as it does in your blood.

So when you finish a race, red-faced and out of breath, remember that billions of hydrogencarbonate ions are quietly catching protons in your blood. Chapter 7 shows a buffer at work in a titration curve, as the long, gently sloping stretch in the middle.

1970s to 2019

The battery in your pocket

M. Stanley Whittingham, John B. Goodenough, Koichi Mizushima, Akira Yoshino

Stockholm, 9 October 2019

When the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 2019 was announced, one of the three winners was 97 years old: John Goodenough, the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize. He shared it with Stanley Whittingham, who was 77, and Akira Yoshino, who was 71. The prize was for something you have almost certainly used today: the lithium-ion battery.

The story behind it took place in an oil company’s laboratory in America, a university in England and a chemical company in Japan, and it begins with a worry about oil.

A battery from an oil company

In the early 1970s, oil prices shot up and people began to worry about what would happen when oil ran short. At the research labs of the oil company Exxon in New Jersey, a young English chemist named Stanley Whittingham was looking for new ways to store energy. He discovered that lithium ions could slip in between the layers of a material called titanium disulfide, like letters sliding into the slots of a letter rack, and slip out again. He used this to build a rechargeable battery with a lithium metal electrode, giving about 2 volts.

It worked, but it had a dangerous habit. Lithium metal reacts fiercely with water and air, and as the battery was charged again and again, thin spikes of lithium could grow inside it and cause short circuits and fires.

More voltage: a discovery in Oxford

At the University of Oxford in 1980, John Goodenough and his team, including the Japanese physicist Koichi Mizushima, reasoned that a metal oxide might hold lithium ions more tightly and give a bigger push. They tried lithium cobalt oxide. It gave about 4 volts, twice as much. Oxford did not see much value in it at the time and did not patent it for itself.

Making it safe: a carbon home for lithium

The last piece came from Japan. In 1985 Akira Yoshino, working for the chemical company Asahi Kasei, replaced the dangerous lithium metal with a special kind of carbon that lithium ions could slip into, between its layers, without ever becoming a lump of reactive metal. With Goodenough’s oxide on one side and Yoshino’s carbon on the other, the battery was light, powerful and much safer. The electronics company Sony started selling lithium-ion batteries in 1991, first in video cameras. Today they are in phones, laptops, electric scooters and cars, and in huge banks that store solar power.

Here is how one works, step by step.

Step 1: why lithium?

Lithium is the lightest metal of all: a mole of lithium atoms has a mass of only 6.94 grams, and each atom can give one electron. Compare lead, used in old car batteries: a mole of lead has a mass of 207 grams and gives two electrons.

Lithium: 1,000 g ÷ 6.94 g per mole ≈ 144 moles of electrons per kilogram.
Lead: (1,000 g ÷ 207.2 g per mole) × 2 ≈ 9.7 moles of electrons per kilogram.
Kilogram for kilogram, lithium can move about 15 times as many electrons.

A whole battery has much more in it than just the metal, so a real lithium-ion battery stores several times as much energy per kilogram as a lead-acid one, not 15 times. But that lightness is why you can carry one in your pocket.

Step 2: two shelves for lithium

A lithium-ion cell has two electrodes, and both are like bookshelves with gaps between the shelves. On one side are layers of carbon, graphite. On the other are layers of a metal oxide, such as cobalt oxide. Lithium ions can slide in between the layers of either one. Between the two electrodes is a liquid called the electrolyte, which lets lithium ions through, and a thin plastic separator that keeps the electrodes from touching.

Step 3: discharging, while you use your phone

When the battery is charged, most of the lithium is tucked between the graphite layers. When you switch your phone on, lithium atoms in the graphite each give up an electron. The lithium ions, Li⁺, travel the short way, through the electrolyte, to the oxide. The electrons cannot go that way. They take the long way round, through the wires and chips of the phone, doing useful work as they go, and meet up with the lithium ions at the oxide.

Step 4: charging, when you plug it in

The charger pushes everything back: it drives electrons back to the graphite through the wire, and lithium ions follow through the electrolyte, sliding back between the carbon layers. The reaction runs uphill, storing energy, ready for next time. Nothing is used up; the same lithium shuttles back and forth, hundreds or thousands of times.

How much lithium moves when you use a full charge?
A phone battery labelled 4,000 mAh can deliver a current of 4 amps for 1 hour.
Charge = 4 A × 3,600 s = 14,400 coulombs.
One mole of electrons carries about 96,485 coulombs, so that is 14,400 ÷ 96,485 ≈ 0.149 moles of electrons.
That means 0.149 moles of lithium ions, about 0.149 × 6.94 ≈ 1.0 gram of lithium, crossing from one side to the other.

About one gram of lithium moving back and forth runs your phone for a day.

Careful

“Charging fills the battery up with electrons from the wall.”

The battery has the same number of electrons when it is full as when it is flat. Charging only moves them, together with the lithium ions, from one electrode to the other, into the arrangement with more stored energy. That is why a charged battery is no heavier than a flat one.

Be a battery detective

Look at the labels on a power bank, a phone box or a laptop charger (do not open or damage any battery). Find the numbers marked mAh or Wh and V. Using the working above, estimate how many grams of lithium shuttle across the power bank when it is used from full to empty. Then remember the safety rule every battery engineer knows: never puncture, crush or heat a lithium-ion battery, and tell an adult if one ever looks swollen.

From an oil crisis in America to an oxide in Oxford to a carbon shelf in Japan: the battery in your pocket was built by people who never worked in the same room. Chapter 11 follows the lithium ions inside a real cell.

1909

Sørensen's brewery and the pH scale

Søren Sørensen, Fritz Haber, Zygmunt Klemensiewicz, Arnold Beckman

The Carlsberg Laboratory, Copenhagen, 1909

The Carlsberg brewery in Copenhagen had something unusual for a beer company: its own science laboratory, set up in 1875 by the brewery’s founder, J. C. Jacobsen, who believed that better science would make better beer. In 1901 a chemist called Søren Peder Lauritz Sørensen became head of its chemistry department.

Sørensen was studying enzymes: the proteins that turn grain into sugar and sugar into alcohol. He kept noticing that his enzymes worked beautifully in some solutions and hardly at all in others, and the difference seemed to depend on how acidic the liquid was. So he needed to measure acidity, and to write it down, again and again, for hundreds of experiments. That is where his problem began.

Step 1: the numbers are horrible

Acidity depends on how many hydrogen ions, really hydronium ions, H₃O⁺, are floating in each litre. Chemists count them in moles per litre. Here are some real values:

Stomach acid: about 0.01 mol/L
Lemon juice: about 0.006 mol/L
Pure water: 0.000 000 1 mol/L
Baking soda solution: about 0.000 000 005 mol/L

Imagine writing numbers like 0.000 000 005 in a lab notebook a hundred times a day, and trying not to lose a zero. The numbers stretch over more than a hundred million million times from the most acidic to the most basic. Sørensen wanted something shorter.

Step 2: just count the zeros

Sørensen’s idea was simple. Write the concentration as a power of ten, and use the number of decimal places, the power, as the measure.

0.1 mol/L = 10⁻¹ → pH 1
0.01 mol/L = 10⁻² → pH 2
0.001 mol/L = 10⁻³ → pH 3
0.000 000 1 mol/L = 10⁻⁷ → pH 7

That is the whole pH scale. A pH number tells you “the concentration of hydronium is ten to the minus this many moles per litre”. For numbers in between, like 0.006, the pH comes out in between too (about 2.2). Mathematicians call this kind of counting-the-power a logarithm, but you do not need the word to use it: pH just counts how many places the decimal point has moved.

Nobody is completely sure what the “p” originally stood for. Sørensen wrote it as pH, with a small H, and people have guessed it meant potenz (German for power), puissance (French for power), or simply the letter he used for a quantity in his equations. Whatever its origin, it stuck.

Step 3: the upside-down part

Because pH counts how many places the number has shrunk, a smaller pH means more hydronium. pH 1 is far more acidic than pH 3. This trips almost everyone up the first time.

Step 4: every step is ten times

Each step of 1 on the pH scale is a factor of ten. So:

pH 4 has 10 times as much hydronium as pH 5.
pH 3 has 10 × 10 = 100 times as much as pH 5.
pH 2 has 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times as much as pH 5.

That is why a small-looking change in pH can be a big deal. When the surface of the ocean goes from pH 8.2 to 8.1, the hydronium in it has gone up by about 26%.

Careful

“pH 6 is twice as acidic as pH 3, because 6 is twice 3.”

It is the other way round, and much more than twice. pH 3 has 1,000 times as much hydronium as pH 6. Remember: lower number, more acidic; each step, ten times.

Step 5: neutral is 7, and why

Even perfectly pure water is never quite without ions. Now and then two water molecules pass a proton between them, making one H₃O⁺ and one OH⁻. At 25 °C this happens just enough to leave 10⁻⁷ mol/L of each. Equal amounts of the two means neutral, so neutral water is pH 7. Below 7, there is more H₃O⁺ than OH⁻: acidic. Above 7, there is less: basic.

Measuring it: a glass that feels acid

Sørensen measured acidity with electrical cells and with colour indicators, carefully chosen dyes that change at known pH values. A few years earlier, the German scientist Max Cremer had found that a thin wall of glass develops a tiny voltage that depends on the acidity of the liquid around it. In the same year as Sørensen’s scale, 1909, Fritz Haber and his young Polish colleague Zygmunt Klemensiewicz in Germany turned this into a practical glass electrode, which became the heart of the pH meter.

The pH meter as a handy instrument came from an unexpected place. In the 1930s California’s lemon growers needed to test the acidity of lemon juice quickly, and a young chemist named Arnold Beckman built them a sturdy electronic meter in 1934. It was so useful that it started a whole company of scientific instruments. Today a pH meter sits in almost every lab, hospital and water-treatment plant in the world.

Put your kitchen in order

If you have made red cabbage indicator (see the story Sour and slippery: what is an acid?), use it to line up kitchen liquids from most acidic to most basic: lemon juice, vinegar, a fizzy drink, milk, tap water, and a little baking soda in water. Pinker means more acidic; bluer or greener means more basic. You are building your own pH scale, without any numbers.

So pH is a shortcut invented by a brewer’s chemist to save himself from writing zeros. Every time you see a pH number in Chapter 7, read it as “count the zeros”: pH 2 means 0.01 mol/L of hydronium, and every step is ten times.

1777 to today

Rust, fire and moving electrons

Antoine Lavoisier, Humphry Davy

The Royal Institution, London, October 1807

Humphry Davy had a new toy: one of the most powerful batteries in Britain, hundreds of metal plates stacked in troughs of acid. He was using it to tear substances apart with electricity. On 6 October 1807 he pointed it at a lump of potash, a substance made from wood ash that chemists had long suspected contained an unknown metal but had never managed to split.

He took a small piece of potash, just damp enough from the air to carry a current, and passed the current through it until it began to melt. At one wire, tiny bright globules of metal appeared, “having a high metallic lustre”, as he wrote. Some of them burst into flame at once. Davy’s cousin Edmund, who was assisting him, later remembered that Humphry was so delighted he danced about the room. He had discovered potassium. A few days later he did the same with soda and found sodium.

Why was it so hard to get these metals out, and why did they burst into flame the moment they appeared? The answer is one of the most important ideas in chemistry, and it began with rust.

Step 1: the old meaning, adding oxygen

When Lavoisier showed in the 1770s that burning is a reaction with oxygen, chemists started calling any reaction that adds oxygen to a substance oxidation. Iron slowly combining with oxygen and water to make flaky red rust is oxidation. So is wood burning, and a cut apple turning brown. The reverse, taking oxygen away from a compound to get the metal back, they called reduction, from a Latin word meaning “to lead back”: the metal was led back out of its ore. People had been doing reduction for thousands of years without the word, every time they heated iron ore with charcoal in a furnace to make iron.

Step 2: the new meaning, moving electrons

After the electron was discovered in 1897, chemists looked again at these reactions and saw something deeper. When iron combines with oxygen, the iron atoms lose electrons and the oxygen atoms gain them. And exactly the same kind of electron loss happens in many reactions that involve no oxygen at all, like zinc reacting with copper ions in Chapter 8. So the words were widened:
