Oxidation is losing electrons.
Reduction is gaining electrons.

A favourite way to remember it is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

Step 3: always together

Electrons do not float around loose in a beaker; if one substance loses them, another must gain them. So oxidation and reduction always happen together, as a pair. Chemists call the pair a redox reaction (from REDuction and OXidation). Here is one you can picture:

Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

Each zinc atom loses two electrons (it is oxidised); each copper ion gains them (it is reduced). Count the charge on each side: +2 before, +2 after. Electrons were passed, not created.

Step 4: who gives electrons most easily?

Line up metals by how readily they lose electrons in reactions like this and you get the reactivity series. Near the top are potassium and sodium, which give up electrons so readily that they react with water and air almost instantly; that is why Davy’s globules burst into flame. Lower down come magnesium, zinc and iron; further down, copper, silver and gold, which hardly react at all. That is why gold coins dug up after two thousand years still shine, while an iron nail rusts in a single wet monsoon.

It also explains why Davy needed his giant battery. Metals at the top of the series are the hardest to get back from their compounds, because their atoms have lost electrons so readily. To push the electrons back onto them takes a big electrical shove.

Careful

“Oxidation always involves oxygen.”

It used to mean that, and the name comes from oxygen. But today chemists use it for any loss of electrons. When magnesium burns in chlorine gas, there is no oxygen anywhere, yet the magnesium is oxidised, because it loses electrons to the chlorine.

Redox all around you

A green statue: the Statue of Liberty in New York was a shiny copper colour when it was put up in 1886. Over the next few decades, rain and air slowly oxidised the copper surface into a crust of green copper compounds, and that crust now protects the metal underneath. Indian temple bells and old copper pots go green in the same way.

A tarnished spoon: silver turns black when it meets traces of sulfur compounds in air or food (eggs are famous for it), because the silver is oxidised to black silver sulfide.

Your own breath: inside your cells, the food you eat is slowly oxidised by the oxygen you breathe, passing electrons step by step along a chain of proteins. That controlled redox reaction is where your energy comes from.

And every battery, from Volta’s pile to the one in your pocket, is a redox reaction arranged so that the electrons have to take the long way round through a wire.

The browning apple test

You need an apple, a knife (ask an adult), a lemon and a plate. Cut two slices of apple. Squeeze lemon juice all over one slice and leave the other bare. Put both on the plate and look every 15 minutes for an hour. The bare slice turns brown as natural substances in the apple are oxidised by oxygen from the air, helped along by an enzyme. The lemon slice stays pale for much longer: the acid slows the enzyme down, and the vitamin C in lemon juice is oxidised more easily than the apple’s own substances, so it takes the hit first. You can eat both slices afterwards.

So rust on a gate, a flame in a grate and an apple on a plate are the same story, told with electrons. Chapter 8 follows those electrons one at a time.

1823 to 1830

Two chemists, two silver salts

Justus von Liebig, Friedrich Wöhler, Jöns Jacob Berzelius

Paris and Stockholm, 1823

Imagine two young chemists, both in their early twenties, working in two different cities. In Paris, Justus von Liebig is studying a silver compound called silver fulminate. It is dangerous stuff: a pinch of it explodes with a sharp crack if you tap it or warm it. (Tiny amounts are what make the bang in snap toys and party crackers.) In Stockholm, in the laboratory of the great Berzelius, Friedrich Wöhler is studying a different silver compound, silver cyanate. It is calm and well behaved: it does not explode at all.

Both chemists did what chemists of the time did with a new substance: they broke it down and weighed what came out, to find exactly which elements it contained and in what proportions. And when their results were published, there was a problem. The two answers were the same. Silver, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, one atom of each, in exactly the same proportions. Yet one substance exploded and the other did not.

Step 1: somebody must be wrong

In the 1820s nearly every chemist believed that a substance’s composition decided what it was. If two samples had the same elements in the same proportions, they had to be the same substance. So when Liebig saw Wöhler’s result, he assumed Wöhler had made a mistake in his analysis, and he said so. He even repeated the cyanate analysis himself, expecting to find the error.

He found that Wöhler was right. Both analyses were correct. Two different substances, with completely different behaviour, really did contain exactly the same atoms in the same numbers.

Step 2: from rivals to friends

The story could have turned into a bitter feud. Instead, when the two young men met a few years later, they discovered they liked each other enormously. They became lifelong friends and worked together for decades, writing hundreds of letters and publishing famous research side by side. It is one of the warmest friendships in the history of science, and it began with each of them thinking the other had got his sums wrong.

There were more puzzles like theirs. Wöhler’s urea, made in 1828 from ammonium cyanate, had the same formula as the ammonium cyanate he started with. Two acids from wine-making, tartaric acid and “racemic acid”, had the same composition but behaved differently. Something new was going on.

Step 3: Berzelius gives it a name

In 1830 Berzelius, who had a gift for naming things, proposed a word for substances with the same composition but different properties: isomers, from the Greek isos, “equal”, and meros, “part”. Equal parts, different substances.

But why could equal parts make different substances? Nobody yet knew how atoms were arranged inside molecules. The full answer had to wait for the 1850s and 1860s, when chemists worked out that atoms are joined by bonds in a definite order, and then for 1874, when van ’t Hoff and Le Bel showed that molecules have shapes in space.

The answer, when it came, was simple: same atoms, joined in a different order. Both contain a little group of three atoms, one carbon, one nitrogen and one oxygen. In cyanate the carbon sits in the middle: O–C–N. In fulminate the nitrogen sits in the middle: C–N–O. That small change in who is holding hands with whom changes everything about how the substance behaves.

Careful

Silver fulminate is a genuinely dangerous explosive. It is part of chemistry’s history, not something to make. Chemists who handle compounds like it work with tiny amounts behind blast shields.

Step 4: isomers you can understand with your own eyes

Here are two isomers you met in Chapter 10. Both have the formula C₂H₆O: two carbons, six hydrogens, one oxygen.

  • In ethanol, the oxygen sits at the end of the chain with a hydrogen attached to it, an –OH group. Ethanol boils at 78.4 °C and mixes with water.
  • In dimethyl ether, the oxygen sits in the middle, between the two carbons, and every hydrogen is attached to a carbon. It boils at −24.8 °C: it is a gas on any day in Mumbai.

Same atoms, a difference in boiling point of more than 100 °C, just because of where one oxygen sits.

Step 5: how many ways can you arrange the atoms?

Small formulas allow only a few arrangements, but the number grows astonishingly fast as molecules get bigger. Here is how many different alkanes (chains and branches of carbon with hydrogens) exist for each number of carbon atoms:

Formula Different isomers
CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈ 1 each
C₄H₁₀ 2
C₅H₁₂ 3
C₆H₁₄ 5
C₁₀H₂₂ 75
C₂₀H₄₂ 366,319

That explosion of possibilities is one reason there are so many millions of carbon compounds. Carbon atoms can be arranged in more ways than anyone could ever list by hand.

Finding the isomers of C₄H₁₀ step by step
Start with the four carbons in a straight row: C–C–C–C. Fill in hydrogens so every carbon has four bonds: that is butane.
Now try a branch: three carbons in a row, with the fourth attached to the middle one. Fill in hydrogens: that is isobutane (2-methylpropane).
Any other drawing you try, such as bending the straight chain, turns out to be one of these two, just turned round. So C₄H₁₀ has exactly 2 isomers.

Build isomers from peas and toothpicks

Use soaked dried peas (or small balls of play dough) for atoms and toothpicks for bonds; ask an adult, as toothpicks are sharp. Make 4 big “carbon” balls and 10 small “hydrogen” balls. Every carbon must end up with exactly four toothpicks, every hydrogen with exactly one. How many genuinely different molecules can you build? (Turning a model round, or bending it, does not count as different: only changing which atom is joined to which does.) You should find exactly two: butane and isobutane. Then try five carbons and twelve hydrogens and see if you can find all three.

Liebig and Wöhler’s quarrel that never happened taught chemistry a lesson it has never forgotten: a formula tells you which atoms are present, but only the arrangement tells you what the substance really is.

1958

The man who measured the air

Charles David Keeling, Roger Revelle, Ralph Keeling

Big Sur, California, 1955

Charles David Keeling was in his late twenties, and he was camping. Not for a holiday: he was collecting air. Day and night, in the forests and mountains of California, he filled glass flasks with air and carried them back to his laboratory, where he measured, with an instrument he had built himself, how much carbon dioxide each flask contained.

Other people had measured carbon dioxide before, and their numbers were all over the place. Keeling was more careful than anyone. He found that if you measured clean air, away from cities and forests breathing on it, the amount was almost the same everywhere he went: about 310 parts in every million. That steadiness was the first surprise. It meant the whole atmosphere was well mixed, and that a careful person in the right place could measure the whole planet at once.

Step 1: the volcano with the cleanest air

In 1958 Keeling, now working at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography with the ocean scientist Roger Revelle, set up an instrument near the top of Mauna Loa, a huge volcano in Hawaii. At 3,400 metres up, in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, the air has travelled thousands of kilometres from the nearest city. It is about as “average” as air gets.

The first measurements, in March 1958, were about 313 parts per million. Keeling expected the number to stay put. Instead, within a couple of years, he saw two things that nobody had seen before.

Step 2: the Earth breathes

The first discovery was beautiful. Every year, the amount of carbon dioxide fell from late spring to autumn, and rose again through winter, by about 6 parts per million. Why? The northern half of the Earth has far more land, and far more forests and fields, than the southern half. In the northern summer, billions of leaves are growing, and plants take carbon dioxide out of the air to build themselves. In winter, leaves fall and rot, and the carbon dioxide comes back. Keeling was watching the whole planet breathe in and out, once a year.

Step 3: the line keeps rising

The second discovery was more worrying. Underneath the yearly breathing, the line kept climbing, year after year, without ever coming back down. It is now called the Keeling curve, and the measurements have continued without a break ever since. After Charles Keeling died in 2005, his son Ralph carried on the work.

The rise comes from burning coal, oil and gas. Every fuel made of carbon compounds turns its carbon into carbon dioxide when it burns, and humans now burn enormous amounts. Before the industrial age, air bubbles trapped in ancient ice show that the level was about 280 parts per million. It has now passed 420: half as much again.

Step 4: what “parts per million” means, step by step

The number looks small, so let us hold it in our hands.

420 parts per million
Out of every million molecules in the air, about 420 are carbon dioxide.
As a percentage: 420 ÷ 1,000,000 × 100 = 0.042%.
One breath of air (about half a litre) contains roughly 1.2 × 10²² molecules.
The carbon dioxide in it: 1.2 × 10²² × 420 ÷ 1,000,000 ≈ 5 × 10¹⁸ molecules.

So carbon dioxide is a tiny fraction of the air, and yet there are still about five million million million molecules of it in every breath you take. A small fraction of a huge number is still a huge number. And small fractions can matter enormously: carbon dioxide traps heat radiating from the Earth’s surface, so even a small change in how much there is changes the climate.

Step 5: the ocean as a sponge

Not all of the carbon dioxide we release stays in the air. Roughly a quarter to a third of it has dissolved into the oceans. That has slowed the rise in the air, but it has a cost, because carbon dioxide dissolving in water makes a weak acid, carbonic acid.

This is called ocean acidification. The sea is not acidic: its pH is still above 7, so it is slightly basic. But it is becoming less basic. The average surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1. Because each step on the pH scale is a factor of ten, that small-looking drop means about 26% more hydrogen ions (10 to the power 0.1 is about 1.26). Corals, oysters and tiny sea snails called pteropods build their shells from calcium carbonate, and they need carbonate ions to do it. As carbonate gets scarcer, building shells gets harder. Since 1988 scientists at a station called ALOHA, in the ocean north of Hawaii, have measured the seawater regularly, and they have watched its pH slowly fall, just as Keeling watched the air.

Careful

“If the oceans are absorbing carbon dioxide, that solves the problem.”

It slows the rise in the air, but it moves the problem into the sea rather than removing it, and the ocean cannot keep absorbing at the same rate forever. Chapter 11 follows this chemistry step by step.

Make carbon dioxide change a colour

Ask an adult to help you chop a few leaves of red cabbage and soak them in warm tap water for half an hour, then strain the purple water into a clear glass. This is a natural pH indicator: it turns pinker when something acidic is added and greener or bluer when something basic is added. Put a straw in the glass and blow gently through it (blow out only, never suck, and do not drink it) for a few minutes. The carbon dioxide in your breath dissolves and makes a little carbonic acid, and the colour shifts slightly towards pink. Compare it with a glass of the same juice you did not blow into. That is ocean acidification in a glass, made with your own breath.

Keeling’s lesson for every chemist is about patience and care. He did not discover anything by being clever in a single afternoon. He discovered it by measuring the same thing, very carefully, in the same place, every day for decades, and refusing to let the numbers be sloppy. Some of the most important facts about our planet were found exactly that way.

1828

Life's chemistry is just chemistry

Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Friedrich Wöhler, Hermann Kolbe, Asima Chatterjee

Berlin, February 1828

Friedrich Wöhler was 27 years old, and he had been trying to make something quite ordinary: a salt called ammonium cyanate. He mixed his chemicals, heated the solution, and let it cool. White crystals appeared. But when he tested them, they were not ammonium cyanate at all. They behaved exactly like a substance that, until then, had only ever come from living bodies: urea, the main waste chemical in the urine of mammals, including you.

On 22 February 1828 he wrote excitedly to his old teacher, the great Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius: he could make urea “without needing kidneys, or even an animal, whether man or dog.”

Why was that so exciting? To understand, you need to know what most chemists believed at the time.

Step 1: two kinds of chemistry?

Around 1806 Berzelius had started using a name for the chemistry of substances that came from living things: sugar, oils, wax, alcohol, urea. He called it organic chemistry, because these substances came from organisms. Everything else, such as salt, metals, rocks and water, was “inorganic”.

Many people felt there was a deep difference between the two. Rocks and salts could be made and remade in a flask. But the substances of life seemed different: they burned easily, they rotted, and nobody could make them from scratch. Perhaps, people thought, only a living body could make them, using some special “life force” that ordinary chemistry did not have. This belief is called vitalism.

Step 2: Wöhler’s crystals

Wöhler had started with substances that nobody would call “living”. Yet out came urea, a substance of life. A flask had done what was supposed to need a kidney.

It also showed something else that puzzled chemists. Ammonium cyanate and urea contain exactly the same atoms in the same numbers: one carbon, one oxygen, two nitrogens and four hydrogens, CH₄N₂O. Heating had simply rearranged them. Two different substances with the same formula: Wöhler and his friend Justus von Liebig had already stumbled on this kind of puzzle with silver salts, and it led to the idea of isomers.

Careful

“Wöhler’s urea killed vitalism overnight.”

This is how the story is often told, but it is too neat. Wöhler’s starting chemicals had themselves been prepared, a few steps back, from animal materials, so a determined vitalist could still argue that the “life force” had sneaked in. Belief in vitalism faded slowly over the next few decades, as chemists made more and more substances of life from simple starting materials. In 1845 Hermann Kolbe made acetic acid (the acid in vinegar) starting from carbon itself, and in the 1850s Marcellin Berthelot made many more, including fats. Wöhler’s crystals were the first famous crack in the wall, not a single blow that knocked it down.

Step 3: so what does “organic” mean now?

Once chemists saw that the same rules apply everywhere, the old meaning of “organic” stopped making sense. But the name stayed, with a new meaning. Today, organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, especially carbon joined to hydrogen, and often to oxygen and nitrogen as well.

Why give carbon a whole branch of chemistry to itself? Because carbon is a champion builder. A carbon atom forms four bonds, and it bonds strongly to other carbon atoms. So carbon atoms can link into chains, branches and rings of almost any size, with other atoms decorating them. The great majority of the many millions of compounds chemists have described contain carbon.

So the word “organic” in a chemistry book means “built on carbon”. It does not mean “alive”, and it does not mean “grown without pesticides”, which is the meaning on a vegetable packet in the supermarket. Plastic, petrol and paracetamol are all organic compounds in the chemist’s sense.

Step 4: the same rules all the way through

The big lesson of this story is simple, and it runs through this whole book. The atoms in your body are the same kinds of atom as in a rock, the air or a test tube. They obey the same rules: they are counted the same way, they attract and repel the same way, and they rearrange the same way in reactions. Living things are made of extraordinarily complicated and beautifully organised chemistry, but it is chemistry. There is no separate “life chemistry” with different laws.

That is not a sad thought. It is what allows medicine to work. If the molecules of life follow ordinary rules, then chemists can study them, copy them, and design new molecules that fix things when they go wrong.

Kolkata, 1944

Here is one person who did exactly that. Asima Chatterjee grew up in Kolkata and became fascinated by the medicinal plants of India. In 1944 she became the first woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science degree by an Indian university, the University of Calcutta. She spent her career working out the structures of carbon compounds made by plants, including alkaloids from the Madagascar periwinkle (which led elsewhere to important cancer drugs), and her team developed medicines against epilepsy and malaria from plant compounds. Her work rested on Wöhler’s discovery: a molecule made by a plant is a molecule like any other, and it can be studied, understood and, sometimes, made in a flask.

Step 5: reading an organic molecule

Every organic molecule is built from two parts, and once you can spot them, organic chemistry stops looking like alphabet soup:

  1. A carbon skeleton: the chain, branch or ring of carbon atoms, with hydrogens filling the spare bonds.
  2. Functional groups: small groups of other atoms attached to the skeleton, such as –OH or –COOH. These are the parts that do most of the chemistry.

Ethane, C₂H₆, is a two-carbon skeleton and nothing else: a gas that does not mix with water. Swap one hydrogen for an –OH group and you get ethanol, a liquid that mixes perfectly with water. Same skeleton, new functional group, new behaviour.

Find the organic chemistry in your kitchen

Go round your kitchen with an adult and sort things into two piles in your head: substances built on carbon, and substances that are not. Sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁), cooking oil, flour (mostly starch, long chains of sugar units), vinegar (acetic acid, CH₃COOH) and butter are all organic. Salt (NaCl), baking soda (NaHCO₃: it contains one carbon atom, but chemists usually count simple carbonates as inorganic) and water are not. Here is a clue you can see without doing anything risky: look at a piece of toast that has been left in the toaster too long. The black, crumbly part is mostly carbon, left behind when the heat broke apart the carbon compounds in the bread. That is the carbon skeleton of organic molecules, with everything else driven off.

Wöhler went on to a long career, but those white crystals from 1828 were his most famous result. They opened the door to the chemistry of carbon, which is the subject of Chapter 10, and to the medicines, plastics and fabrics that organic chemists have built since.

1874

Molecules in three dimensions

Louis Pasteur, August Kekulé, Jacobus van ’t Hoff, Joseph Achille Le Bel, Hermann Kolbe

Utrecht, 1874

In September 1874 a 22-year-old Dutch chemist called Jacobus van ’t Hoff published a little pamphlet, only a dozen or so pages long, with an idea so simple it seems obvious today and so new that it made some famous chemists furious. The idea was this: molecules are not flat. The four bonds of a carbon atom do not lie on paper like the arms of a plus sign. They point out into space, towards the four corners of a tetrahedron.

A few months later, in Paris, a young French chemist called Joseph Achille Le Bel published the same idea, worked out quite independently. When two people reach the same answer on their own, it is often a sign that the answer is right, and that the puzzles of the time were pointing straight at it.

So what were those puzzles?

Step 1: chemists drew molecules flat

By the late 1850s, August Kekulé in Germany and Archibald Scott Couper in Scotland had worked out that a carbon atom forms four bonds, and that carbon atoms can join to each other in chains. Chemists began to draw molecules as diagrams of atoms joined by lines, called structural formulas. Methane, CH₄, looked like a carbon with four hydrogens arranged like a plus sign.

That was a huge step forward. But flat drawings could not explain some strange observations.

Step 2: the mystery of the mirror-image crystals

Back in 1848 the young Louis Pasteur had been looking at crystals of a salt of “racemic acid”, a form of tartaric acid that turned up in the crust that forms inside wine barrels. Under his magnifying lens he noticed that the crystals came in two shapes, which were mirror images of each other, like a left glove and a right glove. Patiently, with tweezers, he sorted them into two piles. Dissolved in water, the two piles behaved differently with polarised light: one twisted the light to the left, the other twisted it to the right, by exactly the same amount.

Yet the two substances had the same formula, and on paper they looked identical. Something about the molecules themselves had to be “left-handed” or “right-handed”. But a flat molecule cannot be left- or right-handed. Flip a flat drawing over and it matches itself.

Step 3: the answer is a shape in space

Van ‘t Hoff and Le Bel saw how to solve it. If a carbon atom’s four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, then a carbon with four different things attached can be built in two ways, which are mirror images of each other and cannot be turned to match, just like your two hands. Hold your hands palm to palm: they are mirror images. Now try to place your right hand exactly on top of your left, both palms down, thumbs on the same side. You cannot. That “handedness” is the secret of Pasteur’s crystals.

Why a tetrahedron? Because the four bonds are pairs of electrons, and electrons repel each other. Four things pushing each other away around a centre settle as far apart as they can be, and in three dimensions that means the corners of a tetrahedron, with every bond at an angle of about 109.5° to every other. On a flat plus sign they would only be 90° apart: crowded closer than they need to be.

Careful

“The 109.5° angle is just a number to memorise.”

It is not arbitrary. It is the angle you get when four things around a point get as far from each other as they possibly can. Mathematicians can calculate it exactly: it is the angle whose cosine is −1/3, which works out at 109.47°. Nature found it long before mathematicians did.

Step 4: not everyone was pleased

In 1877 the powerful German professor Hermann Kolbe wrote a famously scornful review of van ’t Hoff’s idea. He sneered that van ’t Hoff, then teaching at the veterinary school in Utrecht, seemed to have mounted Pegasus, the flying horse, borrowed from the veterinary school’s stables, and flown off into fantasy. Kolbe thought that guessing at the arrangement of atoms in space was not science.

Kolbe was a great chemist, but this time he was wrong, and the evidence piled up against him. In 1901, van ’t Hoff became the very first person ever to receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. (He was honoured for later work on reaction rates and solutions, not for the tetrahedron, but the tetrahedron is what every chemistry student remembers him for.) About forty years after his pamphlet, X-ray crystallography let scientists measure the positions of atoms directly, and the tetrahedral carbon was there, just as he had said.

Step 5: drawing molecules, step by step

Today chemists use several kinds of drawing, each good for a different job:

  1. The molecular formula, such as C₄H₁₀, only counts the atoms. It tells you nothing about how they are joined.
  2. A structural formula shows every atom and every bond as a line. It tells you exactly which atom is joined to which, but it is drawn flat.
  3. A skeletal formula is a shorthand for big molecules. Each corner or end of a zig-zag line is a carbon atom; hydrogens on carbons are not drawn at all (you work them out, because every carbon has four bonds). Only other atoms, such as O or N, are written as letters.
  4. A 3D model, like the ones you can turn in the live figures of Chapter 10, shows the true shape.

Reading a skeletal formula
A zig-zag line with three segments has 4 corners and ends: that is 4 carbon atoms.
Each end carbon has 1 bond in the drawing, so it needs 3 hydrogens. Each middle carbon has 2 bonds drawn, so it needs 2 hydrogens.
Total hydrogens: 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10. So the zig-zag is C₄H₁₀: butane.

Build a tetrahedron with balloons

Blow up four balloons to about the same size and tie them together at their knots (twist the knots round each other, or tie them with a short piece of string). Let go and watch: the balloons push each other into a tetrahedron, all by themselves. Look at it from different sides; no direction is special. That is what the four bonds around a carbon atom do, and for the same reason: things that push each other away settle as far apart as they can. Now try it with three balloons (they make a flat triangle) and with two (a straight line). Those are the shapes of the carbons in ethene and in carbon dioxide.

So when you see a zig-zag chain in this book, remember the two young chemists who first imagined molecules standing up off the page. Every molecule in your body has a shape in space, and in living things that shape matters enormously: for many medicines, one of the two mirror-image forms works much better than the other.

thinking tool

Weighted averages, step by step

Francis Aston

Cambridge, 1920

For a hundred years, chlorine had been an embarrassment. Almost every other light element had a relative atomic mass close to a whole number: carbon 12, nitrogen 14, oxygen 16. Chlorine stubbornly measured 35.46 (the value used then), no matter how carefully it was purified. Some chemists wondered whether atoms of one element could have different weights. Others thought the idea was absurd.

Francis Aston, working in Cambridge, settled it with his new mass spectrograph, a machine that sorts atoms by mass. Chlorine split into two clean streams: one at 35 and one at 37, and nothing at all at 35.5. Chlorine is a mixture of two kinds of atom, and its famous “35.45” is a weighted average. To understand what that means, start at the market.

Step 1: the plain average

You buy two mangoes: one has a mass of 200 g and one 300 g. Their average mass is (200 + 300) ÷ 2 = 250 g. Neither mango weighs 250 g; the average describes the pair, not either one.

Step 2: when there are more of one kind

Now suppose a crate holds 3 small mangoes of 200 g and 1 big mango of 300 g. The plain average of “200 and 300” would still be 250 g, but that is wrong for this crate, because most of the mangoes are small.

Total mass = 3 × 200 + 1 × 300 = 900 g. Number of mangoes = 4.
Average mass = 900 ÷ 4 = 225 g.

The average is pulled towards 200 because there are more 200 g mangoes. That is a weighted average: each value counts according to how common it is.

Step 3: the shortcut with fractions

You can do the same sum using fractions (or percentages) instead of counts. Three out of four mangoes are small, so the fraction of small mangoes is 0.75; the fraction of big ones is 0.25.

Weighted average = 0.75 × 200 + 0.25 × 300 = 150 + 75 = 225 g.

Same answer. Multiply each value by its fraction, then add up. The fractions must add to 1 (here 0.75 + 0.25 = 1), because together they cover everything in the crate.

Step 4: chlorine

Natural chlorine is about 75.8% chlorine-35 and 24.2% chlorine-37. The precise masses of the two isotopes are 34.969 u and 36.966 u.

Average atomic mass = 0.758 × 34.969 + 0.242 × 36.966
= 26.51 + 8.95
= 35.45 u

That 35.45 is what you see printed on a periodic table. It is the right number to use when you weigh out a spoonful of salt, because a spoonful contains countless chlorine atoms in exactly that mixture. But it describes the crowd, not any single atom.

Careful

“The average of 35 and 37 is 36, so chlorine’s atomic mass should be 36.”

That would only be true if there were equal numbers of each. There are about three chlorine-35 atoms for every chlorine-37, so the average is pulled down towards 35. Always weight each value by how common it is.

Average a bag of coins

Take a handful of mixed coins. Weigh each kind separately on a kitchen scale (several at once, then divide to get one coin’s mass) and count how many of each you have. Work out the average mass of a coin in the handful in two ways: total mass divided by number of coins, and the weighted-average shortcut with fractions. Do you get the same answer? Now add ten more of the heaviest coins and see how the average moves.

Weighted averages appear wherever things come in mixtures: the average atomic mass of every element on the periodic table, a class’s average mark, the average speed of the molecules in a gas. In each case, the average describes the whole mixture, and it can be a value that no single member has.

thinking tool

Counting zeros: logarithms without fear

John Napier, Henry Briggs

Merchiston Castle, Edinburgh, 1614

In the early 1600s, astronomers and sailors spent weeks of their lives doing sums. Working out where a planet would be, or where a ship was on the ocean, meant multiplying long numbers like 7,382,915 by 4,106,447, by hand, over and over, and a single slip could wreck everything.

John Napier, the laird of Merchiston Castle near Edinburgh, was a mathematician (and, his neighbours suspected, a bit of a wizard). He spent about twenty years building tables of special numbers that would turn hard multiplications into easy additions. In 1614 he published them and gave them a name he invented: logarithms. An English professor, Henry Briggs, was so excited that he travelled all the way to Edinburgh to meet him, and together they agreed to make a version based on powers of ten, which Briggs published over the following ten years. Astronomers like Johannes Kepler seized on them. It was said that logarithms doubled the working life of an astronomer, by halving the time spent on sums.

Step 1: a logarithm counts tens

You already know powers of ten (if not, read powers of ten first). A logarithm just asks the question backwards.

1,000 = 10³. So the logarithm of 1,000 is 3.
1,000,000 = 10⁶. So the logarithm of a million is 6.
10 = 10¹. The logarithm of 10 is 1.
1 = 10⁰. The logarithm of 1 is 0.

For a number that is a 1 followed by zeros, the logarithm is simply how many zeros. That is all a (base-ten) logarithm is: a way of counting zeros.

Step 2: small numbers have minus logarithms

0.001 = 10⁻³. So the logarithm of 0.001 is −3.
0.000 000 1 = 10⁻⁷. The logarithm is −7.

The smaller the number, the more negative its logarithm. It is still counting the zeros, just on the other side of the decimal point.

Step 3: what about numbers in between?

Numbers that are not neat powers of ten have logarithms in between. Here is one worth remembering:

2 is about 10⁰·³, so the logarithm of 2 is about 0.3.
That means: multiplying by 2 adds 0.3 to the logarithm.
Multiplying by 10 adds exactly 1.

This is Napier’s trick in action: multiplying numbers is the same as adding their logarithms. Before calculators, sailors and engineers looked logarithms up in printed tables, added them, and looked the answer back up. Slide rules, which engineers used to design bridges, aeroplanes and even the rockets that flew to the Moon, are just two logarithm rulers sliding past each other.

Step 4: why chemists love logarithms

The amount of hydronium ions in water can be anything from about 1 mole per litre (in strong acid) to about 0.000 000 000 000 01 moles per litre (in strong alkali). Those numbers are horrible to compare. Their logarithms are 0 and −14: easy.

That is exactly why the pH scale was invented. pH is the logarithm of the hydronium concentration, with the minus sign removed so the numbers come out positive:

Hydronium at 0.001 mol/L = 10⁻³ mol/L, so pH = 3.
Hydronium at 0.000 000 1 mol/L = 10⁻⁷ mol/L, so pH = 7.
Each step of 1 in pH is a factor of 10 in hydronium.
A step of 0.3 in pH is a factor of about 2.

Careful

“pH 4 is twice as acidic as pH 2, because 4 is twice 2.”

Logarithm scales do not work like that. pH 2 has 100 times more hydronium than pH 4 (two steps, ten times each), so it is much more acidic, not less. Whenever you see a logarithm scale, translate each step into “times ten”.

Logarithms turn up in more places than chemistry. The loudness of sound in decibels, the strength of earthquakes and the brightness of stars all use logarithm scales, for the same reason: the real numbers stretch across too many powers of ten to handle comfortably.

A logarithm ruler on your wall

Take a long strip of paper and mark 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 at equal steps of 10 cm. Above them write 1, 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000. Now find where 2 goes: it is about 0.3 of the way from the 0 mark to the 1 mark, so 3 cm along. Where does 20 go? (Hint: 20 is 10 × 2, so add the steps.) You have just made the scale that a slide rule, a pH meter and an earthquake scale all use.

So when you meet pH in Chapter 7, remember Napier in his castle: a logarithm is simply a way of counting zeros, so that numbers spanning many powers of ten fit on one friendly ruler.

What is a scientific model?

A Mumbai local train, the morning rush

Look at the route map above the doors of a Mumbai local train. The stations are evenly spaced dots on straight coloured lines. The real tracks curve, the real stations are close together in some places and far apart in others, and the real city is full of buildings, roads and the sea, none of which appear on the map at all. The map is “wrong” about almost everything.

And yet it is exactly what you need. It tells you which stations come in which order, where to change trains, and how many stops are left. A map that showed every building and every curve would be much harder to use. The route map works because it leaves things out.

That is what scientists mean by a model. A model is a simplified picture, drawing, set of rules or piece of mathematics that captures the part of the truth you need for a particular job, and leaves out the rest on purpose.

Step 1: every model has a job

A globe is a model of the Earth. It gets the shapes of the continents right, but it is far too smooth: on a globe the size of a football, Mount Everest would be a bump about as high as one or two sheets of paper are thick. A model car shows the shape of a car but not how the engine works. Neither is a failure. Each one is good at its own job.

The pictures of atoms in this book are the same. The counting diagrams in Chapter 1 are good at one job: counting protons, neutrons and electrons. They are useless for size (the real nucleus would be invisibly small on the page) and wrong about where electrons are. That is fine, as long as you know which job a picture is for.

Step 2: models improve when evidence surprises them

The history of the atom is a parade of models, each one replaced when an experiment showed something it could not explain.

John Dalton pictured atoms as solid, uncuttable balls. That explained why chemicals combine in fixed proportions. Then J. J. Thomson found electrons coming out of atoms, so atoms could not be solid and uncuttable: he imagined a positive ball with electrons dotted through it. Then Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment showed a tiny, heavy centre, so the model became a nucleus with electrons around it. Niels Bohr added energy levels to explain the colours of light that atoms give out. Today we describe electrons as clouds of likelihood, worked out with quantum physics.

Notice that the old models were not thrown away in shame. Dalton’s solid balls are still perfectly good for balancing chemical equations. Each model is the right tool for some jobs.

Step 3: how to read any model

Whenever you meet a new diagram or rule in this book, ask three questions:

  1. What job is this model doing? (Counting? Showing shape? Predicting a number?)
  2. What does it get right, and how do we know?
  3. Where does it stop being trustworthy?

Careful

“If scientists keep changing their models, they must not really know anything.”

Changing a model is how science gets more right, not less. Each new model explains everything the old one did, plus something new. A map gets better when someone surveys a road that was missing; that does not make the old roads disappear.

The British statistician George Box summed it up in a famous line: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” The skill is knowing which ones are useful, for what, and why.

Make a model, then break it

Make a “model” of a water molecule from a large orange and two small grapes held on with toothpicks, bent at an angle. Write down three things your model shows truthfully (for example: one oxygen, two hydrogens, a bent shape) and three things it gets wrong (sizes, colours, the fact that real atoms are not solid fruit). Then eat the model.

Chemistry is built from models like these. The trick, all the way through this book, is to use each one boldly for its own job, and to remember that it is a map, not the city.

thinking tool

Powers of ten, step by step

Archimedes, Brahmagupta

Syracuse, Sicily, about 2,250 years ago

The Greek mathematician Archimedes once set himself a strange challenge: to count how many grains of sand it would take to fill the whole universe. People said the grains of sand were beyond number. Archimedes disagreed. The problem, he saw, was not the sand. It was that the Greek way of writing numbers ran out at a myriad, ten thousand. So in a little book called The Sand Reckoner he invented a way of building bigger and bigger numbers by stacking “myriads of myriads” on top of each other, and came up with an answer, which in our notation is less than 10⁶³ grains.

His answer about the universe was wrong (it is much bigger than he thought), but his idea was right: to handle huge numbers, you need a way of writing how many times you multiply by ten. Some centuries later, mathematicians in India developed the place-value digits we still use, with zero as a digit, and in 628 Brahmagupta wrote down rules for calculating with zero. That made writing big numbers easy. And today we have the neatest shorthand of all: powers of ten.

Step 1: counting the tens

You already know that 100 = 10 × 10 and 1,000 = 10 × 10 × 10. A power of ten just counts how many tens are multiplied:

10¹ = 10
10² = 10 × 10 = 100
10³ = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000
10⁶ = a million (six tens multiplied; also six zeros after the 1)
10⁷ = ten million: one crore

The little raised number tells you how many zeros follow the 1. In India you already use a few special names for powers of ten: a lakh is 10⁵ (1,00,000) and a crore is 10⁷ (1,00,00,000). Scientists just use the little number instead of a name, so it works for any size.

Step 2: going smaller

What about very small numbers? Each step down divides by ten, and we write it with a minus sign:

10⁰ = 1 (no tens at all)
10⁻¹ = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1
10⁻² = 1 ÷ 100 = 0.01
10⁻³ = 1 ÷ 1,000 = 0.001, a thousandth (a millimetre is 10⁻³ metres)
10⁻⁹ = a billionth (a nanometre is 10⁻⁹ metres)

The minus sign does not mean “negative”. It means “divide by ten this many times”.

Step 3: writing any number this way

Most numbers are not neat powers of ten. So we write them as an ordinary number between 1 and 10, multiplied by a power of ten. This is called scientific notation (or standard form).

602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 = 6.02 × 10²³ (count the places the decimal point moves: 23)
0.000 000 000 3 metres = 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (the point moves 10 places the other way)

A quick check: a big power means a big number; a minus power means a small one.

Step 4: multiplying and dividing the easy way

Here is the real magic. To multiply powers of ten, add the little numbers. To divide, subtract them.

10³ × 10⁴ = 10⁷ (a thousand times ten thousand is ten million)
10²³ ÷ 10²¹ = 10²
(6 × 10²³) × (3 × 10⁻²³) = 18 × 10⁰ = 18

That last line is a real chemistry sum: about 6 × 10²³ water molecules, each with a mass of about 3 × 10⁻²³ grams, make 18 grams of water. The giant number and the tiny number cancel out, and you are left with a gulp of water you can hold.

Careful

“10⁻³ is a negative number.”

It is a small positive number: one thousandth. A powers-of-ten number is never negative or zero, however big the minus sign in the little number. 10⁻¹⁰⁰ is unimaginably small, but it is still more than nothing.

Fold your way to the Moon (on paper)

Take a sheet of paper, about 0.1 mm thick, and fold it in half again and again. Each fold doubles the thickness. You will probably manage six or seven folds before it gets too stiff. Now work it out with a calculator: after 10 folds the stack would be about 10 cm thick; after 20 folds, about 100 metres; after 42 folds, about 440,000 km: more than the distance to the Moon. Doubling grows fast, and powers of ten are how we keep track of numbers that grow like that.

Every big and small number in this book, from 10⁻¹⁰ metres for an atom to 6.022 × 10²³ for a mole, is written in this shorthand. Once you can count the tens, those numbers stop being scary and start being useful.

thinking tool

Doubling and halving: proportion

Robert Boyle, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac

Your kitchen, making chai

Chai for two people needs, say, 1 cup of water, 1 cup of milk and 2 teaspoons of tea leaves. Now four people want chai. You do not need a scientist to tell you what to do: double everything. Two cups of water, two of milk, four teaspoons of tea. If you only doubled the water, the chai would be weak and watery.

You have just used one of the most powerful ideas in science. When two quantities go up and down together, always by the same factor, they are proportional. And there is a second pattern, its mirror image, that is just as important. Between them, they explain a surprising amount of chemistry.

Step 1: going up together

Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other, tripling one triples the other, and halving one halves the other.

People: 2, 4, 6. Tea leaves: 2, 4, 6 teaspoons. (Always 1 teaspoon per person.)
Moles of water: 1, 2, 3. Mass: 18, 36, 54 grams. (Always 18 grams per mole.)

The giveaway is that the ratio stays the same: tea per person, grams per mole. Draw a graph of one against the other and you get a straight line that passes through zero.

Step 2: going opposite ways

Now a different situation. You have a fixed job, say 12 samosas to make, and more friends join in to help. With 1 person it takes 12 minutes; with 2 people, 6 minutes; with 3 people, 4 minutes; with 4 people, 3 minutes. As one number doubles, the other halves. These are inversely proportional.

People × minutes = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 = 12, always.

Here the product stays the same. On a graph it makes a curve that swoops down and flattens out, never quite touching the axes.

Step 3: the two patterns in gases

In 1662, Robert Boyle found that if you squeeze a trapped bubble of air into half the space, its pressure doubles: pressure and volume are inversely proportional (when the temperature stays the same). About 140 years later, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and others found that if you heat a trapped gas, its pressure rises steadily with temperature: directly proportional, as long as you measure temperature in the right way.

Step 4: the trap, and why kelvin exists

That “right way” matters. Try doubling the temperature of a gas from 10 °C to 20 °C. Does its pressure double? No: it only rises by about 3.5%. Proportion only works if zero on your scale means none of the thing at all. Zero degrees Celsius is just the freezing point of water, not “no temperature”.

The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where the molecules have no more energy to give up. On that scale, 10 °C is 283 K and 20 °C is 293 K, and pressure really is proportional to temperature: double the kelvins, double the pressure.

Is going from 10 °C to 20 °C “doubling”?
In kelvin: 283 K to 293 K. The ratio is 293 ÷ 283 ≈ 1.035, a rise of about 3.5%, not 100%.
To double the pressure you would need 566 K, which is about 293 °C.

Careful

“If two things both increase, they must be proportional.”

Not necessarily. Your height increased as you got older, but you are not twice as tall at 12 as you were at 6. Proportional means increasing by the same factor, with a straight-line graph through zero. Always check the ratio (for direct) or the product (for inverse).

Proportion with a balloon and a fridge

Blow up a balloon, not too tightly, and measure its distance around the middle with a piece of string. Put it in the freezer for half an hour (ask first), then measure again quickly. It has shrunk, because the cold gas inside takes up less space. Now let it warm up in the sun. In kelvin, the freezer is about 255 K and a warm room about 298 K: a change of about 17%, so expect a noticeable, but not enormous, change in size.

Whenever this book says “double this and that doubles” or “halve this and that doubles”, it is using one of these two patterns. Look for what stays the same: the ratio, or the product.

thinking tool

The unit-cancelling trick

Mars, 23 September 1999

After a journey of more than nine months, NASA’s Mars Climate Orbiter fired its engine to slip into orbit around Mars. Then it passed behind the planet, and was never heard from again. It had flown far too low and was almost certainly destroyed in the Martian atmosphere.

The investigation found the cause. One team’s software reported the push from the spacecraft’s small thrusters in American units (pound-force seconds). The navigation team’s software expected metric units (newton seconds). One pound-force is about 4.45 newtons, so every number was off by a factor of more than four, and nobody’s computer noticed. A spacecraft worth around 125 million dollars was lost because a number was written without its unit being checked.

Chemists juggle grams, moles, litres, molecules and kilojoules all day. This tool is the habit that keeps them, and you, from crashing into Mars.

Step 1: a unit is part of the number

“18” means nothing on its own. 18 grams? 18 moles? 18 molecules? These are wildly different amounts. So in science, a number always travels with its unit, and you treat the unit almost like a word that is multiplied by the number: 18 g means “18 × gram”.

Step 2: units cancel like fractions

You know from fractions that 3 × (5 ÷ 3) = 5: the 3s cancel. Units do the same.

2 hours × 60 minutes/hour = 120 minutes
The word “hour” appears on top and on the bottom, so it cancels, leaving minutes.

The “60 minutes per hour” is a conversion factor. It is really just a fancy way of writing 1, because 60 minutes and 1 hour are the same amount of time. Multiplying by 1 never changes an amount; it only changes the units you describe it in.

Step 3: chemistry’s favourite chain

The most useful chain in this book goes from grams to moles to particles. Each link is a conversion factor, and the units tell you whether to multiply or divide.

How many molecules in 36 g of water?
36 g × (1 mol / 18 g) = 2 mol (grams cancel)
2 mol × (6.022 × 10²³ molecules / 1 mol) = 1.2 × 10²⁴ molecules (moles cancel)

If you set up a chain and the units do not cancel to what you want (for example you end up with g² per mol), you have flipped a factor upside down. The units have caught your mistake before it caught you.

Careful

“To get from grams to moles I just multiply by the molar mass.”

Check the units: 36 g × 18 g/mol gives 648 g² per mol, which is nonsense. Grams to moles needs the factor written so that grams cancel: 36 g × (1 mol / 18 g) = 2 mol. Whenever you are not sure whether to multiply or divide, write the units in and let them decide.

Step 4: the habit

Write every number with its unit. Write every conversion factor as a fraction. Cross out units that appear on top and bottom. If what is left is the unit you wanted, the method is right, even before you check the arithmetic.

A recipe in two languages

Find a recipe that gives amounts in cups or spoons. Using a kitchen scale, find how many grams of flour (or sugar, or rice) are in one cup. Write it as a conversion factor, like “130 g / 1 cup”. Now convert the whole recipe into grams, writing the units at every step. Then make the recipe (with an adult) using the scale instead of the cups. Do the units cancel properly all the way through?

Every calculation in this book, from moles to concentrations to energies, is a little chain of conversion factors. Write the units, let them cancel, and you will always know where you are.

The adventure in time

The ideas in this book were not found in the order a textbook teaches them. Here they are in the order they actually happened: two and a half thousand years of people asking what everything is made of.

  1. The ancient world
  2. about 450 BCE to 1908
    Can you cut forever? The long argument about atoms

    For more than two thousand years people argued about whether matter is made of tiny uncuttable pieces. A Manchester schoolteacher turned the argument into science.

  3. about 300 to 1700
    Two thousand years of trying to make gold

    The alchemists never made gold, but they invented the laboratory, and one of them found a glowing element while boiling down buckets of urine.

  4. The 1600s
  5. 1659 to 1691
    The sceptical chymist

    The fourteenth child of the richest man in Ireland, who taught chemists to doubt, to test and to write down exactly what they did.

  6. about 450 BCE to 2016
    From four elements to 118

    For two thousand years people believed everything was made of earth, air, fire and water. Here is how that changed.

  7. 1643 to 1804
    Air has weight: pumps, tubes and balloons

    How a pump that would not pump, a glass tube of mercury and a race of balloons revealed that air is a crowd of particles pressing on everything.

  8. 1669 to 1696
    The last of the magicians

    The man who explained gravity and light also spent decades as a secret alchemist, chasing the one thing chemistry can never do.

  9. The 1700s
  10. 1770 to 1786
    The pharmacist who found everything first

    A quiet chemist in a small-town pharmacy discovered oxygen before anyone else, and lost the credit because his printer was slow.

  11. 1767 to 1794
    The minister who invented fizzy water

    A stammering clergyman with a lab in his kitchen invented soda water, found oxygen, and was chased out of England for his opinions.

  12. 1774 to 1794
    The man who weighed everything

    How a careful Parisian with a very good balance proved that nothing is lost when things burn, and gave oxygen its name.

  13. 1798 to 1815
    The boy from Penzance who lit up London

    A woodcarver’s son from the edge of England who breathed laughing gas, tore new metals out of rocks with electricity, and made chemistry the most exciting show in London.

  14. 1772 to 2010
    Pencils, diamonds and footballs

    The softest grey smudge and the hardest gem are the same element. It took a giant burning lens to prove it.

  15. The 1800s
  16. 1780s to 1836
    Frogs’ legs and the first battery

    An argument between two Italian professors about twitching frogs’ legs produced the first battery, and with it the age of electricity.

  17. 1794 to 1808
    The schoolteacher who weighed the invisible

    A weaver’s son who started teaching at twelve, studied his own colour blindness, and gave every element its own kind of atom.

  18. 1799 to 1884
    The lakes of Egypt and the balance that never stops

    How a chemist travelling with Napoleon saw a reaction running backwards in the desert, and found that chemical change is a two-way street.

  19. 1777 to today
    Rust, fire and moving electrons

    Rusting nails, burning wood and browning apples turn out to be the same kind of change: electrons moving from one substance to another.

  20. 1808 to 1961
    How do you weigh an atom?

    Nobody can put one atom on a scale, so chemists learned to weigh atoms against each other instead.

  21. 1811 to 1860
    The forgotten idea: Avogadro, and the congress that found him again

    An Italian professor guessed how gases are built, and almost nobody listened for fifty years.

  22. 1812 to 1860
    The bookbinder’s apprentice

    A blacksmith’s son who left school early, bound books for a living, and talked his way into a laboratory, where he named the words of electrochemistry and lit up the Christmas Lectures.

  23. 1808 to 1813
    Letters for atoms: the language of chemistry

    How chemists stopped drawing secret signs and circles and started writing H₂O, the shorthand every chemist in the world now shares.

  24. 1828
    Life’s chemistry is just chemistry

    A young chemist accidentally makes a substance from a living body in a flask, and the wall between “living” and “non-living” chemistry starts to crack.

  25. 1817 to today
    The families of the table

    Each column of the periodic table is a family with a character of its own, and you meet every one of them in an ordinary day in Mumbai.

  26. 1823 to 1830
    Two chemists, two silver salts

    Two young rivals analyse two very different silver salts and get exactly the same answer. Each thinks the other has made a mistake. Neither has.

  27. 1833 to 1903
    Charged travellers: Faraday’s ions and Arrhenius’s risky idea

    Why can salty water carry electricity? A bookbinder’s apprentice named the travellers, and a Swedish student nearly failed for explaining them.

  28. 1869 to 1886
    The Siberian who left gaps

    The youngest child of a Siberian family, carried across Russia by a mother who would not give up on him, who arranged the elements so well that he could describe ones nobody had yet found.

  29. 1839 to 1974
    Lucky accidents, and the people who noticed

    Rubber tyres, non-stick pans, sticky notes and the first antibiotic all began with something going wrong in a laboratory.

  30. 1783 to 1850
    Heat is motion

    How a guinea pig in a bucket of ice, a cannon factory and a brewer’s paddle wheel showed that heat is not a substance but the jiggling of particles.

  31. 1593 to 1848
    How cold can cold get?

    Thermometers, a frozen guess at the coldest possible cold, and the Scottish scientist who gave us a temperature scale that starts from nothing at all.

  32. 1894 to 1904
    The man who found a missing column

    A Glasgow chemist who chased a tiny mismatch in the weight of nitrogen and found a whole new family of elements, most of them hiding in the air we breathe.

  33. 1856
    The boy who made the world purple

    An 18-year-old trying to make a malaria medicine in his attic got black sludge instead, and made the first coal-tar dye.

  34. 1738 to 1877
    A storm of tiny billiard balls

    The daring idea that a still, quiet room is full of particles racing faster than a jet plane, and the scientists who proved it with nothing but mathematics.

  35. 1859 to 1895
    Fingerprints of light

    Two friends in Heidelberg found that every element glows with its own colours. With that trick, people discovered new elements in spring water, and found helium in the Sun before anyone found it on Earth.

  36. 1773 to 2019
    How big is Avogadro’s number?

    How people measured the number of atoms in a mole without ever seeing an atom, and how to feel the size of 6 × 10²³.

  37. 1865
    The snake that bit its own tail

    How a German chemist solved the puzzle of benzene’s shape, and the famous daydream he told about it twenty-five years later.

  38. 1891 to 1934
    The girl from the secret university

    A Polish girl who studied in secret, paid for her sister’s education before her own, and found two new elements in a leaking shed in Paris.

  39. 1817 to 2016
    The patience game: the story of the periodic table

    How a Russian professor laid out the elements like a card game, left gaps, and dared nature to fill them.

  40. 1874
    Molecules in three dimensions

    Two young chemists, working separately, realise that molecules have shapes in space, and an older professor mocks them for it.

  41. 1823 to 1889
    Why the match needs striking

    Why paper does not burst into flame by itself, how a lump of platinum lit a lamp without a match, and the hill every reaction must climb.

  42. 1808 to 2019
    The mole, step by step

    How chemists learned to count atoms by weighing them, and why the counting unit they invented is so enormous.

  43. 1889 to 1944
    The chemist who wanted India to make its own

    A teacher in Calcutta discovered a new compound, wrote the history of chemistry in ancient India, started a company in his own rooms, and trained a generation of Indian scientists.

  44. 1896 to 1949
    Atoms that change

    A photographic plate left in a drawer revealed that some atoms are slowly breaking apart. It overturned the oldest idea in chemistry, and it lets us tell the age of ancient bones.

  45. 1897
    The particle in the glowing tube

    A strange green glow inside a glass tube led to the first piece of an atom ever found, and proved that atoms can be broken.

  46. The 1900s
  47. 1901 to today
    Mercury into gold, at last

    The alchemists’ dream came true in the twentieth century, but in a way no alchemist imagined, and it turned out that the gold was not the treasure.

  48. 1827 to 1909
    The dance that proved atoms are real

    A botanist sees specks that will not keep still, a young patent clerk explains why, and a French physicist finally counts the invisible.

  49. 1908 to 1916
    How your blood stays at 7.4

    Your muscles pour acid into your blood every time you run, yet its pH hardly moves. A Harvard doctor worked out why.

  50. 1898 to 1913
    Bread from air

    How chemists learned to pull nitrogen out of the air to make fertiliser, feeding billions of people, and why the same chemist’s story also carries a warning.

  51. 1909 to 1911
    The shell that bounced back

    A student was asked to look for something nobody expected to see. What he found showed that every atom is almost entirely empty space around a tiny, heavy centre.

  52. 1909
    Sørensen’s brewery and the pH scale

    A Danish chemist trying to make better beer needed a simple way to say how acidic something is, and invented a scale every school now uses.

  53. 1895 to 1937
    The boy from the potato field

    A New Zealand farm boy with a booming voice who discovered that atoms have a tiny heart, and became the first person to change one element into another on purpose.

  54. 1913 to 1914
    Henry Moseley’s staircase

    A 26-year-old in Manchester found the true order of the elements by measuring X-rays, and counted the missing ones.

  55. 1913 to 1962
    The goalkeeper who drew the atom’s staircase

    A shy Danish student gave the atom its staircase of energy levels, built an institute where the new physics was born, and kept two Nobel medals hidden in a jar of acid.

  56. 1912 to 1964
    Seeing inside salt: the Braggs and their X-rays

    A father and son found a way to see where atoms sit, and discovered that salt has no molecules at all.

  57. 1910 to 1915
    The young man who counted the elements

    In two short years a young Englishman used X-rays to give every element its true place in the periodic table, and showed exactly which ones were still missing.

  58. 1913 to 1932
    Same element, different weight

    Chemists found atoms that behaved identically but weighed differently. The explanation was a particle with no charge at all, and it took twenty years to catch.

  59. 1913 to 1926
    Why electrons don’t fall in

    Rutherford’s atom should have collapsed in a split second. A young Dane rescued it with a daring idea: electrons can only have certain energies, like steps on a staircase.

  60. 1902 to 1939
    Dots and lines: how atoms hold on to each other

    A professor’s doodles of cubes became the shared pair of electrons, the idea at the heart of almost every molecule.

  61. 1611 to 1920
    The strange case of water

    Why ice floats, why water boils so late, and the invisible links between water molecules that make life on Earth possible.

  62. 1913 to today
    Why the table has that strange shape

    Two tall towers, a sunken middle, a strip floating underneath: the shape of the periodic table is a picture of how electrons fill an atom.

  63. 1664 to 1923
    Sour and slippery: what is an acid?

    For 250 years chemists argued about what makes a thing sour. The answer turned out to be one tiny particle: a bare proton.

  64. 1907 to 1970
    Why is the sea blue?

    A young government accountant in Calcutta did experiments every evening, asked why the Mediterranean is blue, and found an effect that won India its first Nobel Prize in science.

  65. 1912 to 1932
    Who pulls harder? The story of polar molecules

    Why oil and water refuse to mix: some atoms pull shared electrons harder than others, and two scientists learned to measure it.

  66. 1907 to 1939
    A walk in the snow

    Lise Meitner worked in a basement because women were not allowed upstairs, fled her country with almost no money, and on a snowy walk at Christmas worked out what it means for an atom to split.

  67. 1925 to 1994
    The boy who never stopped asking why

    A pharmacist’s son from Oregon who worked his way through college became the chemist who explained how atoms hold together, won two Nobel Prizes, and got some big things wrong too.

  68. 1871 to today
    A map that predicts

    The periodic table lets you describe elements nobody has seen properly, and even some that have never been made. Here is how to play Mendeleev’s game yourself.

  69. 1934 to 1969
    Seeing the shapes of molecules

    A girl who grew crystals at home learned to read X-ray patterns so well that she could see the shapes of the molecules of medicine, and spent thirty-four years on insulin.

  70. 1951 to 1958
    Photo 51

    Rosalind Franklin took the clearest X-ray picture of DNA ever made; others used it to build the double helix, and for years her part was barely mentioned.

  71. 13.8 billion years ago to 2017
    Where the elements come from

    Hydrogen from the Big Bang, carbon and oxygen from stars, gold from colliding dead stars: every atom in you has an address in the history of the universe.

  72. 1958
    The man who measured the air

    A young scientist builds an instrument fussy enough to measure the air properly, takes it to the top of a volcano, and finds the planet breathing, and changing.

  73. 1970s to 2019
    The battery in your pocket

    Three scientists on three continents, working over fifteen years, built the light, rechargeable battery that powers phones and electric cars.

Answers to Check yourself

Try each question before you look. If your answer differs, the reasoning matters more than the words: see whether you used the same idea.

Chapter 0. The chemist’s way of seeing

0.1

Which of these is an observation and which is an inference? (a) “This liquid boils at 100 °C.” (b) “This liquid is made of H₂O molecules.”

(a) is an observation: anyone with a thermometer can check it. (b) is an inference: a very well-tested explanation, but one built from evidence rather than seen directly.

Back to section 0.1

0.2

One mole of water has a mass of about 18 g and contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. Each molecule contains three atoms. How many atoms are in that 18 g of water?

3 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.8 × 10²⁴ atoms: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in each of the 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. Always say what you are counting.

Back to section 0.2

Chapter 1. What makes an atom?

1.1

A counting diagram shows 6 red tokens marked + in the centre, 6 brown tokens, and 6 blue tokens marked − around the outside. Name one thing this diagram reliably tells you, and one thing it does not.

It reliably tells you the numbers: 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons (so this is a carbon atom, and it is neutral). It does not tell you the real size of the nucleus compared with the atom, where the electrons actually are, or what anything looks like; atoms have no colour.

Back to section 1.1

1.2

A particle has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 10 electrons. Which element is it?

Oxygen, because it has 8 protons. The 10 electrons only tell you about its charge (it is an oxide ion, O²⁻), and the 8 neutrons only tell you which isotope it is.

Back to section 1.2

1.2

When a candle burns, its wax (made of carbon and hydrogen) seems to disappear. Do any of its carbon atoms turn into atoms of a different element?

No. Burning is a chemical change, and chemical changes only move electrons and rearrange atoms; they never touch the nucleus. Every carbon atom keeps its 6 protons and ends up, still carbon, in carbon dioxide gas that drifts away into the air.

Back to section 1.2

1.3

A made-up element is a mixture of two isotopes: 75% have mass 10 and 25% have mass 14. What is its average atomic mass? Does any atom have that mass?

0.75 × 10 + 0.25 × 14 = 7.5 + 3.5 = 11. No atom has mass 11: each atom is either 10 or 14. The 11 describes the mixture.

Back to section 1.3

1.4

A sulfide ion has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons. What is its charge?

16 − 18 = −2, so it is written S²⁻. The 16 neutrons do not count towards the charge at all.

Back to section 1.4

1.5

An atom has Z = 7 and A = 15. How many neutrons does it have, and which element is it?

15 − 7 = 8 neutrons. With 7 protons it is nitrogen: this is nitrogen-15, a rare but stable isotope.

Back to section 1.5

1.6

Neutral fluorine has 9 electrons and neutral chlorine has 17. Work out their shell counts. What do they have in common?

Fluorine is 2, 7 and chlorine is 2, 8, 7. Both have 7 electrons in their outermost shell, and indeed they are members of the same chemical family (the halogens). Notice we can say this without claiming that either one “wants” an extra electron.

Back to section 1.6

Chapter 2. How atoms form substances

2.1

Is air an element, a compound or a mixture? Give a reason.

A mixture. Air contains several separate substances, mainly nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂) and argon, not joined to each other. Their proportions can vary (for example, humid air has more water vapour than dry air), which a compound’s proportions never do.

Back to section 2.1

2.2

Two opposite charges are 1 unit apart. They are moved to 3 units apart. What fraction of the original attraction is left?

One ninth. The distance has tripled, and 3 × 3 = 9, so the force is 1/9 as strong. It is still an attraction, because the charges are still opposite.

Back to section 2.2

2.3

Rewrite this sentence so it is scientifically accurate: “Atoms bond because they want to fill their shells.”

One good version: “Atoms bond when sharing or transferring electrons leads to an arrangement with lower energy, because of the electric attraction between nuclei and electrons.” Any answer that talks about attraction and energy, and not about atoms wanting, is right.

Back to section 2.3

2.4

How many oxygen atoms are in four CO₂ molecules?

Eight. Each CO₂ molecule has 2 oxygen atoms, and there are 4 molecules: 4 × 2 = 8. (There are also 4 carbon atoms.)

Back to section 2.4

2.5

Magnesium chloride is an ionic solid with formula MgCl₂. Magnesium ions have a charge of 2+. What does the 2 in MgCl₂ tell you?

That there are two chloride ions (Cl⁻) for every magnesium ion (Mg²⁺) in the crystal. Two charges of −1 balance one charge of +2, so the crystal is neutral. It does not mean there are MgCl₂ molecules.

Back to section 2.5

2.6

Can the formula C tell you whether a sample is graphite or diamond? What extra information do you need?

No. Both are pure carbon, so their formula is the same. You need to know the structure: how each atom is bonded to its neighbours (four neighbours in a 3D network for diamond; three, in flat sheets, for graphite).

Back to section 2.6

2.7

Ammonia (NH₃) is a pyramid, with the nitrogen at the top. Boron trifluoride (BF₃) is flat, with its three fluorines spread 120° apart. Both have three polar bonds. Which molecule is polar overall, and why?

Ammonia is polar; boron trifluoride is not. In flat, evenly spread BF₃, the three bond pulls cancel exactly, like three equal ropes pulling a ring from three evenly spaced directions. In pyramid-shaped NH₃, all three N–H pulls point partly the same way, so they add up instead of cancelling.

Back to section 2.7

Chapter 3. Why matter has different states

3.1

Why is it easy to squash the air in a bicycle pump, but almost impossible to squash a syringe full of water?

In a gas the particles are far apart, with lots of empty space between them, so pushing them closer is easy. In a liquid they are already touching their neighbours, so there is almost no empty space left to squeeze out.

Back to section 3.1

3.2

A sealed, rigid container of gas is warmed from 27 °C to 327 °C. By what factor does its pressure change?

Convert to kelvin first: 27 °C = 300 K and 327 °C = 600 K. The kelvin temperature has doubled, so the pressure doubles. (If you had used Celsius, you would wrongly have said it went up more than twelve times.)

Back to section 3.2

3.3

What observation in a kitchen shows that the steam from a kettle is still water?

When steam touches something cold, such as a window or a pan lid, it condenses back into drops of liquid water. Hydrogen and oxygen gas would not do that at kitchen temperatures.

Back to section 3.3

3.4

A gas at constant temperature is squeezed from 12 litres to 4 litres. What happens to its pressure?

The volume becomes one third as big, so the pressure becomes three times as big. (Pressure × volume stays the same: 12 × P = 4 × 3P.)

Back to section 3.4

3.5

Bottle A holds 1 litre of salt solution at 0.50 mol/L. Bottle B holds 4 litres at 0.25 mol/L. Which tastes saltier? Which holds more salt altogether?

Bottle A tastes saltier, because each litre (and each sip) contains more salt: 0.50 mol/L against 0.25 mol/L. But Bottle B holds more salt altogether: 4 × 0.25 = 1.0 mol, compared with 1 × 0.50 = 0.50 mol in Bottle A.

Back to section 3.5

3.6

Carbon dioxide (CO₂, 22 electrons per molecule) and hydrogen (H₂, 2 electrons) are both non-polar gases at room temperature. Solid CO₂ turns to gas at −78.5 °C, but hydrogen boils at −252.9 °C. Why the difference?

Neither has dipole attractions or hydrogen bonds, so only dispersion forces hold their molecules together. Dispersion forces are much stronger for bigger molecules with more electrons. CO₂, with 22 electrons, attracts its neighbours far more strongly than H₂ with 2, so it needs a much higher temperature to break free.

Back to section 3.6

Chapter 4. What changes in a reaction?

4.1

When a fizzy tablet is dropped into water, bubbles appear and the water cools slightly. Is that enough to prove a chemical reaction has happened? What would you need to test?

Not on its own. Bubbles could be air that was trapped in the tablet, and cooling can happen when some things simply dissolve. You would need to show that a new substance was made: for example, collect the gas and test it (carbon dioxide turns limewater milky; air does not), or show that the dissolved substances left behind are different from what was in the tablet.

Back to section 4.1

4.2

How many hydrogen atoms are there in 4 NH₃? And what is the formula of the compound made from calcium ions, Ca²⁺, and chloride ions, Cl⁻?

4 × 3 = 12 hydrogen atoms (and 4 nitrogen atoms). Calcium chloride is CaCl₂: one Ca²⁺ (+2) needs two Cl⁻ (−1 each) for the charges to cancel.

Back to section 4.2

4.3

Nitrogen and hydrogen react to make ammonia. Why is 1 N₂ + 1 H₂ → 1 NH₃ unbalanced, and what coefficients balance it?

Left: 2 N and 2 H. Right: 1 N and 3 H. Neither element matches. Put 2 in front of NH₃ to fix nitrogen (2 N, 6 H on the right), then 3 in front of H₂ to supply 6 H: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. Check: 2 N and 6 H on each side.

Back to section 4.3

4.4

What does the balanced equation N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ tell you, and what does it not tell you?

It tells you that if nitrogen and hydrogen react to make ammonia, they are used up in a 1 : 3 ratio of molecules and make 2 ammonia molecules for every nitrogen molecule, with every atom accounted for. It does not tell you whether the reaction happens at room temperature, how fast it is, whether it needs a catalyst (it does, and high pressure, in industry), or whether it gives out or takes in energy.

Back to section 4.4

Chapter 5. Energy, speed and balance

5.1

When the solid in a cold pack dissolves, the pack gets cold. Is dissolving it exothermic or endothermic? Which is higher in energy, the start or the end?

Endothermic. The surroundings (the water, the pack, your hand) lose energy and get colder, because the system took energy in. So the end (dissolved) is higher in energy than the start.

Back to section 5.1

5.2

In a schematic profile, the reactants are at 40 units, the products at 10, and the peak at 100. What are the forward barrier, the reverse barrier and the overall energy change?

Forward barrier = 100 − 40 = 60. Reverse barrier = 100 − 10 = 90. Overall change = 10 − 40 = −30 (30 units released). The reverse barrier is bigger because the products sit lower, so they have further to climb.

Back to section 5.2

5.3

In the A ⇌ B model with forward constant 2 and reverse constant 1, what are the forward and reverse rates at the very start, when there are 10 units of A and none of B?

Forward rate = 2 × 10 = 20 units per second. Reverse rate = 1 × 0 = 0, because there is no B yet to turn back. That is why the change is fastest at the start.

Back to section 5.3

5.4

At a fixed temperature, could a catalyst lower the forward barrier by 30 units while lowering the reverse barrier by only 10? Why or why not?

No. Both barriers are measured up to the same peak. The reactants and products stay where they were, so if the peak drops by 30, both barriers drop by 30.

Back to section 5.4

5.5

Set the forward constant to 1 and the reverse constant to 3, starting with 10 units of A. At equilibrium, A = 7.5 and B = 2.5. Show that the rates are equal, and explain why A ends up three times as plentiful as B.

Forward rate = 1 × 7.5 = 7.5 per second. Reverse rate = 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 per second. Equal. B turns back into A three times as readily as A turns into B, so the rates can only balance when there is three times as much A as B.

Back to section 5.5

5.6

Methane burns: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O. Using average bond enthalpies (C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O in CO₂ 799, O–H 463 kJ per mole), estimate the overall energy change. Is it exothermic or endothermic?

Break 4 C–H and 2 O=O: 4 × 413 + 2 × 498 = 2,648 kJ in. Make 2 C=O and 4 O–H: 2 × 799 + 4 × 463 = 3,450 kJ out. Overall 2,648 − 3,450 = −802 kJ: exothermic, which is why methane makes a good cooking gas. (The measured value, with the water as a gas, is also about −802 kJ.)

Back to section 5.6

5.7

The A ⇌ B mixture (forward 2, reverse 1) has settled at 3.33 of A and 6.67 of B. You remove half of B. Which rate is bigger immediately afterwards, and where does the mixture settle?

After removing half the B: A = 3.33, B = 3.33. Forward rate = 2 × 3.33 ≈ 6.7, reverse = 1 × 3.33 ≈ 3.3, so the forward reaction is faster and A turns into B. The total is now 6.67, and it settles when B is twice A: A ≈ 2.22, B ≈ 4.44.

Back to section 5.7

Chapter 6. A quantitative language

6.1

Carbon dioxide is CO₂. A carbon atom has a mass of about 12 units and an oxygen atom about 16. What is the atom ratio of carbon to oxygen, and roughly what is the mass ratio?

The atom ratio is 1 : 2 (one carbon, two oxygens). The mass ratio is 12 : 32, which simplifies to 3 : 8. So although carbon dioxide is “one-third carbon” by atoms, it is only about 27% carbon by mass.

Back to section 6.1

6.2

You have 1 mole of oxygen gas, O₂. How many O₂ molecules is that, and how many oxygen atoms?

6.022 × 10²³ molecules of O₂. Each molecule has two atoms, so there are 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10²⁴ oxygen atoms.

Back to section 6.2

6.3
