A chemist weighs out 36.03 g of pure water. How many moles is that, and how many molecules?

36.03 g ÷ 18.015 g/mol = 2.000 mol. That is 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules. The grams cancel, leaving moles: g ÷ (g/mol) = mol.

Back to section 6.3

6.4

For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, you start with 6 H₂ and 2 O₂. How many water molecules can form, and what is left over?

Each O₂ needs two H₂, so 2 O₂ use 4 H₂ and make 4 H₂O. Oxygen runs out first; 2 H₂ are left over.

Back to section 6.4

6.5

Bottle A holds 1.0 L of salt solution at 0.50 mol/L. Bottle B holds 4.0 L at 0.25 mol/L. Which tastes saltier? Which contains more salt in total?

Bottle A tastes saltier, because its concentration is higher. But bottle B contains more salt in total: 4.0 L × 0.25 mol/L = 1.0 mol, against 1.0 L × 0.50 mol/L = 0.50 mol in A.

Back to section 6.5

6.6

In CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O, how many grams of water form from burning 8.0 g of methane (16.0 g/mol)? Water is 18.0 g/mol.

8.0 g ÷ 16.0 g/mol = 0.50 mol of methane. The equation gives 2 H₂O for every 1 CH₄, so 1.0 mol of water forms: 1.0 mol × 18.0 g/mol = 18 g.

Back to section 6.6

Chapter 7. Acids, bases and passing protons

7.1

When ammonia dissolves in water, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which molecule is the acid (proton donor), and which is the base (proton acceptor)?

Water is the acid: it gives a proton to ammonia, leaving OH⁻. Ammonia is the base: it accepts the proton and becomes NH₄⁺. Water can act as an acid or as a base, depending on its partner.

Back to section 7.1

7.2

Sketch or describe two beakers of particles: (A) a concentrated weak acid and (B) a dilute strong acid. How does your drawing show concentration, and how does it show strength?

Concentration is shown by how many acid particles there are in total in each beaker: lots in A, few in B. Strength is shown by what fraction of them have split into H₃O⁺ and the negative ion: almost none in A (mostly whole HA molecules), all of them in B (no whole HCl left).

Back to section 7.2

7.3

You have 1.0 L of a strong acid at pH 2. How much water must you add to raise its pH to 4?

Going from pH 2 to pH 4 means a hundred times less hydronium per litre, so the acid must be spread through 100 times the volume: a total of 100 L. You need to add 99 L of water. (This works for a strong acid, where every molecule has already given up its proton.)

Back to section 7.3

7.4

Why does a mixture of acetic acid and acetate resist a change in pH when a small amount of sodium hydroxide is added?

The added OH⁻ ions react with intact acetic acid molecules, CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, instead of staying free in the solution. The amounts of acetic acid and acetate only change a little, so their ratio, and hence the pH, changes only a little. It works until the acetic acid runs out.

Back to section 7.4

Chapter 8. Electron transfer and electrochemistry

8.1

In Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which particle is oxidised and which is reduced? How many electrons move for every zinc atom that reacts?

Zinc is oxidised (it loses electrons, Zn → Zn²⁺). Copper ions are reduced (they gain electrons, Cu²⁺ → Cu). Two electrons move for every zinc atom, because zinc goes from a charge of 0 to +2.

Back to section 8.1

8.2

Aluminium forms Al³⁺ and silver ions are Ag⁺. Write the balanced equation for aluminium metal reacting with silver ions, and check that the charge is the same on both sides.

Al(s) + 3 Ag⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + 3 Ag(s). One aluminium atom gives three electrons, and each silver ion takes one, so three silver ions are needed. Charge on the left: 0 + 3 × (+1) = +3. On the right: +3 + 0 = +3. Balanced.

Back to section 8.2

8.3

Magnesium is above zinc in the reactivity series. What happens if you put magnesium ribbon into zinc sulfate solution? What happens if you put zinc into magnesium sulfate solution?

Magnesium in zinc sulfate: magnesium gives electrons to Zn²⁺ ions, so zinc metal forms on the ribbon and Mg²⁺ goes into solution. Zinc in magnesium sulfate: nothing happens, because zinc is below magnesium and cannot push electrons onto Mg²⁺.

Back to section 8.3

8.4

As a Daniell cell runs, which plate gets heavier and which gets lighter? Explain using the half-equations.

The copper plate (cathode) gets heavier, because Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu adds copper atoms to it. The zinc plate (anode) gets lighter, because Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2 e⁻ sends zinc atoms off into the solution as ions.

Back to section 8.4

Chapter 9. The shape of the periodic table

9.1

Sodium (2, 8, 1) is much bigger than lithium (2, 1), even though it has 8 more protons. Why?

Sodium’s outer electron is in a third shell, farther from the nucleus, and it is screened by ten inner electrons instead of two. Being farther away and more screened, it is held more weakly, so the atom is bigger.

Back to section 9.1

9.2

Lithium’s first ionisation energy is 520 kJ/mol and its second is 7,298 kJ/mol. Explain why the second is so much larger.

The first electron comes from the outer shell (n = 2), where it is farther from the nucleus and screened by the two inner electrons. The second must come from the inner shell, close to the nucleus with nothing screening it, and from an ion that is already positive. (Not because the pull is now shared among fewer electrons: every proton pulls on every electron regardless.) So it is held far more tightly: about 14 times more energy is needed.

Back to section 9.2

Chapter 10. Carbon chains and the chemistry of life

10.1

A straight-chain alkane has 5 carbon atoms. How many hydrogen atoms does it have? Check by counting the bonds each carbon needs.

  1. The two end carbons each have one carbon neighbour, so each needs 3 hydrogens (6 in total); the three middle carbons each have two carbon neighbours, so each needs 2 hydrogens (6 more). That is pentane, C₅H₁₂, matching 2 × 5 + 2 = 12.

Back to section 10.1

10.2

Methane does not dissolve in water. Methanol, CH₃OH, mixes with water completely. Explain the difference in terms of what the molecules attract.

Methane’s electrons are shared almost evenly, so it has no charged ends to attract water molecules; water molecules stay stuck to each other instead. Methanol’s –OH group has a slightly negative oxygen and a slightly positive hydrogen, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules, and the two mix.

Back to section 10.2

10.3

Propane boils at −42.1 °C and octane at 125.6 °C. One is sold as a liquid fuel for cars; the other is squeezed into gas cylinders for cooking. Which is which, and why?

Octane, with eight carbons, has much stronger dispersion forces, so it is a liquid at room temperature: that is petrol. Propane, with only three carbons, is a gas at room temperature; it is stored as a liquid only by squeezing it under pressure in a cylinder, and turns back into gas when you open the valve.

Back to section 10.3

10.4

Pentane, C₅H₁₂, has three isomers: a straight chain; a chain of four with one branch; and a “cross” shape with four carbons around a central one, almost a ball. Put them in order of boiling point, highest first, and explain.

Straight chain (36.1 °C), then the singly branched one (27.7 °C), then the ball-shaped one (9.5 °C). The more compact the molecule, the less surface touches its neighbours, the weaker the dispersion forces, and the lower the boiling point.

Back to section 10.4

10.5

Why is a fat whose chains are all straight and saturated more likely to be solid at room temperature than an oil whose chains each have a kinked double bond?

Straight chains pack closely side by side, so a lot of surface touches and the dispersion forces add up; it takes a higher temperature to separate them, so the fat is solid. Kinked chains can’t pack closely, so they attract each other less and the oil melts at a lower temperature.

Back to section 10.5

10.6

Glycine, C₂H₅NO₂, has a mass of 75.07 grams per mole. Two glycine molecules join by a peptide bond. What is the formula of the new molecule, and what is its mass per mole? (Water is 18.02 grams per mole.)

Two glycines contain C₄H₁₀N₂O₄. One water, H₂O, leaves, so the new molecule is C₄H₈N₂O₃. Its mass is 2 × 75.07 − 18.02 = 132.12 grams per mole.

Back to section 10.6

Chapter 11. Earth, materials and energy

11.1

If the surface ocean’s pH fell from 8.1 to 7.8, by what factor would the concentration of H⁺ ions increase?

The pH falls by 0.3, so H⁺ is multiplied by 10⁰·³ ≈ 2.0. The concentration of hydrogen ions would roughly double.

Back to section 11.1

11.2

Why must lithium ions move through the electrolyte at the same time as electrons move through the wire? What would happen if they could not?

Each electron that leaves the graphite side through the wire takes away a negative charge; the Li⁺ ion leaving the same side through the electrolyte takes away a matching positive charge. Together they keep both sides neutral. If the ions could not move, negative charge would pile up on one side and positive on the other, the build-up would push back against the electrons, and the current would stop almost at once.

Back to section 11.2

Words worth knowing

Acid
A substance that can pass a proton (a hydrogen nucleus, H⁺) to another particle. Acids taste sour and turn litmus red. (Never taste anything in a laboratory.) 7
Activation energy
The extra energy that colliding particles need to get over the hump between reactants and products. It decides how easily a reaction starts, not how much energy it releases overall. 5.2
Alkane
A chain of carbon atoms joined by single bonds, with hydrogen everywhere else. Formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂: methane, ethane, propane, butane… 10.1
Allotropes
Different forms of the same element, with their atoms joined in different ways. Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon; O₂ and O₃ (ozone) are allotropes of oxygen. 2.6
Amino acid
A molecule with both an amino group and a carboxyl group. Twenty kinds are used to build the proteins in living things. 10.6
Amino group
–NH₂. A nitrogen with two hydrogens. Its spare pair of electrons can pick up H⁺, so it acts as a weak base. 10.6
Anode and cathode
The anode is the electrode where oxidation happens; the cathode is where reduction happens. In a cell that makes electricity, the anode is the negative terminal. 8.4
Atom ratio
The ratio of the numbers of atoms of each element, such as 2 hydrogen : 1 oxygen in water. 6.1
Atomic number (Z)
The number of protons in an atom’s nucleus. It decides which element the atom is: 1 is hydrogen, 6 is carbon, 8 is oxygen, 79 is gold. 1.2
Average atomic mass
The average mass of an element’s atoms in a natural sample, weighted by how common each isotope is. This is the decimal number printed on most periodic tables. 1.3
Avogadro’s constant
The number of things in one mole, 6.022 140 76 × 10²³. Since 2019 this is an exact number, fixed by definition. 0.2
Balanced equation
A chemical equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides of the arrow. 4.3
Base
A substance that can accept a proton from an acid. 7
Bond enthalpy
The energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in gas molecules. Tables give average values, so calculations with them are good estimates, not exact answers. 5.6
Buffer
A mixture of a weak acid and the particle it forms when it gives up a proton (here, acetic acid and acetate). It resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. 7.4
Calorimeter
A container that measures the energy a reaction gives out or takes in, by measuring the temperature change of water around it. 5.1
Carbonic acid
H₂CO₃, a weak acid formed when carbon dioxide reacts with water. It gives the slight sharpness to fizzy drinks. 11.1
Carboxyl group
–COOH. The functional group of carboxylic acids such as ethanoic acid. It can give an H⁺ to water. 10.6
Catalyst
A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing a route with a lower activation energy. It is not used up overall. 5.4
Change of state
Melting, freezing, boiling (evaporating) or condensing. The substance stays the same; only the arrangement and motion of its particles change. 3.3
Chemical change (reaction)
A change in which atoms are rearranged into new substances, with new properties. The atoms themselves are kept. 4.1
Coefficient
The big number written in front of a formula. It counts how many whole particles there are. 4.2
Compound
A substance made of two or more elements joined together in a fixed ratio, such as water, H₂O. 2.1
Concentration
How much solute there is in each litre of a solution. Concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of solution. 3.5
Condensation reaction
A reaction in which two molecules join and a small molecule, usually water, is released. 10.6
Counting model
A diagram that shows how many particles of each kind there are. It is not a picture of where they are or how big they are. 1.1
Covalent bond
A link between two atoms that share electrons. Both nuclei are attracted to the shared electrons between them. 2.3
Covalent network
A giant structure in which covalent bonds link atoms throughout a whole crystal, with no separate molecules. Diamond is one. 2.6
Dipole
A molecule (or bond) with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end. 2.7
Dispersion forces
Weak attractions between all molecules, caused by electrons briefly bunching up on one side. Stronger for bigger molecules with more electrons. 3.6
Double bond
Two shared pairs of electrons between the same two atoms. A C=C double bond is shorter and stronger than a single bond, and cannot twist. 10.5
Dynamic equilibrium
The state of a reversible reaction when the forward and reverse rates are equal, so the amounts stay constant even though both reactions continue. 5.5
Electrolysis
Using electricity from outside to drive a redox reaction that would not happen by itself. 8.4
Electronegativity
How strongly an atom in a bond pulls shared electrons towards itself. Fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen are among the strongest. 2.7
Element
A substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons. 1.2
Elementary charge
The size of the charge on one proton (+1) or one electron (−1). It is the smallest amount of charge any free particle has. 1.4
Enzyme
A catalyst made by a living thing, usually a protein. 5.4
Equivalence point
The moment in a titration when just enough base has been added to react with all of the acid. 7.4
Excess reactant
A reactant left over once the limiting reactant has run out. 6.4
Exothermic, endothermic
Exothermic: energy flows out of the system and the surroundings get warmer. Endothermic: energy flows into the system and the surroundings get colder. 5.1
Formula unit
The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound. NaCl means 1 Na⁺ for every 1 Cl⁻; MgCl₂ means 1 Mg²⁺ for every 2 Cl⁻. 2.5
Functional group
A small group of atoms on a carbon molecule, such as –OH or –COOH, that gives it its typical behaviour. 10.2
Galvanic cell
Two halves of a redox reaction in separate containers, joined by a wire and a salt bridge, so that the electrons travel through the wire as an electric current. 8.4
Half-equation
One half of a redox reaction written on its own, showing the electrons lost (oxidation) or gained (reduction). 8.2
Hydrogen bond
An attraction between a hydrogen atom attached to N, O or F and a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom on a neighbouring molecule. Still far weaker than a covalent bond. 3.6
Hydronium ion (H₃O⁺)
A water molecule that has accepted an extra proton. More hydronium ions means a more acidic solution. 7.1
Ideal gas law
PV = nRT. It links the pressure, volume, amount and kelvin temperature of a gas. It works well for most gases unless they are very squashed or very cold. 3.4
Inference
A conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence. In chemistry, our ideas about particles we cannot see are inferences, built into models. 0.1
Intermolecular forces
Attractions between separate molecules. They are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule. 3.3
Inverse-square law
A rule where a force gets weaker with the square of the distance: twice as far, one quarter of the force; three times as far, one ninth. 2.2
Ion
An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge, because its numbers of protons and electrons are not equal. 1.4
Ionic lattice
A giant, regular, repeating arrangement of positive and negative ions, held together by their attraction in every direction. 2.5
Ionisation energy
The energy needed to pull one electron completely away from an atom. A high value means the electron is held tightly. 1.6
Isomers
Different compounds with the same molecular formula but atoms joined in a different order. 10.4
Isotopes
Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. 1.3
Kelvin (K)
A temperature scale that starts at absolute zero (−273.15 °C). Kelvin = degrees Celsius + 273.15. 3.2
Le Châtelier’s principle
A rule of thumb: when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the change. For changes in amounts, it follows from the rates. 5.7
Limiting reactant
The reactant that gets used up first, which stops the reaction and limits how much product can form. 6.4
Lithium-ion cell
A rechargeable cell in which lithium ions move back and forth between layers of graphite and layers of a metal oxide, while electrons travel through the outside circuit. 11.2
Mass number (A)
The number of protons plus the number of neutrons in one nucleus. It is always a whole number. 1.3
Mixture
Two or more substances mingled together but not chemically joined. Their proportions can vary, and they can usually be separated by physical means such as evaporating or filtering. 2.1
Molar mass
The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (g/mol). For water it is about 18.0 g/mol. 6.3
Mole
A counting unit, like a dozen, but much bigger: one mole is 6.022 × 10²³ things (atoms, molecules, or whatever you say you are counting). 0.2
Molecule
A group of atoms joined by covalent bonds that acts as a single unit. All the molecules of one substance are identical (apart from tiny differences between isotopes). 2.4
Nucleus
The tiny centre of an atom, holding its protons and neutrons, and almost all of its mass. 1.1
Observation
Something you can see or measure directly, such as a colour, a mass, a temperature, or a change of state. 0.1
Ocean acidification
The slow fall in the pH of seawater as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. 11.1
Orbital
A region around a nucleus where an electron is likely to be found, with a definite shape and energy. Shells are made up of orbitals. 9.1
Organic compound
A compound built around carbon atoms, usually bonded to hydrogen. The name is old: people once thought only living things could make them. 10.1
Oxidation
Losing electrons. Zinc is oxidised when Zn becomes Zn²⁺. 8.1
Partial charges (δ⁺, δ⁻)
Small charges on atoms in a molecule, caused by electrons being shared unequally. They are fractions of a full charge. 2.7
pH
A number that says how acidic a solution is, by counting the powers of ten in its hydronium concentration. pH 7 is neutral; lower is more acidic; higher is more basic. 7.3
Physical change
A change of state, shape or mixing in which no new substance is made. The particles keep their identity. 4.1
Powers of ten
A short way of writing big and small numbers. 10⁶ is a million; 10⁻⁶ is a millionth. Each step of 1 in the little number is a factor of ten. 0.2
Pressure
The push of a gas (or liquid) on each square metre of surface. Measured in pascals (Pa); normal air pressure is about 101,000 Pa, or 101 kPa. 3.2
Proton, neutron, electron
The three particles that atoms are built from. Charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1. A proton or neutron has nearly 2,000 times the mass of an electron. 1.1
Rate of reaction
How quickly a reaction goes: the amount of a substance used up or made per unit of time. 5.3
Reactivity series
A list of metals in order of how readily they give away electrons. A metal will push a lower metal’s ions out of solution, but not a higher one’s. 8.3
Redox reaction
A reaction in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Oxidation and reduction always happen together. 8.1
Reduction
Gaining electrons. Copper ions are reduced when Cu²⁺ becomes Cu. 8.1
Salt bridge
A path of salt solution between the two beakers of a cell. Ions move along it to keep each beaker electrically neutral, completing the circuit. 8.4
Shell
A group of electrons with similar energy in an atom. Shells are energy levels, not circular tracks. 1.6
Shielding
The way inner electrons reduce the pull of the nucleus on outer electrons, by repelling them. Electrons in the same shell shield each other only weakly. 9.1
Skeletal formula
A shorthand drawing of a molecule: lines for the carbon skeleton, a carbon at each corner and end, hydrogens on carbon left out. 10.1
Solute, solvent, solution
The solute is the substance that dissolves (salt); the solvent is what it dissolves in (water); the mixture is a solution. 3.5
Spectator ions
Ions that are present in a reacting mixture but come out unchanged, like the sulfate ions in copper sulfate solution. 8.1
States of matter
Solid, liquid and gas. The same substance can be in any of them, depending on its temperature and the pressure around it. 3.1
Strong acid
An acid that gives up its protons to water almost completely, such as hydrochloric acid. 7.2
Subscript
The small lowered number in a formula. It counts atoms of the element just before it, in one molecule or formula unit. 2.4
Sub-shell
A group of electron places within a shell. There are four kinds, called s, p, d and f, holding 2, 6, 10 and 14 electrons. S71
Successive ionisation energies
The energies needed to remove an atom’s electrons one after another. A large jump shows that the next electron is in an inner shell. 9.2
System and surroundings
The system is the substances you are studying. The surroundings are everything else, which can give energy to the system or take it away. 5.1
Temperature
A measure of how hot something is. In a gas it goes up and down with the average energy of the particles’ motion. 3.2
Tetrahedron
A pyramid with four triangular faces. The four bonds of a carbon atom with only single bonds point to its four corners, about 109.5° apart. 10.1
Thermal motion
The constant random movement of particles. The higher the temperature, the more vigorous it is. 3.6
Titration
Adding a solution of known concentration, a little at a time, to measure exactly how much of something is in another solution. 7.4
Weak acid
An acid that gives up its protons to water only partly, so most of its molecules stay whole, such as acetic acid. 7.2

About the models and numbers in this book

Where the numbers come from

Most numbers in this book are real measurements: boiling points, atomic masses, ionisation energies, bond lengths, the sizes of atoms, the voltage of a cell. They come from the standard reference collections that chemists everywhere rely on, such as the values published by IUPAC (the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry), NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) and the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics. They have been rounded to make them easier to read, so you may find slightly different last digits in another book. That is normal: different sources measure in slightly different conditions, and round differently.

A few numbers are made up on purpose, to make a model easy to follow: the “12 u and 13 u” isotope mixture, the energy profiles drawn “in model units”, and the reaction A ⇌ B with its neat rate constants. Whenever a number is invented, the text says so.

The models, and where they break

Counting models of atoms. Drawing protons, neutrons and electrons as little balls is perfect for counting. It is useless for size (the real nucleus is tens of thousands of times narrower than the atom) and wrong about electrons, which are not little balls sitting in particular places.

Shells. Grouping electrons into shells (2, then 8, then 8) explains a great deal, from the families of the periodic table to the cliffs in ionisation energies. It works neatly only for the first 18 elements. Beyond that, and to explain the small dips in Figure 1.7, you need orbitals: the regions where electrons are likely to be found, described by quantum physics.

Ideal gases. The rule linking pressure, volume, temperature and amount treats gas particles as points that never attract each other. Real gases follow it well at everyday conditions, and badly when squeezed hard or cooled until they are close to turning into liquid.

Average bond energies. Adding up the energy to break bonds and the energy given out by making them gives good estimates of the energy of a reaction. But a bond’s strength depends a little on the molecule it is in, so the answers are estimates, usually close but not exact.

The rate picture of equilibrium. Explaining equilibrium as forward and backward reactions running at equal speeds is true and useful. The simple rate rules in Chapter 5 hold for single-step reactions; most real reactions happen in several steps, and their rates are worked out by experiment.

Diagrams in general. Every picture in this book has been chosen to show one thing clearly. Colours, sizes and distances are almost always for clarity rather than accuracy, and atoms themselves have no colour at all. When you meet a new diagram, the best question to ask is the one this whole book is about: what does this show truthfully, and how do we know?

Further adventures

When you have finished this book, the adventure does not stop. Here are some places to go next, all free.

MIT OpenCourseWare. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology puts many of its courses online for anyone. A few of the ideas in this book were borrowed from them.

  • Chemistry Behind the Magic: short videos of demonstrations that look like magic (glowsticks, colour-changing indicators, elements burning with coloured flames), each followed by the chemistry that explains it. These are for watching, not copying: the real experiments need a lab and a trained chemist.
  • Kitchen Chemistry: a whole MIT course in which every week’s experiment is something you eat, from bread and meringue to ice cream.
  • When you are older: Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry (3.091), where Professor Donald Sadoway tells the history of chemistry alongside the science, and Principles of Chemical Science (5.111), MIT’s first-year chemistry course.

In the lab app. Every numbered section of this book has a matching investigation. Build atoms, squeeze gases and balance reactions yourself.

In the kitchen. Every Try it at home box in this book is a real experiment. Keep a notebook: write what you predicted, what happened, and what surprised you. That notebook is exactly what Lavoisier, Faraday and Marie Curie kept.
